title: Japanese N2
description: The fourth step in Japanese, from N3 to JLPT N2. Grammar lessons cover concession and contrast (ものの, にもかかわらず, とはいえ, 反面), time and occasion (に先立って, に際して, 次第, 上で, 以来, つつ), reasons and grounds (からには, 以上, ばかりに, だけに, に基づいて, に応じて, をめぐって), possibility and judgement (かねない, かねる, ざるを得ない, っこない, に越したことはない, ないことには), scope and emphasis (はもとより, に限らず, を問わず, どころか, ずにはいられない, ものなら, とか), and the written forms of newspapers, columns and essays, with a long reading in every lesson and exam practice at the end. About 2,300 new words build on the 3,700 from the earlier courses for about 6,000 in all, learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pitch accent, conjugation drills and sentence building; 390 new kanji (about 1,040 in all) are learned through notecards, tracing and inside words, with furigana you can turn off. Requires Japanese N3.
author: Erudior

modules.title: Although, despite and on the other hand
Written Japanese and the N2 exam

lessons.title: Although: ものの, とはいえ, からといって
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to N2. You finished N3 able to give reasons and judgements, compare, quote, use keigo at
work and read texts of 400 to 600 characters. This course takes you to the level of the JLPT N2:
about 2,300 new words (about 6,000 with the ones you know), 390 new kanji (1,039 in all), and the
grammar of newspapers, columns, essays, business email and formal speech.

Module 1 is about **[[concession]]** (granting a point, then going against it) and **[[contrast]]**
(setting two things against each other): "although", "despite", "on the other hand", "even if"
and "not exactly". This lesson teaches three ways of saying "although": 〜ものの, 〜とはいえ and
〜からといって. The theme is working life: hiring, contracts, pay, promotion and side jobs.

{内定|ないてい}はもらったものの、まだ{迷|まよ}っている。 — I've had a job offer, but I'm still undecided.
{副業|ふくぎょう}が{認|みと}められたとはいえ、{本業|ほんぎょう}が{最優先|さいゆうせん}だ。 — Side jobs may be allowed now, but your main job still comes first.
{給料|きゅうりょう}が{高|たか}いからといって、いい{会社|かいしゃ}だとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — Just because the pay is high doesn't mean it's a good company.

## What changes at N2

- **Thirteen kanji a lesson.** Each core lesson teaches 13 new **[[kanji]]** (390 in all), with a
  tracing pad for each. Many of them spell words you already know in kana: {採用|さいよう},
  {就職|しゅうしょく}, {担当|たんとう}, {患者|かんじゃ}, {契約|けいやく}. From now on those words appear in
  kanji (with **[[furigana]]**, which you can switch off), though their old vocabulary cards still show
  kana. Each kanji section lists the carried words its kanji let you write.
- **About 77 words a lesson.** N2 adds about 2,300 words to the 3,700 you have. Many are kanji
  compounds of two or more kanji, and many are formal: the words of articles and business.
- **A reading of 500 to 800 characters in every lesson**: articles, columns, essays with a claim
  and a counter-view, business email, notices, interviews, stories and reviews. The questions are
  visible after the text so you can think first; the answers and an English translation are in
  boxes you open.
- **Most N2 patterns live in writing.** 〜ものの, 〜にもかかわらず and 〜に{際|さい}して are rare in
  chat. Each lesson says which style a pattern belongs to: everyday speech, formal speech, or the
  **[[written style]]** (〜である) of articles and essays.
- **The exam.** The JLPT N2 has two timed parts: language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar)
  together with reading, 105 minutes; and listening, 50 minutes. It has three scored sections,
  each 0 to 60: vocabulary and grammar, reading, and listening. You need at least 19 in each
  section and 90 of the 180 in all. New at N2 are a word-formation question, passages compared
  side by side, and a long essay. Lesson 30 goes through it all.
- **No spaces and no romaji**, as in N3. **[[Pitch accent]]** marks appear on vocabulary cards and
  where they matter in lessons: {雇用|こよう:0}, {賃金|ちんぎん:1}, {部署|ぶしょ:1}.

### Kana or kanji

A word is written with kanji when all its kanji are on the course list (N5's 102, N4's 177, N3's
370 and N2's 390); otherwise the whole word is in kana: {契約|けいやく}, but はけん (a temp
agency's dispatch: its second kanji isn't on the list) and しせつ (a facility). Grammar words
stay in kana even when their kanji are listed:

| Kind | Examples | Written |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Auxiliary verbs]]** after the **[[て form]]** | 〜ている, 〜てある, 〜ておく, 〜てみる, 〜てしまう, 〜ていく, 〜てくる, 〜てあげる / くれる / もらう / いただく / ほしい | kana |
| **[[Formal nouns]]** and grammar words | こと, もの, ところ, とき, ため, はず, わけ, つもり, よう, そう, まま, うち, ほう, ほど, くせ, せい, おかげ, おそれ | kana |
| Everyday verbs | ある, いる, する, なる, できる, いい / よい, ください | kana |
| **[[Keigo]]** verbs | {伺|うかが}う, {承|うけたまわ}る, {拝見|はいけん}する, {申|もう}し{上|あ}げる, {存|ぞん}じる in kanji; いただく, めしあがる, いたす, まいる, おる in kana | mixed |

N2 has many **[[compound particles]]** (particles made of several words, such as にもかかわらず). The
course writes these in kanji: {際|さい}して, {先立|さきだ}って, {基|もと}づいて, {応|おう}じて, {限|かぎ}らず,
{限|かぎ}り, を{問|と}わず, {越|こ}したことはない, {過|す}ぎない, {次第|しだい}, {以上|いじょう}, {上|うえ}は,
{以来|いらい}, を{通|つう}じて, を{機|き}に, {末|すえ}に, {折|おり}に, {反面|はんめん}, {一方|いっぽう}, ざるを{得|え}ない,
{割|わり}に. These in kana: にあたって, をめぐって, にそって, にともなって, にわたって, にかかわらず /
にもかかわらず, からには, ばかりに, だけに, どころか, はもとより, のみならず, とはいえ, といえども,
にしろ / にせよ, からといって, かねる / かねない, 〜がたい, 〜つつ, 〜あげく, 〜ものの, 〜ものなら,
〜ことに, 〜をきっかけに, 〜につき, 〜をもって, 〜まい, 〜べく. N3's choices stand: について, にとって,
として, によって in kana; {対|たい}して, {関|かん}して, {比|くら}べて, {通|とお}して in kanji. You don't
have to learn the list now: every lesson writes them this way, and the sheet for this module
(Concession and contrast) repeats it.

A few spellings, fixed for the whole course:

| Written | Not | When |
|---|---|---|
| {付|つ}ける, {付|つ}く | — | attach, add, apply: {名前|なまえ}を{付|つ}ける, {気|き}を{付|つ}ける |
| つける, つく | — | switching on, lighting: {電気|でんき}をつける |
| かかる, かける | — | time, money, phone calls: {時間|じかん}がかかる, {電話|でんわ}をかける |
| {掛|か}ける | — | only hanging and sitting: {腰|こし}を{掛|か}ける |
| {辞|や}める | やめる | quitting a job or school: {会社|かいしゃ}を{辞|や}める |
| やめる | {辞|や}める | stopping an action: たばこをやめる |
| {後|あと} | あと | the noun "after": {会議|かいぎ}の{後|あと}で |
| あと | {後|あと} | the adverb "more, left": あと{五分|ごふん} |
| たぶん, かまわない, {出|で}かける | — | always so |

## Although (written): 〜ものの

〜ものの means "although A, B", where B is not what A would lead you to expect. It belongs to
writing and formal speech; in conversation you'd usually say 〜けど or 〜のに.

{面接|めんせつ}には{合格|ごうかく}したものの、{給与|きゅうよ}の{条件|じょうけん}が{合|あ}わなくて{断|ことわ}った。 — I passed the interview, but the pay didn't suit me, so I turned it down.
{求人|きゅうじん}は{多|おお}いものの、{希望|きぼう}に{合|あ}う{仕事|しごと}はなかなか{見|み}つからない。 — There are plenty of vacancies, but it's hard to find a job that fits what I want.
この{仕事|しごと}は{大変|たいへん}であるものの、やりがいがある。 — This job is hard, but it's worth doing.

The part before ものの is in the **[[plain form]]**, as before a noun:

| Before ものの | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| verb | plain form (often the **[[た form]]**) | {応募|おうぼ}したものの, {雇|やと}ってもらえないものの |
| **[[い-adjective]]** | plain form | {忙|いそが}しいものの, {高|たか}かったものの |
| **[[な-adjective]]** | + な, or + である | {便利|べんり}なものの, {便利|べんり}であるものの |
| noun | + である | {新人|しんじん}であるものの |

The commonest use is 〜たものの: "I did A, but it didn't lead where it should have".

{転職|てんしょく}したものの、{前|まえ}の{会社|かいしゃ}のほうが{働|はたら}きやすかった。 — I changed jobs, but the old company was easier to work at.
{専門家|せんもんか}に{相談|そうだん}したものの、{答|こた}えは{出|で}なかった。 — I asked an expert, but got no answer.

As a sentence opener, とはいうものの means "that said": {昇給|しょうきゅう}が{決|き}まった。とはいうものの、{物価|ぶっか}も{上|あ}がっているので{生活|せいかつ}は{楽|らく}にならない (I've got a pay rise. That said, prices are going up too, so life won't get easier). ぶっか is written {物価|ぶっか} now that 価 is on the list.

### ものの and のに

Both join a fact to a result that goes against it. The difference is feeling:

- のに carries the speaker's surprise, disappointment or complaint, and it can end a sentence:
  {頑張|がんば}ったのに！ (And I tried so hard!) 〜ものの can't end a sentence.
- ものの is cooler. It grants A and moves on to B, so it suits reports:
  {業績|ぎょうせき}は{回復|かいふく}したものの、{雇用|こよう}は{増|ふ}えていない (results have recovered, but
  employment hasn't grown). With のに this sounds like a complaint about it.

{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。 (You should have told me.) has no ものの version at all. And in
both, B is usually a fact, not a request or an invitation.

## Granted, even so: 〜とはいえ

〜とはいえ grants A, then says B holds all the same: "granted that A", "A, but even so". It is
written and formal.

{春|はる}とはいえ、{朝晩|あさばん}はまだ{寒|さむ}い。 — It may be spring, but mornings and evenings are still cold.
{正社員|せいしゃいん}になったとはいえ、{給料|きゅうりょう}はアルバイトのころとあまり{変|か}わらない。 — I may have become a full-time employee, but the pay isn't much different from my part-time days.
{休日|きゅうじつ}とはいえ、{急|いそ}ぎの{電話|でんわ}には{出|で}たほうがいい。 — It's your day off, I know, but you'd better answer urgent calls.

| Before とはいえ | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {認|みと}められたとはいえ, {少|すく}ないとはいえ |
| noun, な-adjective: directly, or + だ | {新人|しんじん}とはいえ / {新人|しんじん}だとはいえ, {便利|べんり}とはいえ |

As a sentence opener, とはいえ is "that said, still": {副業|ふくぎょう}は{自由|じゆう}だ。とはいえ、{会社|かいしゃ}への{届|とど}けは{必要|ひつよう}だ (side jobs are up to you; still, you have to tell the company).

ものの and とはいえ are close. Two differences, both tendencies rather than rules: とはいえ joins
a bare noun ({春|はる}とはいえ), and the part after it can more easily be an opinion or advice
(〜たほうがいい, 〜べきだ), as in the third example. After ものの, B is usually a plain fact.

## Just because: 〜からといって

〜からといって is "just because A": it stops the listener from drawing a conclusion. The second
half denies it, usually with a partial negation: 〜わけではない, 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない, or a plain
negative or a "you shouldn't".

{有名|ゆうめい}な{大学|だいがく}を{出|で}たからといって、{仕事|しごと}ができるわけではない。 — Just because someone graduated from a famous university doesn't mean they're good at their job.
{経歴|けいれき}が{立派|りっぱ}だからといって、うちの{部署|ぶしょ}に{合|あ}うとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — An impressive CV doesn't mean they'll suit our department.
{忙|いそが}しいからといって、{返事|へんじ}をしないのはよくない。 — Being busy is no excuse for not replying.

Plain form + からといって; nouns and な-adjectives take だ: {新人|しんじん}だからといって. Unlike ものの
and とはいえ it's common in speech too, where it shortens to からって:
{副業|ふくぎょう}だからって、{手|て}を{抜|ぬ}いていいわけじゃないよ (just because it's a side job doesn't mean
you can cut corners).

> **Review: 〜といっても (N3 lesson 23).** 〜といっても is "I say A, but it's not much": it
> scales down what you've just said. {昇進|しょうしん}したといっても、{係長|かかりちょう}になっただけです
> (I've been promoted, but only to subsection chief). Compare からといって, which blocks a
> conclusion: {昇進|しょうしん}したからといって、{偉|えら}くなったわけではない (being promoted doesn't make
> you important).

## The four side by side

| Pattern | What it does | Style | What follows |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ものの | grants A; B goes against it | written, formal | usually a fact |
| 〜とはいえ | grants A; B holds anyway | written, formal | a fact, an opinion or advice |
| 〜からといって | A doesn't justify the conclusion | all styles (からって in speech) | わけではない, とは{限|かぎ}らない, a negative |
| 〜といっても | A, but only to a small degree | all styles | what A really amounts to |

The reference sheet for this module sets these next to the patterns of lessons 2 to 5.

## Words for working life

N3 gave you the basic job words ({社員|しゃいん}, {正社員|せいしゃいん}, {転職|てんしょく}, {時給|じきゅう},
{求人|きゅうじん}, {内定|ないてい}). N2 adds the words of contracts, pay slips and personnel news.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| hiring | {雇用|こよう}, {雇|やと}う, {雇|やと}い{主|ぬし}, {解雇|かいこ}, {募|つの}る, {人材|じんざい}, {求職|きゅうしょく}, {選考|せんこう}, {不採用|ふさいよう}, {応募者|おうぼしゃ}, {適性|てきせい} |
| ways of working | {契約社員|けいやくしゃいん}, {終身雇用|しゅうしんこよう}, {正規|せいき} / {非正規|ひせいき}, フリーランス, {無職|むしょく}, {失業|しつぎょう}, {失業率|しつぎょうりつ}, {再就職|さいしゅうしょく}, {専業主婦|せんぎょうしゅふ}, サラリーマン |
| side jobs | {副業|ふくぎょう}, {本業|ほんぎょう}, {専念|せんねん}する |
| pay | {賃金|ちんぎん}, {給与|きゅうよ}, {賞与|しょうよ}, {支給|しきゅう}, {給付|きゅうふ}, {手取|てど}り, {明細|めいさい}, {初任給|しょにんきゅう}, {賃上|ちんあ}げ, {昇給|しょうきゅう}, {福利厚生|ふくりこうせい} |
| careers | {経歴|けいれき}, {職歴|しょくれき}, {学歴|がくれき}, キャリア, スキル, {技能|ぎのう}, {研修|けんしゅう}, {昇進|しょうしん}, {昇格|しょうかく}, {出世|しゅっせ}, {就任|しゅうにん}, {肩書|かたが}き, {実績|じっせき}, {業績|ぎょうせき}, {成果|せいか}, {査定|さてい} |
| the organization | {人事|じんじ}, {部署|ぶしょ}, {部門|ぶもん}, {管理職|かんりしょく}, {主任|しゅにん}, {業界|ぎょうかい}, {業種|ぎょうしゅ}, {人手|ひとで}, {人手不足|ひとでぶそく}, {働|はたら}き{手|て}, リストラ, ノルマ |
| attitudes | {勤勉|きんべん}, {張|は}り{切|き}る, やりがい, {担|にな}う, {負担|ふたん}, {分担|ぶんたん} |

Notes:

- {雇|やと}う is the employer's verb: {会社|かいしゃ}が{人|ひと}を{雇|やと}う. The worker is {雇|やと}われる, or more
  often {採用|さいよう}される. {雇用|こよう} is the formal noun ({雇用|こよう}を{守|まも}る, protect jobs).
- {賃金|ちんぎん} is the word of law and economics; {給与|きゅうよ} is what a company pays, on contracts and
  pay slips; {給料|きゅうりょう} is the everyday word. {賞与|しょうよ} is the formal word for ボーナス.
- {手取|てど}り is take-home pay, after tax and insurance; the slip that shows it is the
  {給与明細|きゅうよめいさい}.
- {昇進|しょうしん} is moving up to a higher post ({課長|かちょう}に{昇進|しょうしん}する); {昇格|しょうかく} is moving up a
  grade or rank; {昇給|しょうきゅう} is a pay rise. {出世|しゅっせ} is getting on in the world, success
  in a career.
- {正規|せいき} and {非正規|ひせいき} describe employment: {非正規|ひせいき}の{社員|しゃいん} are workers on fixed-term,
  part-time or agency contracts. Agency staff are はけん{社員|しゃいん} (the second kanji of はけん isn't on the
  list).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: hiring, roles, pay and results.

### Hiring and taking a job

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 雇 | employ | コ | やと(う) | 12 | {雇用|こよう}, {解雇|かいこ}, {雇|やと}う, {雇|やと}い{主|ぬし} |
| 募 | recruit, gather | ボ | つの(る) | 12 | {募集|ぼしゅう}, {応募|おうぼ}, {募|つの}る |
| 採 | take, pick, adopt | サイ | と(る) | 11 | {採用|さいよう}, {不採用|ふさいよう}, {採|と}る |
| 就 | take up (a post) | シュウ | つ(く) | 12 | {就職|しゅうしょく}, {就任|しゅうにん}, {再就職|さいしゅうしょく}, {就|つ}く |

- Carried words now in kanji: {採用|さいよう}, {就職|しゅうしょく}, {募集|ぼしゅう}, {応募|おうぼ} (応 is lesson 13's
  kanji).
- {採|と}る is the とる of hiring and of picking things in nature: {新人|しんじん}を{採|と}る, きのこを{採|と}る.
  {就|つ}く is the つく of taking up a job: {仕事|しごと}に{就|つ}く, {職|しょく}に{就|つ}く. Both are the same
  verbs you know (とる, つく), with another kanji.
- {募|つの}る is "to call for" (people, money, opinions): {参加者|さんかしゃ}を{募|つの}る. Used of feelings it
  means "to grow stronger": {不安|ふあん}が{募|つの}る.

### Roles and places

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 担 | carry, be in charge | タン | にな(う) | 8 | {担当|たんとう}, {担任|たんにん}, {負担|ふたん}, {分担|ぶんたん}, {担|にな}う |
| 副 | vice-, secondary | フク | — | 11 | {副業|ふくぎょう}, {副社長|ふくしゃちょう}, {副作用|ふくさよう} (lesson 2) |
| 専 | exclusive, special | セン | — | 9 | {専門|せんもん}, {専門家|せんもんか}, {専念|せんねん}, {専業主婦|せんぎょうしゅふ}, {専用|せんよう} |
| 署 | office; sign | ショ | — | 13 | {部署|ぶしょ}, {警察署|けいさつしょ}, {消防署|しょうぼうしょ}, {署名|しょめい} (lesson 7) |

- Carried words now in kanji: {担当|たんとう}, {担当者|たんとうしゃ}, {担任|たんにん}, {専門|せんもん},
  {警察署|けいさつしょ}.
- {担|にな}う is formal: "to carry, to take on" a role or the future. {次|つぎ}の{時代|じだい}を{担|にな}う{人材|じんざい}
  (the people who will carry the next era).
- 副 as a prefix means "vice-" or "side": {副社長|ふくしゃちょう}, {副業|ふくぎょう}. Lesson 27 has it with the
  other prefixes.
- {専用|せんよう} is "for the exclusive use of": {女性専用車|じょせいせんようしゃ} (women-only car),
  {社員専用|しゃいんせんよう} (staff only).

### Pay, results and rising

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 賃 | wages, fee | チン | — | 13 | {賃金|ちんぎん}, {家賃|やちん}, {賃上|ちんあ}げ, {運賃|うんちん} |
| 績 | achievement | セキ | — | 17 | {成績|せいせき}, {業績|ぎょうせき}, {実績|じっせき} |
| 昇 | rise | ショウ | のぼ(る) | 8 | {昇進|しょうしん}, {昇給|しょうきゅう}, {昇格|しょうかく}, {昇|のぼ}る |
| 与 | give | ヨ | あた(える) | 3 | {給与|きゅうよ}, {賞与|しょうよ}, {与|あた}える, {与党|よとう} |
| 張 | stretch | チョウ | は(る) | 11 | {出張|しゅっちょう}, {主張|しゅちょう}, {緊張|きんちょう}, {張|は}る, {引|ひ}っ{張|ぱ}る, {張|は}り{切|き}る, {頑張|がんば}る |

- Carried words now in kanji: {家賃|やちん}, {成績|せいせき}, {出張|しゅっちょう}, {頑張|がんば}る, {緊張|きんちょう}
  (緊 is lesson 4's), {張|は}り{紙|がみ}, {与党|よとう}. Write them so from now on.
- {昇|のぼ}る is the のぼる of the sun and of rising: {日|ひ}が{昇|のぼ}る. Climbing a mountain stays
  {登|のぼ}る and going up stairs {上|のぼ}る.
- {張|は}る is "to stretch, to put up": テントを{張|は}る, {張|は}り{紙|がみ}を{張|は}る. 張 turns up in many
  words about effort and tension: {頑張|がんば}る, {緊張|きんちょう}, {張|は}り{切|き}る (to be full of
  energy for something), {主張|しゅちょう} (a claim).
- {運賃|うんちん} is a fare for transport; {家賃|やちん} is rent.

Memory notes:

- 雇 is a door (戸) over a bird: a house that takes a bird in, like an employer taking in a
  worker.
- 募 has 力 (strength) at the bottom: calling for people's strength.
- 担 is a hand (扌) beside the sun (日) rising over the horizon: shouldering the day's load.
- 専 ends in a hand at the bottom right, holding one thing only: exclusive.
- 署 is a net (罒) over 者 (person): the office where people are assigned their places.
- 賃 is 任 (task) over the "shell" shape that marks money words: money paid for a task.
- 績 has the thread radical (糸): results piled up thread by thread.
- 昇 is the sun (日) over a measuring cup: the sun climbing step by step.
- 張 has a bow on the left: stretching a bowstring.

```trace
雇募採就担副専賃績昇与張署
```

## Dialogue: side jobs and a promotion

Mio and Kenta joined the same company in the same year and talk over lunch. (Casual: colleagues of
the same age.)

```dialogue
# At lunch
みお: ねえ、{聞|き}いた？{来月|らいげつ}から{副業|ふくぎょう}オーケーになるんだって。
= Hey, have you heard? Side jobs are going to be allowed from next month.
けんた: うん、{人事|じんじ}からメール{来|き}てたね。でも、{認|みと}められたとはいえ、{会社|かいしゃ}に{届|とど}けなきゃいけないらしいよ。
= Yeah, there was an email from HR. But even if they're allowed, apparently you have to tell the company.
みお: そっか。{実|じつ}は{私|わたし}、{週末|しゅうまつ}にデザインの{仕事|しごと}、{受|う}けてみようかなって{思|おも}ってて。
= I see. Actually, I've been thinking of taking on some design work at weekends.
けんた: いいじゃん。みおさん、{専門|せんもん}だもんね。
= Sounds good. That's your field, isn't it?
みお: {専門|せんもん}っていっても、{大学|だいがく}でちょっと{勉強|べんきょう}しただけだよ。
= "My field" is putting it strongly. I only studied it a bit at university.
けんた: でも、{去年|きょねん}のポスター、みんなほめてたよ。
= But everyone praised your poster last year.
みお: ありがと。ただ、{始|はじ}めても、{本業|ほんぎょう}が{忙|いそが}しくて{続|つづ}かなかったらどうしようって。
= Thanks. But I'm worried that I'll start and then not keep it up because my main job's so busy.
けんた: {副業|ふくぎょう}だからって、{毎週|まいしゅう}やらなきゃいけないわけじゃないでしょ。
= Just because it's a side job doesn't mean you have to do it every week.
みお: そうだね。けんたくんは？{昇進|しょうしん}の{話|はなし}、{出|で}てるんでしょ？
= True. What about you? There's talk of a promotion, isn't there?
けんた: うん、{係長|かかりちょう}にって。でも、{正直|しょうじき}{迷|まよ}ってるんだ。{昇進|しょうしん}したからって{給料|きゅうりょう}がそんなに{上|あ}がるわけじゃないし、{責任|せきにん}は{重|おも}くなるし。
= Yeah, to subsection chief. But honestly, I can't decide. Being promoted doesn't mean the pay goes up that much, and the responsibility gets heavier.
みお: でも、{業績|ぎょうせき}が{認|みと}められたってことじゃない。
= But it means your results have been recognized.
けんた: それはうれしいんだけどね。{部下|ぶか}を{持|も}つのって、{向|む}いてない{気|き}がして。
= I'm pleased about that. I just feel I'm not cut out for having people under me.
みお: やってみないと{分|わ}からないよ。{私|わたし}も{副業|ふくぎょう}、{思|おも}い{切|き}ってやってみる。
= You won't know till you try. I'm going to take the plunge with my side job too.
けんた: じゃあ、お{互|たが}い{頑張|がんば}ろう。
= Then let's both give it our best.
```

{届|とど}ける here is "to notify, to report" (to the company); {思|おも}い{切|き}って = boldly, taking the
plunge. In speech, からといって shortens to からって and といっても to っていっても. {部下|ぶか} (N4's
ぶか) and {頑張|がんば}る (N5's がんばる) are now written in kanji.

## Reading: side jobs

A newspaper-style article (〜である style, as most N2 texts are).

> {近年|きんねん}、{社員|しゃいん}の{副業|ふくぎょう}を{認|みと}める{企業|きぎょう}が{増|ふ}えている。{以前|いぜん}は{多|おお}くの{会社|かいしゃ}が{就業規則|しゅうぎょうきそく}で{副業|ふくぎょう}を{禁止|きんし}していたが、{社外|しゃがい}での{経験|けいけん}が{人材|じんざい}の{成長|せいちょう}につながるとして、{考|かんが}え{方|かた}が{変|か}わってきた。{人手不足|ひとでぶそく}が{続|つづ}く{企業|きぎょう}にとっては、{副業|ふくぎょう}を{認|みと}めることで{有能|ゆうのう}な{人材|じんざい}を{集|あつ}めやすくなるという{利点|りてん}もある。{実際|じっさい}、{募集|ぼしゅう}の{広告|こうこく}に「{副業|ふくぎょう}{可|か}」と{書|か}く{会社|かいしゃ}も{出|で}てきた。
>
> {都内|とない}のメーカーに{勤|つと}める{木村|きむら}さん（{三十二|さんじゅうに}）は、{二年前|にねんまえ}から{週末|しゅうまつ}に{高校生|こうこうせい}の{家庭教師|かていきょうし}をしている。「{始|はじ}めたものの、{最初|さいしょ}の{半年|はんとし}は{本業|ほんぎょう}との{両立|りょうりつ}に{苦労|くろう}しました」と{話|はな}す。{今|いま}では{収入|しゅうにゅう}が{少|すこ}し{増|ふ}えただけでなく、{人|ひと}に{教|おし}えることで、{会議|かいぎ}での{説明|せつめい}もうまくなったという。ただし、{平日|へいじつ}の{夜|よる}は{働|はたら}かないと{決|き}めている。{本業|ほんぎょう}に{専念|せんねん}する{時間|じかん}を{守|まも}るためだ。
>
> {一方|いっぽう}で、{課題|かだい}もある。{会社|かいしゃ}が{認|みと}めているとはいえ、{働|はたら}く{時間|じかん}が{長|なが}くなれば、{体|からだ}をこわす{人|ひと}も{出|で}てくる。{本業|ほんぎょう}と{副業|ふくぎょう}の{労働時間|ろうどうじかん}をどう{合|あ}わせて{管理|かんり}するのか、まだはっきりした{答|こた}えはない。{情報|じょうほう}の{管理|かんり}を{心配|しんぱい}する{会社|かいしゃ}も{少|すく}なくない。
>
> もちろん、{副業|ふくぎょう}が{自由|じゆう}になったからといって、だれもが{始|はじ}めるべきだというわけではない。{働|はたら}き{方|かた}にくわしい{専門家|せんもんか}は、「まず、{何|なに}のために{副業|ふくぎょう}をするのかを{考|かんが}えてほしい」と{話|はな}す。{収入|しゅうにゅう}のためか、{経験|けいけん}のためか。{目的|もくてき}がはっきりしていれば、{副業|ふくぎょう}は{本業|ほんぎょう}にもいい{影響|えいきょう}を{与|あた}えるだろう。

{企業|きぎょう} = a company, an enterprise (lesson 17's word); {就業規則|しゅうぎょうきそく} = a company's work rules; {社外|しゃがい} = outside the company; {両立|りょうりつ} =
doing both side by side; {副業|ふくぎょう}{可|か} = side jobs allowed (可 is lesson 28's kanji; notices use it, lesson 15); {体|からだ}をこわす = to damage one's health; くわしい = knowledgeable about.

1. Why have many companies changed their view of side jobs?
2. What did Kimura find hard at first, and what has the side job brought?
3. What two worries does the article mention?
4. What does the expert advise people to do before starting a side job?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. They have come to see that experience outside the company helps their staff grow
   ({社外|しゃがい}での{経験|けいけん}が{人材|じんざい}の{成長|せいちょう}につながる).
2. Fitting it in with his main job for the first six months (ものの: he started, but it was hard).
   Now a little more income, and better explanations in meetings.
3. Longer working hours that can damage people's health (and no clear answer yet on how to
   manage the hours of both jobs), and companies' concern about their information.
4. To think first about why they want one: for money or for experience.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

In recent years, more and more companies have been allowing their employees to take side jobs.
In the past, many companies banned side jobs in their work rules, but their thinking has changed
as they've come to see experience outside the company as something that helps their people grow.
For companies short of staff, allowing side jobs also has the advantage of making it easier to
attract capable people. Some companies have even begun writing "side jobs allowed" in their job
advertisements.

Kimura (32), who works for a manufacturer in Tokyo, has been tutoring high-school students at
weekends for two years. "I started, but for the first six months I struggled to balance it with
my main job," Kimura says. Now, according to Kimura, not only has the income gone up a little, but
teaching people has also made it easier to explain things in meetings. Kimura has decided, though,
not to work on weekday evenings, to protect the time given to the main job.

There are problems too, though. Even if the company allows it, if people work longer hours some
of them will damage their health. There's still no clear answer on how to manage the working
hours of the main job and the side job together. Quite a few companies are also worried about how
their information is handled.

Of course, side jobs being free now doesn't mean everyone should start one. "First, I'd like
people to think about what they want a side job for," says an expert on ways of working. Is it
for income, or for experience? If the purpose is clear, a side job will probably have a good
effect on the main job too.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{内定|ないてい}はもらったものの、まだ{迷|まよ}っています。
= I've had a job offer, but I'm still undecided.
{新人|しんじん}とはいえ、{責任|せきにん}はあります。
= I may be new, but I still have responsibilities.
{給料|きゅうりょう}が{高|たか}いからといって、いい{会社|かいしゃ}だとは{限|かぎ}りません。
= High pay doesn't necessarily make it a good company.
{昇進|しょうしん}したといっても、{係長|かかりちょう}になっただけです。
= I've been promoted, but only to subsection chief.
{雇用|こよう}の{条件|じょうけん}を{確認|かくにん}させてください。
= Please let me check the terms of employment.
```

## Common mistakes

- Ending a sentence with ものの. ×{頑張|がんば}ったものの。 ものの needs its second half; for a
  sentence-final complaint use のに: {頑張|がんば}ったのに。
- A noun straight before ものの. ×{新人|しんじん}ものの. Use である: {新人|しんじん}であるものの (or
  {新人|しんじん}だが in plainer writing). Compare とはいえ, which takes the bare noun:
  {新人|しんじん}とはいえ.
- からといって with a positive ending. ×{高|たか}いからといって、いいものだ. からといって blocks a
  conclusion, so the end is a negation: いいものだとは{限|かぎ}らない.
- ものの in casual chat. It sounds bookish between friends: say けど, のに, or からって there.
  とはいえ is heard in adults' everyday speech (as in the dialogue), but it is still on the formal
  side; けど is the casual choice.
- {昇進|しょうしん} for a pay rise. A pay rise is {昇給|しょうきゅう}; {昇進|しょうしん} is a higher post.
- {雇|やと}う for your own job hunt. You don't {雇|やと}う yourself into a company: {会社|かいしゃ}に{採用|さいよう}される,
  {就職|しゅうしょく}する.

## Key points

- Words whose kanji are all on the list (1,039) are written in kanji, carried ones included:
  {採用|さいよう}, {就職|しゅうしょく}, {担当|たんとう}, {成績|せいせき}, {出張|しゅっちょう}, {頑張|がんば}る.
  Auxiliary verbs, formal nouns and the kana compound particles stay in kana.
- 〜ものの: although; written; plain form, な / である after な-adjectives, である after nouns;
  often 〜たものの. Cooler than のに, and it can't end a sentence.
- 〜とはいえ: granted, even so; written; takes nouns directly; also a sentence opener.
- 〜からといって (からって): just because; ends in わけではない, とは{限|かぎ}らない or a negative.
- 〜といっても (N3): I say A, but only so much.
- New kanji: 雇 募 採 就 担 副 専 賃 績 昇 与 張 署.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Despite: にもかかわらず, ながらも, つつも
topics: ながらも and つつも
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1's 〜ものの and 〜とはいえ grant a point and then go against it. This lesson adds three more
ways of saying "despite" or "although": 〜にもかかわらず, the formal "despite" of news and letters;
〜ながらも, which joins a state to something that goes against it; and 〜つつも, the written "even
while". At the end a table sets all of them beside N3's のに and くせに. The theme is medicine:
hospitals, diagnosis, treatment, injuries, infection and looking after the sick.

{雨|あめ}にもかかわらず、{大勢|おおぜい}の{人|ひと}が{検診|けんしん}に{来|き}た。 — Despite the rain, a lot of people came for the check-up.
{小|ちい}さいながらも、{設備|せつび}の{整|ととの}った{診療所|しんりょうじょ}だ。 — It's a small clinic, but a well-equipped one.
{体|からだ}に{悪|わる}いと{知|し}りつつも、つい{夜|よる}{遅|おそ}くまで{起|お}きてしまう。 — I know it's bad for me, but I end up staying up late anyway.

## Despite (formal): 〜にもかかわらず

〜にもかかわらず means "despite A" or "although A": B is surprising, or regrettable, given A. It
belongs to writing, news and formal speech. (かかわらず comes from かかわる, "to be connected": "even
with A, B isn't held back".)

{熱|ねつ}があるにもかかわらず、{彼|かれ}は{仕事|しごと}を{続|つづ}けた。 — Despite having a fever, he went on working.
{治療|ちりょう}を{受|う}けたにもかかわらず、{症状|しょうじょう}はよくならなかった。 — Despite the treatment, the symptoms didn't improve.
{休日|きゅうじつ}にもかかわらず、{病院|びょういん}の{前|まえ}には{長|なが}い{列|れつ}ができていた。 — Although it was a holiday, there was a long queue in front of the hospital.

| Before にもかかわらず | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {注意|ちゅうい}したにもかかわらず, {痛|いた}いにもかかわらず |
| な-adjective: stem, or + である | {危険|きけん}にもかかわらず, {危険|きけん}であるにもかかわらず |
| noun: directly, or + である | {雨|あめ}にもかかわらず, {休日|きゅうじつ}であるにもかかわらず |

Not with だ: ×{雨|あめ}だにもかかわらず. As a sentence opener it is (それ)にもかかわらず, "and yet":
{医者|いしゃ}は{安静|あんせい}にするように{言|い}った。それにもかかわらず、{彼|かれ}は{次|つぎ}の{日|ひ}から{練習|れんしゅう}に{出|で}た (the
doctor told him to rest; and yet he was back at practice the next day).

B is a fact, not a request or a plan of yours: ×{雨|あめ}にもかかわらず、{来|き}てください. In speech
it often expresses thanks: お{忙|いそが}しいにもかかわらず、ありがとうございました (thank you for coming
when you're so busy). And don't confuse it with lesson 21's にかかわらず (without も): "regardless
of". The も makes it "despite".

## Although, while still: 〜ながら(も)

N3 taught 〜ながら for doing two things at once ({歩|ある}きながら) and met 〜ながらも for "although".
At N2 the "although" use goes beyond verbs: 〜ながら(も) takes nouns and adjectives and joins a
state to something that goes against it. も makes the contrast stronger; it is common in writing
and set phrases, and a little formal in speech.

{子供|こども}ながら、{彼|かれ}は{痛|いた}みに{最後|さいご}までたえた。 — Child though he was, he bore the pain to the end.
{貧|まず}しいながらも、{家族|かぞく}は{仲|なか}よく{暮|く}らしていた。 — Poor as they were, the family lived happily together.
{医者|いしゃ}は{悪|わる}いと{知|し}っていながら、{何|なに}も{言|い}わなかった。 — The doctor knew it was bad, but said nothing.

| Before ながら(も) | Example |
|---|---|
| noun: directly, or + でありながら | {子供|こども}ながら(に), {医者|いしゃ}でありながら |
| い-adjective: dictionary form | {小|ちい}さいながらも, {貧|まず}しいながらも |
| な-adjective: stem | {残念|ざんねん}ながら, {不安|ふあん}ながらも |
| verb: ます stem (state verbs) or 〜ていながら | {知|し}りながら, {知|し}っていながら, {言|い}いながらも |

Set phrases you'll meet often: {残念|ざんねん}ながら (unfortunately), {勝手|かって}ながら (we're sorry
for the inconvenience; on notices: "at our own convenience"), {我|わ}ながら (if I say so myself),
{子供|こども}ながらに (even as a child).

With verbs, this ながら is about states, not actions happening at the same time: {知|し}りながら
(knowing it), {分|わ}かっていながら (understanding it), {持|も}っていながら (having it). If the verb is an
ongoing action, ながら is read as "while doing": {薬|くすり}を{飲|の}みながら{仕事|しごと}をする (I work while
taking medicine), not "although".

## Even while (written): 〜つつ(も)

〜つつも takes the ます stem: "even while (thinking, knowing) A, B". The subject of both halves is
the same person, and the verbs are usually about thinking, knowing and saying: {思|おも}いつつも,
{知|し}りつつも, {言|い}いつつも, {気|き}にしつつも. It is written style; in conversation you'd use
けど or のに.

{早|はや}く{病院|びょういん}へ{行|い}かなければと{思|おも}いつつも、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}がたってしまった。 — I kept thinking I had to go to hospital soon, and yet a week went by.
{副作用|ふくさよう}を{心配|しんぱい}しつつも、{医師|いし}を{信|しん}じて{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}み{続|つづ}けた。 — Though worried about side effects, I trusted the doctor and kept taking the medicine.

Without も, つつ can also mean "while" (two things at once, written): lesson 9 teaches that use. For
"although", the も is the safer choice.

## Which "although"? A table

| Pattern | Style | Feeling | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| のに | all styles | surprise, disappointment, complaint; can end a sentence | {薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んだのに、{治|なお}らない。 |
| くせに | speech | blame: someone (usually not you) does something they shouldn't, given A | {医者|いしゃ}のくせに、たばこを{吸|す}っている。 |
| 〜ものの | written, formal | cool: grants A, then B | {退院|たいいん}したものの、まだ{通院|つういん}が{必要|ひつよう}だ。 |
| 〜にもかかわらず | written, formal, news | B is surprising or regrettable given A | {注意|ちゅうい}したにもかかわらず、{事故|じこ}が{起|お}きた。 |
| 〜ながら(も) | written, set phrases | a state, and something against it | {小|ちい}さいながらも{立派|りっぱ}な{病院|びょういん} |
| 〜つつ(も) | written | same person: thinking or knowing, yet doing | {悪|わる}いと{知|し}りつつも{続|つづ}けた。 |

> **Review: くせに and のに (N3 lesson 18).** くせに blames the subject and is spoken, often
> rude: {自分|じぶん}だって{遅|おく}れたくせに (you were late yourself!). It needs the same subject in both
> halves, a person, and is usually about someone else (said of yourself it sounds self-mocking).
> のに only reports that B went against A, with feeling.

### To recognize: 〜ものを

〜ものを at the end of a clause is a regret or a reproach: "if only… (but you didn't)". It is
literary or old-fashioned, and today you'll mostly meet it in writing:
すぐに{医者|いしゃ}に{診|み}せればよかったものを (if only you'd shown it to a doctor straight away). The
everyday version is 〜ばよかったのに.

## Words for medicine

N3 gave you the doctor's visit ({診察|しんさつ}, {症状|しょうじょう}, {患者|かんじゃ}, {治療|ちりょう}, {手術|しゅじゅつ},
{検査|けんさ}, {入院|にゅういん}), all of which you can now write in kanji. N2 adds the words of hospitals,
health news and medical notices.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| the system | {医療|いりょう}, {医療費|いりょうひ}, {医学|いがく}, {診療|しんりょう}, {診療所|しんりょうじょ}, {外来|がいらい}, {主治医|しゅじい}, {病室|びょうしつ} |
| departments | {小児科|しょうにか}, {眼科|がんか}, {皮膚科|ひふか}, {耳鼻科|じびか} |
| diagnosis | {診断|しんだん}, {診断書|しんだんしょ}, {受診|じゅしん}, {検診|けんしん}, {誤診|ごしん}, {人間|にんげん}ドック, {病状|びょうじょう}, {症例|しょうれい}, 〜{症|しょう}, {発症|はっしょう} |
| illness | {病|やまい}, {持病|じびょう}, {急性|きゅうせい}, {重症|じゅうしょう}, {軽症|けいしょう}, {後遺症|こういしょう}, {熱中症|ねっちゅうしょう}, {花粉症|かふんしょう}, {患|わずら}う, {悪化|あっか}, {再発|さいはつ} |
| infection | {感染|かんせん}, {感染症|かんせんしょう}, {伝染|でんせん}, ウイルス, {予防接種|よぼうせっしゅ}, {消毒|しょうどく} |
| injuries | {外傷|がいしょう}, {重傷|じゅうしょう}, {軽傷|けいしょう}, {負傷|ふしょう}, {傷口|きずぐち}, {傷跡|きずあと}, {怪我人|けがにん}, {刺|さ}さる, {処置|しょち} |
| treatment | {療養|りょうよう}, {安静|あんせい}, {通院|つういん}, {処方|しょほう}, {服用|ふくよう}, {医薬品|いやくひん}, {飲|の}み{薬|ぐすり}, {塗|ぬ}り{薬|ぐすり}, {風邪薬|かぜぐすり}, {副作用|ふくさよう}, {完治|かんち}, {延命|えんめい}, {救命|きゅうめい} |
| care | {看護|かんご}, {看病|かんびょう}, お{見舞|みま}い, {寝|ね}たきり |
| poison | {毒|どく}, {毒性|どくせい}, {有毒|ゆうどく}, {中毒|ちゅうどく}, {食中毒|しょくちゅうどく}, {刺激|しげき} |

Notes:

- 〜{症|しょう} is a suffix for a disorder or condition: {熱中症|ねっちゅうしょう} (heatstroke), {花粉症|かふんしょう} (hay
  fever), {後遺症|こういしょう} (after-effects). {重症|じゅうしょう} (a serious case: of illness) and {重傷|じゅうしょう}
  (a serious injury) sound the same; news reports use both, so the kanji matter.
- {診察|しんさつ} is the doctor examining you; {診断|しんだん} is the doctor's judgement (the diagnosis);
  {診療|しんりょう} is examination and treatment together, the word of clinic signs:
  {診療時間|しんりょうじかん} (surgery hours). {受診|じゅしん} is the patient's side: going to see a doctor.
- {看護|かんご} is nursing as a job; {看病|かんびょう} is looking after a sick family member at home.
- {感染|かんせん} is catching an infection ({感染|かんせん}する, {感染|かんせん}を{防|ふせ}ぐ). うつる is the everyday
  verb: {風邪|かぜ}がうつる (catch a cold from someone).
- お{見舞|みま}い is a visit to someone ill or injured, and the gift you take.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: illness and treatment, care, injuries and poison.

### Illness and treatment

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 患 | suffer; illness | カン | わずら(う) | 11 | {患者|かんじゃ}, {患部|かんぶ}, {患|わずら}う |
| 療 | treat, heal | リョウ | — | 17 | {治療|ちりょう}, {医療|いりょう}, {療養|りょうよう}, {診療|しんりょう} |
| 診 | examine (medically) | シン | み(る) | 12 | {診察|しんさつ}, {診断|しんだん}, {受診|じゅしん}, {検診|けんしん}, {診|み}る |
| 症 | symptom, condition | ショウ | — | 10 | {症状|しょうじょう}, {重症|じゅうしょう}, {発症|はっしょう}, {花粉症|かふんしょう} |
| 看 | watch over | カン | — | 9 | {看護|かんご}, {看護師|かんごし}, {看病|かんびょう}, {看板|かんばん} (signboard) |
| 護 | protect | ゴ | — | 20 | {看護|かんご}, {保護|ほご} (protection), {弁護士|べんごし} (lesson 11) |

- Carried words now in kanji: {患者|かんじゃ}, {治療|ちりょう}, {診察|しんさつ}, {症状|しょうじょう}, {看護師|かんごし},
  {健康診断|けんこうしんだん}. Write them so from now on.
- {診|み}る is the みる of a doctor examining a patient: {医者|いしゃ}に{診|み}てもらう. It is the same verb as
  {見|み}る, with the medical kanji.
- 護 has 20 strokes, the most in this lesson.

### Injuries, poison and odd readings

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 傷 | wound | ショウ | きず | 13 | {傷|きず}, {傷口|きずぐち}, {重傷|じゅうしょう}, {負傷|ふしょう}, {傷|きず}つく |
| 怪 | strange | カイ | あや(しい) | 8 | {怪|あや}しい, {怪我|けが} (special reading) |
| 我 | self | ガ | われ, わ | 7 | {怪我|けが}, {我々|われわれ}, {我|わ}ながら |
| 邪 | wicked | ジャ | — | 8 | {風邪|かぜ} (special reading), {無邪気|むじゃき} |
| 針 | needle | シン | はり | 10 | {針|はり}, {方針|ほうしん} (policy), {針金|はりがね} (wire) |
| 毒 | poison | ドク | — | 8 | {毒|どく}, {中毒|ちゅうどく}, {消毒|しょうどく}, {気|き}の{毒|どく} |
| 刺 | pierce | シ | さ(す), さ(さる) | 8 | {刺|さ}す, {刺|さ}さる, {刺激|しげき}, {名刺|めいし} |

- **Special readings.** {風邪|かぜ} (a cold) and {怪我|けが} (an injury) are read as whole words, not
  kanji by kanji. You know both from earlier courses: write {風邪|かぜ}をひく and {怪我|けが}をする from now
  on.
- Other carried words now in kanji: {傷|きず}, {怪|あや}しい, {気|き}の{毒|どく}, {名刺|めいし}, {刺|さ}す (of
  insects and needles), {我々|われわれ}, and {針|はり} (a clock's hand is the same word: {時計|とけい}の{針|はり}).
  じゃま stays in kana: its second kanji isn't on the list, nor is that of がまん.
- {傷|きず}つく / {傷|きず}つける also work for feelings: {言葉|ことば}に{傷|きず}つく (be hurt by words).
- {刺激|しげき} is "stimulus": a sting to the skin or the eyes, and also excitement or inspiration
  ({刺激|しげき}を{受|う}ける, to be inspired). 激 is lesson 4's kanji.

Memory notes:

- 患 is a heart (心) with a skewer through two boxes on top: a heart pierced by worry, suffering.
- 療 and 症 have the sickness radical (疒), a sickbed with a roof.
- 診 is speech (言) and a shape like flowing hair: the doctor's questions and close look.
- 看 is a hand over an eye (目): shading your eyes to watch over someone.
- 傷 has a person (亻) on the left: a person with a wound.
- 針 has metal (金) on the left and 十 on the right: a metal pin.
- 毒 has 母 (mother) at the bottom, under a crown of growing grass: a plant too strong to touch.
- 刺 has a knife (刂) on the right: something sharp that pierces.

```trace
患療診症看護傷怪我邪針毒刺
```

## Dialogue: at the clinic

Yūto has had a fever for days and finally goes to a small neighbourhood clinic. Dr Morita is the
doctor. (Polite: doctor and patient.)

```dialogue
# At the clinic
もりた: {今日|きょう}はどうされましたか。
= What seems to be the problem today?
ゆうと: {先週|せんしゅう}から{熱|ねつ}が{下|さ}がらないんです。{風邪|かぜ}だと{思|おも}って、{風邪薬|かぜぐすり}を{飲|の}んでいたんですが。
= My temperature hasn't gone down since last week. I thought it was a cold and was taking cold medicine.
もりた: {一週間|いっしゅうかん}もですか。{早|はや}く{受診|じゅしん}されればよかったのに。
= A whole week? You should have come in sooner.
ゆうと: はい。{早|はや}く{来|こ}なきゃと{思|おも}いつつも、{仕事|しごと}が{休|やす}めなくて…。
= I know. I kept thinking I had to come, but I couldn't get time off work…
もりた: {熱|ねつ}は{何度|なんど}ありますか。
= How high is your temperature?
ゆうと: {今朝|けさ}は{三十八度|さんじゅうはちど}でした。{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んでいるのに、{全然|ぜんぜん}{下|さ}がらなくて。
= It was thirty-eight this morning. I'm taking medicine, but it won't come down at all.
もりた: {胸|むね}の{音|おと}を{聞|き}きますね。{大|おお}きく{息|いき}を{吸|す}ってください。…はい、けっこうです。せきは{出|で}ますか。
= I'll listen to your chest. Take a deep breath, please. …Thank you, that's fine. Do you have a cough?
ゆうと: {夜|よる}になると、ひどくなります。
= It gets bad at night.
もりた: {念|ねん}のため、{血液|けつえき}{検査|けんさ}をしましょう。{結果|けっか}は{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}ほどで{出|で}ます。
= To be on the safe side, let's do a blood test. The results will be ready in about thirty minutes.
ゆうと: {分|わ}かりました。あの、{仕事|しごと}は{続|つづ}けてもだいじょうぶでしょうか。
= All right. Er, is it all right for me to keep working?
もりた: {診断|しんだん}が{出|で}るまでは、{安静|あんせい}にしてください。{無理|むり}をすると、{悪化|あっか}するおそれもありますから。
= Until we have a diagnosis, please rest. If you push yourself, it could get worse.
ゆうと: {会社|かいしゃ}に{出|だ}す{診断書|しんだんしょ}も、お{願|ねが}いできますか。
= Could I also have a medical certificate for the company, please?
もりた: ええ、{検査|けんさ}の{結果|けっか}を{見|み}てから{書|か}きますね。お{大事|だいじ}に。
= Yes, I'll write it once I've seen the test results. Take care.
```

The doctor's のに (よかったのに) is a gentle reproach, close in meaning to 〜ものを above but
everyday. ゆうと's つつも is a little formal for speech, which suits talking to a doctor. 〜おそれがある
(there's a risk of) is lesson 16's; {念|ねん}のため = to be on the safe side (N3). Lesson 5 owns the
body words ({胸|むね}, {血液|けつえき}); {胸|むね} and {息|いき} are carried.

## Reading: a nurse's column

A column by a hospital nurse in a local paper (〜である style).

> {看護師|かんごし}として{働|はたら}いて{十五年|じゅうごねん}になる。この{間|あいだ}、{何度|なんど}も{同|おな}じような{場面|ばめん}を{見|み}てきた。{体|からだ}の{具合|ぐあい}がおかしいと{気|き}づきつつも、「{忙|いそが}しいから」と{受診|じゅしん}を{先|さき}に{延|の}ばし、{症状|しょうじょう}が{重|おも}くなってから{救急車|きゅうきゅうしゃ}で{運|はこ}ばれてくる{患者|かんじゃ}さんである。そのたびに、「もう{少|すこ}し{早|はや}く{来|き}てくれていれば」と{思|おも}う。
>
> ある{男性|だんせい}は、{会社|かいしゃ}の{健康診断|けんこうしんだん}で{再検査|さいけんさ}が{必要|ひつよう}だと{言|い}われていたにもかかわらず、{半年|はんとし}も{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}かなかった。{入院|にゅういん}したとき、{病状|びょうじょう}はかなり{進|すす}んでいた。「{仕事|しごと}を{休|やす}めなかったんです」と{彼|かれ}は{言|い}ったが、{結局|けっきょく}{二|に}か{月|げつ}も{仕事|しごと}を{休|やす}むことになってしまった。
>
> {病院|びょういん}に{来|く}るのが{遅|おく}れる{理由|りゆう}は、{忙|いそが}しさだけではない。「{大|たい}したことはないだろう」「{病院|びょういん}は{待|ま}ち{時間|じかん}が{長|なが}いから」と{考|かんが}える{人|ひと}も{多|おお}い。{気持|きも}ちは{分|わ}かる。{私|わたし}{自身|じしん}、{看護師|かんごし}でありながら、{自分|じぶん}の{風邪|かぜ}は{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んで{寝|ね}ていれば{治|なお}ると{思|おも}ってしまうことがある。
>
> もちろん、{少|すこ}しの{熱|ねつ}や{痛|いた}みで、すぐに{大|おお}きな{病院|びょういん}へ{行|い}く{必要|ひつよう}はない。まずは{近|ちか}くの{診療所|しんりょうじょ}で{診|み}てもらえばいい。{大切|たいせつ}なのは、{自分|じぶん}の{体|からだ}の{声|こえ}を{聞|き}き{流|なが}さないことだ。
>
> {先日|せんじつ}、{退院|たいいん}した{女性|じょせい}から{手紙|てがみ}が{届|とど}いた。{小|ちい}さな{字|じ}ながらも、ていねいに{書|か}かれた{手紙|てがみ}には、「{入院|にゅういん}{中|ちゅう}は{不安|ふあん}でしたが、{看護師|かんごし}さんの{言葉|ことば}に{何度|なんど}も{救|すく}われました」とあった。{忙|いそが}しい{毎日|まいにち}の{中|なか}で、こうした{言葉|ことば}が{私|わたし}たちの{力|ちから}になっている。

{場面|ばめん} = scene, situation; {先|さき}に{延|の}ばす = to put off (延 is lesson 10's kanji);
{再検査|さいけんさ} = a follow-up test; {聞|き}き{流|なが}す = to let something go in one ear and out the
other; {救|すく}う = to save, to rescue (lesson 16's word).

1. What kind of patient has the writer seen many times?
2. Why did the man end up off work for two months?
3. What does the writer admit, and what does the column say about a slight fever?
4. What did the woman's letter say?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Patients who notice something is wrong but keep putting off seeing a doctor because they're
   busy ({気|き}づきつつも), until they're brought in by ambulance.
2. He was told at his company health check that he needed a follow-up test, but didn't go to
   hospital for six months (にもかかわらず); by the time he was admitted, his illness was well
   advanced.
3. Though a nurse ({看護師|かんごし}でありながら), the writer sometimes thinks a cold of their own will pass with
   medicine and rest. With a slight fever there's no need to rush to a big hospital: see a local
   clinic first, but don't ignore what your body is telling you.
4. That she had been anxious in hospital, but the nurses' words had helped her many times.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

I've been working as a nurse for fifteen years. In that time I've seen the same kind of scene
many times: patients who notice that something is wrong with their body but put off seeing a
doctor "because they're busy", and are brought in by ambulance once their symptoms have become
serious. Each time, I think: if only they had come a little sooner.

One man had been told at his company health check that he needed a follow-up test, and yet he
didn't go to a hospital for six months. When he was admitted, his illness was quite advanced. "I
couldn't take time off work," he said, but in the end he had to take two whole months off.

Busyness isn't the only reason people come late. Many think "it's probably nothing" or "the
wait at hospital is so long". I understand how they feel. Even I, nurse though I am, sometimes
think my own cold will get better if I just take some medicine and stay in bed.

Of course, there's no need to rush to a big hospital at the first sign of a slight fever or pain.
It's enough to see a doctor at a local clinic first. What matters is not to ignore what your
body is telling you.

The other day I received a letter from a woman who had left hospital. In small but careful
handwriting she had written: "I was anxious while I was in hospital, but the nurses' words
helped me again and again." In our busy days, words like these are what keep us going.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{雨|あめ}にもかかわらず、お{越|こ}しいただき、ありがとうございます。
= Thank you for coming despite the rain.
{残念|ざんねん}ながら、{今日|きょう}の{診療|しんりょう}は{終|お}わりました。
= I'm afraid today's surgery hours have finished.
{早|はや}く{行|い}こうと{思|おも}いつつも、{行|い}けませんでした。
= I kept meaning to go soon, but I couldn't.
{風邪|かぜ}をひいてしまいました。
= I've caught a cold.
{傷口|きずぐち}を{消毒|しょうどく}してください。
= Please disinfect the wound.
```

お{越|こ}しいただく is a polite way to say someone came (越 is an N3 kanji; lesson 19 meets it in 〜に{越|こ}したことはない).

## Common mistakes

- だ before にもかかわらず. ×{休日|きゅうじつ}だにもかかわらず → {休日|きゅうじつ}にもかかわらず or
  {休日|きゅうじつ}であるにもかかわらず.
- A request after にもかかわらず. ×{遠|とお}いにもかかわらず、{来|き}てください. Use けれど or が:
  {遠|とお}いですが、ぜひ{来|き}てください.
- にもかかわらず for "regardless". {天気|てんき}にかかわらず{開催|かいさい}します (held whatever the
  weather) has no も; with も it would mean "despite the weather", which is something else (lesson 21).
- Different subjects with つつも. ×{母|はは}が{止|と}めつつも、{私|わたし}は{出|で}かけた. つつも needs one subject:
  {私|わたし}は{悪|わる}いと{思|おも}いつつも{出|で}かけた. For two people, use のに or が.
- くせに about things. ×{雨|あめ}のくせに、{試合|しあい}があった. くせに blames a person; for the weather or
  events, use のに: {雨|あめ}なのに.
- Mixing {重症|じゅうしょう} and {重傷|じゅうしょう}: an illness is {重症|じゅうしょう}; an injury is {重傷|じゅうしょう}.

## Key points

- 〜にもかかわらず: despite; formal and written; plain form, nouns and な-adjectives directly or with
  である; B is a fact. (それ)にもかかわらず opens a sentence.
- 〜ながら(も): although, with a state: nouns ({子供|こども}ながら), adjectives ({貧|まず}しいながらも), state
  verbs ({知|し}りながら). Set phrases: {残念|ざんねん}ながら, {勝手|かって}ながら.
- 〜つつ(も): ます stem; written; one subject thinking or knowing, yet doing.
- のに: feeling, any style; くせに: spoken blame. 〜ものを (to recognize): literary regret.
- Special readings: {風邪|かぜ}, {怪我|けが}.
- New kanji: 患 療 診 症 看 護 傷 怪 我 邪 針 毒 刺.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Two sides: 反面, 一方で, かと思うと, どころか
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 1 and 2 were about concession: granting A, then saying something against it. This lesson is
about **[[contrast]]**: two sides of one thing (〜{反面|はんめん}), two things set side by side
(〜{一方|いっぽう}で), a sudden change (〜たかと{思|おも}うと), and a result that is the opposite of what
was suggested (〜どころか). The theme is geography and the landscape: mountains, valleys, rivers,
coasts, forests, land and sea.

この{町|まち}は{海|うみ}に{近|ちか}くて{景色|けしき}がいい{反面|はんめん}、{台風|たいふう}の{被害|ひがい}も{多|おお}い。 — This town is near the sea and has fine views, but on the other hand it suffers a lot of typhoon damage.
{北|きた}の{海岸|かいがん}は{岩|いわ}が{多|おお}い{一方|いっぽう}で、{南|みなみ}の{海岸|かいがん}はすなはまが{続|つづ}く。 — The northern coast is rocky, whereas the southern coast is one long sandy beach.
{晴|は}れたかと{思|おも}うと、{急|きゅう}に{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。 — No sooner had it cleared up than it suddenly started to rain.
{雨|あめ}は{止|や}むどころか、ますます{強|つよ}くなった。 — Far from stopping, the rain got heavier and heavier.

すなはま is a sandy beach (its second kanji isn't on the list, so the word is in kana).

## Two sides of one thing: 〜{反面|はんめん}

〜{反面|はんめん} is "while A, on the other hand B": one thing, person or situation has a good side and
a bad side (or the reverse). The subject of both halves is the same. It's common in writing and in
careful speech. You'll also see it written {半面|はんめん} (half of the face).

{山|やま}の{生活|せいかつ}は{静|しず}かな{反面|はんめん}、{買|か}い{物|もの}が{不便|ふべん}だ。 — Life in the mountains is quiet, but shopping is inconvenient.
{川|かわ}は{町|まち}に{水|みず}を{運|はこ}んでくれる{反面|はんめん}、{大雨|おおあめ}のときには{危険|きけん}にもなる。 — Rivers bring the town its water, but in heavy rain they can also be dangerous.
{兄|あに}は{頑固|がんこ}である{反面|はんめん}、{涙|なみだ}もろいところもある。 — My brother is stubborn, but he's also easily moved to tears.

{頑固|がんこ} (stubborn) and {涙|なみだ}もろい (easily moved to tears) are lesson 4's words.

| Before 反面 | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {運|はこ}んでくれる{反面|はんめん}, {高|たか}い{反面|はんめん} |
| な-adjective: + な, or + である | {静|しず}かな{反面|はんめん}, {便利|べんり}である{反面|はんめん} |
| noun: + である | {観光地|かんこうち}である{反面|はんめん} |

{反面|はんめん} can also open a sentence (その{反面|はんめん}, "on the other hand"), and as a noun it's
"the other side": {反面|はんめん}{教師|きょうし} (a bad example to learn from).

## On the other hand, whereas: 〜{一方|いっぽう}(で)

N3 met {一方|いっぽう} in two places: 〜{一方|いっぽう}だ (it keeps getting more so, lesson 4) and {一方|いっぽう}
as a connector (lesson 28). As a clause ending, 〜{一方|いっぽう}(で) is "whereas" or "while": it sets two
things side by side, or two sides of one thing.

{東京|とうきょう}は{人口|じんこう}が{増|ふ}えている{一方|いっぽう}で、{地方|ちほう}の{町|まち}は{減|へ}り{続|つづ}けている。 — While Tokyo's population is growing, towns in the regions keep shrinking.
この{島|しま}は{夏|なつ}は{観光客|かんこうきゃく}でにぎわう{一方|いっぽう}、{冬|ふゆ}はほとんど{人|ひと}が{来|こ}ない。 — The island bustles with tourists in summer, whereas in winter hardly anyone comes.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}く{一方|いっぽう}で、{週末|しゅうまつ}は{森林|しんりん}を{守|まも}る{活動|かつどう}をしている。 — As well as working at a company, she does forest conservation at weekends.

The forms are the same as {反面|はんめん}'s (な / である after な-adjectives, である after nouns). At the start
of a sentence it's {一方|いっぽう}, or {一方|いっぽう}で: "meanwhile, on the other hand".

### {反面|はんめん} and {一方|いっぽう}で

| | 〜{反面|はんめん} | 〜{一方|いっぽう}(で) |
|---|---|---|
| what is contrasted | two sides of the same thing | two different things, or two sides of one |
| typical content | good and bad points | any two facts set side by side |
| also | — | "as well as doing A, also B" (third example) |

So {東京|とうきょう}は{増|ふ}えている{一方|いっぽう}で、{地方|ちほう}は{減|へ}っている works only with {一方|いっぽう}で: Tokyo and the
regions are two different places. For one thing's pros and cons, both are possible.

## No sooner than: 〜たかと{思|おも}うと

〜たかと{思|おも}うと (or 〜たかと{思|おも}ったら) means "no sooner had A happened than B": the change
comes quickly and is usually unexpected. It describes things you observe, not your own actions
(×{私|わたし}は{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}ったかと{思|おも}うと、すぐ{出|で}かけた). B is something that has
actually happened, usually in the past tense (a habitual or present scene also works, as in the
second example).

{空|そら}が{暗|くら}くなったかと{思|おも}うと、{強|つよ}い{風|かぜ}が{吹|ふ}いてきた。 — No sooner had the sky gone dark than a strong wind started blowing.
{子供|こども}は{泣|な}いたかと{思|おも}うと、もう{笑|わら}っている。 — One moment the child is crying, and the next it's already laughing.
{波|なみ}が{引|ひ}いたかと{思|おも}ったら、また{大|おお}きな{波|なみ}が{来|き}た。 — The wave had only just gone out when another big one came in.

かと{思|おも}ったら is a little more spoken. Without た the pattern describes things that keep
alternating: {泣|な}いているかと{思|おも}えば、{笑|わら}っている (one minute crying, the next laughing). Notice
the か: literally "the moment I thought 'has it…?'".

## Far from it: 〜どころか

〜どころか says the truth is far from A, often the very opposite: "far from A, (in fact) B". With a
negative at the end it's "not even…, let alone A": A どころか B も〜ない.

{雨|あめ}は{止|や}むどころか、ますます{強|つよ}くなった。 — Far from stopping, the rain got heavier.
この{辺|あた}りは{静|しず}かどころか、{夜中|よなか}まで{車|くるま}の{音|おと}がうるさい。 — Far from being quiet, this area is noisy with traffic until the middle of the night.
{山|やま}に{登|のぼ}るどころか、{坂道|さかみち}を{歩|ある}くだけで{疲|つか}れてしまう。 — Forget climbing mountains: I get tired just walking up a hill.
{海外|かいがい}どころか、{近|ちか}くの{湖|みずうみ}にも{行|い}ったことがない。 — Let alone abroad, I've never even been to the lake nearby.

| Before どころか | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {止|や}むどころか, {安|やす}いどころか |
| な-adjective: stem (or + な) | {静|しず}かどころか |
| noun: directly | {海外|かいがい}どころか |

In the "let alone" use, B is the smaller or easier thing, marked with も or さえ.

### No time for: 〜どころではない

〜どころではない (casual どころじゃない) is "this is no time (or state) for A": circumstances rule A out.

{仕事|しごと}が{忙|いそが}しくて、{旅行|りょこう}どころではない。 — I'm so busy at work that a trip is out of the question.
{雪|ゆき}がひどくて、{景色|けしき}を{楽|たの}しむどころではなかった。 — The snow was so bad we were in no state to enjoy the view.

- 砂 is a stone (石) and 少 (a little): stone broken small, sand.
