it is long and thin, and the climate in the north and the south is completely different.

The main feature of Japan's landscape is that it has many mountains. About two-thirds of the
land is forest, and there is little flat land where people can easily live. As a result, the
population is concentrated on the plains facing the sea. While there are many mountains, on the
other hand the forests store water and give rise to plentiful rivers.

Japanese rivers are said to be short and fast-flowing compared with rivers on the continent.
That's because the distance from the mountains to the sea is short. No sooner has the rain
fallen than the water runs straight down to the river mouths. In heavy rain the water rises all
at once, so since long ago many towns have suffered from floods.

The shape of the coast also varies greatly from place to place. While there are rocky coasts
with intricate inlets, there are also coasts where a sandy beach stretches for kilometres. Inside
the deeply indented bays the waves are calm, so fishing harbours have been built there since
long ago. In such bays, though, the water is also said to rise higher in a tsunami.

On the other hand, the closeness of the mountains and the sea has brought many blessings to life
in Japan. Water carrying the nutrients of the mountains flows into the bays, and fish and
shellfish grow well there. Far from just making life inconvenient, the steep landscape gives
rise to beautiful scenery and rich food.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{便利|べんり}な{反面|はんめん}、{家賃|やちん}が{高|たか}いです。
= It's convenient, but on the other hand the rent is high.
{晴|は}れたかと{思|おも}うと、また{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}しました。
= No sooner had it cleared up than it started raining again.
{雨|あめ}は{止|や}むどころか、{強|つよ}くなりました。
= Far from stopping, the rain got heavier.
{忙|いそが}しくて、{旅行|りょこう}どころではありません。
= I'm too busy to even think of a trip.
{湖|みずうみ}の{向|む}こうに{岩山|いわやま}が{見|み}えます。
= You can see a rocky mountain beyond the lake.
```

## Common mistakes

- 〜{反面|はんめん} for two different things. ×{兄|あに}は{背|せ}が{高|たか}い{反面|はんめん}、{弟|おとうと}は{低|ひく}い. Two people are
  two things: use {一方|いっぽう}(で): {兄|あに}は{背|せ}が{高|たか}い{一方|いっぽう}で、{弟|おとうと}は{低|ひく}い.
- A noun straight before {反面|はんめん}. ×{観光地|かんこうち}{反面|はんめん} → {観光地|かんこうち}である{反面|はんめん}.
- 〜たかと{思|おも}うと for your own actions. ×{私|わたし}は{起|お}きたかと{思|おも}うと、また{寝|ね}た. Use
  〜たらすぐ / 〜てすぐ: {起|お}きてすぐ、また{寝|ね}てしまった.
- A plan after かと{思|おも}うと. B is something that happened: ×{着|つ}いたかと{思|おも}うと、{電話|でんわ}してください.
- どころか with a simple contrast. どころか says A is far from the truth: {寒|さむ}いどころか{暑|あつ}いくらいだ
  (far from cold, it's almost hot). For "A, but B" without that sense, use けど or {一方|いっぽう}で.

## Key points

- 〜{反面|はんめん}: two sides of one thing; plain form, な / である, noun + である.
- 〜{一方|いっぽう}(で): whereas; two things or two sides; also "as well as". {一方|いっぽう} opens sentences.
- 〜たかと{思|おも}うと / 〜たかと{思|おも}ったら: no sooner had A than B; things you observe; B has happened (usually past).
- 〜どころか: far from A (the opposite); A どころか B も〜ない: let alone A. 〜どころではない: no time
  for.
- Special readings: {河原|かわら}, {砂利|じゃり}.
- New kanji: 谷 林 岸 波 岩 坂 河 湖 湾 陸 砂 泥 竹.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Even if: にしても, にしろ, にせよ, としても
topics: にしろ and にせよ
にしては and 割に
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 1 to 3 conceded facts: "although it's true that…". This lesson concedes things that may or
may not be true, and things you don't know yet: "even if", "whatever", "whether A or B". The
patterns are 〜にしても, 〜にしろ and 〜にせよ, which are close in meaning and differ in style, and
〜としても, the hypothetical "even supposing". The theme is the inner life: worry, love and
heartbreak, loneliness, courage, stubbornness, and strong feelings.

{忙|いそが}しいにしても、{連絡|れんらく}ぐらいはできるはずだ。 — Even if you're busy, you should at least be able to get in touch.
{行|い}くにしろ{行|い}かないにしろ、{早|はや}めに{返事|へんじ}をください。 — Whether you're going or not, please let me know soon.
たとえ{反対|はんたい}されたとしても、{自分|じぶん}の{気持|きも}ちを{伝|つた}えたい。 — Even if they're against it, I want to tell them how I feel.

## Even if, granted: 〜にしても

〜にしても grants A (it may well be so) and says B holds anyway: "even if", "granted that". It is
used in speech and writing. B is often a judgement or an opinion: だろう, はずだ, べきだ, 〜てほしい,
〜すぎる.

{失恋|しつれん}したにしても、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}も{学校|がっこう}を{休|やす}むのはよくない。 — Even if you've been dumped, taking a whole week off school isn't good.
じょうだんにしても、{言|い}っていいことと{悪|わる}いことがある。 — Even as a joke, there are things you can say and things you can't.
{頑固|がんこ}な{父|ちち}にしても、{娘|むすめ}の{涙|なみだ}には{勝|か}てなかった。 — Even my stubborn father couldn't hold out against his daughter's tears.

| Before にしても | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {失恋|しつれん}したにしても, {寂|さび}しいにしても |
| な-adjective: stem, or + である | {不安|ふあん}にしても, {不安|ふあん}であるにしても |
| noun: directly, or + である | じょうだんにしても |

In the third example にしても follows a person: "even (someone like) A". This is close to "even
for A": {彼|かれ}にしても{悪気|わるぎ}はなかったのだ (he didn't mean any harm either). {悪気|わるぎ} = ill
intent.

### Whatever, wherever: question word + にしても

With a question word, にしても means "whatever, whoever, wherever":
{何|なに}をするにしても、{勇気|ゆうき}がいる (whatever you do, it takes courage);
どこに{住|す}むにしても、{寂|さび}しさはついてくる (wherever you live, loneliness follows you).

As set phrases, {何|なに}にしても, いずれにしても and いずれにせよ mean "anyway, in any case": いずれにしても、
{明日|あした}{話|はな}そう (anyway, let's talk tomorrow).

## The same, more formal: 〜にしろ, 〜にせよ

〜にしろ and 〜にせよ come from the imperatives of する (しろ, せよ: "let it be"). They mean the same as
にしても and join the same way, but sound firmer and more formal; にせよ is the most written of the
three.

{理由|りゆう}が{何|なん}であるにせよ、{暴力|ぼうりょく}は{許|ゆる}されない。 — Whatever the reason, violence is unforgivable.
じょうだんにしろ、そんなことを{言|い}われたらだれでも{傷|きず}つく。 — Even as a joke, anyone would be hurt to be told that.

### Whether A or B: A にしろ B にしろ

Doubled, these patterns give "whether A or B": both cases lead to the same B. にしろ〜にしろ and
にせよ〜にせよ are the usual forms; にしても〜にしても is also heard.

{賛成|さんせい}するにしろ{反対|はんたい}するにしろ、{理由|りゆう}を{説明|せつめい}してください。 — Whether you agree or disagree, please explain why.
{勝|か}つにせよ{負|ま}けるにせよ、{最後|さいご}まで{全力|ぜんりょく}を{出|だ}そう。 — Win or lose, let's give it everything to the end.

## Even supposing: 〜としても, たとえ〜としても

〜としても is "even supposing A": A is a hypothesis, something that may not be the case. It often
comes with たとえ ("even if"). Compare N3's たとえ〜ても: the meaning is close, but としても makes A
more clearly a supposition ("even assuming that").

たとえ{失敗|しっぱい}したとしても、こうかいはしない。 — Even if I fail, I won't regret it.
{今|いま}から{急|いそ}いだとしても、{最終|さいしゅう}{電車|でんしゃ}には{間|ま}に{合|あ}わないだろう。 — Even if we hurry now, we probably won't make the last train.
{彼|かれ}が{本当|ほんとう}のことを{言|い}っているとしても、しょうこがない。 — Even supposing he's telling the truth, there's no proof.

Plain form + としても; nouns and な-adjectives take だ: {本当|ほんとう}だとしても, {無理|むり}だとしても.
こうかい (regret) is in kana: its second kanji isn't on the list.

### にしても or としても?

| | 〜にしても / にしろ / にせよ | 〜としても |
|---|---|---|
| A is | often a fact or a likely situation granted for argument | a supposition |
| after a noun | directly (じょうだんにしても) | with だ (じょうだんだとしても) |
| question words | yes: {何|なに}をするにしても | yes, mostly with ある: {何|なに}があったとしても |
| A or B | yes: 〜にしろ〜にしろ | rare |

## Review: 〜にしては and 〜{割|わり}に

> **Review (N3 lesson 18).** 〜にしては and 〜{割|わり}に look like にしても but mean "for, considering":
> A sets an expectation and the fact goes against it. {初|はじ}めてにしては{上手|じょうず}だ (it's good for a
> first try). {年|とし}の{割|わり}に{若|わか}く{見|み}える (looks young for their age). にしても concedes
> ("even if A, still B"); にしては measures against A ("for an A, surprisingly B").

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {彼女|かのじょ}は{初|はじ}めてにしては{落|お}ち{着|つ}いていた。 | For her first time, she was calm. (surprising) |
| {初|はじ}めてにしても、{準備|じゅんび}が{足|た}りない。 | Even granting it's her first time, she's under-prepared. |
| {値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}に{快適|かいてき}なホテルだった。 | It was a comfortable hotel for the price. |

### To recognize: 〜といえども

〜といえども (very written) is "even, although": {子供|こども}といえども{一人|ひとり}の{人間|にんげん}だ (a child,
but still a person in their own right); {専門家|せんもんか}といえども{間違|まちが}えることはある (even experts make
mistakes). You'll meet it in editorials and speeches; in your own writing, にしても or でも is
enough.

## Words for feelings

N3 gave you the basic emotions ({感情|かんじょう}, {感動|かんどう}, {喜|よろこ}び, {悲|かな}しみ, {不安|ふあん}). Now
you can write several carried words in kanji: {寂|さび}しい, {恋人|こいびと}, {恋愛|れんあい}, {片思|かたおも}い,
{涙|なみだ}, {驚|おどろ}く, {頑張|がんば}る, {緊張|きんちょう}, {離婚|りこん}.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| worry and pain | {悩|なや}む, {悩|なや}み, {悩|なや}ましい, {苦悩|くのう}, {苦|くる}しみ, {苦痛|くつう}, {絶望|ぜつぼう}, プレッシャー, {弱音|よわね} |
| love and heartbreak | {恋|こい}しい, {初恋|はつこい}, {恋心|こいごころ}, {恋愛結婚|れんあいけっこん}, {失恋|しつれん}, {未練|みれん}, {好意|こうい}, {切|せつ}ない |
| loneliness and parting | {寂|さび}しさ, {寂|さび}しがる, {寂|さび}しがり{屋|や}, {離|はな}れる, {離|はな}す, {離|はな}れ{離|ばな}れ |
| anger and hate | {激怒|げきど}, {憎|にく}む, {憎|にく}い, {憎|にく}しみ, {憎|にく}らしい, {憎悪|ぞうお}, {憎|にく}まれ{口|ぐち} |
| surprise and tears | {驚|おどろ}き, {驚|おどろ}かす, {叫|さけ}ぶ, {叫|さけ}び, {叫|さけ}び{声|ごえ}, {涙|なみだ}ぐむ, {涙|なみだ}もろい, {涙声|なみだごえ} |
| courage and stubbornness | {勇気|ゆうき}, {勇|いさ}ましい, {勇気|ゆうき}づける, {頑固|がんこ}, {頑|かたく}な, {頑|がん}として, {強情|ごうじょう}, {意地|いじ}, {意地|いじ}っ{張|ぱ}り, {頑張|がんば}り |
| comfort and discomfort | {快|こころよ}い, {快適|かいてき}, {快感|かいかん}, {不快|ふかい}, {心地|ここち}, {心地|ここち}よい, {居心地|いごこち}, {気楽|きらく}, {安|やす}らぐ, {支|ささ}え, {心強|こころづよ}い, {気|き}まずい, {照|て}れくさい, もどかしい |
| strong feelings | {激|はげ}しい, {感激|かんげき}, {情熱|じょうねつ}, {熱意|ねつい}, {感情的|かんじょうてき}, {感傷的|かんしょうてき}, {刺激的|しげきてき}, {過激|かげき} |
| inside and outside | {本音|ほんね}, {反省|はんせい}, {罪悪感|ざいあくかん}, {気分転換|きぶんてんかん} |

Notes:

- {寂|さび}しい is how you feel; {寂|さび}しがる is how someone else shows it (〜がる, N4). The same goes for
  N3's {怖|こわ}がる.
- {憎|にく}い is "hateful", but {憎|にく}らしい is often milder, even affectionate: {憎|にく}らしいことを{言|い}う{子|こ}
  (a cheeky child). {憎|にく}めない{人|ひと} is someone you can't help liking.
- {頑固|がんこ} (stubborn) is a character; {頑|かたく}な (obstinate) describes an attitude; {頑|がん}として
  (flatly) goes with refusing: {頑|がん}として{認|みと}めない.
- {本音|ほんね} is what you really think, as opposed to たてまえ (what you say in public).
  {弱音|よわね}をはく is "to whine, to admit you're beaten" (the verb's kanji isn't on the list).
- {快|こころよ}い is "pleasant" and also "willing": {快|こころよ}く{引|ひ}き{受|う}ける (to agree gladly).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: troubled feelings, love and tears, and strength.

### Troubled feelings

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 悩 | worry | ノウ | なや(む) | 10 | {悩|なや}む, {悩|なや}み, {悩|なや}ましい, {苦悩|くのう} |
| 憎 | hate | ゾウ | にく(む), にく(い) | 14 | {憎|にく}む, {憎|にく}い, {憎|にく}しみ, {憎|にく}らしい, {憎悪|ぞうお} |
| 寂 | lonely | ジャク | さび(しい) | 11 | {寂|さび}しい, {寂|さび}しさ, {静寂|せいじゃく} (silence) |
| 驚 | be surprised | キョウ | おどろ(く) | 22 | {驚|おどろ}く, {驚|おどろ}き, {驚|おどろ}かす |
| 叫 | shout | キョウ | さけ(ぶ) | 6 | {叫|さけ}ぶ, {叫|さけ}び, {絶叫|ぜっきょう} (a scream) |

- Carried words now in kanji: {寂|さび}しい (N4's さびしい), {驚|おどろ}く (N3's おどろく). 驚 has 22 strokes,
  the most in this module.
- 驚 has a horse (馬) at the bottom: a startled horse.

### Love, tears and comfort

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 恋 | romantic love | レン | こい, こい(しい) | 10 | {恋|こい}, {恋人|こいびと}, {恋愛|れんあい}, {失恋|しつれん}, {初恋|はつこい}, {恋|こい}しい |
| 涙 | tears | ルイ | なみだ | 10 | {涙|なみだ}, {涙|なみだ}ぐむ, {涙|なみだ}もろい, {感涙|かんるい} (tears of emotion) |
| 快 | pleasant | カイ | こころよ(い) | 7 | {快適|かいてき}, {不快|ふかい}, {快晴|かいせい}, {快速|かいそく}, {快|こころよ}い |
| 離 | separate | リ | はな(れる), はな(す) | 19 | {離|はな}れる, {離|はな}す, {離婚|りこん}, {離島|りとう} |

- Carried words now in kanji: {恋|こい}, {恋人|こいびと}, {恋愛|れんあい}, {片思|かたおも}い, {涙|なみだ}, {離婚|りこん},
  {快速|かいそく} (a rapid train).
- {快晴|かいせい} is a perfectly clear sky, the weather forecast's word.
- {離|はな}す (let go of, keep apart) sounds like {話|はな}す (speak) and {放|はな}す (release): the kanji tell
  them apart. {目|め}を{離|はな}す = to take one's eyes off.

### Strength and tension

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 勇 | brave | ユウ | いさ(ましい) | 9 | {勇気|ゆうき}, {勇|いさ}ましい, {勇気|ゆうき}づける |
| 頑 | stubborn | ガン | かたく(な) | 13 | {頑固|がんこ}, {頑張|がんば}る, {頑|かたく}な, {頑|がん}として |
| 緊 | tight, tense | キン | — | 15 | {緊張|きんちょう}, {緊急|きんきゅう} (emergency) |
| 激 | violent, intense | ゲキ | はげ(しい) | 16 | {激|はげ}しい, {感激|かんげき}, {激怒|げきど}, {刺激|しげき}, {激減|げきげん} |

- Carried words now in kanji: {頑張|がんば}る, {緊張|きんちょう}.
- 激〜 as a prefix means "sharply, violently": {激減|げきげん} (a sharp fall), {激増|げきぞう} (a sharp rise).
  In casual speech it means "super-": {激|げき}{安|やす} (rock-bottom prices).

Memory notes:

- 悩 and 憎 have the heart radical (忄) on the left, like many feeling kanji.
- 恋 has the heart (心) at the bottom: a heart that's tied up.
- 涙 is water (氵) and 戻 (return): water that keeps coming back to your eyes.
- 寂 has a roof (宀) on top: a quiet, empty house.
- 勇 is a man (男) with 力 (strength) inside: courage.
- 離 has a bird on the right: a bird flying away.
- 叫 is a mouth (口) and a twisting cry: shouting.

```trace
悩憎恋寂驚叫涙快勇頑緊激離
```

## Dialogue: after the break-up

Haruka's boyfriend has broken up with her. Her friend Natsuki calls round. (Casual: friends.)

```dialogue
# After the break-up
なつき: はるか、だいじょうぶ？ {昨日|きのう}から{連絡|れんらく}つかないから、{心配|しんぱい}したよ。
= Haruka, are you all right? I couldn't get hold of you yesterday, so I was worried.
はるか: ごめん…。{実|じつ}は、{振|ふ}られちゃった。
= Sorry… The thing is, I got dumped.
なつき: えっ、たくまくんに？ {急|きゅう}にどうして？
= What, by Takuma? Why, all of a sudden?
はるか: {仕事|しごと}が{忙|いそが}しくて、{一緒|いっしょ}にいる{時間|じかん}がないって。
= He said he's too busy with work and has no time to be with me.
なつき: {忙|いそが}しいにしても、そんな{言|い}い{方|かた}ないよね。
= Even if he's busy, that's no way to put it.
はるか: うん…。でも、{私|わたし}にも{悪|わる}いところがあったのかも。{寂|さび}しいって、{毎日|まいにち}{言|い}ってたし。
= Yeah… But maybe it was partly my fault too. I kept saying I was lonely, every day.
なつき: {寂|さび}しいと{思|おも}うのは{当然|とうぜん}でしょ。はるかのせいだとしても、{一言|ひとこと}{話|はな}し{合|あ}うべきだったよ。
= It's natural to feel lonely. Even if it was your fault, he should have talked it over with you.
はるか: {今|いま}{思|おも}えば、{最後|さいご}のころは{会|あ}ってもけんかばかりだったな。
= Thinking back, by the end all we did when we met was argue.
なつき: そっか…。{何|なに}にしても、{今|いま}はゆっくり{休|やす}みなよ。{泣|な}きたいときは{泣|な}いていいんだから。
= I see… Anyway, take it easy for now. When you want to cry, it's fine to cry.
はるか: ありがとう。なつきが{来|き}てくれて、{心強|こころづよ}いよ。
= Thanks. It's a real comfort that you came.
なつき: {週末|しゅうまつ}、{気分転換|きぶんてんかん}にどこか{行|い}こうよ。{海|うみ}にしろ{山|やま}にしろ、はるかの{好|す}きなところでいいから。
= Let's go somewhere this weekend for a change of scene. Sea or mountains, wherever you like.
はるか: うん、{行|い}きたい。{少|すこ}し{元気|げんき}{出|で}てきた。
= Yes, I'd like that. I'm feeling a bit better already.
```

{振|ふ}る is "to dump" (end a relationship), so {振|ふ}られる is "to be dumped"; {連絡|れんらく}がつく = to be
able to reach someone; 〜なよ is the casual "do…" (from 〜なさい). Count the concessions: にしても,
としても, {何|なに}にしても, and にしろ〜にしろ.

## Reading: an advice column

A reader's letter and the reply, from the advice page of a magazine (です / ます style).

> 「{三年|さんねん}{付|つ}き{合|あ}った{恋人|こいびと}と{別|わか}れました。{理由|りゆう}は{彼|かれ}の{転勤|てんきん}です。えんきょりでも{続|つづ}けられると{思|おも}っていましたが、{彼|かれ}は『{離|はな}れて{暮|く}らすのは{無理|むり}だ』と{言|い}いました。{半年|はんとし}たった{今|いま}も、{彼|かれ}のことを{思|おも}い{出|だ}すと{涙|なみだ}が{出|で}ます。{新|あたら}しい{出会|であ}いを{探|さが}す{勇気|ゆうき}もありません。」（{会社員|かいしゃいん}、{二十九歳|にじゅうきゅうさい}）
>
> お{手紙|てがみ}、ありがとうございます。{三年|さんねん}も{一緒|いっしょ}にいた{人|ひと}と{離|はな}れたのですから、{寂|さび}しいのは{当然|とうぜん}です。{半年|はんとし}で{忘|わす}れられなくても、{自分|じぶん}を{責|せ}める{必要|ひつよう}はありません。{悩|なや}みを{一人|ひとり}で{抱|かか}え{込|こ}まないことも{大切|たいせつ}です。{話|はな}しにくいにしても、{信頼|しんらい}できる{友|とも}だちや{家族|かぞく}に{気持|きも}ちを{聞|き}いてもらうだけで、{心|こころ}は{少|すこ}し{軽|かる}くなるものです。{涙|なみだ}が{出|で}るのは、{心|こころ}が{回復|かいふく}しようとしている{証|しるし}だとも{言|い}われます。
>
> {別|わか}れの{理由|りゆう}が{何|なん}であったにせよ、あなたは{三年間|さんねんかん}、{本気|ほんき}で{人|ひと}を{愛|あい}しました。それは{恥|は}ずかしいことではなく、むしろほこっていいことです。
>
> たとえ{今|いま}は{前|まえ}に{進|すす}めないとしても、{毎日|まいにち}の{生活|せいかつ}を{大切|たいせつ}にしてください。{好|す}きな{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}くにしろ、{友|とも}だちと{食事|しょくじ}をするにしろ、{小|ちい}さな{楽|たの}しみを{積|つ}み{重|かさ}ねていくうちに、{気持|きも}ちは{少|すこ}しずつ{変|か}わっていきます。
>
> {新|あたら}しい{恋|こい}は、{急|いそ}いで{探|さが}すものではありません。いずれにしても、{心|こころ}が{本当|ほんとう}に{元気|げんき}になったとき、{自然|しぜん}に{始|はじ}まるものだと{思|おも}います。

{付|つ}き{合|あ}う = to go out with; {転勤|てんきん} = a transfer (N3); えんきょり = long-distance (a
relationship); {責|せ}める = to blame; {本気|ほんき}で = seriously, with all one's heart; ほこる = to be proud of;
{積|つ}み{重|かさ}ねる = to pile up, build up; {抱|かか}え{込|こ}む = to carry (a problem) alone; {証|しるし} = a
sign (証 is lesson 7's kanji). えんきょり and ほこる are in kana: one of their kanji isn't on
the list.

1. Why did the reader and the partner split up?
2. What does the reader say there's no courage for?
3. What does the writer say about the reason for the break-up?
4. What does the writer advise the reader to do now?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. He was transferred, and he said living apart wasn't possible for him.
2. Looking for someone new.
3. Whatever the reason was (〜にせよ), the reader loved someone seriously for three years, which is
   nothing to be ashamed of and something to be proud of.
4. Even if the reader can't move on yet (〜としても), to take care of daily life and build up small
   pleasures, such as listening to music or eating with friends (〜にしろ〜にしろ); new love will
   come by itself when the reader is truly well again.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"I've split up with the partner I'd been going out with for three years. The reason was his
transfer. I thought we could keep going long-distance, but he said, 'Living apart is impossible.'
Now, six months later, I still cry when I think of him. I don't even have the courage to look
for someone new." (Office worker, 29)

Thank you for your letter. You've parted from someone you were with for three years, so of
course you're lonely. Even if you can't forget him in six months, there's no need to blame
yourself. It's also important not to carry your worries alone. Even if it's hard to talk about,
just having a friend or family member you trust listen to how you feel will make your heart a
little lighter. Tears are even said to be a sign that your heart is trying to recover.

Whatever the reason for the break-up, you loved someone seriously for three years. That's
nothing to be ashamed of; if anything, it's something to be proud of.

Even if you can't move forward just now, please take good care of your daily life. Whether it's
listening to music you love or having a meal with friends, as you build up small pleasures, your
feelings will gradually change.

A new love isn't something to go looking for in a hurry. In any case, I think it's something that
starts by itself, when your heart is truly well again.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{忙|いそが}しいにしても、{連絡|れんらく}ぐらいください。
= Even if you're busy, at least get in touch.
{行|い}くにしろ{行|い}かないにしろ、{教|おし}えてください。
= Whether you're going or not, please tell me.
たとえ{反対|はんたい}されたとしても、{気持|きも}ちは{変|か}わりません。
= Even if they're against it, my feelings won't change.
いずれにしても、{明日|あした}また{話|はな}しましょう。
= Anyway, let's talk again tomorrow.
{初|はじ}めてにしては、{上手|じょうず}ですね。
= That's good for a first try.
```

## Common mistakes

- だ before にしても with a noun. ×じょうだんだにしても → じょうだんにしても. としても is the one that
  takes だ: じょうだんだとしても.
- にしても for "for (considering)". ×{初|はじ}めてにしても{上手|じょうず}だ → {初|はじ}めてにしては{上手|じょうず}だ. にしても
  concedes; にしては compares with an expectation.
- Only one half of A にしろ B にしろ. ×{行|い}くにしろ、{連絡|れんらく}してください (for "whether or not you go").
  Say both: {行|い}くにしろ{行|い}かないにしろ.
- にせよ in chat. It's correct but stiff: friends say にしても or でも.
- {寂|さび}しい about someone else's feelings in a statement. ×{母|はは}は{寂|さび}しい → {母|はは}は{寂|さび}しがっている, or
  {寂|さび}しそうだ. Feeling adjectives state your own feelings.
- Mixing {離|はな}す and {話|はな}す. {手|て}を{離|はな}す is "to let go of someone's hand"; {話|はな}す is "to speak".

## Key points

- 〜にしても: even if, granted; question word + にしても = whatever, wherever. {何|なに}にしても /
  いずれにしても / いずれにせよ = anyway.
- 〜にしろ / 〜にせよ: the same, firmer and more formal (にせよ most). A にしろ B にしろ = whether A or B.
- 〜としても / たとえ〜としても: even supposing; nouns take だ.
- 〜にしては / 〜{割|わり}に (N3): for, considering. 〜といえども (to recognize): very written "even".
- New kanji: 悩 憎 恋 寂 驚 叫 涙 快 勇 頑 緊 激 離. Write {寂|さび}しい, {恋人|こいびと}, {涙|なみだ}, {驚|おどろ}く,
  {頑張|がんば}る, {緊張|きんちょう}, {離婚|りこん} in kanji.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Not exactly: というわけではない, ないこともない, ないとも限らない
topics: ないこともない and なくもない
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last four lessons granted a point and then went against it. This lesson is about the softer
side of the same skill: saying that something is only partly true. Japanese speakers and writers
**[[hedge]]** a great deal: "it's not exactly that…", "I wouldn't say no", "it could just happen",
"you can't really say that". Most of these patterns are built on N3's 〜わけではない and
〜ないことはない, and the lesson ends with a table of how strong each one is. The theme is the body:
body parts, organs, skin, bones and blood, posture and strength.

{運動|うんどう}がきらいというわけではないが、{時間|じかん}がない。 — It's not that I dislike exercise; I just don't have the time.
{肩|かた}こりは{治|なお}らないこともない。 — Stiff shoulders can be cured, in fact.
{若|わか}くても、{骨折|こっせつ}しないとも{限|かぎ}らない。 — Even when you're young, you could still break a bone.

きらい (dislike) is in kana here: its kanji isn't on the list.

## It's not (exactly) that: 〜というわけではない

> **Review (N3 lesson 7).** 〜わけではない denies a conclusion the listener might draw: "it's not
> that…". With {全部|ぜんぶ}, いつも, みんな it gives **[[partial negation]]**: {全部|ぜんぶ}{分|わ}かるわけではない
> (I don't understand all of it).

〜というわけではない adds という, "it's not the case that…". The meaning is the same, but という
wraps A up as a quoted idea, so it sounds a little more explicit and is very common when you
correct someone's guess. A noun or な-adjective goes straight before という, without な:

「{具合|ぐあい}が{悪|わる}いの？」「ううん、{病気|びょうき}というわけじゃないんだけど、{少|すこ}し{疲|つか}れてて。」 — "Are you unwell?" "No, it's not that I'm ill; I'm just a bit tired."
{背|せ}が{高|たか}いからバスケットボールが{得意|とくい}だというわけではない。 — Being tall doesn't automatically make you good at basketball.
{毎日|まいにち}{走|はし}っているが、{健康|けんこう}のためというわけでもない。 — I run every day, but it's not exactly for my health, either.

| Before というわけではない | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, い-adjective: plain form | {痛|いた}いというわけではない |
| な-adjective: stem (+ だ) | きらいというわけではない, {得意|とくい}だというわけではない |
| noun (+ だ) | {病気|びょうき}というわけではない |

Casual: というわけじゃない, or just ってわけじゃない. 〜というわけでもない adds "nor that".

## I could, in fact: 〜ないこともない, 〜なくもない

> **Review (N3 lesson 8).** 〜ないことはない / 〜ないこともない is a double negative: "it's not that
> I don't…", so "I do, up to a point". なっとうは{食|た}べないこともない (I do eat natto, sort of).

〜なくもない is the same idea in fewer words, a little more written: {分|わ}からなくもない (I can
sort of understand it). Both sound hesitant: the speaker admits something without enthusiasm.

{腕|うで}の{力|ちから}には{自信|じしん}がないが、{一人|ひとり}で{運|はこ}べなくもない。 — I'm not confident in my arm strength, but I could carry it on my own.
{医者|いしゃ}に{言|い}われてみれば、{最近|さいきん}{胃|い}の{調子|ちょうし}が{悪|わる}い{気|き}もしなくもない。 — Now the doctor mentions it, I do have a feeling my stomach has been off lately.
「{日曜日|にちようび}、{走|はし}りに{行|い}かない？」「{行|い}けないこともないけど…{朝|あさ}{早|はや}いのはちょっと。」 — "Want to go running on Sunday?" "I could go, I suppose… but not too early."

{自信|じしん} = confidence. Joining: the ない form + こともない, or the ない form with ない turned into
なくもない: {行|い}かないこともない, {行|い}かなくもない, {高|たか}くなくもない, {便利|べんり}でなくもない.
In practice the verb forms are by far the commonest.

The third example shows the typical use: a half-agreement that leaves room for a "but". To agree
fully, just say {行|い}けるよ.

### To recognize: 〜{気|き}がしないでもない

〜{気|き}がしないでもない (literally "it's not that I don't have the feeling") is a very soft "I
have a slight feeling that…": {言|い}われてみれば、{少|すこ}し{太|ふと}った{気|き}がしないでもない (now you
mention it, I do have a vague feeling I've put on a little weight). You'll meet it in essays and
in careful speech.

## It could just happen: 〜ないとも{限|かぎ}らない

〜ないとも{限|かぎ}らない is "it isn't certain that A won't happen", so "A could happen": a small
possibility, usually something unwelcome, given as a reason to be careful. It's mostly written or
formal; the second half is often a precaution.

{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}らないとも{限|かぎ}らないから、かさを{持|も}っていこう。 — It might rain, so let's take an umbrella.
{運動|うんどう}{中|ちゅう}に{怪我|けが}をしないとも{限|かぎ}らないので、{保険|ほけん}に{入|はい}っておいた。 — You can always get hurt while exercising, so I took out insurance.
{検査|けんさ}で{何|なに}も{見|み}つからなかったが、{病気|びょうき}が{再発|さいはつ}しないとも{限|かぎ}らない。 — Nothing was found in the tests, but the illness could still come back.

かさ (umbrella) is in kana: its kanji isn't on the list. Joining: ない form + とも{限|かぎ}らない. It
follows the same idea as N3's 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない ("not necessarily"), turned round: "it's not
certain that it won't".

> **Review (N3 lesson 8).** {必|かなら}ずしも〜とは{限|かぎ}らない: "not necessarily".
> {高|たか}い{薬|くすり}が{必|かなら}ずしもよく{効|き}くとは{限|かぎ}らない (expensive medicine doesn't necessarily work
> better).

## Can't say, could say: 〜とは{言|い}えない, 〜とも{言|い}える

〜とは{言|い}えない ("you can't say that…") denies a claim politely, and 〜とも{言|い}える ("one could
also say…") offers a second way of seeing something. Both are the stock hedges of essays and
discussions.

{体重|たいじゅう}が{軽|かる}いからといって、{健康|けんこう}だとは{言|い}えない。 — Being light doesn't mean you can say you're healthy.
{肩|かた}こりは、{体|からだ}からの{注意|ちゅうい}のサインとも{言|い}える。 — Stiff shoulders could be called a warning sign from your body.
いちがいに{悪|わる}いとは{言|い}えない。 — You can't simply say it's bad.

いちがいに (wholesale, as a blanket rule) goes with a negative: いちがいに〜とは{言|い}えない is "you
can't generalize". Plain form + とは{言|い}えない / とも{言|い}える; nouns and な-adjectives take だ.

## How strong is it?

From a full "yes" to a full "no", with the hedges in between:

| Statement | Strength | English |
|---|---|---|
| {運動|うんどう}が{好|す}きだ。 | yes | I like exercise. |
| {運動|うんどう}が{好|す}きだとも{言|い}える。 | a possible way of putting it | You could say I like exercise. |
| {運動|うんどう}がきらいではない。 | yes, without enthusiasm | I don't dislike exercise. |
| {運動|うんどう}が{好|す}きでないこともない。 | a reluctant yes | I don't not like it. |
| {運動|うんどう}が{好|す}きな{気|き}がしないでもない。 | a vague yes | I have a feeling I sort of like it. |
| {運動|うんどう}がきらいというわけではない。 | denies a guess, no claim either way | It's not that I dislike exercise. |
| {必|かなら}ずしも{好|す}きとは{限|かぎ}らない。 | not always | I don't necessarily like it. |
| {好|す}きとは{言|い}えない。 | close to no, said politely | I can't say I like it. |
| {運動|うんどう}が{好|す}きではない。 | no | I don't like exercise. |

And for possibilities: {怪我|けが}をする (it will happen) → {怪我|けが}をするかもしれない (it may) →
{怪我|けが}をしないとも{限|かぎ}らない (it can't be ruled out) → {怪我|けが}をするとは{限|かぎ}らない (it won't
necessarily) → {怪我|けが}をすることはない (there's no chance, no need to worry).

The middle of the table is where Japanese is most at home. A blunt {好|す}きではない can sound cold;
きらいというわけではない or {好|す}きとは{言|い}えない does the same job more gently.

## Words for the body

N5 to N3 gave you the outside of the body ({頭|あたま}, {顔|かお}, {首|くび}, {背中|せなか}, {指|ゆび}, ひざ,
{髪|かみ}) and several words that you can now write in kanji: {鼻|はな}, {腕|うで}, {腰|こし}, {胸|むね},
{骨|ほね}, {鼻水|はなみず}. N2 adds the inside of the body and the words of health checks and fitness.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| head and face | {脳|のう}, {頭脳|ずのう}, {脳|のう}みそ, {鼻先|はなさき}, {鼻声|はなごえ}, {鼻血|はなぢ}, {髪|かみ}の{毛|け}, まつ{毛|げ} |
| upper body | {肩|かた}, {肩|かた}こり, {肩幅|かたはば}, {胸元|むなもと}, {胸板|むないた}, {腕力|わんりょく}, {腕前|うでまえ}, {腕組|うでぐ}み, {腕時計|うでどけい}, {手首|てくび}, {手|て}のひら, {指先|ゆびさき}, {上半身|じょうはんしん} |
| lower body | {腰痛|ようつう}, {足腰|あしこし}, {太|ふと}もも, {足首|あしくび}, {下半身|かはんしん} |
| inside | {内臓|ないぞう}, {臓器|ぞうき}, {心臓|しんぞう}, {心臓病|しんぞうびょう}, {胃|い}, {胃痛|いつう}, {胃袋|いぶくろ}, {神経|しんけい}, {体内|たいない}, {消化|しょうか} |
| skin and hair | {皮膚|ひふ}, {皮|かわ}, {毛|け}, {体毛|たいもう}, {毛皮|けがわ}, {毛布|もうふ} |
| blood and bones | {血|ち}, {血液|けつえき}, {血液型|けつえきがた}, {血管|けっかん}, {血圧|けつあつ}, {高血圧|こうけつあつ}, {血行|けっこう}, {血流|けつりゅう}, {出血|しゅっけつ}, {貧血|ひんけつ}, {血|ち}の{気|け}, {骨折|こっせつ}, {骨格|こっかく}, {骨組|ほねぐ}み, {背骨|せぼね}, {骨太|ほねぶと} |
| build and posture | {体格|たいかく}, {体型|たいけい}, {体|からだ}つき, {体質|たいしつ}, {生|う}まれつき, {姿勢|しせい}, {猫背|ねこぜ}, {正座|せいざ}, しゃがむ, {寝返|ねがえ}り, {曲|ま}げる, {反|そ}らす, {弱|よわ}る |
| sayings | {骨|ほね}が{折|お}れる (to be hard work), {鼻|はな}が{高|たか}い (to be proud), {胸|むね}を{張|は}る (to hold one's head high), {肩代|かたが}わり (taking over someone's burden), {皮肉|ひにく} (irony, sarcasm) |

Notes:

- 毛 is け on its own and in {髪|かみ}の{毛|け}, but げ after another word (まつ{毛|げ}, eyelashes) and モウ in
  kanji compounds ({毛布|もうふ}, {体毛|たいもう}).
- 胸 becomes むな before some words: {胸元|むなもと}, {胸板|むないた}. 血 becomes ぢ in some compounds: {鼻血|はなぢ}.
- {血行|けっこう} (circulation) sounds like N3's {結構|けっこう} (quite): context, and in writing the kanji,
  tell them apart.
- {姿勢|しせい} is both posture and attitude: {姿勢|しせい}がいい (good posture), {前向|まえむ}きな{姿勢|しせい} (a positive
  attitude). 姿 is lesson 22's kanji.
- {皮|かわ} is skin or peel (りんごの{皮|かわ}: apple peel) and also hide; the skin of the body is
  {皮膚|ひふ}, or in everyday speech {肌|はだ} (lesson 24).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: the outside of the body, and the inside.

### The outside

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 毛 | hair, fur | モウ | け | 4 | {毛|け}, {髪|かみ}の{毛|け}, {毛布|もうふ}, {体毛|たいもう}, まつ{毛|げ} |
| 皮 | skin, peel | ヒ | かわ | 5 | {皮|かわ}, {皮膚|ひふ}, {皮肉|ひにく}, {毛皮|けがわ} |
| 膚 | skin | フ | — | 15 | {皮膚|ひふ}, {皮膚科|ひふか} (lesson 2) |
| 鼻 | nose | ビ | はな | 14 | {鼻|はな}, {鼻水|はなみず}, {鼻血|はなぢ}, {耳鼻科|じびか} |
| 胸 | chest | キョウ | むね, むな | 10 | {胸|むね}, {胸元|むなもと}, {胸板|むないた}, {胸囲|きょうい} (chest size) |
| 肩 | shoulder | — | かた | 8 | {肩|かた}, {肩|かた}こり, {肩幅|かたはば}, {肩書|かたが}き (lesson 1) |
| 腕 | arm | ワン | うで | 12 | {腕|うで}, {腕力|わんりょく}, {腕前|うでまえ}, {腕時計|うでどけい} |
| 腰 | lower back | ヨウ | こし | 13 | {腰|こし}, {腰痛|ようつう}, {足腰|あしこし}, {腰掛|こしか}ける |

- Carried words now in kanji: {鼻|はな} (N5's はな), {鼻水|はなみず}, {胸|むね}, {腕|うで}, {腰|こし}. Mind the
  homophones: {鼻|はな:0} (nose) and {花|はな:2} (flower) differ in pitch; {肩|かた:1} (shoulder) and N5's
  [かた:2] (person, polite) too.
- {腰掛|こしか}ける is "to sit down (on a chair)": 掛 is the かける of sitting (lesson 1's spelling
  table). You'll also see it written {腰|こし}かける.
- 腕 also means skill: {腕前|うでまえ}, {腕|うで}がいい (skilful).

### The inside

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 血 | blood | ケツ | ち | 6 | {血|ち}, {血液|けつえき}, {血管|けっかん}, {出血|しゅっけつ}, {鼻血|はなぢ} |
| 骨 | bone | コツ | ほね | 10 | {骨|ほね}, {骨折|こっせつ}, {骨格|こっかく}, {背骨|せぼね} |
| 脳 | brain | ノウ | — | 11 | {脳|のう}, {頭脳|ずのう}, {脳|のう}みそ, {首脳|しゅのう} (leaders, lesson 21) |
| 胃 | stomach | イ | — | 9 | {胃|い}, {胃痛|いつう}, {胃袋|いぶくろ} |
| 臓 | internal organ | ゾウ | — | 19 | {心臓|しんぞう}, {内臓|ないぞう}, {臓器|ぞうき} |

- Carried word now in kanji: {骨|ほね} (N3's ほね).
- 血 is ケツ, shortened to ケッ before k: {血管|けっかん}, {血行|けっこう}.
- 骨 is コツ, shortened to コッ before s and k: {骨折|こっせつ}, {骨格|こっかく}.

Memory notes:

- Most body kanji have the "flesh" radical (月, from 肉), usually on the left: 胸, 腕, 腰, 脳 and
  臓; at the bottom in 肩 and 胃.
- 毛 is a single hair with three short strands.
- 皮 has a hand at the bottom right, pulling the skin off.
- 鼻 has 自 (self) at the top: people point to their nose when they mean "me".
- 血 is a dish (皿) with a drop on top: the blood of an offering.
- 骨 is a joint over the flesh radical.
- 胃 is a field (田) over flesh: the stomach full of food.
- 肩 is a door (戸) over flesh: the shoulder, which opens like a door.

```trace
毛皮血骨鼻胸脳肩腕腰胃臓膚
```

## Dialogue: stiff shoulders

Two colleagues, Riku and Emi, at the office. Emi keeps rubbing her shoulders. (Casual: colleagues
of the same age.)

```dialogue
# At the office
りく: えみさん、さっきから{肩|かた}ばっかり{触|さわ}ってるけど、だいじょうぶ？
= Emi, you've been rubbing your shoulders all this time. Are you all right?
えみ: うん、ひどい{肩|かた}こりで。{痛|いた}いってわけじゃないんだけど、{重|おも}くて。
= Yeah, my shoulders are really stiff. It's not that they hurt; they just feel heavy.
りく: {一日中|いちにちじゅう}パソコンだもんね。{姿勢|しせい}が{悪|わる}いんじゃない？
= You're at the computer all day. Maybe it's your posture?
えみ: そうかも。{気|き}がつくと{猫背|ねこぜ}になってるんだよね。
= Could be. Whenever I notice, I'm hunched over.
りく: ぼく、{最近|さいきん}ジムに{通|かよ}い{始|はじ}めたんだ。{一緒|いっしょ}に{行|い}かない？
= I've just started going to the gym. Do you want to come along?
えみ: ジムか…。{行|い}かないこともないけど、{続|つづ}くかなあ。
= The gym… I wouldn't say no, but I wonder if I'd keep it up.
りく: {毎日|まいにち}{行|い}かなきゃいけないってわけじゃないよ。{週|しゅう}に{一回|いっかい}でも{違|ちが}うって。
= It's not as if you have to go every day. They say even once a week makes a difference.
えみ: でも、{急|きゅう}に{運動|うんどう}すると、{腰|こし}を{痛|いた}めないとも{限|かぎ}らないし。
= But if I suddenly start exercising, I might hurt my back.
りく: それなら{最初|さいしょ}はストレッチだけにすれば？ {無理|むり}をしなければ、{怪我|けが}をすることはないよ。
= Then why not just do stretches at first? If you don't overdo it, there's no need to worry about getting hurt.
えみ: そうだね。{実|じつ}は{健康|けんこう}{診断|しんだん}で「{運動不足|うんどうぶそく}」って{書|か}かれたし…。
= You're right. Actually, my health check said "lack of exercise"…
りく: じゃあ、{決|き}まりだね。{土曜日|どようび}の{朝|あさ}、{駅前|えきまえ}のジムで。
= Then it's settled. Saturday morning, at the gym by the station.
えみ: {朝|あさ}か…。まあ、{起|お}きられなくもないけど。
= Morning, huh… Well, I suppose I could get up.
```

{触|さわ}る = to touch (N5); {痛|いた}める = to hurt (a part of your body); {決|き}まり = settled. Count
the hedges: ってわけじゃない (twice), ないこともない, ないとも{限|かぎ}らない, ことはない and なくもない.

## Reading: why do our shoulders get stiff?

An explanatory piece from the health page of a newspaper (〜である style).

> {肩|かた}こりに{悩|なや}む{人|ひと}は{多|おお}い。{机|つくえ}に{向|む}かう{時間|じかん}が{長|なが}い{会社員|かいしゃいん}や{学生|がくせい}だけでなく、{家事|かじ}や{育児|いくじ}で{同|おな}じ{姿勢|しせい}を{続|つづ}ける{人|ひと}にもよく{見|み}られる。{最近|さいきん}は{子供|こども}にも{増|ふ}えているという。
>
> {人|ひと}の{頭|あたま}は、{体重|たいじゅう}の{一割|いちわり}ほどの{重|おも}さがあると{言|い}われる。その{重|おも}い{頭|あたま}を、{首|くび}と{肩|かた}が{一日中|いちにちじゅう}{支|ささ}えているのである。スマホを{見|み}るときのように{頭|あたま}が{前|まえ}に{出|で}た{姿勢|しせい}では、{首|くび}や{肩|かた}にかかる{負担|ふたん}はさらに{大|おお}きくなる。きんにくが{固|かた}くなると{血行|けっこう}が{悪|わる}くなり、こりや{痛|いた}みにつながる。
>
> {肩|かた}こりは{日本人|にほんじん}に{特|とく}に{多|おお}いと{言|い}われることもある。しかし、{本当|ほんとう}に{多|おお}いのかどうかは、はっきりしない。{英語|えいご}などには「{肩|かた}こり」にぴったり{合|あ}う{言葉|ことば}がなく、{同|おな}じ{症状|しょうじょう}を{首|くび}や{背中|せなか}の{痛|いた}みとして{表|あらわ}すことが{多|おお}いため、{比|くら}べにくいのだという。
>
> もっとも、{肩|かた}こりの{原因|げんいん}は{姿勢|しせい}だけというわけではない。{冷|ひ}えやストレス、{目|め}の{疲|つか}れが{関係|かんけい}していることもある。まれに、{心臓|しんぞう}や{内臓|ないぞう}の{病気|びょうき}のサインである{場合|ばあい}もないとは{言|い}えない。{痛|いた}みが{強|つよ}いときや、{長|なが}く{続|つづ}くときは、{一度|いちど}{医師|いし}に{診|み}てもらったほうがいい。
>
> {予防|よぼう}のためには、{一時間|いちじかん}に{一度|いちど}は{立|た}ち{上|あ}がって、{肩|かた}を{回|まわ}したり{背中|せなか}を{伸|の}ばしたりするといい。「{運動|うんどう}は{苦手|にがて}だ」という{人|ひと}も、これならできなくもないだろう。{体|からだ}を{動|うご}かすことは、{肩|かた}こりだけでなく、{心|こころ}の{疲|つか}れにも{効|き}くとも{言|い}える。

{机|つくえ}に{向|む}かう = to sit at a desk; {育児|いくじ} = childcare (lesson 23's word); {一割|いちわり} = ten per
cent; きんにく = muscle (N4; in kana, as its first kanji isn't on the list); こり = stiffness; {冷|ひ}え = getting chilled; まれに =
rarely; {伸|の}ばす = to stretch (lesson 30's word).

1. Who suffers from stiff shoulders, according to the writer?
2. Why does looking at a smartphone make it worse, and why is it hard to say whether Japanese
   people suffer more?
3. Is posture the only cause? What else can be involved?
4. What does the writer suggest for people who don't like exercise?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Many people: not only office workers and students who sit at desks for a long time, but also
   people who keep the same posture doing housework or looking after children.
2. The head sticks forward, which puts an even bigger load on the neck and shoulders. Other
   languages have no exact word for it and describe the same symptoms as neck or back pain, so
   comparison is hard.
3. No (〜というわけではない): getting chilled, stress and tired eyes can play a part, and rarely it
   can even be a sign of heart or other internal illness (ないとは{言|い}えない).
4. Standing up once an hour to roll the shoulders and stretch the back: something even they could
   probably manage (できなくもない).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Many people suffer from stiff shoulders. It's often seen not only in office workers and students
who spend long hours at their desks, but also in people who keep the same posture while doing
housework or looking after children. Recently, it's said to be on the rise among children too.

A person's head is said to weigh about a tenth of their body weight. The neck and shoulders
support that heavy head all day long. In a posture with the head pushed forward, as when looking
at a smartphone, the load on the neck and shoulders becomes even greater. When the muscles
stiffen, circulation gets worse, which leads to stiffness and pain.

It's sometimes said that stiff shoulders are especially common among Japanese people. But
whether they really are more common isn't clear. Languages such as English have no word that
matches {肩|かた}こり exactly, and the same symptoms are often described as neck or back pain, so
it's hard to compare, apparently.

That said, posture isn't the only cause of stiff shoulders. Getting chilled, stress and tired
eyes can also be involved. In rare cases, one can't rule out that it's a sign of a disease of the
heart or other internal organs. When the pain is strong or goes on for a long time, it's best to
see a doctor once.

To prevent it, stand up once an hour and roll your shoulders or stretch your back. Even people
who say they're "no good at exercise" could probably manage this. Moving your body works not
only on stiff shoulders but, one could say, on a tired mind too.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{痛|いた}いというわけではないんですが、{少|すこ}し{重|おも}いんです。
= It's not that it hurts exactly; it just feels a bit heavy.
{行|い}けないこともないですけど…。
= I could go, I suppose…
{怪我|けが}をしないとも{限|かぎ}らないので、{気|き}を{付|つ}けてください。
= You never know, you might get hurt, so please be careful.
いちがいに{悪|わる}いとは{言|い}えません。
= You can't simply say it's bad.
{鼻|はな}が{高|たか}いです。
= I'm proud (of it).
```

## Common mistakes

- な before というわけではない. ×きらいなというわけではない → きらいというわけではない. という follows the
  bare stem or だ.
- 〜ないとも{限|かぎ}らない for something likely. It's for a small, unwelcome chance: for "it'll probably
  rain", say {降|ふ}るだろう. And for "it won't necessarily rain", say {降|ふ}るとは{限|かぎ}らない.
- Taking ないこともない as a no. {行|い}かないこともない is a (reluctant) yes: "I could go". It's easy to
  hear the two ない and stop listening.
- Doubling the hedges. {好|す}きでないこともないというわけではない is a puzzle, not a sentence. One
  hedge is enough.
- きんにく (muscle) in kanji. Its first kanji isn't on the list, so the course writes it in kana.
- {血行|けっこう} and {結構|けっこう}: same sound, different words.

## Key points

- 〜というわけではない (casual ってわけじゃない): it's not (exactly) that; nouns and な-adjectives
  straight before という.
- 〜ないこともない / 〜ないことはない / 〜なくもない: I do, up to a point; a reluctant yes.
- 〜ないとも{限|かぎ}らない: it could just happen; usually with a precaution.
- 〜とは{言|い}えない / 〜とも{言|い}える: can't say / could also say. いちがいに〜とは{言|い}えない: you can't
  generalize. 〜{気|き}がしないでもない (to recognize): a vague feeling.
- New kanji: 毛 皮 血 骨 鼻 胸 脳 肩 腕 腰 胃 臓 膚. Write {鼻|はな}, {胸|むね}, {肩|かた}, {腕|うで}, {腰|こし},
  {骨|ほね} in kanji.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Rakugo and manzai
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan has two great traditions of spoken comedy. In {落語|らくご}, one performer sits alone on a
cushion and tells a long funny story, playing every character with nothing but a fan and a hand
towel. In まんざい, two people stand at a microphone and trade jokes at speed. This honors lesson
explains how each works, retells one classic rakugo story in modern Japanese, and gives you an
original manzai sketch to read and listen to. It uses the concessions of lessons 1 to 4 to talk
about them.

The dialogues and phrases here are read by your device's voice. Rakugo and manzai depend on timing,
voices and pauses that a computer voice can't give: once you can follow the scripts, listen to real
performers (many theatres and broadcasters put recordings online).

## {落語|らくご}: one person, every voice

| | |
|---|---|
| performer | a {落語家|らくごか}, also called a はなしか (its first kanji is outside N2) |
| stage | the {高座|こうざ}, a raised platform, with a {座布団|ざぶとん} (floor cushion) on it |
| props | a folding fan, せんす (its first kanji is outside N2), and a {手|て}ぬぐい (cotton hand towel) |
| costume | a kimono |
| where | the {寄席|よせ}, theatres that put on rakugo and other variety arts every day, and halls, TV and radio |

{寄席|よせ} is a **special reading**: the two kanji are read together as よせ. Both kanji are on
the list, but the reading isn't the sum of their readings.

The performer never stands up and never changes costume. To switch between two characters, they
turn the head slightly to one side and then the other, changing voice and manner: this is called
かみしも, and an audience quickly learns to follow it. The fan becomes chopsticks, a pipe, a brush
or an oar; the towel becomes a wallet, a book or a letter. Everything else lives in the audience's
imagination.

### How a performance runs

1. まくら: the opening chat. The performer talks about everyday things, the weather, the news,
   their own life, and warms up the audience. A good まくら also leads into the story's theme.
2. The story itself, mostly dialogue between the characters.
3. The オチ (also called サゲ): the punchline that ends the story, often a pun or a twist on
   something set up earlier. Rakugo is written with {落|らく} (fall, drop) for this reason: the story
   "drops" at the end.

### A little history

Rakugo is usually traced back to storytellers of the Edo period (1603–1868). By the late 17th
century, people in Kyoto, Osaka and Edo were telling funny stories to paying audiences, and
theatres for story-telling grew up in Edo around the turn of the 19th century. Today there are two
main styles: Edo (Tokyo) rakugo and Kamigata (Osaka and Kyoto) rakugo. Kamigata performers often
use a small desk, the {見台|けんだい}, and strike it with a wooden clapper, こびょうし, to mark scene
changes; their stories are told in Kansai dialect. Details vary from performer to performer.

Many stories are centuries old and belong to no one: these are the classic stories, performed by
generation after generation of {落語家|らくごか}. Newly written ones are called {新作|しんさく} (new works).

## A classic retold: the soba seller

Here is a classic story, "Toki soba", retold in modern Japanese in this course's own words. It
needs one fact: in the Edo period, the hours of the night were counted with numbers. Around
midnight was 「{九|ここの}つ」, and about two hours earlier was 「{四|よ}つ」.

> {冬|ふゆ}の{夜|よる}、{一人|ひとり}の{男|おとこ}がそばの{屋台|やたい}にやってきた。{男|おとこ}はそばを{食|た}べながら、「いい{店|みせ}だねえ」「おいしいねえ」と、{主人|しゅじん}をほめ{続|つづ}ける。{食|た}べ{終|お}わると、お{金|かね}を{払|はら}う{番|ばん}だ。そばは{十六文|じゅうろくもん}。
>
> 「{細|こま}かいお{金|かね}しかないから、{手|て}を{出|だ}してくれ。{一|ひと}つ、{二|ふた}つ、{三|みっ}つ……{八|やっ}つ。ところで、{今|いま}{何時|なんどき}だい？」
>
> 「へい、{九|ここの}つで。」
>
> 「{十|とお}、{十一|じゅういち}、{十二|じゅうに}……{十六|じゅうろく}。じゃあな。」
>
> {男|おとこ}は{帰|かえ}っていった。それを{見|み}ていた{別|べつ}の{男|おとこ}は、{一文|いちもん}ごまかしたことに{気|き}づいて、{感心|かんしん}する。{自分|じぶん}もまねしようと、{次|つぎ}の{夜|よる}、{早|はや}めに{家|いえ}を{出|で}た。ところが、{入|はい}った{屋台|やたい}のそばは、{伸|の}びていてまずい。それでも{男|おとこ}はがまんして{食|た}べ、{同|おな}じように{数|かぞ}え{始|はじ}める。
>
> 「{一|ひと}つ、{二|ふた}つ……{八|やっ}つ。{今|いま}{何時|なんどき}だい？」
>
> 「へい、{四|よ}つで。」
>
> 「{五|いつ}つ、{六|むっ}つ、{七|なな}つ、{八|やっ}つ……。」

(The first man asked the time after eight coins; the answer "nine" let him skip a coin. The second
man went out too early: the answer "four" makes him count five, six, seven, eight all over again,
so he pays four coins too many. The オチ is simply the counting, and the audience laughs before
he finishes.)

{屋台|やたい} = food stall (N3); {主人|しゅじん} = the owner; {十六文|じゅうろくもん} = sixteen mon ({文|もん} was a
coin of the time); へい = yes (old shopkeepers' word); ごまかす = to cheat; {感心|かんしん}する = to
admire; まねする = to copy; {伸|の}びる (of noodles) = to go soggy; がまんする = to put up with it (N4: its
second kanji isn't on the list, so the course writes it in kana).

Rakugo is cheap to stage and hard to perform: the performer is the whole show. A story like this
one is short on paper, yet a {落語家|らくごか} may take fifteen minutes over it, with the まくら, the
praise of the first stall, and the slow misery of the second.

## まんざい: two at the microphone

まんざい (its first kanji is outside N2) is comedy for two, performed standing. One plays the ボケ,
who says silly or mistaken things; the other is the ツッコミ, who points out the mistake, often
with a quick tap on the head or the shoulder and a line such as 「なんでやねん！」 ("Why, though?!",
Kansai dialect). The pair are each other's {相方|あいかた} (comedy partner). Modern manzai grew up
mainly in Osaka in the 20th century, which is one reason so many {芸人|げいにん} (comedians) speak
Kansai dialect on stage; but there are pairs from all over Japan, and many use standard Japanese.

Where rakugo is told and acted by one person, manzai lives on the speed of the exchange. The
ツッコミ's job is to say what the audience is thinking, a moment before they think it.

### An original manzai: the job interview

A pair called 「{晴|は}れと{曇|くも}り」 ("Sunny and Cloudy"). Yū is the ボケ, Kai the ツッコミ. (Casual,
with a little Kansai dialect.)

```dialogue
# Sunny and Cloudy
ゆう: どうも、{晴|は}れと{曇|くも}りです！ よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
= Hello, we're Sunny and Cloudy! Thanks for having us.
かい: {最近|さいきん}、{相方|あいかた}が{就職|しゅうしょく}{活動|かつどう}してるんですよ。
= My partner's been job-hunting lately.
ゆう: そうなんです。{芸人|げいにん}とはいえ、{生活|せいかつ}がありますから。
= That's right. I may be a comedian, but I've got a living to make.
かい: じゃあ、ぼくが{面接官|めんせつかん}をやるから、{練習|れんしゅう}しよう。…では、しぼう{動機|どうき}を{教|おし}えてください。
= Then I'll play the interviewer, and we'll practise. …Now, please tell me why you're applying.
ゆう: はい。おんしゃの{社員|しゃいん}{食堂|しょくどう}が{安|やす}いからです。
= Yes. Because your company's staff canteen is cheap.
かい: {理由|りゆう}、そこかい！ {正直|しょうじき}すぎるやろ。
= That's your reason?! That's way too honest.
ゆう: でも、{安|やす}いからといって、{毎日|まいにち}{食|た}べるわけではありません。
= But just because it's cheap doesn't mean I'll eat there every day.
かい: いや、そこは{食|た}べてええねん！ …{次|つぎ}、あなたの{長所|ちょうしょ}は？
= No, eating there's fine! …Next: your strong points?
ゆう: {頑固|がんこ}なところです。
= My stubbornness.
かい: それ、{短所|たんしょ}やないか！
= That's a weak point!
ゆう: {頑固|がんこ}な{反面|はんめん}、{一度|いちど}{決|き}めたら{最後|さいご}までやります。
= I'm stubborn, but on the other hand, once I decide something I see it through.
かい: お、ちょっとええやん。で、{最後|さいご}に{何|なに}か{質問|しつもん}は？
= Oh, that's not bad. And finally, any questions?
ゆう: {社員|しゃいん}{食堂|しょくどう}は、{何時|なんじ}まで{開|あ}いてますか。
= What time does the staff canteen stay open till?
かい: {結局|けっきょく}そこかい！ もうええわ。
= Back to that again?! I give up.
ふたり: どうも、ありがとうございました！
= Thank you very much!
```

もうええわ ("that's enough") is a classic way for the ツッコミ to end a manzai, and the pair bow out
together. Kansai forms in the script: やろ (= だろう), ええ (= いい), ねん (sentence-final, = のだ), や
(= だ), やないか (= じゃないか). おんしゃ is "your company" (polite, spoken in interviews: N4's word). しぼう{動機|どうき} = reason for applying (しぼう's first kanji isn't on the list); {長所|ちょうしょ} / {短所|たんしょ} = strong / weak
points. Spot the lesson grammar:
とはいえ, からといって〜わけではない and {反面|はんめん}.

## Say it

```speak
{寄席|よせ}で{落語|らくご}を{聞|き}きました。
= I heard rakugo at a variety theatre.
{落語家|らくごか}は{一人|ひとり}で{何人|なんにん}もの{役|やく}を{演|えん}じる。
= A rakugo performer plays many roles alone.
{面白|おもしろ}かったとはいえ、{全部|ぜんぶ}{分|わ}かったわけではない。
= It was funny, but I didn't understand all of it.
なんでやねん！
= Why, though?! (the ツッコミ's line)
```

## Key points

- {落語|らくご}: one seated performer, a fan and a towel, every role; かみしも (turning the head) switches
  speakers. Structure: まくら → story → オチ / サゲ.
- {寄席|よせ}: special reading; theatres of rakugo and variety arts. {高座|こうざ}: the raised stage.
- Edo-period origins, as usually told; Tokyo and Kamigata styles.
- まんざい: two performers, ボケ and ツッコミ, {相方|あいかた} to each other; much of it in Kansai dialect.
