workshops became factories with machines, and mass-produced plates and bowls were shipped all over
the country. But as cheap imports increased, the number of factories in the town just kept falling.

It's only in the last ten years or so that the trend has started to change. As Japanese food has
become popular abroad, dishes that craftspeople make one at a time have attracted attention. People especially
value how they feel in the hand and the beauty of their shapes, it's said. Now
nearly half of the town's products are exported.

The third-generation owner of one workshop keeps up the traditional techniques while also
bringing in new machines. "If we did everything by hand, we couldn't keep up with the orders. But
the last stage, adding the colour, can only be done by human hands." Recently, the number of
visitors from abroad who come to watch the work is growing too, apparently.

There are challenges as well. The craftspeople are getting older, and quite a few workshops can't
find anyone to pass their skills on to. So the town has set up a school where young people can
learn pottery techniques, and is recruiting students from all over the country. Some of its
graduates have stayed in the town and opened workshops of their own.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きつつ、{作業|さぎょう}を{進|すす}めた。
= I got on with the work while listening to music.
{町|まち}の{様子|ようす}は{少|すこ}しずつ{変|か}わりつつある。
= The town is gradually changing.
{人口|じんこう}の{減少|げんしょう}にともない、{学校|がっこう}の{数|かず}も{減|へ}っている。
= Along with the falling population, the number of schools is falling too.
{物価|ぶっか}は{上|あ}がるばかりだ。
= Prices just keep going up.
{伝統|でんとう}を{守|まも}りつつ、{新|あたら}しいことも{始|はじ}めたい。
= I want to keep up tradition while starting new things too.
```

{物価|ぶっか} (N3's ぶっか) can now be written with kanji: {価|か} is lesson 12's kanji.

## Common mistakes

- つつ with two subjects: ×{母|はは}が{料理|りょうり}をしつつ、{私|わたし}は{掃除|そうじ}をした. Use
  〜{間|あいだ}に: {母|はは}が{料理|りょうり}をしている{間|あいだ}に、{私|わたし}は{掃除|そうじ}をした.
- つつある with an ordinary action: ×{今|いま}、{昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べつつある. Use 〜ている.
- つつある in casual speech: it sounds like a news report. Say 〜てきている: だんだん{寒|さむ}くなってきている.
- にともなって with a person: ×{父|ちち}にともなって{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}した. Use と{一緒|いっしょ}に, or the
  event: {父|ちち}の{転勤|てんきん}にともなって{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}した.
- ばかりだ with the た form for a trend: ×{悪|わる}くなったばかりだ means "has only just got worse".
  The trend is {悪|わる}くなるばかりだ.
- Reading {貨物|かもつ} as かぶつ, or {型|かた} as がた when it stands alone.

## Key points

- ます stem + つつ: while (written); one subject; often with thought and attitude verbs.
- ます stem + つつも: although (lesson 2).
- ます stem + つつある: in the process of changing (written, news); speech uses 〜てきている.
- 〜にともなって / にともない / にともなう: B comes along with a change or event A (formal).
- 〜とともに, 〜につれて: as (review); only とともに works with people.
- dictionary form + ばかりだ: only gets worse; 〜{一方|いっぽう}だ: keeps going one way.
- New kanji: 製 造 材 械 型 築 設 技 農 輸 貿 貨 管. Write {機械|きかい}, {材料|ざいりょう}, {取材|しゅざい},
  {設定|せってい}, {競技|きょうぎ} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Triggers and occasions: をきっかけに, を機に, につけ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last lesson of module 2 is about what sets things off: the event that started a change,
the moment someone seized to make a decision, and the things that stir a feeling whenever they
happen. It also reviews N3's "every time" and "the moment".

{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}しをきっかけに、{料理|りょうり}を{始|はじ}めた。 — Moving house got me started on cooking.
{退職|たいしょく}を{機|き}に、{田舎|いなか}に{移|うつ}り{住|す}んだ。 — I took retirement as the chance to move to the countryside.
この{写真|しゃしん}を{見|み}るにつけ、{学生|がくせい}{時代|じだい}を{思|おも}い{出|だ}す。 — Whenever I see this photo, I'm reminded of my student days.

The theme is moving things and people: flights, the post and parcels, packing, parking, and
moving house or offices. {荷物|にもつ}, {袋|ふくろ}, {郵便局|ゆうびんきょく} and {駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう} (N5),
{包|つつ}む, {延期|えんき}, {両替|りょうがえ}, {片道|かたみち}, {片付|かたづ}ける and {指輪|ゆびわ} (N4), {延長|えんちょう},
{停電|ていでん}, {着替|きが}える and {駐輪場|ちゅうりんじょう} (N3) are now written with kanji.

This lesson owns the term **[[trigger]]** (〜をきっかけに).

## The trigger: 〜をきっかけに

きっかけ is "the thing that sets something off": a trigger, a chance, a start. 〜をきっかけに(して)
/ 〜をきっかけとして means "with A as the trigger, B began or changed". A is an event, often
unplanned; B is a new start or a change that followed.

{留学|りゅうがく}をきっかけに、{日本|にほん}の{歴史|れきし}が{好|す}きになった。 — Studying abroad got me into Japanese history.
{友|とも}だちに{誘|さそ}われたのをきっかけに、{山登|やまのぼ}りを{始|はじ}めた。 — A friend invited me along, and that's how I took up hiking.
{震災|しんさい}をきっかけとして、{多|おお}くの{会社|かいしゃ}が{防災|ぼうさい}を{見直|みなお}した。 — The earthquake disaster prompted many companies to review their disaster planning.

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| noun + をきっかけに(して) | {入院|にゅういん}をきっかけに |
| clause + のをきっかけに | {誘|さそ}われたのをきっかけに |
| 〜がきっかけで | {一冊|いっさつ}の{本|ほん}がきっかけで (a book was what started it) |
| 〜のきっかけ | {話|はなし}のきっかけ (something to start a conversation) |
| written: 〜を{契機|けいき}に | {事故|じこ}を{契機|けいき}に、{法律|ほうりつ}が{変|か}わった |

B is usually something that has started and continues: 〜ようになった, 〜を{始|はじ}めた, 〜が{変|か}わった.
It doesn't fit a single, finished event with no change after it.

## Taking the chance: 〜を{機|き}に

{機|き} is an occasion or an opportunity, as in {機会|きかい} (a chance). 〜を{機|き}に / 〜を{機|き}として means
"taking A as the opportunity, (I / we) did B". A is a turning point in life or business
(marriage, retirement, a move, an anniversary); B is a decision someone made on purpose. It's
formal and written.

{結婚|けっこん}を{機|き}に、{会社|かいしゃ}を{辞|や}めて{独立|どくりつ}した。 — I took my marriage as the chance to quit the company and go independent.
{開店|かいてん}{十周年|じゅっしゅうねん}を{機|き}に、{店|みせ}の{名前|なまえ}を{変|か}えることにした。 — We decided to take our tenth anniversary as the chance to rename the shop.
{事務所|じむしょ}の{移転|いてん}を{機|き}に、{書類|しょるい}をすべてデータにした。 — With the office move, we took the opportunity to put all our paperwork into digital form.

### きっかけ or {機|き}?

| | 〜をきっかけに | 〜を{機|き}に |
|---|---|---|
| A | any event, often by chance | a turning point you can see coming |
| B | a change that followed (may be unplanned) | a decision someone made deliberately |
| register | spoken and written | formal, written |
| example | {病気|びょうき}をきっかけに{健康|けんこう}に{気|き}を{付|つ}けるようになった | {定年|ていねん}を{機|き}に{田舎|いなか}に{移住|いじゅう}した |

Many sentences take both. Because を{機|き}に is about choosing, it sounds odd with a change nobody
chose: {事故|じこ}をきっかけに{車|くるま}が{怖|こわ}くなった is natural; ×{事故|じこ}を{機|き}に{車|くるま}が{怖|こわ}くなった is not.

## Whenever: 〜につけ(て)

Dictionary form + につけ(て) means "whenever (I see, hear or think of A), (a feeling comes)". It's
written, and it goes with verbs of perceiving and thinking: {見|み}るにつけ, {聞|き}くにつけ,
{思|おも}うにつけ, {考|かんが}えるにつけ. The second half is a feeling or a thought that comes by itself.
It's kana in this course.

{古|ふる}い{写真|しゃしん}を{見|み}るにつけ、{亡|な}くなった{祖母|そぼ}のことが{思|おも}い{出|だ}される。 — Whenever I look at old photos, I'm reminded of my late grandmother.
{事故|じこ}のニュースを{聞|き}くにつけ、{安全|あんぜん}の{大切|たいせつ}さを{感|かん}じる。 — Every time I hear news of an accident, I feel how important safety is.

Two set uses:

- {何|なに}かにつけ(て): "at every opportunity, for one reason or another": {母|はは}は{何|なに}かにつけて
  {電話|でんわ}をしてくる (my mother phones me at the slightest excuse).
- A につけ B につけ: "whether A or B": {雨|あめ}につけ{風|かぜ}につけ, うれしいにつけ{悲|かな}しいにつけ. The
  old form よきにつけ{悪|あ}しきにつけ ("for better or worse") turns up in writing: recognize it.

### たびに or につけ?

> **Review (N3 lesson 2).** 〜たびに: every time A, B ({会|あ}うたびに{大|おお}きくなっている).
> 〜たとたん(に): the moment A, B (unexpected): {外|そと}に{出|で}たとたん、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した.

〜たびに is neutral and goes with any repeated event and any result. 〜につけ is narrower: a
perception (seeing, hearing, thinking) that brings a feeling with it. {駅|えき}を{通|とお}るたびに{本屋|ほんや}に
{寄|よ}る (I drop into the bookshop every time I pass the station) can't take につけ: dropping into a
shop isn't a feeling.

## Half done: 〜かけ (review)

> **Review (N3 lesson 3).** ます stem + かける / かけの: started but not finished:
> {読|よ}みかけの{本|ほん} (a half-read book), {言|い}いかけてやめた (started to say something and stopped).

It's handy on moving day: {荷造|にづく}りしかけの{箱|はこ} (a half-packed box),
{食|た}べかけのお{弁当|べんとう}, {書|か}きかけの{送|おく}り{状|じょう}.

## Flights, the post and moving house

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| triggers | きっかけ, {契機|けいき}, {転機|てんき}, {好機|こうき} |
| flights | {航空|こうくう}, {航空券|こうくうけん}, {航空便|こうくうびん}, {航空会社|こうくうがいしゃ}, {航空機|こうくうき}, {航路|こうろ}, {欠航|けっこう}する, {運航|うんこう}, {航海|こうかい}, {機内|きない}, {着陸|ちゃくりく}する, {離陸|りりく}する, とうじょうする, {便|びん}, {直行便|ちょっこうびん}, キャンセル{待|ま}ち, {手荷物|てにもつ} |
| delays | {延着|えんちゃく}, {振替|ふりかえ} |
| parking and stops | {駐車|ちゅうしゃ}する, {駐車違反|ちゅうしゃいはん}, {停車|ていしゃ}する, {停止|ていし}する, {停留所|ていりゅうじょ}, バス{停|てい} |
| the post | {郵便|ゆうびん}, {郵送|ゆうそう}する, {郵便物|ゆうびんぶつ}, {郵便受|ゆうびんう}け, {郵便番号|ゆうびんばんごう}, {小包|こづつみ}, {速達|そくたつ}, {送|おく}り{状|じょう}, {受取人|うけとりにん}, {差出人|さしだしにん}, {着払|ちゃくばら}い, {配送|はいそう}する, {再配達|さいはいたつ}, {集荷|しゅうか}, {入荷|にゅうか}する |
| packing | {包装|ほうそう}する, {包装紙|ほうそうし}, {包|つつ}み, {紙袋|かみぶくろ}, {手袋|てぶくろ}, {詰|つ}める, {詰|つ}まる, {詰|つ}め{込|こ}む, {箱詰|はこづ}め, {荷造|にづく}り, {割|わ}れ{物|もの}, こんぽうする, ガムテープ, {輪|わ}ゴム |
| moving | {移動|いどう}する, {移転|いてん}する, {移|うつ}る, {移|うつ}す, {移住|いじゅう}する, {移|うつ}り{住|す}む, {移民|いみん}, {転居|てんきょ}, {新居|しんきょ}, {業者|ぎょうしゃ}, {運送|うんそう}, {積|つ}み{込|こ}む, {荷台|にだい} |
| other | {輪|わ}, {車輪|しゃりん}, {五輪|ごりん}, {片方|かたほう}, {片手|かたて}, {足袋|たび} |

Notes:

- A flight is {欠航|けっこう} when it's cancelled; a cancelled train service is {運休|うんきゅう}. {欠航|けっこう} [けっこう:0] and the adverb {結構|けっこう}
  [けっこう:1] are told apart by pitch and context.
- {移転|いてん} is for offices, shops and institutions; people {引|ひ}っ{越|こ}す, or in formal writing
  {転居|てんきょ}する.
- {便|びん} counts and names transport services and post: {午後|ごご}の{便|びん}, {航空便|こうくうびん},
  {宅配便|たくはいびん}. {便|べん} is read ベン in {便利|べんり}.
- {延|の}びる / {延|の}ばす are the same words as {伸|の}びる / {伸|の}ばす (lesson 30): {延|の}びる for time and
  distance ({出発|しゅっぱつ}が{延|の}びた: the departure was put back), {伸|の}びる for growing and
  stretching.
- {替|か}える is N3's かえる "exchange, replace", now with its kanji: お{金|かね}を{両替|りょうがえ}する,
  {電池|でんち}を{取|と}り{替|か}える, {着替|きが}える.
- {足袋|たび} is a special reading: {足|あし} + {袋|ふくろ}, the split-toe socks worn with kimono.
- {航海|こうかい} (a voyage) is [こうかい:1]; N3's {公開|こうかい} (making public) is [こうかい:0].

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: flying and stopping, the post, packing, and moving.

### Flying, stopping and the post

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 航 | sail, fly | コウ | — | 10 | {航空|こうくう}, {航空券|こうくうけん}, {航路|こうろ}, {欠航|けっこう}, {航海|こうかい} |
| 駐 | stop, stay | チュウ | — | 15 | {駐車|ちゅうしゃ}, {駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう}, {駐輪場|ちゅうりんじょう} |
| 停 | stop | テイ | — | 11 | {停車|ていしゃ}, {停止|ていし}, {停留所|ていりゅうじょ}, {停電|ていでん}, {各駅停車|かくえきていしゃ} |
| 郵 | post | ユウ | — | 11 | {郵便|ゆうびん}, {郵便局|ゆうびんきょく}, {郵送|ゆうそう}, {郵便物|ゆうびんぶつ} |
| 延 | extend, delay | エン | の(びる), の(ばす) | 8 | {延期|えんき}, {延長|えんちょう}, {延着|えんちゃく}, {遅延|ちえん}, {延|の}びる |

- {駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう} and {郵便局|ゆうびんきょく} (N5), {延期|えんき} (N4), {延長|えんちょう}, {遅延|ちえん},
  {停電|ていでん}, {各駅停車|かくえきていしゃ} and {駐輪場|ちゅうりんじょう} (N3) are now written with kanji.
- 駐 and 停 both mean "stop": 駐 is staying put (parking, being stationed), 停 is coming to a
  halt.

### Moving and packing

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 移 | move | イ | うつ(る), うつ(す) | 11 | {移動|いどう}, {移転|いてん}, {移住|いじゅう}, {移|うつ}る, {移|うつ}す |
| 荷 | load, luggage | カ | に | 10 | {荷物|にもつ}, {荷造|にづく}り, {手荷物|てにもつ}, {出荷|しゅっか}, {入荷|にゅうか} |
| 包 | wrap | ホウ | つつ(む) | 5 | {包|つつ}む, {包|つつ}み, {包装|ほうそう}, {小包|こづつみ} |
| 袋 | bag | — | ふくろ | 11 | {袋|ふくろ}, {紙袋|かみぶくろ}, {手袋|てぶくろ}, {足袋|たび} |
| 詰 | pack, cram | — | つ(める), つ(まる) | 13 | {詰|つ}める, {詰|つ}まる, {詰|つ}め{込|こ}む, {箱詰|はこづ}め |
| 替 | exchange | — | か(える), か(わる) | 12 | {両替|りょうがえ}, {着替|きが}える, {取|と}り{替|か}える, {振替|ふりかえ} |
| 輪 | ring, wheel | リン | わ | 15 | {輪|わ}, {輪|わ}ゴム, {車輪|しゃりん}, {五輪|ごりん}, {指輪|ゆびわ} |
| 片 | one side, piece | ヘン | かた | 4 | {片方|かたほう}, {片手|かたて}, {片道|かたみち}, {片付|かたづ}ける |

- {荷物|にもつ} and {袋|ふくろ} (N5), {包|つつ}む, {両替|りょうがえ}, {指輪|ゆびわ}, {片道|かたみち} and {片付|かたづ}ける
  (N4), {着替|きが}える, {取|と}り{替|か}える and {片思|かたおも}い (N3) are now written with kanji.
- 袋, 詰 and 替 have rarely used on'yomi; learn them by their kun'yomi.
- 包 becomes づつみ after こ: {小包|こづつみ} (rendaku). 袋 becomes ぶくろ: {紙袋|かみぶくろ}, {手袋|てぶくろ}.
- {足袋|たび} is a special reading: learn it as a word.

Memory notes:

- 航 is a boat shape on the left and a shape like a long neck: a boat heading far out, sailing.
- 駐 is a horse (馬) and 主 (master, N3): a horse waiting for its master, staying put.
- 停 is a person (亻) and a tall pavilion: a person stopping to rest at a roadside shelter.
- 郵 is a hanging shape and a village (阝): messages carried from village to village, the post.
- 延 is a long road stroke with a foot on it: a road that stretches on, extending.
- 移 is grain (禾) and 多 (many, N5): moving lots of seedlings to a new field.
- 荷 is grass (艹) over 何 (what, N5): what's that bundle of straw on your back? A load.
- 包 is a wrapping shape round a curled-up baby: wrapped up.
- 袋 is 代 (replace, N4) over clothes (衣): cloth that holds things in place of your hands, a bag.
- 詰 is words (言) and a lucky sign (士 over 口): packing a container full, like good words crammed
  into a fortune.
- 替 is two husbands (夫夫) over the sun (日): one man takes over from the other, exchange.
- 輪 is a cart (車) and a shape like spokes in order: a wheel.
- 片 is half a tree, split down the middle: one side, a piece.

```trace
航駐停郵延移荷包袋詰替輪片
```

## Dialogue: moving day for the office

The design office where まな and こうき work is moving next week. (Casual speech between
colleagues.)

```dialogue
# Packing up the office
まな: こうきさん、その{箱|はこ}、{割|わ}れ{物|もの}{入|はい}ってる？
= Kōki, has that box got breakables in it?
こうき: うん、コーヒーカップ。{新聞紙|しんぶんし}で{包|つつ}んでから{詰|つ}めたからだいじょうぶ…だと{思|おも}う。
= Yeah, coffee cups. I wrapped them in newspaper before I packed them, so they should be fine… I think.
まな: {一応|いちおう}「{割|わ}れ{物|もの}{注意|ちゅうい}」って{書|か}いておいて。{業者|ぎょうしゃ}さん、{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}{来|く}るから。
= Write "fragile" on it, just in case. The removal people are coming tomorrow morning.
こうき: {了解|りょうかい}。それにしても、{移転|いてん}をきっかけに{物|もの}をずいぶん{捨|す}てたね。
= Got it. Still, the move has made us throw out a lot of stuff.
まな: {社長|しゃちょう}が「{移転|いてん}を{機|き}に{全部|ぜんぶ}データにする」って{決|き}めたからね。{書類|しょるい}の{山|やま}がなくなってすっきりした。
= That's because the boss decided "we'll take the move as the chance to go fully digital". It's nice not having piles of paper.
こうき: {古|ふる}いファイルを{見|み}るにつけ、{入社|にゅうしゃ}したころを{思|おも}い{出|だ}すよ。
= Whenever I look at the old files, it takes me back to when I joined the company.
まな: なに、{急|きゅう}に。……あ、{新|あたら}しい{事務所|じむしょ}って{駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう}あったっけ？
= What's got into you? …Oh, does the new office have a car park?
こうき: ないんだって。{近|ちか}くのコインパーキングを{使|つか}うしかないみたい。{路上|ろじょう}に{止|と}めると{駐車違反|ちゅうしゃいはん}になるし。
= No, apparently. We'll have to use a pay car park nearby. If you park on the street you get a ticket.
まな: そっか。じゃあ{電車|でんしゃ}で{移動|いどう}したほうがいいね。あと、{郵便物|ゆうびんぶつ}の{転送|てんそう}、{手続|てつづ}きした？
= I see. Then we'd better travel by train. Oh, and did you do the paperwork to forward the mail?
こうき: あ、まだだ。{危|あぶ}なかった。{今日|きょう}{郵便局|ゆうびんきょく}に{行|い}ってくる。
= Oh, not yet. That was close. I'll go to the post office today.
まな: お{願|ねが}い。それと、そこの{書|か}きかけの{送|おく}り{状|じょう}、{住所|じゅうしょ}が{途中|とちゅう}までしか{書|か}いてないよ。
= Thanks. And that half-written shipping label there only has half the address on it.
こうき: ごめん、{電話|でんわ}が{鳴|な}ったとたん、{忘|わす}れちゃった。
= Sorry, the moment the phone rang, I forgot all about it.
```

{一応|いちおう} = just in case; {了解|りょうかい} = got it; コインパーキング = a coin-operated car
park; {路上|ろじょう} = on the street; {転送|てんそう} = forwarding (mail). Count the patterns:
きっかけに (what the move led to), を{機|き}に (the boss's decision), {見|み}るにつけ (a feeling that
comes back), {書|か}きかけ (half done), {鳴|な}ったとたん (the moment).

## Reading: a reader's essay

From the readers' page of a magazine on living in the countryside (だ/である style).

> {私|わたし}が{今|いま}の{島|しま}に{移|うつ}り{住|す}んで、{五年|ごねん}になる。きっかけは、{東京|とうきょう}の{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}いていたころに{出|で}かけた{一人旅|ひとりたび}だった。{飛行機|ひこうき}が{着陸|ちゃくりく}する{直前|ちょくぜん}、{窓|まど}から{見|み}えた{青|あお}い{海|うみ}を、{今|いま}もはっきり{覚|おぼ}えている。
>
> {移住|いじゅう}を{決|き}めたのは、その{三年後|さんねんご}、{会社|かいしゃ}の{事務所|じむしょ}が{移転|いてん}したときだ。{通勤|つうきん}に{片道|かたみち}{二時間|にじかん}かかることになり、{会社|かいしゃ}を{辞|や}めるかどうか{迷|まよ}った{末|すえ}、それを{機|き}に{島|しま}で{暮|く}らそうと{決|き}めた。{荷造|にづく}りをしながらも、{本当|ほんとう}にこれでいいのかと{何度|なんど}も{考|かんが}えた。{家族|かぞく}には{反対|はんたい}されたが、{今|いま}では{両親|りょうしん}も{年|ねん}に{一度|いちど}{遊|あそ}びに{来|く}る。
>
> {島|しま}の{生活|せいかつ}は{便利|べんり}とは{言|い}えない。{本土|ほんど}との{間|あいだ}は{船|ふね}と{小|ちい}さな{飛行機|ひこうき}だけで、{台風|たいふう}が{来|く}れば{何日|なんにち}も{欠航|けっこう}する。ネットで{注文|ちゅうもん}した{荷物|にもつ}も、{本土|ほんど}より{二日|ふつか}は{遅|おそ}れて{届|とど}く。{最初|さいしょ}の{冬|ふゆ}は、{船|ふね}が{止|と}まって{店|みせ}から{牛乳|ぎゅうにゅう}が{消|き}えたこともあった。{去年|きょねん}の{台風|たいふう}のときは{停電|ていでん}が{三日間|みっかかん}にわたって{続|つづ}いたが、{島|しま}の{人|ひと}たちは{慣|な}れた{様子|ようす}で{助|たす}け{合|あ}っていた。
>
> それでも、{不便|ふべん}さを{感|かん}じるにつけ、{人|ひと}とのつながりのありがたさも{感|かん}じる。{船|ふね}が{止|と}まると、{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}が{野菜|やさい}や{魚|さかな}を{分|わ}けてくれる。{私|わたし}も{何|なに}かにつけて{島|しま}の{人|ひと}に{助|たす}けてもらっている。
>
> {今|いま}は{島|しま}の{特産品|とくさんひん}を{包装|ほうそう}して{全国|ぜんこく}に{郵送|ゆうそう}する{仕事|しごと}をしている。{始|はじ}めたころに{比|くら}べると、{注文|ちゅうもん}は{少|すこ}しずつ{増|ふ}えつつある。{小包|こづつみ}を{一|ひと}つ{送|おく}り{出|だ}すたびに、{島|しま}と{外|そと}の{世界|せかい}が{少|すこ}しだけつながる{気|き}がする。

{本土|ほんど} = the mainland; {特産品|とくさんひん} = local speciality products; {直前|ちょくぜん} = just
before (N3). Note how the writer separates the trigger (きっかけは、…{一人旅|ひとりたび}だった) from the
decision (それを{機|き}に…{決|き}めた).

1. What first drew the writer to the island?
2. When and why did the writer decide to move?
3. What are the inconveniences of island life mentioned, and what does the writer feel because of
   them?
4. What work does the writer do now, and how do they feel about it?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A trip they took alone while working in Tokyo: they still remember the blue sea seen from the
   plane window just before it landed (きっかけは…{一人旅|ひとりたび}だった).
2. Three years later, when the office moved and the commute became two hours each way. After
   agonizing over whether to quit, they took that as the chance to live on the island
   (それを{機|き}に…{決|き}めた).
3. Only boats and small planes link it to the mainland, and they're cancelled for days in a
   typhoon; parcels arrive at least two days later than on the mainland; once milk vanished from
   the shops. But whenever they feel the inconvenience, they also feel how precious the ties with
   people are ({不便|ふべん}さを{感|かん}じるにつけ).
4. They wrap the island's local products and post them all over Japan. Each time they send a
   parcel, they feel the island and the outside world are connected a little.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

It's five years since I moved to this island. What set it off was a trip I took on my own when I
was working for a company in Tokyo. I still clearly remember the blue sea I saw from the window
just before the plane landed.

I decided to move three years after that, when my company's office relocated. The commute was
going to take two hours each way, and after agonizing over whether to quit, I took it as the
chance to decide to live on the island. Even while I was packing, I kept asking myself whether
this was really the right thing. My family were against it, but now even my parents come to
visit once a year.

Island life can't be called convenient. The only links with the mainland are boats and small
planes, and when a typhoon comes, they're cancelled for days. Even parcels I order online arrive
at least two days later than on the mainland. In my first winter, the boats stopped and milk
disappeared from the shops. In last year's typhoon the power was out for three days, but the
islanders helped each other as if they were used to it.

Even so, whenever I feel the inconvenience, I also feel how precious the ties with people are.
When the boats stop, the neighbours share their vegetables and fish with me. And I'm helped by
the islanders at every turn.

Now I work wrapping the island's local products and posting them all over Japan. Compared with when I
started, the orders are slowly growing. Every time I
send off a parcel, I feel that the island and the outside world are linked just a little.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{留学|りゅうがく}をきっかけに、{考|かんが}え{方|かた}が{変|か}わりました。
= Studying abroad changed the way I think.
{結婚|けっこん}を{機|き}に、{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}すことにしました。
= We decided to take our marriage as the chance to move.
この{歌|うた}を{聞|き}くにつけ、ふるさとを{思|おも}い{出|だ}します。
= Whenever I hear this song, I think of home.
{台風|たいふう}のため、{午後|ごご}の{便|びん}は{欠航|けっこう}となりました。
= Owing to the typhoon, the afternoon flights have been cancelled.
{荷物|にもつ}が{届|とど}き{次第|しだい}、{開|あ}けて{確認|かくにん}してください。
= Please open and check the parcel as soon as it arrives.
```


## Common mistakes

- を{機|き}に with a change nobody chose: ×{病気|びょうき}を{機|き}に{体|からだ}が{弱|よわ}くなった. Use
  をきっかけに, or make B a decision: {病気|びょうき}を{機|き}に{禁煙|きんえん}した.
- 〜につけ with an ordinary repeated action: ×{駅|えき}に{行|い}くにつけ、{本屋|ほんや}に{寄|よ}る. That's
  たびに. につけ needs a perception and a feeling.
- Forgetting の after a clause: ×{誘|さそ}われたをきっかけに → {誘|さそ}われたのをきっかけに.
- {移転|いてん} for a person moving house: say {引|ひ}っ{越|こ}す (or {転居|てんきょ}する in writing).
- Reading {小包|こづつみ} as こつつみ, or {紙袋|かみぶくろ} as かみふくろ.
- {延|の}びる vs {伸|の}びる: a schedule {延|の}びる; a child's height {伸|の}びる.

## Key points

- 〜をきっかけに / をきっかけとして / がきっかけで: the trigger that started a change.
- 〜を{機|き}に / を{契機|けいき}に: taking a turning point as the chance to decide something (formal).
- 〜につけ(て): whenever (seeing, hearing, thinking), a feeling comes; {何|なに}かにつけて; A につけ B につけ.
- たびに (every time, neutral), たとたん (the moment), かけ (half done): review.
- New kanji: 航 駐 停 郵 延 移 荷 包 袋 詰 替 輪 片. Write {荷物|にもつ}, {袋|ふくろ}, {郵便局|ゆうびんきょく},
  {駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう}, {包|つつ}む, {延期|えんき}, {両替|りょうがえ}, {片道|かたみち}, {片付|かたづ}ける,
  {着替|きが}える with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The tea ceremony and wagashi
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 6 gave you the language of formal occasions: に{先立|さきだ}って, にあたって, に{際|さい}して. Few
occasions in Japan are as formal, or as carefully planned, as a tea gathering. This honors lesson
introduces the tea ceremony, its rooms and manners, the sweets that go with it, and the idea
behind it, and then has you read an invitation to a tea gathering, written in exactly the style
of lesson 6.

Tea schools differ in their details, and so do teachers within a school. What follows is a
common pattern, not the one correct way. If you ever go to a gathering, the host or the person
next to you will show you what to do, and nobody expects a guest from abroad to know it all.

## {茶道|さどう} and its words

The tea ceremony is {茶道|さどう}, N4's word. Most people today read it さどう; ちゃどう is also
used, and some tea schools prefer it. The older name is {茶|ちゃ}の{湯|ゆ} ("hot water for tea").

At its simplest, a host makes powdered green tea, まっちゃ (its first kanji is outside N2), for one
or more guests, in a set order of movements, in a room prepared for the occasion. A formal
gathering ({茶会|ちゃかい}) can last several hours and include a meal; a short one is a bowl of tea
and a sweet.

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {茶室|ちゃしつ} | the tea room, usually a small Japanese-style room with tatami |
| {床|とこ}の{間|ま} | the alcove, with a hanging scroll (かけじく) and seasonal flowers |
| {茶道具|ちゃどうぐ} | tea utensils: the bowl, the whisk, the tea scoop, the kettle |
| {茶|ちゃ}わん | the tea bowl (its second kanji is outside N2) |
| {薄茶|うすちゃ} / {濃茶|こいちゃ} | thin tea (frothy, the usual kind) / thick tea (much stronger, in formal gatherings) |
| {正座|せいざ} | sitting formally on your heels |
| {作法|さほう} | the etiquette, the right way of doing things (N3) |
| もてなし | hospitality: the host's care for the guest |

Many tea rooms have a very low entrance that guests crawl through. It's often explained as a way of
making everyone equal: whoever you are, you bow your head to enter. Treat that as the common
explanation rather than settled history.

## {千利休|せんのりきゅう}

The person most associated with the tea ceremony is {千利休|せんのりきゅう}, a tea master of the 16th
century. He is credited with bringing to completion the simple, quiet style of tea called わびちゃ
(わび: its kanji is outside N2), which values plain, rough, old things over showy ones. He served
the most powerful warlords of his age, and in 1591 he died by his own hand on the order of the
ruler とよとみひでよし (two of the name's kanji are outside N2). Why he was ordered to die is still
debated.

After him, his descendants founded three schools that are still the best known today: the
{表千家|おもてせんけ}, the {裏千家|うらせんけ} and the {武者小路千家|むしゃのこうじせんけ}. There are many other
schools too, and they differ in small things, such as how far you turn the bowl.

## A guest's part

Here, in outline, is what a guest does with a bowl of thin tea. Details vary from school to school.

1. Bow to the host when the sweet is brought, and eat it first: the sweetness prepares the mouth
   for the bitter tea. You usually eat it from a sheet of paper you've brought.
2. When the bowl is placed in front of you, bow to the guest next to you ("excuse me for going
   before you"), then to the host ("thank you for the tea").
3. Pick up the bowl, hold it in the palm of your left hand, and turn it a little clockwise, so that
   you don't drink from its front (the side with the best pattern faces you when it's served).
4. Drink it in a few sips. Many people finish with a small slurp, to show the bowl is empty.
5. Wipe the place where your lips touched with your fingers, turn the bowl back, and put it down.
6. Look at the bowl and admire it: its shape, colour and weight.

Questions such as {何回|なんかい}{回|まわ}しますか (how many times do I turn it?) are perfectly polite to
ask. In many schools it's turned twice, but not in all.

## {和菓子|わがし} and the seasons

The sweets of the tea ceremony are {和菓子|わがし}, Japanese-style sweets ({菓|か} is lesson 19's kanji).
Two broad kinds are served:

- {主菓子|おもがし}: moist sweets, often made from bean paste, served before thick tea or at the
  start of a gathering.
- {干菓子|ひがし}: small dry sweets, made from sugar or rice flour, served with thin tea.

What makes them special is the season. A tea sweet is often shaped and named after the time of year:
a cherry blossom or a young leaf in spring, cool, clear shapes that look like water in summer, a red
maple leaf in autumn, snow or a camellia in winter. The scroll in the alcove, the flowers and the
bowl are chosen the same way, so that the guest feels the season in every part of the room. This
seasonal sense runs through Japanese letters too (lesson 6's {時候|じこう}のあいさつ).

## {一期一会|いちごいちえ}

{一期一会|いちごいちえ} means "one time, one meeting": this gathering, with these people, in this
season, will never happen again in exactly the same way, so host and guest should treat it with
their whole heart. The phrase is closely tied to the tea ceremony, and today it's used far beyond
it: shops, hotels and wedding speeches use it for "we treasure every encounter".

{期|ご} is read ゴ here, not キ: a rarer on'yomi of 期, also heard in {最期|さいご} (one's last moments).

## Dialogue: a first tea gathering

A student, ルーカス, has been invited by his Japanese teacher, よしこ, to a small tea gathering at
a community centre. (Polite speech.)

```dialogue
# Before the gathering
ルーカス: {先生|せんせい}、{茶会|ちゃかい}に{参加|さんか}するにあたって、{何|なに}か{準備|じゅんび}しておくことはありますか。
= Is there anything I should prepare before taking part in the tea gathering?
よしこ: そうですね。{白|しろ}い{靴下|くつした}を{持|も}ってきてください。{茶室|ちゃしつ}に{入|はい}る{際|さい}に、はき{替|か}えるといいですよ。
= Let me see. Please bring white socks. It's good to change into them when you go into the tea room.
ルーカス: {分|わ}かりました。{正座|せいざ}はどのくらいしますか。{慣|な}れていないので、ちょっと{心配|しんぱい}で…。
= I see. How long will we sit formally? I'm not used to it, so I'm a little worried…
よしこ: {今日|きょう}は{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}ぐらいです。{足|あし}が{痛|いた}くなったら、{無理|むり}をしないで{楽|らく}に{座|すわ}ってもかまいません。
= About thirty minutes today. If your legs start to hurt, don't force it: you can sit more comfortably.
ルーカス: ありがとうございます。お{菓子|かし}は、お{茶|ちゃ}の{前|まえ}に{食|た}べるんですよね。
= Thank you. The sweet comes before the tea, doesn't it?
よしこ: ええ。{甘|あま}いものを{先|さき}に{食|た}べると、まっちゃの{味|あじ}がよく{分|わ}かるんです。{今日|きょう}のお{菓子|かし}は{秋|あき}らしく、{紅葉|もみじ}の{形|かたち}だそうですよ。
= Yes. Eating something sweet first lets you taste the matcha properly. I hear today's sweets are autumnal, in the shape of maple leaves.
ルーカス: きれいでしょうね。{茶|ちゃ}わんは{回|まわ}してから{飲|の}むんですか。
= They must be beautiful. Do I turn the bowl before drinking?
よしこ: はい、{正面|しょうめん}を{避|さ}けるためです。{何回|なんかい}{回|まわ}すかは{流派|りゅうは}によって{違|ちが}うので、となりの{人|ひと}を{見|み}てまねすればだいじょうぶです。
= Yes, to avoid the front. How many times you turn it depends on the school, so just watch the person next to you and copy them.
ルーカス: {作法|さほう}を{間違|まちが}えたら、{失礼|しつれい}になりませんか。
= Won't it be rude if I get the etiquette wrong?
よしこ: {大切|たいせつ}なのは{形|かたち}より{心|こころ}です。{一期一会|いちごいちえ}と{言|い}って、この{時間|じかん}を{一緒|いっしょ}に{楽|たの}しむことが{一番|いちばん}のもてなしになるんですよ。
= What matters is the spirit more than the form. There's the phrase {一期一会|いちごいちえ}: enjoying this time together is the best hospitality there is.
ルーカス: なるほど。{楽|たの}しみにしています。
= I see. I'm looking forward to it.
```

{楽|らく}に{座|すわ}る = to sit comfortably; {正面|しょうめん} = the front; {流派|りゅうは} = a school (of an
art).
Note the lesson 6 patterns: {参加|さんか}するにあたって, {入|はい}る{際|さい}に.

## Reading: an invitation to a tea gathering

A notice from a community centre's tea club (です/ます, formal).

> {秋|あき}の{茶会|ちゃかい}のご{案内|あんない}
>
> {秋|あき}も{深|ふか}まってまいりました。{皆様|みなさま}にはお{元気|げんき}でお{過|す}ごしのことと{存|ぞん}じます。
>
> さて、{当|とう}{茶道|さどう}クラブでは、{例年|れいねん}どおり{秋|あき}の{茶会|ちゃかい}を{催|もよお}すことになりました。{初|はじ}めての{方|かた}も{気軽|きがる}にご{参加|さんか}いただけるよう、{開会|かいかい}に{先立|さきだ}って{十五分|じゅうごふん}ほど、{作法|さほう}の{簡単|かんたん}な{説明|せつめい}を{行|おこな}います。
>
> {日時|にちじ}：{十一月|じゅういちがつ}{十五日|じゅうごにち}（{土|ど}）{午後|ごご}{一時|いちじ}〜{三時|さんじ}
>
> {場所|ばしょ}：{市民|しみん}センター{二階|にかい}　{和室|わしつ}
>
> {会費|かいひ}：{五百円|ごひゃくえん}（{薄茶|うすちゃ}と{和菓子|わがし}{付|つ}き）
>
> ご{参加|さんか}に{際|さい}しては、{白|しろ}い{靴下|くつした}をご{用意|ようい}ください。{正座|せいざ}が{難|むずか}しい{方|かた}のために、いすの{席|せき}も{設|もう}けております。お{申|もう}し{込|こ}みは{十一月|じゅういちがつ}{八日|ようか}までに、{受付|うけつけ}またはお{電話|でんわ}でお{願|ねが}いいたします。{定員|ていいん}になり{次第|しだい}、{受付|うけつけ}を{終了|しゅうりょう}いたします。
>
> {皆様|みなさま}のお{越|こ}しを{心|こころ}よりお{待|ま}ちしております。

{当|とう}〜 = this (our) …; {定員|ていいん} = the number of places; {終了|しゅうりょう} = ending (its second kanji, {了|りょう},
is lesson 27's).

1. Is this the first time the club has held the gathering?
2. What is done for newcomers, and when?
3. What should participants bring, and what has been arranged for people who find formal sitting hard?
4. When do applications close?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. No: it's held as usual, every year ({例年|れいねん}どおり).
2. A short explanation of the etiquette, for about fifteen minutes before the gathering begins
   ({開会|かいかい}に{先立|さきだ}って).
3. White socks ({参加|さんか}に{際|さい}しては…); seats on chairs have been set up ({設|もう}けております).
4. On 8 November, or earlier if all the places are taken ({定員|ていいん}になり{次第|しだい}).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Invitation to the autumn tea gathering

Autumn is deepening. We trust you are all well.

Our tea club will hold its autumn tea gathering as usual this year. So that newcomers too can join
in easily, we will give a short explanation of the etiquette for about fifteen minutes before the
gathering begins.

Date and time: Saturday 15 November, 1–3 p.m.

Place: the Japanese-style room, second floor, Civic Centre

Fee: 500 yen (thin tea and a Japanese sweet included)

When you come, please bring white socks. For those who find formal sitting difficult, we have
also arranged seats on chairs. Please apply at reception or by phone by 8 November. Applications
will close as soon as all places are taken.

We sincerely look forward to welcoming you.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
お{先|さき}に{失礼|しつれい}します。
= Excuse me for going before you. (to the next guest)
お{点前|てまえ}ちょうだいいたします。
= Thank you for the tea (I humbly receive it). (to the host)
{結構|けっこう}なお{茶|ちゃ}わんですね。
= What a fine bowl.
{一期一会|いちごいちえ}を{大切|たいせつ}にしたいと{思|おも}います。
= I want to treasure each encounter.
```

お{点前|てまえ} is the host's making of the tea; ちょうだいいたします is a humble "I receive it" (its
kanji are outside N2).
Schools differ in the exact phrases: follow your host.

## Key points

- {茶道|さどう} (also ちゃどう), {茶|ちゃ}の{湯|ゆ}: the tea ceremony; まっちゃ, {薄茶|うすちゃ}, {濃茶|こいちゃ}.
- {茶室|ちゃしつ}, {床|とこ}の{間|ま}, {茶道具|ちゃどうぐ}, {茶|ちゃ}わん; {正座|せいざ}, {作法|さほう}, もてなし.
- {千利休|せんのりきゅう} (16th century) and わびちゃ; the three {千家|せんけ}; schools differ in details.
- The guest eats the sweet first, bows, turns the bowl away from its front, drinks and admires it.
- {和菓子|わがし}: {主菓子|おもがし} and {干菓子|ひがし}, shaped by the season.
- {一期一会|いちごいちえ}: treasure each meeting; {期|ご} is read ゴ.

lessons.title: Akutagawa and "The Spider's Thread"
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1's honors lesson met {夏目|なつめ}{漱石|そうせき}. This one meets a writer Sōseki encouraged,
{芥川|あくたがわ}{龍之介|りゅうのすけ}, and one of the best-known short stories in Japanese, 『くもの{糸|いと}』
("The Spider's Thread"). You'll read the story retold in modern Japanese, think about what it
means, and learn about the literary prize that carries the writer's name.

The writer's name has three kanji outside N2 ({芥|あくた}, {龍|りゅう} and {之|の}), and the story's real title has two more
({蜘蛛|くも}, the spider): they're shown with furigana here, as names and titles, and you aren't expected
to learn them. The story was published in 1918 and is in the public domain; what follows is this
course's own retelling, not the original text.

## The writer

{芥川|あくたがわ}{龍之介|りゅうのすけ} (1892–1927) was born in Tokyo and studied English literature at
university. He wrote short stories ({短編|たんぺん}) rather than novels, and many of them take an old
tale, from a collection of medieval stories or from Buddhist legend, and retell it with a modern,
often dark, view of human nature. One early story, 『{鼻|はな}』 ("The Nose", 1916), was praised by
Sōseki, and that praise is often said to have launched his career. He died in 1927, at the age of
35.

His style is clear and carefully built, and his stories are short: that's why they're read at
school, and why they're a good first step into real Japanese literature after N2.

## 『くもの{糸|いと}』

『くもの{糸|いと}』 was published in 1918 in 『{赤|あか}い{鳥|とり}』, a magazine of stories and songs for
children that began that year. It's one of the stories he wrote for children ({童話|どうわ}), and it's
built on a Buddhist idea of paradise and hell. Words you'll need:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {極楽|ごくらく} | paradise (the Buddhist Pure Land) |
| じごく | hell (its second kanji is outside N2) |
| おしゃかさま | the Buddha (two of its kanji are outside N2) |
| {罪人|ざいにん} | a sinner |
| {悪人|あくにん} | a wicked person, a villain |
| じひ | mercy, compassion (its first kanji is outside N2) |
| くも | a spider; written in kana here, like くも (cloud), which is lesson 16's {雲|くも} |
| {糸|いと} | thread (lesson 24's kanji) |
| {身勝手|みがって} | selfish |
| {教訓|きょうくん} | the lesson, the moral of a story |

くも (spider) and {雲|くも} (cloud) have the same sound and the same pitch, [くも:1]: in speech, only
context tells them apart.

## The story, retold

> ある{朝|あさ}、おしゃかさまは{極楽|ごくらく}の{池|いけ}のほとりを{一人|ひとり}で{歩|ある}いていた。{池|いけ}には{白|しろ}い{花|はな}が{咲|さ}き、あたりにはいい{香|かお}りが{広|ひろ}がっていた。
>
> おしゃかさまがふと{池|いけ}をのぞくと、{水|みず}の{下|した}のずっと{深|ふか}いところに、じごくの{様子|ようす}が{見|み}えた。{大勢|おおぜい}の{罪人|ざいにん}が{苦|くる}しんでいる。その{中|なか}に、カンダタという{男|おとこ}がいた。カンダタは{人|ひと}を{殺|ころ}したり、{家|いえ}に{火|ひ}をつけたりした{大|だい}{悪人|あくにん}だった。
>
> しかし、そんなカンダタにも、たった{一|ひと}つだけいいことをした{思|おも}い{出|で}があった。{森|もり}の{中|なか}で{小|ちい}さなくもをふみそうになったとき、「この{小|ちい}さな{命|いのち}も{大切|たいせつ}だ」と{思|おも}い{直|なお}して、くもを{助|たす}けてやったのだ。
>
> おしゃかさまはそれを{思|おも}い{出|だ}し、じひの{心|こころ}から、{極楽|ごくらく}のくもの{糸|いと}を{一本|いっぽん}、じごくへまっすぐ{下|お}ろした。
>
> {暗|くら}いじごくで、カンダタは{上|うえ}から{光|ひか}る{糸|いと}が{下|お}りてくるのに{気|き}づいた。これを{登|のぼ}っていけば、じごくから{出|で}られるにちがいない。カンダタは{糸|いと}をつかみ、いっしょうけんめい{登|のぼ}り{始|はじ}めた。
>
> ところが、{途中|とちゅう}で{一休|ひとやす}みして{下|した}を{見|み}ると、{数|かず}え{切|き}れないほどの{罪人|ざいにん}が、{同|おな}じ{糸|いと}を{登|のぼ}ってくるではないか。こんなに{大勢|おおぜい}がつかまったら、{細|ほそ}い{糸|いと}は{切|き}れてしまう。カンダタは{大声|おおごえ}で{叫|さけ}んだ。「この{糸|いと}はおれのものだ。おまえたちは{下|お}りろ！」
>
> その{時|とき}、{糸|いと}はカンダタのすぐ{上|うえ}で、ぷつりと{切|き}れた。カンダタは{罪人|ざいにん}たちと{一緒|いっしょ}に、また{暗|くら}いじごくの{底|そこ}へ{落|お}ちていった。
>
> {極楽|ごくらく}の{池|いけ}のほとりで、おしゃかさまはそれを{最後|さいご}まで{見|み}ていたが、やがて{悲|かな}しそうな{顔|かお}をして、また{歩|ある}き{出|だ}した。{池|いけ}の{花|はな}は{何|なに}も{知|し}らないように、{静|しず}かにゆれていた。{極楽|ごくらく}は、もうすぐお{昼|ひる}になるところだった。

ほとり = the edge (of a pond); ふむ = to step on (N4; its kanji is outside N2); いっしょうけんめい = with all one's might
(one of its kanji is outside N2); {数|かず}え{切|き}れない
= countless; 〜ではないか = isn't it! (written surprise); ぷつりと = with a snap; ゆれる = to sway
(N4; its kanji is outside N2). The original has more detail and a famously calm, almost uncaring last paragraph: this
retelling only keeps the outline.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

One morning, the Buddha was walking alone at the edge of the pond in paradise. White flowers were
blooming in the pond, and a lovely scent filled the air.

When the Buddha happened to look into the pond, far, far below the water he could see hell. Crowds
of sinners were suffering there. Among them was a man called Kandata. Kandata was a great villain
who had killed people and set fire to houses.

But even Kandata had the memory of one single good deed. Once, in a forest, when he was about to
step on a little spider, he changed his mind, thinking "this little life matters too", and let
the spider live.

The Buddha remembered this, and out of compassion he let down a single spider's thread from
paradise, straight down into hell.

In the darkness of hell, Kandata noticed a shining thread coming down from above. If he climbed
it, he would surely get out of hell. He grabbed the thread and began climbing with all his might.

But when he stopped for a rest halfway and looked down, what should he see but countless sinners
climbing up the same thread! If so many held on, the thin thread would break. Kandata shouted at
the top of his voice: "This thread is mine! Get off, all of you!"

At that moment the thread snapped, just above Kandata. Together with the other sinners, he fell
back down into the depths of hell.

At the edge of the pond in paradise, the Buddha watched it all to the end, then, with a sad face,
began to walk again. The flowers in the pond swayed quietly, as if they knew nothing. In paradise,
it was nearly noon.

</details>

## What does it mean?

The usual reading is simple: Kandata was given a chance to be saved because of one small act of
kindness, and he lost it through one act of selfishness. The thread could hold everyone as long as
nobody tried to keep it for himself. The moment he said "this is mine", it broke.

The story leaves some questions open, which is part of why it's still discussed:

- Was the Buddha's kindness really kind, if it ended in more suffering? Some readers find his
  sad but calm walk away the most unsettling part.
- Was Kandata's shout so wicked? Anyone might panic on a thin thread. The story seems to say that
  the test was exactly the moment when it was hardest to think of others.
- What does the quiet, beautiful paradise at the end add? Some read it as showing that paradise
  goes on untouched, whatever happens below.

Lesson 1's concessions are useful for talking about it: {身勝手|みがって}だったとはいえ、{怖|こわ}かったのも
{無理|むり}はない (granted, he was selfish, but it's no wonder he was scared), or
{一度|いちど}だけいいことをしたからといって、{助|たす}かるべきだとは{限|かぎ}らない.

## The Akutagawa Prize

In 1935 the writer and publisher きくちかん (Kikuchi Kan: his family name's first kanji is outside
N2), a friend of Akutagawa's, founded two literary prizes in memory of his friends: the
あくたがわしょう (Akutagawa Prize; {芥|あくた} is outside N2) and the {直木賞|なおきしょう} (Naoki Prize). Both are
awarded twice a year. The Akutagawa Prize goes to new or little-known writers of "pure
literature" ({純文学|じゅんぶんがく}, literary fiction), usually for a short novel or a long short
story; the Naoki Prize to popular fiction. The announcements are big news in Japan, and the
winning works often sell very well.

## Dialogue: a book club

Two members of a library reading group, ひなた and そうま, talk about the story. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# After the reading group
ひなた: 『くもの{糸|いと}』、{子供|こども}のころ{読|よ}んだきりだったけど、{大人|おとな}になって{読|よ}むと{全然|ぜんぜん}{違|ちが}うね。
= I hadn't read "The Spider's Thread" since I was a kid, but it's completely different reading it as an adult.
そうま: そうそう。{昔|むかし}は「{悪|わる}いことをしちゃだめ」っていう{教訓|きょうくん}の{話|はなし}だと{思|おも}ってた。
= Exactly. I used to think it was just a story with the moral "don't do bad things".
ひなた: でも、カンダタってそんなに{特別|とくべつ}{悪|わる}い{人|ひと}かな。あの{場面|ばめん}で{叫|さけ}んじゃうのは、だれにでもありそう。
= But is Kandata so specially wicked? Anyone might shout in that situation.
そうま: {確|たし}かに。{自分|じぶん}だけ{助|たす}かろうとするのは{身勝手|みがって}だけど、{怖|こわ}かったんだろうね。
= True. Trying to save only yourself is selfish, but he must have been scared.
ひなた: あと、おしゃかさまが{最後|さいご}に{悲|かな}しそうに{歩|ある}いていっちゃうところ。あれ、ちょっと{冷|つめ}たくない？
= And the bit at the end where the Buddha just walks off looking sad. Isn't that a bit cold?
そうま: {読|よ}むたびに{感|かん}じ{方|かた}が{変|か}わるんだよね。{芥川|あくたがわ}って、そこがうまいんだと{思|おも}う。
= The way you feel about it changes every time you read it. I think that's what Akutagawa's good at.
ひなた: {短編|たんぺん}なのに、いろいろ{考|かんが}えさせられるよね。
= It's only a short story, but it makes you think about so much.
そうま: これをきっかけに、ほかの{作品|さくひん}も{読|よ}んでみようかな。『{鼻|はな}』とか。
= Maybe I'll use this as a start and try his other works. "The Nose", say.
ひなた: いいね。{来月|らいげつ}の{本|ほん}、それにしようよ。
= Good idea. Let's make that next month's book.
```

〜きり = only once, and not since (N3); {場面|ばめん} = scene.

## Key points

- {芥川|あくたがわ}{龍之介|りゅうのすけ} (1892–1927): short stories ({短編|たんぺん}), many retelling old tales.
- 『くもの{糸|いと}』 (1918), in the children's magazine 『{赤|あか}い{鳥|とり}』: the Buddha lets down a
  spider's thread; Kandata loses his chance through selfishness.
- Words: {極楽|ごくらく}, じごく, {罪人|ざいにん}, {悪人|あくにん}, じひ, {身勝手|みがって}, {童話|どうわ}, {教訓|きょうくん}.
- The Akutagawa Prize: founded in 1935, awarded twice a year to new writers of literary fiction.

lessons.title: Since it's so: からには, 以上は, 上は
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is about reasons and the **[[grounds]]** a statement stands on. N3 gave you the everyday
causes (から, ので, ため, おかげで, せいで). N2 adds patterns that say what kind of reason it is:
a reason that commits you (this lesson), a reason with a bad or a fitting result (lesson 12), the
basis a decision rests on (13), the issue a debate is about (14) and the reasons printed on
notices (15).

This lesson's patterns all mean "since (this is so), (then it follows that…)". The first half
states a fact or a decision that can't be taken back; the second half says what that fact
commits someone to.

{弁護士|べんごし}になると{決|き}めたからには、{毎日|まいにち}{勉強|べんきょう}するしかない。 — Now that I've decided to become a lawyer, I have no choice but to study every day.
{契約書|けいやくしょ}にサインした{以上|いじょう}、{条件|じょうけん}は{守|まも}っていただきます。 — Since you've signed the contract, we'll ask you to keep to its terms.
こうなった{上|うえ}は、{裁判|さいばん}で{争|あらそ}うしかない。 — Now that it's come to this, there's nothing for it but to fight it out in court.

The theme is law, rights and justice: courts, trials and lawyers, rights and duties, rules and
bans, and punishment. Crime, the police and suspects were N3's ({犯罪|はんざい}, {容疑者|ようぎしゃ},
{犯人|はんにん} are carried); politics is lesson 21's. Many carried words now take kanji:
{法律|ほうりつ}, {規則|きそく}, {権利|けんり}, {裁判|さいばん}, {禁止|きんし}, {被害|ひがい}.

## 〜からには: now that, so you must

〜からには joins a fact or decision to what it commits the speaker or listener to. The first half
is usually something done or decided ({決|き}めた, {引|ひ}き{受|う}けた, {来|き}た); the second half
is a duty, a resolve, a piece of advice or a firm conclusion.

| Before からには | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {引|ひ}き{受|う}けたからには / やるからには |
| noun + である | {学生|がくせい}であるからには |
| な-adjective + である | {自由|じゆう}であるからには |

{引|ひ}き{受|う}けたからには、{最後|さいご}まで{責任|せきにん}を{持|も}ってやります。 — Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たからには、{日本語|にほんご}で{話|はな}したい。 — Now that I'm in Japan, I want to speak Japanese.
やるからには、{一番|いちばん}を{目指|めざ}そう。 — If we're going to do it, let's aim for first place.
{法律|ほうりつ}で{禁|きん}じられているからには、やめるべきだ。 — Since it's forbidden by law, you should stop.
{親|おや}であるからには、{子供|こども}を{守|まも}る{義務|ぎむ}がある。 — Being a parent, you have a duty to protect your child.

What comes after it:

| Second half | Example |
|---|---|
| duty: なければならない, べきだ, 〜しかない | {約束|やくそく}したからには、{守|まも}らなければならない。 |
| resolve: 〜つもりだ, 〜(よ)う, 〜たい | {始|はじ}めたからには、{最後|さいご}までやるつもりだ。 |
| advice or a request: 〜てください, 〜なさい | {出|で}ると{決|き}めたからには、しっかり{準備|じゅんび}してください。 |
| a firm conclusion: 〜はずだ, 〜に{違|ちが}いない | あの{人|ひと}が「やる」と{言|い}ったからには、やるに{違|ちが}いない。 |

Two things to notice:

- *It isn't a plain report of a cause.* "It rained, so the match was cancelled" is just から or
  ので: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ったので、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}になった. Using からには here sounds wrong,
  because nothing follows from the rain that anyone is committed to.
- *The first half is usually settled.* A decision, a fact, a role. That's why the た form is so
  common: {決|き}めたからには, {来|き}たからには. With the dictionary form it means "if (we're) going
  to…": やるからには, {出|で}るからには.

You'll also meet からは with the same meaning ({約束|やくそく}したからは). It sounds older and more
written; からには is the everyday form.

## 〜{以上|いじょう}(は): since, given that

〜{以上|いじょう} (often 〜{以上|いじょう}は) works like からには but sounds more formal and more logical: it's
the "given that" of rules, contracts, official explanations and arguments. It joins the same way.

| Before {以上|いじょう} | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {契約|けいやく}した{以上|いじょう} / {認|みと}めない{以上|いじょう} |
| noun + である | {学生|がくせい}である{以上|いじょう} |
| な-adjective + である | {不可能|ふかのう}である{以上|いじょう} |

{会社|かいしゃ}に{入|はい}った{以上|いじょう}、{規則|きそく}を{守|まも}る{義務|ぎむ}がある。 — Now that you've joined the company, you have a duty to follow its rules.
{利用|りよう}{規約|きやく}に{同意|どうい}した{以上|いじょう}、それに{従|したが}う{必要|ひつよう}がある。 — Since you agreed to the terms of use, you have to follow them. ({従|したが}う = to follow, obey: lesson 28)
{被告人|ひこくにん}が{否認|ひにん}している{以上|いじょう}、{裁判|さいばん}は{長|なが}くなるだろう。 — Given that the defendant denies the charge, the trial is likely to be a long one.

Because it reasons from a condition, {以上|いじょう} goes easily with a negative: "as long as… not", "unless".

{本人|ほんにん}が{認|みと}めない{以上|いじょう}、{処分|しょぶん}はできない。 — As long as he won't admit it, no disciplinary action can be taken.
{規則|きそく}がない{以上|いじょう}、{禁|きん}じることはできない。 — As long as there's no rule, you can't ban it.

からには can follow a negative too, but it's less common; {以上|いじょう} is the safer choice there.

Don't mix this up with the other {以上|いじょう} you know: "more than" ({二十歳|はたち}{以上|いじょう}) and "the
above, that's all" ({以上|いじょう}です at the end of a report). The "since" {以上|いじょう} always follows a
clause.

## 〜{上|うえ}は: since, now that (very formal; to recognize)

〜{上|うえ}は means the same, mostly after a past verb, and sounds formal and a little old-fashioned.
You'll meet it in written Japanese, in speeches and in set phrases rather than in conversation.

こうなった{上|うえ}は、{裁判|さいばん}で{争|あらそ}うしかない。 — Now that it's come to this, there's nothing for it but to fight it out in court.
{判決|はんけつ}が{出|で}た{上|うえ}は、{結果|けっか}を{受|う}け{入|い}れるほかない。 — Now that the verdict has been given, we must accept the outcome.

Three {上|うえ} patterns now look alike. Lesson 7 taught the other two:

| Pattern | Reading | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜た{上|うえ}は | うえ | since, now that | {決|き}まった{上|うえ}は、やるしかない |
| 〜た{上|うえ}で | うえ | after doing (properly) | よく{考|かんが}えた{上|うえ}で{決|き}める |
| 〜{上|じょう} | じょう | in terms of | {法律上|ほうりつじょう}は{問題|もんだい}ない |

## Reminder: 〜のだから

> **Review (N3).** 〜のだから (spoken 〜んだから) gives a reason that both people know, and pushes a
> conclusion, advice or a complaint: もう{大人|おとな}なんだから、{自分|じぶん}で{決|き}めなさい (you're an
> adult now, so decide for yourself). It's everyday speech; からには and {以上|いじょう} are its formal,
> "committed" cousins.

## 〜ことだし: since (casual reasons)

〜ことだし gives one reason among others, softly, and leads to a suggestion or a decision. It's
spoken and friendly, often with も. Plain form; nouns and な-adjectives take である or な less often,
so learn it after verbs and い-adjectives.

{天気|てんき}もいいことだし、{歩|ある}いて{帰|かえ}ろうか。 — The weather's nice, so shall we walk home?
みんな{集|あつ}まったことだし、そろそろ{始|はじ}めましょう。 — Everyone's here, so let's get started.
もう{遅|おそ}いことだし、{今日|きょう}はここまでにしよう。 — It's late, so let's stop here for today.

It isn't for duties or strong conclusions: ことだし sounds relaxed ("what with… and all"), the
opposite of からには.

## Which one?

| Pattern | Register | What usually follows | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| からには | spoken and written | duty, resolve, advice, firm conclusion | {出|で}るからには{勝|か}ちたい |
| {以上|いじょう}(は) | formal, logical; rules and contracts | duty, logical conclusion, "can't"; also after negatives | {契約|けいやく}した{以上|いじょう}、{守|まも}るべきだ |
| {上|うえ}は | very formal, old-fashioned (recognize) | resolve, "there's nothing for it but" | こうなった{上|うえ}は、やるしかない |
| のだから | spoken (んだから) | advice, criticism, conclusion | {大人|おとな}なんだから{自分|じぶん}でやりなさい |
| ことだし | casual-polite speech | suggestion, decision | {雨|あめ}もやんだことだし、{出|で}かけよう |

The first three overlap a great deal. Speakers choose からには for personal resolve, {以上|いじょう} when they
argue from a rule or a condition, and {上|うえ}は in formal or fixed phrases. のだから and ことだし are
everyday reasons, not grounds for a duty.

1. What do people who defend strict school rules say?
2. According to the writer, what must every rule be able to do?
3. What did the student council at one high school do, and what was the outcome?
4. What is the writer's conclusion?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That once you've entered a school you should follow its rules ({入学|にゅうがく}したからには、{規則|きそく}は{守|まも}るべきだ), and that some discipline is needed when many people live together.
2. Its reason must be explainable: if the only answer is "it's always been so", it should be reviewed.
3. It ran a school-wide questionnaire and discussed the rules without clear reasons one by one. The hair-colour rule went; the ban on phones in class stayed.
4. Real discipline only comes when those who follow rules understand them, so those who make rules have a duty to explain them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Quite a few Japanese junior and senior high schools have detailed rules on hair colour and dress.
There are even rules such as "underwear must be white", and some people say this is a question of
pupils' human rights.

On the other hand, many people think that "once you've entered a school, you should keep its
rules". It's true that when many people live together, some degree of discipline is probably
needed. If everyone did as they liked, lessons might become impossible.

But since a rule is a rule, it ought to be possible to explain why it's needed. If, when asked
the reason, all you can say is "because that's how it has always been", shouldn't the rule be
reviewed?

Recently some schools have started changing their rules through discussion between pupils and
teachers. At one high school, the student council ran a questionnaire across the whole school
and took up, one by one, the rules whose reasons weren't clear. As a result, the rule on hair
colour went, but the ban on phones in class stayed. The head teacher says, "Since they decided
themselves, the pupils will surely keep the rules responsibly."

We tend to think of rules as something handed down from above. But unless those who keep them
understand why, real discipline doesn't come about. Rules made only for the convenience of
those who enforce them will one day stop being kept. Those who make the rules have a duty to
explain them too.

</details>
