*The Town with the Lighthouse*, by Chinatsu Aoki (Kitakaze Shuppan)

This is a full-length novel set in a small seaside town. The main character, Misaki, who works for a
publisher in Tokyo, goes back to the town she grew up in for the first time in ten years when her
father falls ill.

The story itself is simple. Nothing dramatic happens. But as you read on, each ordinary
conversation starts to take on meaning. The author won high praise for the previous book, a
collection of short stories, but this is said to be the author's first novel. Even so, the power to make
you read a work of over three hundred pages to the end in one go is remarkable.

What stays with you most is the scene between father and daughter in chapter five. Her father
says, "I'm nothing more than the keeper of an old lighthouse", and little by little Misaki comes to
understand the feelings behind those words.

The townspeople are very good too. The old woman who sells fish at the harbour every morning, Kenta,
Misaki's childhood friend who runs a small bookshop in the town: every one of them is written as
someone who might really exist. Through her conversations with them, Misaki comes to realize what
she truly wants to hold on to.

The book isn't without faults. The first half has rather a lot of explanation, and some readers
may find it slow to develop. But as far as this reviewer knows, no novel in the last few years has
moved the heart so quietly. On long autumn nights, there's nothing like taking your time over a
book like this.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
それは{一|ひと}つの{例|れい}に{過|す}ぎません。
= That's no more than one example.
{夏|なつ}は{冷|つめ}たいそばに{限|かぎ}る。
= In summer, nothing beats cold soba.
{急|いそ}いでいるときに{限|かぎ}って、{電車|でんしゃ}が{遅|おく}れる。
= The train's always late just when I'm in a hurry.
{私|わたし}が{知|し}っている{限|かぎ}りでは、まだ{発売|はつばい}されていません。
= As far as I know, it hasn't come out yet.
できる{限|かぎ}りのことはします。
= I'll do everything I can.
```

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out である after a な-adjective: before に{過|す}ぎない, a な-adjective usually takes である
  ({偶然|ぐうぜん}であるに{過|す}ぎない). With {偶然|ぐうぜん}, which is also a noun, {偶然|ぐうぜん}に{過|す}ぎない
  is common too, so for this word it's a matter of style.
- Using 〜に{限|かぎ}る for a general truth. It's your own recommendation; for "obviously best", use
  〜に{越|こ}したことはない.
- Mixing up に{限|かぎ}って and に{限|かぎ}り. A notice says {本日|ほんじつ}に{限|かぎ}り (today only); a
  complaint says {雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}に{限|かぎ}って (always on a rainy day).
- ×{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}る{限|かぎ}り for "unless it rains". "Unless" is ない{限|かぎ}り: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}らない
  {限|かぎ}り.
- ×{三冊|さんざつ}. The counter 〜{冊|さつ} doesn't change after さん: {三冊|さんさつ}. It does after
  いっ, はっ, じゅっ: {一冊|いっさつ}, {八冊|はっさつ}, {十冊|じゅっさつ}.
- {評判|ひょうばん} for a formal rating. "The product was rated highly" is {高|たか}く{評価|ひょうか}された;
  {評判|ひょうばん}がいい is "it has a good reputation".

## Key points

- 〜に{過|す}ぎない: no more than, merely (written; spoken 〜だけだ); often with ただ, {単|たん}なる, わずか.
- 〜に{限|かぎ}る: the best thing is (the speaker's own recommendation); compare
  〜に{越|こ}したことはない (general, often "…but").
- 〜に{限|かぎ}って: always just when (bad luck); X of all people wouldn't.
- 〜に{限|かぎ}り: only (notices).
- 〜{限|かぎ}り(は): as long as; 〜ない{限|かぎ}り: unless; 〜{限|かぎ}りでは: as far as; できる{限|かぎ}り: as
  much as possible.
- New kanji: 刊 誌 版 刷 冊 巻 章 編 著 筆 述 詞 評. Write {雑誌|ざっし}, {印刷|いんさつ}, 〜{冊|さつ},
  {文章|ぶんしょう}, {巻|ま}く, {筆者|ひっしゃ}, {歌詞|かし} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: How Japan works: work-style reform
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan has long had a reputation for long working hours, and the language shows it: {残業|ざんぎょう}
(overtime) and {過労死|かろうし} (death from overwork) are everyday words, and the second is known well
beyond Japan. Since the late 2010s the country has been trying to change this under the slogan
{働|はたら}き{方|かた}{改革|かいかく}, "work-style reform". This lesson explains what the reform did, in
Japanese you can now read: the module's patterns (〜ざるを{得|え}ない, 〜かねない, 〜に{限|かぎ}る,
〜に{過|す}ぎない) are everywhere in articles about it.

The facts below are as published by Japan's labour ministry ({厚生労働省|こうせいろうどうしょう}); rules
change, so check the ministry's own pages before relying on any figure.

## The law of 2018

In June 2018 the Diet passed a package of laws usually called the {働|はたら}き{方|かた}{改革|かいかく}{関連法|かんれんほう}
(the work-style reform laws). It changed several existing laws at once, above all the Labour
Standards Act. Two of its changes matter most for ordinary workers.

### A legal cap on overtime

Before the reform there was guidance on overtime but no upper limit in the law itself. The reform
set one:

- As a rule, overtime ({時間外労働|じかんがいろうどう}) may not exceed 45 hours a month and 360
  hours a year.
- With an agreement between employer and workers, and only for exceptional, temporary reasons,
  it may go higher, but never above 720 hours a year, under 100 hours in any one month,
  and no more than an average of 80 hours a month over any two to six months (both of these
  including work on days off); the 45-hour line may be crossed in at most six months of the year.
- The cap applied to large companies from April 2019 and to small and medium-sized
  companies from April 2020. Some kinds of work, such as construction, driving and doctors'
  work, were given more time; the ministry says the cap has applied to them too since April 2024,
  with special rules.
- Employers who break the cap can be punished.

{原則|げんそく}として、{時間外労働|じかんがいろうどう}の{上限|じょうげん}は{月|つき}{四十五時間|よんじゅうごじかん}、{年|ねん}{三百六十時間|さんびゃくろくじゅうじかん}だ。 — As a rule, the cap on overtime is 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year.

{原則|げんそく} (principle, rule) is lesson 11's word; {上限|じょうげん} is the upper limit.

### Five days of paid leave a year

Japanese workers have a legal right to paid annual leave ({年次有給休暇|ねんじゆうきゅうきゅうか}, whose last kanji
is outside N2, usually shortened to N4's {有休|ゆうきゅう}), but many didn't take it, partly so
as not to burden colleagues. Since April 2019, employers must make sure that every worker who
is given ten or more days of leave a year actually takes at least five of them.

{有休|ゆうきゅう}が{十日|とおか}{以上|いじょう}ある{人|ひと}は、{年|ねん}に{五日|いつか}は{必|かなら}ず{休|やす}まなければならない。 — Anyone who has ten or more days of paid leave must take at least five days a year.

Note the readings: {十日|とおか}, {五日|いつか} are the native counting of days.

## Working from home

When the coronavirus spread in 2020, many companies, especially large ones in big cities, moved
office work home almost overnight: テレワーク (telework) and {在宅|ざいたく}{勤務|きんむ} (working from
home, N3's word) entered daily speech. Some companies have kept it; others have brought people
back to the office, and practice varies a great deal by company and by job.

## For and against

People argue about the reform as much as they do about any law. Some typical views, put in the
module's patterns:

- For. {長時間労働|ちょうじかんろうどう}が{続|つづ}けば、{健康|けんこう}を{損|そこ}なう{人|ひと}が{増|ふ}えかねない。
  {上限|じょうげん}は{必要|ひつよう}だ。 — If long working hours go on, more people could ruin their
  health. A cap is necessary.
- Against (or worried). {仕事|しごと}の{量|りょう}が{減|へ}らないまま{時間|じかん}だけ{短|みじか}くしても、
  {家|いえ}に{持|も}ち{帰|かえ}って{働|はたら}かざるを{得|え}ない{人|ひと}が{出|で}てくる。 — If you only shorten the
  hours without reducing the work, some people will have no choice but to take it home.
- Small companies. {人手不足|ひとでぶそく}の{会社|かいしゃ}にとって、{残業|ざんぎょう}を{減|へ}らすのは
  {簡単|かんたん}ではない。 — For companies short of staff, cutting overtime isn't easy.
- A sceptic. {法律|ほうりつ}が{変|か}わっても、{職場|しょくば}の{空気|くうき}が{変|か}わらない{限|かぎ}り、{休|やす}み
  にくさは{変|か}わらない。 — Even if the law changes, as long as the atmosphere at work stays the same,
  it'll stay hard to take time off.

## Dialogue: leaving on time

Two colleagues, Saki and Ryō, at five past six. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# Going home
さき: あれ、りょうさん、もう{帰|かえ}るの？{珍|めずら}しいね。
= Oh, Ryō, you're going already? That's unusual.
りょう: うん。{今月|こんげつ}はもう{残業|ざんぎょう}が{四十時間|よんじゅうじかん}{近|ちか}くて、これ{以上|いじょう}は{課長|かちょう}に{止|と}められてるんだ。
= Yeah. I'm already close to forty hours of overtime this month, and the section chief's told me no more.
さき: そうか、{上限|じょうげん}があるもんね。でも、{仕事|しごと}、{終|お}わるの？
= Right, there's a cap. But will you get your work done?
りょう: {正直|しょうじき}、{厳|きび}しい。でも、{家|いえ}でやったら{意味|いみ}がないし。{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}、{早|はや}めに{来|く}るよ。
= Honestly, it's tight. But there's no point doing it at home. I'll come in early tomorrow.
さき: それも{実質|じっしつ}{残業|ざんぎょう}じゃない？
= Isn't that overtime in all but name?
りょう: …{言|い}われてみれば、そうかも。{仕事|しごと}の{量|りょう}が{同|おな}じなら、{時間|じかん}を{減|へ}らすのにも{限界|げんかい}があるよね。
= …Now you mention it, maybe it is. If the amount of work's the same, there's a limit to how far you can cut the hours.
さき: だから{来週|らいしゅう}の{会議|かいぎ}で、{仕事|しごと}の{分|わ}け{方|かた}を{見直|みなお}してもらおうよ。{二人|ふたり}で{言|い}えば、{課長|かちょう}も{検討|けんとう}せざるを{得|え}ないでしょ。
= So let's get them to rethink how the work's shared out at next week's meeting. If we both say it, the chief will have to consider it.
りょう: そうだね。じゃ、{今日|きょう}は{帰|かえ}る。{疲|つか}れたときは{早|はや}く{寝|ね}るに{限|かぎ}る。
= You're right. Well, I'm off. When you're tired, there's nothing like an early night.
さき: お{疲|つか}れさま。
= See you tomorrow.
```

{厳|きび}しい = tough, tight (lesson 11's kanji);
{実質|じっしつ} = in substance, in effect; {見直|みなお}す = to review (N3's word).

## Reading: a column on rest

An opinion column (だ/である style).

> 「{有休|ゆうきゅう}を{取|と}ると、どうりょうにめいわくをかけかねない」。そう{考|かんが}えて、{休|やす}みを{取|と}らない{人|ひと}は{今|いま}も{少|すく}なくない。{法律|ほうりつ}で{年|ねん}{五日|いつか}の{取得|しゅとく}が{義務|ぎむ}になったとはいえ、それはあくまで{最低限|さいていげん}に{過|す}ぎない。
>
> {休|やす}みにくさの{原因|げんいん}は、{個人|こじん}の{気持|きも}ちだけではない。{一人|ひとり}が{休|やす}むと{仕事|しごと}が{止|と}まってしまう{職場|しょくば}では、{休|やす}まざるを{得|え}ない{日|ひ}でさえ、{電話|でんわ}やメールに{追|お}われる。{休|やす}める{仕組|しく}みを{作|つく}らない{限|かぎ}り、{法律|ほうりつ}がいくら{変|か}わっても{状況|じょうきょう}は{変|か}わらないだろう。
>
> では、どうすればいいのか。まずは、{仕事|しごと}の{内容|ないよう}を{複数|ふくすう}の{人|ひと}で{共有|きょうゆう}することだ。そして、{管理職|かんりしょく}が{率先|そっせん}して{休|やす}むことである。{上|うえ}の{人|ひと}が{休|やす}まない{限|かぎ}り、{部下|ぶか}は{休|やす}みにくい。{休|やす}むことはなまけることではない。よく{働|はたら}くためには、よく{休|やす}むに{限|かぎ}るのである。

どうりょう = a colleague (its second kanji is off the list); {取得|しゅとく} = taking (leave),
obtaining; {最低限|さいていげん} = the minimum; {仕組|しく}み = a system, set-up; {共有|きょうゆう} = sharing;
{管理職|かんりしょく} = managers; {率先|そっせん}して = taking the lead; {部下|ぶか} = subordinates;
なまける = to be lazy (its kanji is off the list).

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"If I take paid leave, I could easily cause trouble for my colleagues." Plenty of people still
think that way and don't take time off. The law may now require five days a year, but that is no
more than the minimum.

What makes leave hard to take isn't only individual feelings. In workplaces where the work stops
when one person is away, people are chased by phone calls and emails even on days when they have
no choice but to be off. Unless we build systems that let people take time off, the situation
probably won't change however much the law does.

So what should be done? First, share the content of each job among several people. And managers
should take the lead in taking time off. As long as the people at the top don't rest, their staff
will find it hard to. Resting isn't laziness. If you want to work well, there's nothing like
resting well.

</details>

## Key points

- {働|はたら}き{方|かた}{改革|かいかく}: the reform laws passed in June 2018.
- Overtime cap: 45 hours a month and 360 a year as a rule; with special agreements no more than
  720 a year, under 100 in a month and an average of 80 over two to six months; large companies
  from April 2019, smaller ones from April 2020.
- Paid leave: at least five days a year must be taken by workers given ten or more days (from
  April 2019).
- {過労死|かろうし}, {長時間労働|ちょうじかんろうどう}, {時間外労働|じかんがいろうどう}, {上限|じょうげん},
  テレワーク, {人手不足|ひとでぶそく} (lesson 1): the words of the debate.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Miyazawa Kenji: 雨ニモマケズ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

「{雨|あめ}ニモマケズ」 ("Unbeaten by the rain", or "Not losing to the rain") is probably the best-known
modern poem in Japan. Schoolchildren learn it, it's carved on monuments, and people quote it in
hard times. It was written by {宮沢賢治|みやざわけんじ} (Miyazawa Kenji): his family name's two kanji
are outside N2, so they always come with furigana here.

This lesson reads the poem line by line in its original katakana, with a modern-Japanese
paraphrase and an English version of our own, explains its old spellings, and introduces his best
-known story. You'll see that the poem is built from grammar you know: the ず form, conditions,
and one last, plain wish.

## Who was Miyazawa Kenji?

- Born in 1896 in Hanamaki ({花巻|はなまき}), Iwate, in north-east Japan, into a well-off family.
  He studied agriculture and was a devout Buddhist, a follower of the Lotus Sutra.
- In the early 1920s he taught at the local agricultural school ({農学校|のうがっこう}); he left in
  1926 to live and work among the farmers ({農民|のうみん}), teaching them about soil and fertilizer.
  Cold summers and failed harvests were a real danger in Iwate, and they run through his writing.
- In 1924 he published, at his own expense, a book of poems, 『{春|はる}と{修羅|しゅら}』 (Spring and
  Asura), and a book of children's stories ({童話|どうわ}), 『{注文|ちゅうもん}の{多|おお}い{料理店|りょうりてん}』 (The
  Restaurant of Many Orders). Neither sold well, and he was little known in his lifetime
  ({生前|せいぜん}).
- He died of illness in September 1933, at 37. Most of his work became famous only after his death.
- He gave his home region an imaginary name, イーハトーブ (Ihatov, spelled in several ways): an
  ideal Iwate where his stories take place.

{修羅|しゅら}'s second kanji and the other off-list kanji in this lesson always have furigana; you
don't need to learn them.

## How the poem was found

The poem was never meant for publication. Kenji wrote it in pencil in a small black notebook,
under the date 3 November (of 1931), while he was ill. After his death the notebook was found in
a pocket of his trunk, and the poem was printed in 1934. It has no title: people call it by its
first line, and scholarly editions print that in brackets, 〔{雨|あめ}ニモマケズ〕. On the facing page of the
notebook are lines of Buddhist invocation.

## The poem

The text below is the one printed in most editions (checked against several published
transcriptions, which differ only in small details such as old kanji forms; the line breaks follow
most printed editions). The second column is our own paraphrase in modern
Japanese, the third our own English. Several kanji are outside N2 ({丈|じょう}, {慾|よく}, {瞋|いか}, {玄|げん},
{噌|そ}, {松|まつ}, {蔭|かげ}, {萓|かや}, {稲|いね}); read them with their furigana.

| | Kenji's text | Modern Japanese | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | {雨|あめ}ニモマケズ | {雨|あめ}にも{負|ま}けず | Not giving in to the rain |
| 2 | {風|かぜ}ニモマケズ | {風|かぜ}にも{負|ま}けず | not giving in to the wind |
| 3 | {雪|ゆき}ニモ{夏|なつ}ノ{暑|あつ}サニモマケヌ | {雪|ゆき}にも{夏|なつ}の{暑|あつ}さにも{負|ま}けない | beaten by neither snow nor summer heat |
| 4 | {丈夫|じょうぶ}ナカラダヲモチ | {丈夫|じょうぶ}な{体|からだ}を{持|も}ち | with a strong body, |
| 5 | {慾|よく}ハナク | {欲|よく}はなく | without greed, |
| 6 | {決|けっ}シテ{瞋|いか}ラズ | {決|けっ}して{怒|おこ}らず | never angry, |
| 7 | イツモシヅカニワラッテヰル | いつも{静|しず}かに{笑|わら}っている | always quietly smiling; |
| 8 | {一日|いちにち}ニ{玄米|げんまい}{四合|よんごう}ト | {一日|いちにち}に{玄米|げんまい}を{四合|よんごう}と | eating, each day, four gō of brown rice, |
| 9 | {味噌|みそ}ト{少|すこ}シノ{野菜|やさい}ヲタベ | みそと{少|すこ}しの{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べ | miso and a few vegetables; |
| 10 | アラユルコトヲ | どんなことも | in everything |
| 11 | ジブンヲカンジョウニ{入|い}レズニ | {自分|じぶん}のことは{考|かんが}えに{入|い}れないで | leaving myself out of the count, |
| 12 | ヨクミキキシワカリ | よく{見|み}て、{聞|き}いて、{理解|りかい}し | seeing, listening, understanding well, |
| 13 | ソシテワスレズ | そして{忘|わす}れない | and not forgetting; |
| 14 | {野原|のはら}ノ{松|まつ}ノ{林|はやし}ノ{蔭|かげ}ノ | {野原|のはら}の{松|まつ}の{林|はやし}のかげにある | in the shade of the pines on the moor, |
| 15 | {小|ちい}サナ{萓|かや}ブキノ{小屋|こや}ニヰテ | {小|ちい}さなかやぶきの{小屋|こや}に{住|す}んで | living in a little thatched hut; |
| 16 | {東|ひがし}ニ{病気|びょうき}ノコドモアレバ | {東|ひがし}に{病気|びょうき}の{子供|こども}がいれば | if there's a sick child to the east, |
| 17 | {行|い}ッテ{看病|かんびょう}シテヤリ | {行|い}って{看病|かんびょう}してあげ | going to nurse the child; |
| 18 | {西|にし}ニツカレタ{母|はは}アレバ | {西|にし}に{疲|つか}れた{母親|ははおや}がいれば | if there's a tired mother to the west, |
| 19 | {行|い}ッテソノ{稲|いね}ノ{束|たば}ヲ{負|お}ヒ | {行|い}ってその{稲|いね}の{束|たば}を{背負|せお}い | going to carry her sheaves of rice; |
| 20 | {南|みなみ}ニ{死|し}ニサウナ{人|ひと}アレバ | {南|みなみ}に{死|し}にそうな{人|ひと}がいれば | if there's someone dying to the south, |
| 21 | {行|い}ッテコハガラナクテモイヽトイヒ | {行|い}って{怖|こわ}がらなくてもいいと{言|い}い | going to say there's no need to be afraid; |
| 22 | {北|きた}ニケンクヮヤソショウガアレバ | {北|きた}にけんかや{裁判|さいばん}があれば | if there's a quarrel or a lawsuit to the north, |
| 23 | ツマラナイカラヤメロトイヒ | つまらないからやめなさいと{言|い}い | telling them to stop, it isn't worth it; |
| 24 | ヒデリノトキハナミダヲナガシ | {日照|ひで}りのときは{涙|なみだ}を{流|なが}し | shedding tears in times of drought, |
| 25 | サムサノナツハオロオロアルキ | {寒|さむ}い{夏|なつ}にはおろおろと{歩|ある}き | wandering at a loss in a cold summer; |
| 26 | ミンナニデクノボートヨバレ | みんなに「でくのぼう」と{呼|よ}ばれ | called a fool by everyone, |
| 27 | ホメラレモセズ | ほめられもせず | neither praised |
| 28 | クニモサレズ | {人|ひと}の{重荷|おもに}にもならない | nor a burden to anyone: |
| 29 | サウイフモノニ | そういう{人|ひと}に | that is the kind of person |
| 30 | ワタシハナリタイ | {私|わたし}はなりたい | I want to be. |

Notes on the paraphrase: {四合|よんごう} is four gō (a gō, about 180 ml, is the traditional measure for
rice; some readers say しごう); でくのぼう is a wooden puppet, so a useless, slow person; line 28,
クニモサレズ, literally "not even made a {苦|く} (a pain, a worry)", is read in more than one way, and
our paraphrase is one common reading.

## Reading the old spelling

The poem uses the kana spelling of its time (before the 1946 reform) and a few classical forms.
Each is easy once you know it.

| In the poem | Today | What's happening |
|---|---|---|
| ワラッテヰル, {小屋|こや}ニヰテ | {笑|わら}っている, {小屋|こや}にいて | ヰ is an old kana now written い |
| {負|お}ヒ, トイヒ | {背負|せお}い, と{言|い}い | ヒ in the middle or at the end of a word was later spelled い |
| シヅカ | しずか | old spelling of ず |
| サウナ, サウイフ | そうな, そういう | サウ was later spelled そう |
| コハガラナクテモ | {怖|こわ}がらなくても | ハ inside a word, now わ |
| イヽ | いい | ヽ (the katakana repeat mark; ゝ in hiragana) repeats the kana before it |
| ケンクヮ | けんか | クヮ is an old spelling of か |
| {萓|かや} | {萱|かや} | Kenji's notebook uses a variant form of the kanji for thatch grass; most editions keep it |
| マケズ, {瞋|いか}ラズ, ワスレズ | {負|ま}けず, {怒|おこ}らず, {忘|わす}れず | the ず form (N3): "without, not" |
| マケヌ | {負|ま}けない | classical ぬ (lesson 26) |
| {病気|びょうき}ノコドモアレバ | {病気|びょうき}の{子供|こども}がいれば | classical style uses ある for people too |

ヒデリ or ヒドリ? Line 24 reads ヒドリ in Kenji's notebook. When the poem was first printed,
the editors corrected it to ヒデリ ({日照|ひで}り, drought), which fits the next line about cold
summers, and most editions and schoolbooks print ヒデリ. A few scholars think Kenji meant ヒドリ,
read as "day labour" (working for a day's wage) or a slip for ヒトリ (alone). There's no agreed
answer; this lesson prints the usual text.

## Why katakana?

Nobody knows for sure why Kenji wrote this in katakana; it was a private notebook. Some points
people make:

- In his day, kanji mixed with katakana was the usual style of laws, official documents and
  telegrams, and the primary-school readers of the time taught katakana before hiragana. It wasn't as
  unusual then as it looks now.
- Kenji often used katakana in his notebooks and drafts.
- Many readers feel the style makes the poem sound like a vow or a prayer rather than a
  conversation.

## The wish at the end

Grammatically, the whole poem is one sentence. Lines 1–28 pile up descriptions, all in the
connective forms you know (〜ず, 〜ずに, and the ます stem used as "and": モチ, タベ, イヒ,
ナガシ, アルキ), and every one of them hangs on 「サウイフモノ」 (that kind of person) in line 29. Only line 30
has an ordinary verb at the end: ナリタイ, "I want to become". The poem doesn't say "I am like
this"; it says "I want to be". That is part of why it moves people: it's a wish, and a modest one.

Compare the patterns of this module: Kenji doesn't say {負|ま}けるものか (as if I'd lose!) or
{負|ま}けるわけにはいかない (I can't lose). He describes a person who simply isn't beaten.

## Night on the Galactic Railroad

『{銀河鉄道|ぎんがてつどう}の{夜|よる}』 (Night on the Galactic Railroad) is Kenji's best-known story. On
the night of a star festival, a lonely boy, Giovanni (ジョバンニ), finds himself on a train
travelling along the Milky Way ({天|あま}の{川|がわ}, lesson 18) with his friend Campanella
(カムパネルラ). They meet strange passengers and see the constellations up close, and Giovanni
slowly comes to understand that Campanella will not be coming back. Kenji rewrote it many times
and never finished it; it was published after his death, and it has been made into films, plays
and anime. Lesson 18's {銀河|ぎんが}, {星座|せいざ} and {天|あま}の{川|がわ} are all in it.

## Dialogue: in a literature class

Two university students, Haruka and Takumi, after a seminar. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# After the seminar
はるか: 「{雨|あめ}ニモマケズ」って、{小学校|しょうがっこう}で{暗記|あんき}させられたよね。
= We had to learn 「{雨|あめ}ニモマケズ」 by heart at primary school, didn't we?
たくみ: うん。でも、{正直|しょうじき}、{意味|いみ}はよく{分|わ}かってなかったな。
= Yeah. But to be honest, I didn't really understand what it meant.
はるか: {今日|きょう}{先生|せんせい}が、あれは{作品|さくひん}として{発表|はっぴょう}したものじゃなくて、{手帳|てちょう}に{書|か}いたメモに{過|す}ぎないって{言|い}ってたでしょ。びっくりした。
= Today the lecturer said it wasn't a work he published, just a note he wrote in a notebook. That surprised me.
たくみ: {病気|びょうき}で{寝|ね}ていたときに{書|か}いたらしいね。だから「なりたい」なのかな。
= Apparently he wrote it while he was ill in bed. Maybe that's why it says "I want to be".
はるか: そうかも。{自分|じぶん}はそうなれていないって{思|おも}っていたのかもしれない。
= Could be. Maybe he felt he hadn't managed to become like that.
たくみ: 「でくのぼう」と{呼|よ}ばれたいなんて、{普通|ふつう}は{思|おも}わないよね。
= You wouldn't normally want to be called a fool.
はるか: でも、ほめられなくてもいいから、{困|こま}っている{人|ひと}のそばにいたいってことでしょ。そう{考|かんが}えると、{簡単|かんたん}にはまねできないよ。
= But it means he wants to be there for people in trouble, even if nobody praises him. Seen that way, it's not something you can easily copy.
たくみ: {確|たし}かに。{読|よ}めば{読|よ}むほど、{言葉|ことば}で{説明|せつめい}しようがない{感|かん}じがする。
= True. The more I read it, the more I feel there's no way to explain it in words.
```

{暗記|あんき}する = to learn by heart; {手帳|てちょう} = a notebook (its second kanji is outside N2);
まねする = to copy, imitate.

## Key points

- {宮沢賢治|みやざわけんじ} (1896–1933), from Hanamaki in Iwate: poet, writer of children's stories,
  agricultural scientist; little known in his lifetime.
- 「{雨|あめ}ニモマケズ」: written in a notebook in 1931 while he was ill, found after his death,
  printed in 1934; no title of its own.
- Old spellings: ヰ → い, word-internal ヒ / ハ → い / わ, サウ → そう, シヅ → しず, ヽ repeats,
  クヮ → か; ず and ぬ are negatives.
- The whole poem is one sentence ending in a wish: サウイフモノニ / ワタシハナリタイ.
- 『{銀河鉄道|ぎんがてつどう}の{夜|よる}』: his unfinished, best-loved story.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Not only, regardless of: はもとより, のみならず, を問わず, に限らず
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about **[[scope]]**, emphasis and feeling. Scope is how far a statement reaches: does
it cover only A, A and B, or everyone whatever their age or nationality? This lesson gives the
written and formal ways to widen a statement: "not to mention A", "not only A", "regardless of
A", "not just A". Lessons 22 and 23 add strong feelings and exclamations, 24 hearsay and
"as if", and 25 "if only" and "if you dare".

{政治|せいじ}はもとより、{経済|けいざい}にもくわしい。 — They know a lot about the economy, not to mention politics.
この{問題|もんだい}は{日本|にほん}のみならず、{世界|せかい}{各国|かっこく}に{共通|きょうつう}している。 — This problem is shared not only by Japan but by countries all over the world.
{年齢|ねんれい}を{問|と}わず、だれでも{参加|さんか}できます。 — Anyone can take part, regardless of age.
{選挙|せんきょ}は{天候|てんこう}にかかわらず{行|おこな}われる。 — The election goes ahead whatever the weather.
{子供|こども}に{限|かぎ}らず、{大人|おとな}にも{人気|にんき}がある。 — It's popular not just with children but with adults too.

The theme is government, politics and the world: ministries and agencies, prefectures, parties
and elections, international relations, Europe and the West. N3 gave you the basics ({政治|せいじ},
{選挙|せんきょ}, {政府|せいふ}, {国会|こっかい}, {首相|しゅしょう}); this lesson's kanji let you write
several of them, and many more, with kanji: {政党|せいとう}, {与党|よとう}, {野党|やとう},
{大臣|だいじん}, {九州|きゅうしゅう}, {領収書|りょうしゅうしょ}.

Most of these patterns live in writing and formal speech: news, notices, job adverts, speeches.
In a chat with friends you'd use their everyday cousins: はもちろん, だけじゃなくて, {関係|かんけい}なく.

## Not to mention: 〜はもとより

N3 lesson 20 taught 〜はもちろん: A はもちろん B も, "B too, not to mention A". 〜はもとより
means the same and is more formal and more written. A is the obvious case; B is the one that
widens the statement, and it usually takes も (or まで, さえ).

{県庁|けんちょう}の{職員|しょくいん}はもとより、{市町村|しちょうそん}の{職員|しょくいん}も{研修|けんしゅう}に{参加|さんか}した。 — Not only the prefectural office's staff but also the staff of the cities, towns and villages took part in the training.
このニュースは{国内|こくない}はもとより、{欧米|おうべい}でも{大|おお}きく{報道|ほうどう}された。 — The news was widely reported in Europe and America, never mind at home.
{外交|がいこう}には{語学力|ごがくりょく}はもとより、{相手|あいて}の{文化|ぶんか}への{理解|りかい}が{欠|か}かせない。 — Diplomacy needs an understanding of the other side's culture, not to mention language skills.

| Pattern | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A はもちろん B も | everyday, spoken and written | {子供|こども}はもちろん、{大人|おとな}も{楽|たの}しめる |
| A はもとより B も | formal, mostly written | {子供|こども}はもとより、{大人|おとな}も{楽|たの}しめる |

Before はもとより you normally have a noun. With a verb, make it a noun with の:
{読|よ}むのはもとより、{書|か}くのも{得意|とくい}だ (good at writing, never mind reading).

もとより on its own is an adverb, "from the start; of course": {失敗|しっぱい}はもとより{承知|しょうち}の{上|うえ}だ
(I knew from the start that it might fail). You'll meet it in writing; {承知|しょうち} (awareness, N3
keigo's {承知|しょうち}しました) is the same word.

## Not only (written): 〜のみならず

のみ is the written word for だけ ("only"): {関係者|かんけいしゃ}のみ (staff only), {現金|げんきん}のみ (cash
only). 〜のみならず is the written だけでなく: "not only A but (also) B". The second part often
has も, まで or さえ.

| Before のみならず | Example |
|---|---|
| noun | {国内|こくない}のみならず |
| verb, plain form | {増|ふ}えるのみならず, {増|ふ}えたのみならず |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}いのみならず |
| な-adjective or noun + である | {便利|べんり}であるのみならず, {問題|もんだい}であるのみならず |

{少子化|しょうしか}は{日本|にほん}のみならず、アジアの{多|おお}くの{国|くに}が{抱|かか}える{問題|もんだい}だ。 — The falling birth rate is a problem not only for Japan but for many countries in Asia.
{新|あたら}しい{政策|せいさく}は{費用|ひよう}がかかるのみならず、{効果|こうか}も{疑問|ぎもん}だ。 — The new policy is not only expensive; its effect is doubtful too.
{大統領|だいとうりょう}の{発言|はつげん}は{国内|こくない}のみならず、{諸外国|しょがいこく}からも{批判|ひはん}を{受|う}けた。 — The president's remarks were criticized not only at home but by foreign countries too.

At the start of a sentence, のみならず means "moreover, what's more" (written):
{建設|けんせつ}{費|ひ}は{予算|よさん}を{大|おお}きく{超|こ}えた。のみならず、{工事|こうじ}も{一年|いちねん}{遅|おく}れている。 —
The construction costs went well over budget. What's more, the work is a year behind.

ただ〜のみならず and ひとり〜のみならず (to recognize) are stronger, very written versions: ひとり
{日本|にほん}のみならず (not Japan alone).

## Regardless of: 〜を{問|と}わず

{問|と}う is a formal verb, "to ask; to question; to make an issue of". 〜を{問|と}わず (its ず form,
N3 lesson 10) means "without making an issue of A": regardless of, irrespective of. It follows a
noun that covers a range of values, very often a pair of opposites:

| Range | Example |
|---|---|
| {年齢|ねんれい}, {性別|せいべつ}, {国籍|こくせき}, {学歴|がくれき} | {国籍|こくせき}を{問|と}わず{応募|おうぼ}できる (anyone can apply, whatever their nationality) |
| {男女|だんじょ}, {昼夜|ちゅうや}, {内外|ないがい}, {有無|うむ} | {昼夜|ちゅうや}を{問|と}わず{工事|こうじ}が{続|つづ}く (the work goes on day and night) |
| {老若男女|ろうにゃくなんにょ} | {老若男女|ろうにゃくなんにょ}を{問|と}わず{楽|たの}しめる (young and old, men and women can all enjoy it) |
| {経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ} | {経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}を{問|と}わず (with or without experience) |
| 〜かどうか | {参加|さんか}するかどうかを{問|と}わず (whether you take part or not) |

この{仕事|しごと}は、{経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}を{問|と}わず{応募|おうぼ}できます。 — You can apply for this job with or without experience.
この{問題|もんだい}は、{与党|よとう}・{野党|やとう}を{問|と}わず{議論|ぎろん}すべきだ。 — This issue should be debated by all parties, in government or in opposition.
{国|くに}の{内外|ないがい}を{問|と}わず、{多|おお}くの{人|ひと}がこの{映画|えいが}を{見|み}た。 — Many people at home and abroad saw this film.

In job adverts and notices you'll often see the plain verb at the end: {経験|けいけん}は{問|と}いません
(experience not required), {年齢|ねんれい}{不問|ふもん} (age no object). {問|と}う also has its own
meanings: {責任|せきにん}を{問|と}う (to hold someone responsible), {国民|こくみん}に{信|しん}を{問|と}う (to go to
the country, call an election).

## Regardless of: 〜にかかわらず, 〜にかかわりなく

〜にかかわらず (written in kana in this course) also means "regardless of". Like を{問|と}わず it
follows a noun with a range of values, and it can also follow a verb pair (dictionary form +
ない form) or adjective pair:

{天候|てんこう}にかかわらず、{試合|しあい}は{予定|よてい}どおり{行|おこな}います。 — The match will go ahead as planned whatever the weather.
{参加|さんか}するしないにかかわらず、{返事|へんじ}をください。 — Please reply whether or not you're taking part.
{金額|きんがく}の{大小|だいしょう}にかかわらず、{領収書|りょうしゅうしょ}をもらってください。 — Get a receipt, however large or small the amount.

〜にかかわりなく is the same meaning ({関係|かんけい}なく in everyday speech): {年齢|ねんれい}にかかわりなく
(regardless of age). {好|この}むと{好|この}まざるとにかかわらず ("whether you like it or not") is a written set
phrase to recognize.

### にかかわらず or にもかかわらず?

One も makes a big difference. 〜にもかかわらず (lesson 2) is "despite": A is a fact, and B
happens against what you'd expect. 〜にかかわらず is "regardless of": A can be anything, and B
doesn't change.

| | 〜にかかわらず (regardless of) | 〜にもかかわらず (despite) |
|---|---|---|
| What A is | a range of possibilities (weather, age, yes/no) | one fact that is true |
| What the sentence says | B is the same, whatever A is | B happened although A |
| Example | {雨天|うてん}にかかわらず{行|おこな}う (we'll hold it, rain or shine) | {雨|あめ}にもかかわらず{大勢|おおぜい}{来|き}た (lots of people came despite the rain) |
| Time | often rules and plans (future, general) | often a past event |

{選挙|せんきょ}の{日|ひ}は、{天気|てんき}にかかわらずとうひょうじょが{開|ひら}く。 — On election day the polling stations open whatever the weather.
{大雪|おおゆき}にもかかわらず、とうひょうに{来|き}た{人|ひと}は{多|おお}かった。 — Despite the heavy snow, many people came to vote.

(とうひょう, "voting", is written in kana in this course: its second kanji isn't on the list.)

If you can add "whatever it is" or "whether or not", you want にかかわらず. If you can add "and
yet", you want にもかかわらず.

### を{問|と}わず or にかかわらず?

With nouns like {年齢|ねんれい}, {性別|せいべつ}, {経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ} they usually mean the same, and
both are formal. を{問|と}わず is a little more written and is the usual choice with pairs of
nouns ({男女|だんじょ}を{問|と}わず, {昼夜|ちゅうや}を{問|と}わず); にかかわらず is the usual choice after a
verb pair ({行|い}く{行|い}かないにかかわらず). Speakers vary, so treat this as a tendency.

## Not just: 〜に{限|かぎ}らず

〜に{限|かぎ}らず (written with kanji: lesson 20 teaches {限|かぎ}る in full) says that A isn't the
limit: "not just A (but others too)". It's common in speech as well as writing.

この{問題|もんだい}は{若者|わかもの}に{限|かぎ}らず、どの{世代|せだい}にも{関係|かんけい}がある。 — This issue isn't limited to young people; it concerns every generation.
{首都|しゅと}に{限|かぎ}らず、{地方|ちほう}の{都市|とし}でも{人口|じんこう}が{減|へ}っている。 — It's not just the capital: regional cities are losing people too.
{日本|にほん}に{限|かぎ}らず、どの{国|くに}でも{選挙|せんきょ}の{前|まえ}は{議論|ぎろん}がさかんになる。 — Not only in Japan but in every country, debate heats up before an election.

に{限|かぎ}らず and のみならず are close, but they lean differently. のみならず adds B to A ("not
only A, B as well") and is written. に{限|かぎ}らず takes away a limit ("this isn't true only of
A") and is often followed by a whole group: どの〜も, {全般|ぜんぱん}, だれでも. Lesson 20's
〜に{限|かぎ}り (only) and 〜に{限|かぎ}って (of all times) are a different family.

> **Review: 〜ばかりか, 〜ばかりでなく, 〜をはじめ (N3 lessons 20 and 12).** A ばかりか B まで / さえ is
> "not only A but even B", with surprise: {彼|かれ}は{地元|じもと}ばかりか、{海外|かいがい}でも{知|し}られている.
> ばかりでなく is a neutral "not only". A をはじめ(として) B など names A as the leading example of a
> group: {首相|しゅしょう}をはじめ、{各|かく}{大臣|だいじん}が{出席|しゅっせき}した (the prime minister and the
> ministers attended).

## The scope patterns side by side

| Pattern | Meaning | Register | Typical partner |
|---|---|---|---|
| A はもとより B も | B too, not to mention A (A is obvious) | formal, written | も, まで |
| A のみならず B も | not only A but also B | written | も, まで, さえ |
| A を{問|と}わず | regardless of A (A has many values) | formal, written | pairs: {男女|だんじょ}, {昼夜|ちゅうや} |
| A にかかわらず | regardless of A | formal | verb pairs: する・しない |
| A に{限|かぎ}らず | not just A | spoken and written | どの〜も, だれでも |
| A ばかりか B まで | not only A but even B (surprise) | neutral | まで, さえ |
| A にもかかわらず | despite A (one fact) | formal | a past event |

The sheet "Scope and emphasis" has the whole module's patterns in one place.

## Government and the world: words

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| the state | {政府|せいふ}, {行政|ぎょうせい} (administration), {省庁|しょうちょう} (ministries and agencies), {省|しょう}, {庁|ちょう}, {外務省|がいむしょう}, {気象庁|きしょうちょう}, {役人|やくにん} (an official) |
| the regions | {都道府県|とどうふけん}, {府|ふ} ({京都府|きょうとふ}, おおさか{府|ふ}), {県庁|けんちょう}, {都庁|とちょう}, {市町村|しちょうそん}, {各地|かくち}, {州|しゅう} (a state in the US or Australia) |
| leaders | {総理大臣|そうりだいじん}, {大臣|だいじん}, {大統領|だいとうりょう}, {首脳|しゅのう} (leaders, heads of government), {委員|いいん}, {委員会|いいんかい} |
| parties and power | {党|とう}, {党首|とうしゅ}, {与党|よとう}, {野党|やとう}, {与野党|よやとう}, {政権|せいけん} (the government in power), {勢力|せいりょく}, {優勢|ゆうせい}, {勢|いきお}い, {情勢|じょうせい} (the situation), {改革|かいかく}, {民主主義|みんしゅしゅぎ} |
| elections | {選挙区|せんきょく}, {選挙権|せんきょけん}, {有権者|ゆうけんしゃ}, {立候補|りっこうほ}する, {議席|ぎせき}, {過半数|かはんすう}, {総選挙|そうせんきょ}, {支持率|しじりつ} |
| deciding | {可決|かけつ}する, {否決|ひけつ}する, {賛否|さんぴ} (for and against), {委|ゆだ}ねる (to leave a decision to) |
| the world | {各国|かっこく}, {諸国|しょこく}, {諸外国|しょがいこく}, {先進国|せんしんこく}, {途上国|とじょうこく}, {国連|こくれん}, {首脳会談|しゅのうかいだん}, サミット, {条約|じょうやく}, {協定|きょうてい}, {合意|ごうい}, {大使|たいし}, {領事館|りょうじかん}, {主権|しゅけん}, {領土|りょうど}, {領域|りょういき}, {移民|いみん}, {難民|なんみん} |
| Europe and the West | {欧米|おうべい}, {欧州|おうしゅう}, {西欧|せいおう}, {東欧|とうおう}, {北欧|ほくおう}, {北米|ほくべい}, {南米|なんべい}, {中東|ちゅうとう} |

Notes:

- Japan has 47 {都道府県|とどうふけん}: one {都|と} (Tokyo), one {道|どう} (Hokkaido), two {府|ふ}
  (Kyoto and Osaka) and 43 {県|けん}. Each has its own office: {都庁|とちょう}, {道庁|どうちょう},
  {府庁|ふちょう}, {県庁|けんちょう}. {都立|とりつ}, {府立|ふりつ}, {県立|けんりつ} mean "run by the
  prefecture" ({都立|とりつ}{高校|こうこう}).
- {省|しょう} is a ministry and {庁|ちょう} an agency, often under a ministry: {外務省|がいむしょう}
  (Foreign Ministry), {気象庁|きしょうちょう} (Meteorological Agency). {省庁|しょうちょう} is both
  together, "the ministries".
- {各|かく}〜 is "each": {各国|かっこく} (each country, every country), {各地|かくち}, {各自|かくじ}.
  {諸|しょ}〜 is "the various": {諸国|しょこく}, {諸外国|しょがいこく}. Lesson 27 has more of these
  prefixes. Note the sound change in {各国|かっこく} (かく + こく).
- {大勢|おおぜい} (a lot of people) and {勢|いきお}い (force, momentum) share 勢: {大勢|おおぜい} is
  read おおぜい, not ×おおせい.
- {政権|せいけん} is the party or leader in power; {政府|せいふ} is the government as an
  institution.
- {有権者|ゆうけんしゃ} are the people with the vote ({選挙権|せんきょけん}); {立候補|りっこうほ}する is
  to stand for election.
- {問|と}う isn't in the conjugation drills (the app can't yet build its forms), and のみ is a
  particle, so neither is drilled.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: the state, the world, and gathering together.

### The state

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 党 | party (political) | トウ | — | 10 | {党|とう}, {党首|とうしゅ}, {政党|せいとう}, {与党|よとう}, {野党|やとう}, {与野党|よやとう} |
| 臣 | minister, retainer | シン, ジン | — | 7 | {大臣|だいじん}, {総理大臣|そうりだいじん} |
| 府 | seat of government | フ | — | 8 | {政府|せいふ}, {府|ふ}, {京都府|きょうとふ}, {都道府県|とどうふけん} |
| 庁 | government office, agency | チョウ | — | 5 | {庁|ちょう}, {県庁|けんちょう}, {都庁|とちょう}, {気象庁|きしょうちょう}, {省庁|しょうちょう} |
| 省 | ministry; leave out; reflect | ショウ, セイ | はぶ(く) | 9 | {省|しょう}, {外務省|がいむしょう}, {省|はぶ}く, {反省|はんせい}する, {帰省|きせい}する |
| 委 | entrust, committee | イ | ゆだ(ねる) | 8 | {委員|いいん}, {委員会|いいんかい}, {委|ゆだ}ねる |

- {政党|せいとう}, {与党|よとう}, {野党|やとう} (N3) and {大臣|だいじん} (N3) are now written with kanji,
  and so is {政府|せいふ}.
- 臣 is ジン only in {大臣|だいじん}; elsewhere シン.
- 省 has three jobs. As ショウ it's a ministry. As セイ it's "look back on": {反省|はんせい}する (to
  reflect on what you did wrong), {帰省|きせい}する (to go back to your home town). As はぶ(く) it's
  "leave out, cut": {手間|てま}を{省|はぶ}く (save trouble). Lesson 7's {省略|しょうりゃく} (omission) uses
  the ショウ reading with that meaning.

### The world

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 州 | state, province; sandbank | シュウ | — | 6 | {州|しゅう}, {欧州|おうしゅう}, {本州|ほんしゅう}, {九州|きゅうしゅう} |
| 欧 | Europe | オウ | — | 8 | {欧米|おうべい}, {欧州|おうしゅう}, {西欧|せいおう}, {東欧|とうおう}, {北欧|ほくおう} |
| 領 | territory; govern; receive | リョウ | — | 14 | {領土|りょうど}, {領域|りょういき}, {大統領|だいとうりょう}, {領事館|りょうじかん}, {領収書|りょうしゅうしょ} |
| 諸 | various, many | ショ | — | 15 | {諸国|しょこく}, {諸外国|しょがいこく} |

- {九州|きゅうしゅう} (N3) and {領収書|りょうしゅうしょ} (N3) can now be written with kanji.
  {本州|ほんしゅう} is Japan's largest island.
- 欧 stands for Europe because it was used to write the first sound of an old name for Europe.
  {欧米|おうべい} is "Europe and America", the West; 米 is America (as in {米国|べいこく}, the USA).
- 領 is "receive" in {領収書|りょうしゅうしょ} (a receipt) and "govern, territory" elsewhere.

### Gathering and acting

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 挙 | raise; hold; all | キョ | あ(げる) | 10 | {選挙|せんきょ}, {選挙区|せんきょく}, {選挙権|せんきょけん}, {例|れい}を{挙|あ}げる |
| 各 | each | カク | — | 6 | {各国|かっこく}, {各地|かくち}, {各自|かくじ}, {各駅停車|かくえきていしゃ} |
| 勢 | force, power | セイ, ゼイ | いきお(い) | 13 | {勢力|せいりょく}, {優勢|ゆうせい}, {情勢|じょうせい}, {勢|いきお}い, {大勢|おおぜい} |

- {選挙|せんきょ} (N3) and {各駅停車|かくえきていしゃ} (N3) are now written with kanji.
- {挙|あ}げる is N4's あげる in its "raise up, put forward" senses: {例|れい}を{挙|あ}げる (give an
  example), {手|て}を{挙|あ}げる (raise your hand), {式|しき}を{挙|あ}げる (hold a wedding). It's the
  same word, so it isn't a new item; {上|あ}げる is also correct for raising a hand.
- 勢 is ゼイ in {大勢|おおぜい}.

Memory notes:

- 党 is a roof with something shining under it over 儿 (legs): people under one roof, a party.
- 府 is 广 (a building) with 付 (attach, N3 lesson 21) inside: the building everything is attached to,
  the seat of government.
- 庁 is the same building, 广, with a T-shape inside: a smaller government office.
- 省 is 少 (few, N4) over 目 (eye, N5): look closely and cut it down to a few.
- 委 is 禾 (grain) over 女 (woman, N5): handing the harvest over to someone you trust.
- 州 is a river with three dots in it: sandbanks, land between the streams.
- 諸 is 言 (word) and 者 (person, N4): words to many people.
- 勢 is 埶 over 力 (power, N4): power in action.
- 各 is 夂 (feet) over 口: each person arrives at their own door.

```trace
党臣府庁省州欧領挙委各諸勢
```

## Dialogue: an election for high school students

A local radio programme. The presenter, ゆい, talks to まさき from the prefecture's election committee.
(Polite speech. とうひょう, voting, is in kana: its second kanji isn't on the course list.)

```dialogue
# On the radio
ゆい: {今日|きょう}は、{県|けん}の{選挙|せんきょ}{管理|かんり}{委員会|いいんかい}のさとうまさきさんに{来|き}ていただきました。よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
= Today we're joined by Masaki Satō from the prefecture's election committee. Welcome.
まさき: よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
= Thank you.
ゆい: {来月|らいげつ}、{高校生|こうこうせい}が{選挙|せんきょ}を{体験|たいけん}するイベントがあるそうですね。
= I hear there's an event next month where high school students get to experience an election.
まさき: はい。{県内|けんない}の{高校生|こうこうせい}なら、{学年|がくねん}を{問|と}わず{参加|さんか}できます。{本当|ほんとう}のとうひょう{箱|ばこ}を{使|つか}って、{選挙|せんきょ}を{一|いち}から{体験|たいけん}してもらいます。
= Yes. Any high school student in the prefecture can take part, whatever year they're in. We'll use real ballot boxes and they'll go through an election from start to finish.
ゆい: {高校生|こうこうせい}に{限|かぎ}らず、{中学生|ちゅうがくせい}も{参加|さんか}できるんでしょうか。
= Can junior high school students take part too, or is it just high school students?
まさき: {今回|こんかい}、とうひょうできるのは{高校生|こうこうせい}のみです。ただ、{見学|けんがく}は{年齢|ねんれい}にかかわらず、どなたでも{大|だい}かんげいです。
= This time only high school students can vote. But anyone is very welcome to come and watch, whatever their age.
ゆい: どうしてこういうイベントを？
= Why hold an event like this?
まさき: {若|わか}い{人|ひと}のとうひょう{率|りつ}が{低|ひく}いのは、この{県|けん}はもとより、{全国的|ぜんこくてき}な{課題|かだい}なんです。{一度|いちど}{体験|たいけん}しておくと、{本番|ほんばん}でも{行|い}きやすくなると{言|い}われています。
= Low turnout among young people is a problem across the country, not to mention in this prefecture. They say that if you've done it once, it's easier to go when it's for real.
ゆい: {候補者|こうほしゃ}はどなたが？
= And who are the candidates?
まさき: {大学生|だいがくせい}のボランティアが{三人|さんにん}、{候補者|こうほしゃ}になります。それぞれ{公約|こうやく}を{発表|はっぴょう}して、{演説|えんぜつ}もします。
= Three university student volunteers will be the candidates. Each one announces their pledges and gives a speech.
ゆい: テーマは{何|なん}ですか。
= What's the theme?
まさき: {県|けん}の{予算|よさん}をどう{使|つか}うか、です。{子育|こそだ}てや{交通|こうつう}のみならず、{観光|かんこう}や{環境|かんきょう}まで、いろいろな{意見|いけん}が{出|で}ると{思|おも}います。
= How to spend the prefecture's budget. I think there'll be all sorts of opinions, not only on childcare and transport but on tourism and the environment too.
ゆい: {結果|けっか}も{楽|たの}しみですね。
= I'm looking forward to the result.
まさき: はい。{結果|けっか}は{県庁|けんちょう}のロビーはもとより、ホームページでも{公表|こうひょう}する{予定|よてい}です。
= Yes. We plan to publish it on our website, as well as in the lobby of the prefectural office, of course.
ゆい: {本日|ほんじつ}はありがとうございました。
= Thank you very much for coming in today.
```

{選挙|せんきょ}{管理|かんり}{委員会|いいんかい} = election committee; とうひょう{箱|ばこ} = ballot box;
とうひょう{率|りつ} = turnout; {本番|ほんばん} = the real thing; {大|だい}かんげい = very welcome
(its second kanji is off-list); {公表|こうひょう}する = to make public (N3). Notice that the official uses を{問|と}わず,
のみ, はもとより: formal words for a formal setting. In a chat with friends you'd say
{学年|がくねん}{関係|かんけい}なく and {高校生|こうこうせい}だけ.

## Reading: a newspaper article

A short news article (である style, as newspapers write). ひかり{県|けん} is invented.

> ひかり{県|けん}は、{県内|けんない}に{住|す}む{外国人|がいこくじん}のための{相談|そうだん}{窓口|まどぐち}を、{来年|らいねん}{四月|しがつ}から{大|おお}きく{広|ひろ}げると{発表|はっぴょう}した。{現在|げんざい}、{窓口|まどぐち}は{県庁|けんちょう}の{中|なか}にしかないが、{今後|こんご}は{県庁|けんちょう}のみならず、{県内|けんない}{各地|かくち}の{市役所|しやくしょ}や{町村|ちょうそん}の{役場|やくば}にも{置|お}かれる{予定|よてい}だ。
>
> {県|けん}によると、{県内|けんない}の{外国人|がいこくじん}{住民|じゅうみん}はこの{十年|じゅうねん}で{約|やく}{二倍|にばい}に{増|ふ}えた。{欧米|おうべい}はもとより、アジアや{南米|なんべい}など、{出身|しゅっしん}の{国|くに}はおよそ{八十|はちじゅう}か{国|こく}に{及|およ}ぶ。{特|とく}に{増|ふ}えているのは、{工場|こうじょう}や{農業|のうぎょう}の{現場|げんば}で{働|はたら}く{若|わか}い{世代|せだい}だという。
>
> {新|あたら}しい{窓口|まどぐち}では、{国籍|こくせき}を{問|と}わず、だれでも{無料|むりょう}で{相談|そうだん}できる。{仕事|しごと}や{住|す}まい、{子供|こども}の{学校|がっこう}のことに{限|かぎ}らず、{病院|びょういん}のかかり{方|かた}や{災害|さいがい}への{備|そな}えなど、{生活|せいかつ}に{関|かん}することなら{何|なん}でも{受|う}け{付|つ}けるという。{使|つか}える{言語|げんご}も、{英語|えいご}や{中国語|ちゅうごくご}はもとより、ポルトガル{語|ご}やベトナム{語|ご}など{十二|じゅうに}の{言語|げんご}に{増|ふ}やす。
>
> また、{窓口|まどぐち}は{平日|へいじつ}のみならず、{土曜日|どようび}にも{開|ひら}く。{仕事|しごと}の{都合|つごう}で{平日|へいじつ}には{来|こ}られないという{声|こえ}が{多|おお}かったためだ。{相談|そうだん}は{窓口|まどぐち}に{限|かぎ}らず、{電話|でんわ}やオンラインでもできるようにする。{予約|よやく}がなくても{相談|そうだん}できるという。
>
> {県|けん}の{担当者|たんとうしゃ}は「{言葉|ことば}が{分|わ}からないために、{困|こま}っていても{相談|そうだん}できない{人|ひと}は{少|すく}なくない。{年齢|ねんれい}や{国籍|こくせき}にかかわらず、だれもが{安心|あんしん}して{暮|く}らせる{県|けん}にしたい」と{話|はな}している。
>
> {一方|いっぽう}で、{相談|そうだん}{員|いん}の{数|かず}が{足|た}りないという{課題|かだい}もある。{県|けん}は、{外国語|がいこくご}ができる{人|ひと}を{広|ひろ}く{募集|ぼしゅう}しており、{経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}は{問|と}わないとしている。

{窓口|まどぐち} = service desk; {役場|やくば} = town or village office; {及|およ}ぶ = to reach (lesson 17's
kanji); {備|そな}え = preparation; {相談|そうだん}{員|いん} = adviser.

1. Where are the advice desks now, and where will they be from April?
2. Who can use the new desks, and what can they ask about?
3. Why will the desks also open on Saturdays?
4. What problem does the prefecture still have, and what is it doing about it?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Now they're only inside the prefectural office; from April they'll also be in city halls and
   town and village offices across the prefecture ({県庁|けんちょう}のみならず、{県内|けんない}{各地|かくち}の…).
2. Anyone, whatever their nationality, free of charge ({国籍|こくせき}を{問|と}わず、だれでも{無料|むりょう}で); anything to do with
   daily life, not just work, housing and school but also using hospitals and preparing for
   disasters.
3. Many people said they couldn't come on weekdays because of work.
4. There aren't enough advisers. It's recruiting widely among people who speak foreign
   languages, with or without experience ({経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}は{問|と}わない).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Hikari Prefecture has announced that from next April it will greatly expand its advice desks for
foreign residents. At present the only desk is inside the prefectural office, but from now on
desks are to be set up not only there but in city halls and town and village offices across the
prefecture.

According to the prefecture, the number of foreign residents has roughly doubled in the last ten
years. They come from about eighty countries: from Asia and South America, among others, as well
as, of course, from Europe and North America.

At the new desks anyone can get advice free of charge, whatever their nationality. They will
reportedly deal with anything to do with daily life: not just work, housing and children's
schooling, but also how to use hospitals and how to prepare for disasters. The languages offered
will also increase to twelve, among them Portuguese and Vietnamese as well as, of course, English
and Chinese.

The desks will also open not only on weekdays but on Saturdays. This is because many people said
they couldn't come on weekdays because of work. Advice will be available not only at the desks
but also by phone and online.

The official in charge said: "There are quite a few people who can't ask for help even when
they're in trouble, because they don't understand the language. We want this to be a prefecture
where everyone can live without worry, regardless of age or nationality."

On the other hand, there is a shortage of advisers. The prefecture is recruiting widely among
people who speak foreign languages and says that experience is not required.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{子供|こども}はもとより、{大人|おとな}も{楽|たの}しめます。
= Adults can enjoy it too, not to mention children.
{経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}は{問|と}いません。
= Experience is not required.
{天候|てんこう}にかかわらず、{行|おこな}います。
= It will go ahead whatever the weather.
{日本|にほん}に{限|かぎ}らず、どこの{国|くに}でも{同|おな}じです。
= It's the same in any country, not just Japan.
{国内|こくない}のみならず、{海外|かいがい}でも{知|し}られています。
= It's known not only at home but abroad.
```

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up にかかわらず and にもかかわらず. {雨|あめ}にもかかわらず{出|で}かけた is "I went out despite
  the rain" (it was raining). {雨|あめ}にかかわらず{出|で}かける would be "I'll go out regardless of rain",
  and for the weather the natural words are {天候|てんこう}にかかわらず or {雨天|うてん}にかかわらず.
- を{問|と}わず after a single fixed thing. ×{田中|たなか}さんを{問|と}わず doesn't work: the noun must
  cover a range ({年齢|ねんれい}, {男女|だんじょ}, {経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}). For "not just Tanaka", use
  {田中|たなか}さんに{限|かぎ}らず.
- はもとより after a verb without の: ×{読|よ}むはもとより → {読|よ}むのはもとより.
- のみならず after a noun or な-adjective with だ: ×{問題|もんだい}だのみならず → {問題|もんだい}のみならず
  or {問題|もんだい}であるのみならず.
- Using these in casual chat. 「{子供|こども}はもとより、{大人|おとな}も{楽|たの}しめるよ」 sounds like a
  brochure; with friends, say はもちろん or だけじゃなくて.
- {大勢|おおぜい} read ×おおせい, and {各国|かっこく} read ×かくこく.

## Key points

- A はもとより B も: B too, not to mention A (formal; the written はもちろん).
- A のみならず B も: not only A but also B (written; のみ = だけ). At the start of a sentence: what's
  more.
- A を{問|と}わず: regardless of A, where A has a range of values ({年齢|ねんれい}, {男女|だんじょ},
  {経験|けいけん}の{有無|うむ}); 〜は{問|と}いません in adverts.
- A にかかわらず / にかかわりなく: regardless of A, also after verb pairs (する・しない). Don't confuse it
  with にもかかわらず (despite).
- A に{限|かぎ}らず: not just A; common in speech and writing.
- New kanji: 党 臣 府 庁 省 州 欧 領 挙 委 各 諸 勢. Write {政党|せいとう}, {与党|よとう}, {野党|やとう},
  {大臣|だいじん}, {政府|せいふ}, {選挙|せんきょ}, {九州|きゅうしゅう}, {領収書|りょうしゅうしょ} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 widened a statement. This lesson turns up its strength: feelings and sensations so
strong you can't bear them, thoughts that come by themselves, and actions you can't stop
yourself doing. These are **[[emphatic expressions]]**: patterns whose job is to say "very, too
much, I can't help it".

{明日|あした}の{公演|こうえん}が{楽|たの}しみでたまらない。 — I can't wait for tomorrow's show.
{彼|かれ}の{演技|えんぎ}には、どこか{寂|さび}しさがあるように{思|おも}えてならない。 — I can't help feeling there's a kind of loneliness in his acting.
あまりに{美|うつく}しい{歌声|うたごえ}に、はくしゅしないではいられなかった。 — The singing was so beautiful I couldn't help applauding.

(はくしゅ, applause, is written in kana in this course: its first kanji isn't on the list.)

The theme is the arts and performance: theatre and comedy, music, painting and patterns, film
and photography, scent, exhibitions. N3 lesson 20 gave many arts words in kana that you can now
write with kanji: {芸術|げいじゅつ}, {演劇|えんげき}, {劇場|げきじょう}, {俳優|はいゆう}, {演奏|えんそう},
{影響|えいきょう}, {踊|おど}る, {撮|と}る.

## Unbearably: 〜てたまらない

たまらない means "can't stand it, can't bear it". After the て form of an adjective or a
feeling verb, it says the feeling or sensation is so strong you can hardly bear it. N3 met it
for recognition; here it's yours to use.

| Before てたまらない | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| い-adjective → 〜くて | {暑|あつ}くてたまらない | unbearably hot |
| 〜たい → 〜たくて | {会|あ}いたくてたまらない | dying to see them |
| な-adjective → 〜で | {心配|しんぱい}でたまらない | worried sick |
| feeling verb → て form | {気|き}になってたまらない | can't stop thinking about it |

{初日|しょにち}の{舞台|ぶたい}の{前|まえ}は、{緊張|きんちょう}してたまらなかった。 — Before the opening night I was unbearably nervous.
{好|す}きな{劇団|げきだん}の{新作|しんさく}が{見|み}たくてたまらない。 — I'm dying to see my favourite theatre company's new play.
{撮影所|さつえいじょ}の{中|なか}は{照明|しょうめい}のせいで{暑|あつ}くてたまらない。 — It's unbearably hot inside the film studio because of the lights.

{照明|しょうめい} (lighting) is lesson 30's word.

Points to note:

- In a statement it describes your own feelings. For someone else, add a word that shows you
  can only see it from outside: {弟|おとうと}は{発表会|はっぴょうかい}が{楽|たの}しみでたまらないようだ
  (my brother seems to be really looking forward to the recital). In stories the narrator can use
  it freely about characters.
- In casual speech: 〜てたまんない.
- たまらない on its own (and casual たまらん) is praise: このコーヒーの{香|かお}り、たまらない (the smell
  of this coffee is irresistible).

## Can't help feeling: 〜てならない

〜てならない means much the same as てたまらない, but it's more written and it suits feelings
that rise by themselves, without your wanting them: worry, regret, a hunch. It's very common
with the "spontaneous" verbs {思|おも}える, {気|き}がする, {感|かん}じられる, {思|おも}い{出|だ}される.

{最近|さいきん}、だれかに{見|み}られているような{気|き}がしてならない。 — Lately I can't shake the feeling that someone's watching me.

あの{悲劇|ひげき}の{結末|けつまつ}は、{今|いま}でも{残念|ざんねん}に{思|おも}えてならない。 — Even now I can't help feeling sorry about the ending of that tragedy.
{初|はじ}めて{来|き}た{町|まち}なのに、なつかしく{感|かん}じられてならない。 — It's a town I've never been to, but I can't help feeling it's familiar.

| | 〜てたまらない | 〜てならない |
|---|---|---|
| Register | spoken and written | more written, a little formal |
| Best with | sensations and desires: {暑|あつ}い, {痛|いた}い, {眠|ねむ}い, 〜たい | feelings that come by themselves: {気|き}がする, {思|おも}える, {心配|しんぱい}, {残念|ざんねん} |
| Example | {足|あし}が{痛|いた}くてたまらない | {失敗|しっぱい}しそうな{気|き}がしてならない |

The two overlap a lot ({心配|しんぱい}でたまらない and {心配|しんぱい}でならない are both fine). The
clearest difference is with {気|き}がする and {思|おも}える: {気|き}がしてならない is the natural phrase, and
{気|き}がしてたまらない sounds odd to many speakers. With plain physical sensations, たまらない is
the everyday choice.

## Review: 〜てしょうがない (N3 lesson 10)

> **Review.** 〜てしょうがない and 〜てしかたがない ("it can't be helped") work like てたまらない, but
> they're casual and often used for annoyances: {眠|ねむ}くてしょうがない (I'm so sleepy),
> となりの{工事|こうじ}がうるさくてしょうがない (the building work next door is driving me mad). In
> casual speech: 〜てしょうがない, 〜てしかたない.

## Can't help doing: 〜ないではいられない

N3 lesson 10 taught 〜ずにはいられない: "can't stop yourself doing". 〜ないではいられない is the same
pattern with the ない form; it's a little less written. It's about actions, not feelings.

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| ない form + ではいられない | {笑|わら}わないではいられない |
| ず form + にはいられない | {笑|わら}わずにはいられない |
| する verbs | {心配|しんぱい}しないではいられない / {心配|しんぱい}せずにはいられない |

あの{喜劇|きげき}は{何度|なんど}{見|み}ても、{笑|わら}わないではいられない。 — However many times I see that comedy, I can't help laughing.
{素晴|すば}らしい{演奏|えんそう}だったので、{終|お}わったとたんに{立|た}ち{上|あ}がらないではいられなかった。 — It was a wonderful performance, so the moment it ended I couldn't help standing up.
{好|す}きな{俳優|はいゆう}の{写真集|しゃしんしゅう}が{出|で}ると{聞|き}いて、{買|か}わないではいられなかった。 — When I heard my favourite actor's photo book was coming out, I just had to buy it.

とたんに is N3's "the moment"; ず form: する → せず (×しず).

Compare: {悲|かな}しくてたまらない (a feeling: I'm terribly sad) and {泣|な}かないではいられない (an
action: I can't stop myself crying).

## To recognize: 〜ずにはおかない

〜ずにはおかない (often with a causative) says that something will inevitably cause a reaction:
"it can't fail to…". The subject is usually a thing, a work or an event, not a person's will.

この{映画|えいが}は、{見|み}る{人|ひと}を{感動|かんどう}させずにはおかない。 — This film can't fail to move anyone who sees it.
{彼女|かのじょ}の{歌声|うたごえ}は、{聞|き}く{人|ひと}の{心|こころ}を{動|うご}かさずにはおかない。 — Her singing can't fail to touch the hearts of those who hear it.

It's written, and you'll mostly meet it in reviews and essays. With a person as the subject it
can also mean "I won't let it go without…" ({謝|あやま}らせずにはおかない: I'll make them apologize);
that use is rarer. 〜ずにはすまない (lesson 17, "can't get away without") is a different pattern.

## The five side by side

| Pattern | What it's about | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜てたまらない | feelings, sensations, wishes: unbearably | neutral | {会|あ}いたくてたまらない |
| 〜てならない | feelings that come by themselves | written | {気|き}がしてならない |
| 〜てしょうがない | feelings and annoyances | casual | {眠|ねむ}くてしょうがない |
| 〜ないではいられない / ずにはいられない | actions you can't hold back | neutral / written | {笑|わら}わないではいられない |
| 〜ずにはおかない | a thing that inevitably causes a reaction | written | {感動|かんどう}させずにはおかない |

Memory notes:

- 芸 is grass (艹) over a figure like two lines and a hook: plants trained by skill, an art.
- 劇 has 刂 (a sword) on the right: drama with swords, intense.
- 俳 is a person (亻) and 非 (not, N3): a person who is not themselves, an actor.
- 奏 has hands raised (the top) over 天 shape: playing music up to heaven.
- 踊 is 足 (foot) and 甬: feet that leap.
- 模 is 木 (wood) and 莫: a wooden model or pattern.
- 姿 is 次 (next, N3) over 女 (woman): the figure of a person.
- 影 is 景 (scene, N3's 景色) and three strokes of light: the scene and its shadow.
- 鏡 is 金 (metal) and 竟: a metal mirror, as old mirrors were.
- 撮 is 扌 (hand) and 最 (most, N4): the hand grabbing the best moment.
- 紅 is 糸 (thread, lesson 24) and 工: dyed thread, deep red.
- 香 is 禾 (grain) over 日: the smell of grain in the sun.

## Dialogue: after the show

Two friends come out of a small theatre after a comedy. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# After the show
あおい: いやー、{面白|おもしろ}かった！{途中|とちゅう}から{笑|わら}いすぎて、おなかが{痛|いた}くてたまんなかったよ。
= Wow, that was great! I laughed so much from halfway through that my stomach hurt like mad.
れん: ほんと。あの{主演|しゅえん}の{人|ひと}、{出|で}てくるだけで{笑|わら}わないではいられないよね。
= Seriously. That lead actor, you can't help laughing the moment they walk on.
あおい: {芸名|げいめい}、なんだっけ？{前|まえ}はテレビの{芸人|げいにん}だったんでしょ？
= What's their stage name again? They used to be a comedian on TV, didn't they?
れん: そうそう。{芸能界|げいのうかい}をやめて、この{劇団|げきだん}に{入|はい}ったんだって。
= That's right. Apparently they quit show business and joined this company.
あおい: へえ。でも{最後|さいご}の{場面|ばめん}は、ちょっと{悲|かな}しかったな。{喜劇|きげき}なのに。
= Huh. But the last scene was a bit sad, wasn't it? Even though it's a comedy.
れん: うん。{一人|ひとり}で{舞台|ぶたい}に{残|のこ}る{後|うし}ろ{姿|すがた}が、なんか{寂|さび}しそうに{見|み}えてしょうがなかった。
= Yeah. Seen from behind, standing alone on the stage, they looked so lonely.
あおい: {音楽|おんがく}もよかったね。{生演奏|なまえんそう}だったでしょ？
= The music was good too. That was live, wasn't it?
れん: そう、{客席|きゃくせき}の{横|よこ}にバイオリンの{人|ひと}がいたよ。{小|ちい}さい{劇場|げきじょう}だから、{音|おと}がよく{響|ひび}くんだよね。
= Yes, there was a violinist by the seats. It's a small theatre, so the sound really carries.
あおい: {台本|だいほん}も{役者|やくしゃ}さんが{書|か}いてるんだっけ？
= The actors write the script themselves too, don't they?
れん: {劇作家|げきさっか}は{別|べつ}にいるらしいよ。でも、{毎回|まいかい}{少|すこ}しずつ{変|か}わるんだって。
= Apparently there's a separate playwright. But it changes a little every night, they say.
あおい: え、じゃあもう{一回|いっかい}{見|み}たくてたまらないんだけど。
= What, then I'm dying to see it again.
れん: {千秋楽|せんしゅうらく}のチケット、まだあるかな。{帰|かえ}ったらすぐ{調|しら}べよう。
= I wonder if there are still tickets for the last night. Let's check as soon as we get home.
```

{途中|とちゅう} = partway; {千秋楽|せんしゅうらく} = the last performance of a run (originally a sumo
and kabuki word); たまんない = たまらない (casual). The speaker uses たまらない for a sensation and a
wish, ないではいられない for an action, and しょうがない in a casual "it looked so…".
