> {舞台|ぶたい}は{毎晩|まいばん}{違|ちが}う。{同|おな}じ{台本|だいほん}、{同|おな}じ{役者|やくしゃ}でも、{客席|きゃくせき}の{反応|はんのう}によって、{間|ま}の{取|と}り{方|かた}も{声|こえ}の{響|ひび}きも{変|か}わる。{役者|やくしゃ}が{観客|かんきゃく}の{笑|わら}い{声|ごえ}を{聞|き}いて、ほんの{少|すこ}し{間|ま}を{置|お}いてからせりふを{言|い}う。そのいっしゅんに、{舞台|ぶたい}と{客席|きゃくせき}は{一|ひと}つになる。そういう{夜|よる}に{出会|であ}うと、{劇場|げきじょう}を{出|で}て{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}く{間|あいだ}も、{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}ったあともだれかに{話|はな}さないではいられない。
>
> もちろん、{舞台|ぶたい}はいつもうまくいくわけではない。せりふを{忘|わす}れる{役者|やくしゃ}もいれば、{途中|とちゅう}で{眠|ねむ}くてたまらなくなる{夜|よる}もある。しかし、{失敗|しっぱい}するかもしれない{生|なま}のものだからこそ、うまくいった{夜|よる}は{見|み}る{者|もの}を{感動|かんどう}させずにはおかないのだろう。{今夜|こんや}も{私|わたし}は、{暗|くら}くなる{客席|きゃくせき}でそのしゅんかんを{待|ま}っている。

けいたい = mobile phone; せき = a cough; しゅんかん = moment, いっしゅん = an instant (their kanji are off-list);
{間|ま} = timing, a pause; せりふ = lines (in a play); {見|み}る{者|もの} =
those who watch (written style).

1. What moment does the writer love, and why?
2. What advantage of watching at home does the writer accept?
3. According to the writer, why is every performance different?
4. Why, in the writer's view, can a good night at the theatre move people so much?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The moment the auditorium goes dark: everyone falls silent and looks the same way, and the
   expectation that something is about to begin is almost painful ({好|す}きでたまらない).
2. At home you can watch films from all over the world when you like, and watch them again as
   often as you want if you record them; there are no expensive tickets, and no coughing neighbours.
3. Because the actors respond to the audience: their timing and their voices change with the
   audience's reactions.
4. Because theatre is live and might fail; that's exactly why a night that goes well can't fail
   to move the audience ({感動|かんどう}させずにはおかない).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

I love the moment the auditorium goes dark more than I can say. The talking stops, phone
screens go out, and hundreds of people look the same way. Sitting in that silence, the
expectation that something is about to begin almost makes my chest hurt.

People say that in the age of video, fewer and fewer people bother to go to the theatre. It's
true that at home you can watch films from all over the world whenever you like. Record them and
you can watch them again as many times as you want. You don't have to pay for expensive tickets,
and you aren't bothered by the coughing of the person in the next seat. Even so, I can't help feeling that the stage
has a power of its own.

The stage is different every night. With the same script and the same actors, the timing and the
ring of the voices change with the audience's reactions. An actor hears the audience laughing
and pauses for just a moment before speaking a line. In that instant, stage and audience become one. When I
come across a night like that, I can't stop myself telling someone about it, on the walk to
the station and even after I get home.

Of course, the stage doesn't always succeed. Some actors forget their lines, and some nights I
get so sleepy I can hardly bear it. But perhaps it's precisely because it is a live thing that
might fail that a night that goes well can't fail to move those who watch. Tonight, too, I'm
waiting for that moment as the auditorium goes dark.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{会|あ}いたくてたまりません。
= I'm dying to see you.
そんな{気|き}がしてならないんです。
= I just can't shake that feeling.
{笑|わら}わないではいられませんでした。
= I couldn't help laughing.
この{作品|さくひん}は、{見|み}る{人|ひと}を{感動|かんどう}させずにはおかない。
= This work can't fail to move those who see it.
{香|かお}りがたまらないですね。
= The smell is irresistible, isn't it?
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{楽|たの}しいでたまらない: an い-adjective takes くて: {楽|たの}しくてたまらない. A な-adjective
  takes で: {心配|しんぱい}でたまらない.
- Using てたまらない for someone else's feelings as a plain fact: ×{妹|いもうと}は{寂|さび}しくてたまらない.
  Say {寂|さび}しくてたまらないようだ / らしい, or {寂|さび}しがっている.
- てならない with deliberate actions: ×{走|はし}ってならない. It goes with feelings and
  impressions; for actions you can't hold back, use ないではいられない.
- ないではいられない with feelings: ×{悲|かな}しくないではいられない. Use an action
  ({泣|な}かないではいられない) or a feeling pattern ({悲|かな}しくてたまらない).
- だれ, しゅんかん, けいたい, はくしゅ: these words have kanji outside the course list, so this
  course writes them in kana. In print you'll often see them with kanji.
- ずにはおかない with your own feelings: ×{私|わたし}は{感動|かんどう}せずにはおかない. The subject is the
  thing that causes the feeling; for yourself, use {感動|かんどう}せずにはいられない.

## Key points

- 〜てたまらない: unbearably, dying to (feelings, sensations, wishes); about yourself in statements.
- 〜てならない: can't help feeling; written; best with {気|き}がする, {思|おも}える, {心配|しんぱい}.
- 〜てしょうがない: the casual version, also for annoyances (review).
- 〜ないではいられない = 〜ずにはいられない: can't stop yourself doing (actions).
- 〜ずにはおかない (to recognize): a thing can't fail to cause a reaction.
- New kanji: 芸 劇 俳 奏 模 踊 姿 影 響 鏡 紅 香 撮. Write {芸術|げいじゅつ}, {演劇|えんげき},
  {劇場|げきじょう}, {俳優|はいゆう}, {演奏|えんそう}, {影響|えいきょう}, {影|かげ}, {踊|おど}る, {撮|と}る,
  {紅茶|こうちゃ} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Exclamations: ものがある, ことに, 限りだ
topics: ことか and ものだ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 22 was about feelings too strong to bear. This lesson is about saying how something
strikes you: "there's something really moving about it", "to my surprise", "I couldn't be
happier", "how quickly they grow!". These are **[[exclamative]]** patterns: they don't add
information so much as show the speaker's surprise, admiration, joy or regret.

この{子|こ}の{絵|え}には、{大人|おとな}を{驚|おどろ}かせるものがある。 — There's something about this child's drawings that astonishes adults.
{驚|おどろ}いたことに、{三歳|さんさい}の{孫|まご}がひらがなを{全部|ぜんぶ}{読|よ}めるようになった。 — To my surprise, my three-year-old grandchild can now read all the hiragana.
{皆様|みなさま}に{応援|おうえん}していただき、{心強|こころづよ}い{限|かぎ}りです。 — Your support is a great comfort to us.
{子供|こども}の{成長|せいちょう}は、なんと{早|はや}いことか。 — How quickly children grow!

The theme is children, family and education: childcare and nursery, classes and levels,
courses and lectures, respect between the generations. N3 lesson 18 had school, pupils and
tests; many of its words are carried, and this lesson's kanji let you write them:
{授業|じゅぎょう}, {講義|こうぎ}, {教授|きょうじゅ}, {訓練|くんれん}, {仲間|なかま}, {机|つくえ}, {孫|まご},
{幼|おさな}い, {敬語|けいご}.

## There's something about it: 〜ものがある

〜ものがある says that a person or thing has a quality that makes a strong impression on you. The
part before it is an evaluation: a feeling, a verb like "move" or "astonish", or 〜べき.

| Before ものがある | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {心|こころ}を{打|う}つものがある (there's something that touches the heart) |
| い-adjective | {厳|きび}しいものがある (it's really tough) |
| な-adjective + な | {見事|みごと}なものがある (it's truly impressive) |
| 〜べき | {見|み}るべきものがある (there's something worth seeing) |

{彼女|かのじょ}の{講演|こうえん}には、{聞|き}く{人|ひと}の{心|こころ}を{動|うご}かすものがあった。 — There was something in her lecture that moved everyone who heard it.
{一人|ひとり}で{三人|さんにん}の{子供|こども}を{育|そだ}てる{苦労|くろう}には、{大変|たいへん}なものがある。 — Raising three children on your own is really hard work.
{新人|しんじん}{講師|こうし}だが、{教|おし}え{方|かた}には{光|ひか}るものがある。 — They're a new lecturer, but there's something brilliant about the way they teach.

Points:

- It's about a quality, not a thing you can point at: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}に{本|ほん}がある is just
  "there's a book on the desk". ものがある gives your judgement of something you've observed.
- It sounds measured and a little formal: commentaries, reviews, speeches. In casual speech
  you'd say {心|こころ}に{響|ひび}くよね or すごいよね.
- {光|ひか}るものがある (shows real promise) and {見|み}るべきものがある (has merit) are common set
  combinations.

## To my surprise: 〜ことに

〜ことに goes at the start of a sentence and says how you feel about what follows: "to my
surprise", "sadly", "luckily".

| Form | Examples |
|---|---|
| verb, た form + ことに | {驚|おどろ}いたことに, {困|こま}ったことに, {感心|かんしん}したことに |
| い-adjective + ことに | うれしいことに, ありがたいことに, {悲|かな}しいことに |
| な-adjective + なことに | {残念|ざんねん}なことに, {不思議|ふしぎ}なことに, {幸|さいわ}いなことに |

{残念|ざんねん}なことに、{雨|あめ}で{運動会|うんどうかい}が{中止|ちゅうし}になった。 — Unfortunately, the sports day was cancelled because of rain.
ありがたいことに、{近所|きんじょ}に{評判|ひょうばん}のいい{保育園|ほいくえん}がある。 — Luckily, there's a nursery with a good reputation in our neighbourhood.
{不思議|ふしぎ}なことに、{兄弟|きょうだい}でも{性格|せいかく}はまったく{違|ちが}う。 — Strangely enough, even siblings can have completely different personalities.

The feeling is the speaker's, and the fact that follows is real. So it doesn't go with requests,
orders or the volitional: ×{残念|ざんねん}なことに、{帰|かえ}ってください. It's written or formal
speech; in conversation, {驚|おどろ}いたことに is also common, but casual speakers more often say
びっくりしたんだけど, {残念|ざんねん}だけど.

## I couldn't be more…: 〜{限|かぎ}りだ

〜{限|かぎ}りだ (written with kanji, like the other {限|かぎ}り patterns in this course) says your feeling
is as strong as it gets: "extremely", "I couldn't be more…". It follows a feeling adjective in
its dictionary form (な-adjectives with な).

うれしい{限|かぎ}りだ (I couldn't be happier) · {心強|こころづよ}い{限|かぎ}りだ (most reassuring) ·
{頼|たの}もしい{限|かぎ}りだ (so dependable) · {寂|さび}しい{限|かぎ}りだ (so lonely, so sad) ·
うらやましい{限|かぎ}りだ (I'm so envious) · {残念|ざんねん}な{限|かぎ}りだ (most regrettable) ·
{喜|よろこ}ばしい{限|かぎ}りだ (a cause for great joy)

{孫|まご}が{三人|さんにん}も{集|あつ}まってくれて、うれしい{限|かぎ}りです。 — As many as three of my grandchildren came to see me: I couldn't be happier.
{子供|こども}の{数|かず}が{減|へ}って{学校|がっこう}が{閉|と}じるのは、{寂|さび}しい{限|かぎ}りだ。 — It's so sad that the school is closing because there are fewer children.
{若|わか}い{先生|せんせい}たちが{本当|ほんとう}に{頼|たの}もしい{限|かぎ}りです。 — The young teachers are so dependable.

Points:

- It's about your own feeling (or your side's), like てたまらない: ×{田中|たなか}さんはうれしい{限|かぎ}りだ.
- It's formal: speeches, letters, greetings. With friends: めっちゃうれしい, ほんとにうれしい.
- Don't confuse it with lesson 20's 〜{限|かぎ}り(は) "as long as" and できる{限|かぎ}り "as much as
  possible". {限|かぎ}りだ at the end of a sentence after a feeling word is the exclamation.

## Review: 〜ことか and 〜ものだ (N3 lessons 20 and 9)

> **Review.** どれだけ / どんなに / なんと 〜ことか is "how…!": {子供|こども}の{笑顔|えがお}にどれだけ{救|すく}われた
> ことか (how much my child's smile has saved me!). 〜ものだ is a feeling about something in general
> or in the past: {子供|こども}はすぐ{大|おお}きくなるものだ (children do grow up fast),
> {子供|こども}のころはよく{川|かわ}で{遊|あそ}んだものだ (I used to play in the river as a child).

## To recognize: 〜といったらない

〜といったらない ("there are no words for it") is an informal-sounding but strong exclamation:
"indescribably, unbelievably". It usually follows a noun, often one made with 〜さ.

{初|はじ}めて{孫|まご}を{抱|だ}いたときのうれしさといったらなかった。 — I can't tell you how happy I was the first time I held my grandchild.
{朝|あさ}の{電車|でんしゃ}の{混|こ}み{方|かた}といったらない。 — The crush on the morning trains is something else.

In casual speech: 〜ったらない. It can be positive or negative; context tells which.

## Exclamation patterns compared

| Pattern | What it shows | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ものがある | a strong impression of a quality | formal, measured | {心|こころ}を{打|う}つものがある |
| 〜ことに | your feeling about the fact that follows | written, formal | {残念|ざんねん}なことに |
| 〜{限|かぎ}りだ | your feeling at its strongest | formal (speeches, letters) | うれしい{限|かぎ}りだ |
| どれだけ〜ことか | how much…! | neutral, written | どれだけ{泣|な}いたことか |
| 〜ものだ | a feeling about how things are, or were | neutral | {早|はや}いものだ |
| 〜といったらない | indescribably (to recognize) | spoken, strong | うれしさといったらない |

## Children and education: words

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| young children | {幼児|ようじ}, {乳児|にゅうじ}, {新生児|しんせいじ}, {児童|じどう}, {幼少期|ようしょうき}, おむつ, {授乳|じゅにゅう}, {寝|ね}かしつける, {子守|こもり} |
| childcare | {育児|いくじ}, {保育|ほいく}, {保育園|ほいくえん}, {保育士|ほいくし}, {学童保育|がくどうほいく}, {児童館|じどうかん}, {小児科|しょうにか}, {甘|あま}やかす, {見守|みまも}る |
| family | {孫|まご}, {孫娘|まごむすめ}, ひ{孫|まご}, {子孫|しそん}, {父母|ふぼ}, {姉妹|しまい}, {次男|じなん}, {一家|いっか}, {授|さず}かる, {仲人|なこうど} |
| school | {学級|がっきゅう}, {学級委員|がっきゅういいん}, {同級生|どうきゅうせい}, {進級|しんきゅう}, {在校生|ざいこうせい}, {新入生|しんにゅうせい}, {母校|ぼこう}, {保護者|ほごしゃ}, {参観|さんかん}, {自習|じしゅう}, {教材|きょうざい}, {家庭教師|かていきょうし}, {優等生|ゆうとうせい} |
| levels | {級|きゅう}, {初級|しょきゅう}, {中級|ちゅうきゅう}, {上級|じょうきゅう}, {高級|こうきゅう}, {年長|ねんちょう}, {年少|ねんしょう} |
| courses and lectures | {講師|こうし}, {講座|こうざ}, {講演|こうえん}, {講演会|こうえんかい}, {受講|じゅこう}, {講習|こうしゅう}, {休講|きゅうこう}, {教養|きょうよう}, {童話|どうわ} |
| respect and wisdom | {尊敬|そんけい}, {尊重|そんちょう}, {尊|とうと}い, {尊|とうと}ぶ, {敬|うやま}う, {敬意|けいい}, {敬老|けいろう}, {年長者|ねんちょうしゃ}, {賢|かしこ}い, {賢明|けんめい}, {教訓|きょうくん}, {家訓|かくん}, {弟子|でし}, {仲|なか}, {仲間入|なかまい}り |
| feelings for {限|かぎ}りだ | {心強|こころづよ}い, {頼|たの}もしい, {喜|よろこ}ばしい, {大人|おとな}びる (to act grown-up) |

Notes:

- {保育園|ほいくえん} is a day nursery (for children of working parents, from babies up);
  ようちえん, kindergarten, is a school for ages three to five (its second kanji is off-list).
  {年少|ねんしょう}, {年中|ねんちゅう}, {年長|ねんちょう} are the three year groups there, youngest first.
  {学童保育|がくどうほいく} is after-school care for primary school children.
- {児童|じどう} is the formal word for children, especially primary school pupils
  ({児童|じどう}{数|すう}, number of pupils). Sounds like N4's {自動|じどう} (automatic).
- {講演|こうえん} is a lecture or talk to an audience; it sounds like N5's {公園|こうえん} (park) and
  N3's {公演|こうえん} (performance). {講座|こうざ} (a course) sounds like {口座|こうざ} (a bank account).
- {敬老|けいろう}の{日|ひ} is a national holiday in September for honouring older people.
- {仲人|なこうど} (a go-between at a wedding) is a special reading: 仲 is usually なか or チュウ.
- {授|さず}かる is to be blessed with, often of children ({子供|こども}を{授|さず}かる).
- {甘|あま}やかす is to spoil (a child); it's the causative-like partner of {甘|あま}える (lesson 19).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: children and family, teaching and learning, people and respect.

### Children and family

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 童 | child | ドウ | — | 12 | {児童|じどう}, {童話|どうわ}, {学童保育|がくどうほいく} |
| 児 | child, infant | ジ, ニ | — | 7 | {児童|じどう}, {幼児|ようじ}, {育児|いくじ}, {乳児|にゅうじ}, {新生児|しんせいじ}, {小児科|しょうにか} |
| 幼 | very young | ヨウ | おさな(い) | 5 | {幼|おさな}い, {幼|おさな}なじみ, {幼児|ようじ}, {幼少期|ようしょうき} |
| 孫 | grandchild | ソン | まご | 10 | {孫|まご}, {孫娘|まごむすめ}, ひ{孫|まご}, {子孫|しそん} |

- {幼|おさな}い, {幼|おさな}なじみ (N3) and {孫|まご} (N4) are now written with kanji.
- 児 is ニ only in {小児科|しょうにか} (paediatrics).

### Teaching and learning

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 訓 | teach; Japanese reading | クン | — | 10 | {訓|くん}, {訓練|くんれん}, {教訓|きょうくん}, {家訓|かくん} |
| 授 | give, grant; teach | ジュ | さず(ける), さず(かる) | 11 | {授業|じゅぎょう}, {授業料|じゅぎょうりょう}, {教授|きょうじゅ}, {授乳|じゅにゅう}, {授|さず}かる |
| 講 | lecture | コウ | — | 17 | {講義|こうぎ}, {講演|こうえん}, {講師|こうし}, {講座|こうざ}, {受講|じゅこう}, {休講|きゅうこう} |
| 机 | desk | キ | つくえ | 6 | {机|つくえ} |
| 級 | grade, level, class | キュウ | — | 9 | {級|きゅう}, {学級|がっきゅう}, {初級|しょきゅう}, {中級|ちゅうきゅう}, {上級|じょうきゅう}, {同級生|どうきゅうせい} |

- {訓練|くんれん}, {授業|じゅぎょう}, {授業料|じゅぎょうりょう}, {教授|きょうじゅ}, {講義|こうぎ} (N3) and
  {机|つくえ} (N5) are now written with kanji.
- {訓|くん} is a kanji's Japanese reading (kun'yomi): {音|おん}と{訓|くん}. It sounds like the name suffix
  〜くん.
- 級 has a sound change in {学級|がっきゅう} (がく + きゅう).

### People and respect

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 仲 | relationship; go-between | チュウ | なか | 6 | {仲|なか}, {仲間|なかま}, {仲良|なかよ}し, {仲直|なかなお}り, {仲間入|なかまい}り, {仲人|なこうど} |
| 尊 | precious, respect | ソン | とうと(い), とうと(ぶ) | 12 | {尊敬|そんけい}, {尊重|そんちょう}, {尊敬語|そんけいご}, {尊|とうと}い, {尊|とうと}ぶ |
| 敬 | respect | ケイ | うやま(う) | 12 | {敬語|けいご}, {敬具|けいぐ}, {敬|うやま}う, {敬意|けいい}, {敬老|けいろう} |
| 賢 | wise, clever | ケン | かしこ(い) | 16 | {賢|かしこ}い, {賢明|けんめい} |

- {仲間|なかま}, {仲良|なかよ}し, {仲直|なかなお}り (N3), {敬語|けいご}, {尊敬語|そんけいご} and
  {敬具|けいぐ} (N4) are now written with kanji.
- {尊|とうと}い and {尊|とうと}ぶ are also read たっとい, たっとぶ; とうとい is the more common today.

Memory notes:

- 童 is 立 (stand, N5) over 里 (village): the children standing about the village.
- 児 is 旧 (old, lesson 8) shape over 儿 (legs): a toddler's head and wobbly legs.
- 幼 is 幺 (a tiny thread) and 力 (strength): only a little strength.
- 孫 is 子 (child) and 系 (line, lineage): the next child in the family line.
- 訓 is 言 (words) and 川 (river): words that flow down to the next person.
- 授 is a hand (扌) and 受 (receive, N3): one hand gives and the other receives.
- 講 is 言 (words) and a frame built up of crossed sticks: words built up, a lecture.
- 机 is 木 (wood) and 几 (a small table): a wooden desk.
- 級 is 糸 (thread) and 及 (reach, lesson 17): the steps of thread that reach up, grades.
- 仲 is a person (亻) and 中 (middle): the person in the middle, the go-between.
- 尊 is a wine jar over 寸 (a hand): a jar offered with respect.
- 敬 has 攵 (strike) on the right: discipline, respect.
- 賢 has 貝 (shell, money) at the bottom: clever with resources.

```trace
童児幼孫訓授講机仲尊敬賢級
```

## Dialogue: at the nursery gate

まき comes to pick up her son ゆうと, and his teacher, なつみ, tells her about the day. (Polite speech; the
teacher uses keigo to the parent.)

```dialogue
# Pick-up time
なつみ: あ、ゆうとくんのお{母|かあ}さん、お{帰|かえ}りなさい。
= Ah, Yūto's mother, welcome back.
まき: {先生|せんせい}、{今日|きょう}もありがとうございました。{何|なに}か{変|か}わったことはありませんでしたか。
= Thank you again for today. Did anything unusual happen?
なつみ: それが、{驚|おどろ}いたことに、ゆうとくんが{初|はじ}めて{自分|じぶん}から「{手伝|てつだ}う」って{言|い}ってくれたんですよ。{年少|ねんしょう}さんのお{昼寝|ひるね}の{準備|じゅんび}を。
= Well, to our surprise, Yūto offered to help for the first time, all on his own. Getting the youngest ones ready for their nap.
まき: えっ、うちの{子|こ}がですか。{家|いえ}では{甘|あま}えてばかりなのに。
= What, my son? At home he does nothing but act like a baby.
なつみ: {年長|ねんちょう}さんになって、ずいぶん{大人|おとな}びてきましたね。{小|ちい}さい{子|こ}への{優|やさ}しさには、{見|み}ていて{感心|かんしん}するものがあります。
= Now that he's in the oldest group, he's really grown up. The kindness he shows the little ones is something to see.
まき: そうですか。うれしい{限|かぎ}りです。
= Really? That makes me so happy.
なつみ: それから、{来週|らいしゅう}の{保育|ほいく}{参観|さんかん}ですが、お{父|とう}さんもいらっしゃいますか。
= And about next week's open day, will his father be coming too?
まき: はい、{二人|ふたり}で{伺|うかが}います。{残念|ざんねん}なことに、{祖父母|そふぼ}は{遠|とお}くて{来|こ}られないんですけど。
= Yes, we'll both come. Unfortunately his grandparents live far away and can't make it.
なつみ: では、{当日|とうじつ}の{写真|しゃしん}をれんらくちょうと{一緒|いっしょ}にお{渡|わた}ししましょうか。
= Then shall I give you some photos from the day, with his notebook?
まき: ありがとうございます。{先生|せんせい}がいてくださって、{本当|ほんとう}に{心強|こころづよ}い{限|かぎ}りです。
= Thank you so much. It's such a comfort to have you as his teacher.
なつみ: いえいえ。ゆうとくん、お{母|かあ}さん{来|き}たよー。
= Oh, not at all. Yūto, your mum's here!
ゆうと: ママー！{今日|きょう}ね、{小|ちい}さい{子|こ}にえほん{読|よ}んであげたんだよ！
= Mummy! Today I read a picture book to the little ones!
まき: すごいね。{家|いえ}でも{読|よ}んでくれるとうれしいな。
= Wow. I'd be happy if you read to me at home too.
```

{昼寝|ひるね} = nap; {保育|ほいく}{参観|さんかん} = open day at a nursery; れんらくちょう = the notebook that
goes between nursery and home (its last kanji is off-list); {当日|とうじつ} = on the day. The teacher speaks of the parent's family with
honorific いらっしゃる; the parent humbles herself with {伺|うかが}う. Note that the formal
{限|かぎ}りです and ことに come from the adults; the child speaks casual Japanese.

## Reading: a letter to a former teacher

A letter from a former pupil, now a primary school teacher, to the teacher they had at the same
age (です/ます style; letters have their own opening and closing words).

> {山下先生|やましたせんせい}
>
> {秋|あき}も{深|ふか}まってまいりましたが、お{元気|げんき}でいらっしゃいますか。{小学校|しょうがっこう}で{先生|せんせい}の{学級|がっきゅう}にいた{森|もり}です。
>
> {実|じつ}は、この{春|はる}から{私|わたし}も{小学校|しょうがっこう}の{教師|きょうし}になりました。うれしいことに、{初|はじ}めての{勤務|きんむ}{先|さき}は、{私|わたし}の{母校|ぼこう}です。{担当|たんとう}は{三年生|さんねんせい}で、{先生|せんせい}が{私|わたし}たちを{受|う}け{持|も}ってくださったのと{同|おな}じ{学年|がくねん}です。
>
> {毎日|まいにち}{子供|こども}たちの{前|まえ}に{立|た}つと、{先生|せんせい}のことを{思|おも}い{出|だ}します。{先生|せんせい}はどんなに{忙|いそが}しくても、{児童|じどう}{一人一人|ひとりひとり}の{話|はなし}を{最後|さいご}まで{聞|き}いてくださいました。{今|いま}になって、それがどれだけ{大変|たいへん}なことだったか、よく{分|わ}かります。{教室|きょうしつ}の{机|つくえ}に{向|む}かって、{遅|おそ}くまで{連絡|れんらく}ノートに{返事|へんじ}を{書|か}いていらっしゃった{姿|すがた}も、よく{覚|おぼ}えています。
>
> {子供|こども}たちの{力|ちから}には、{驚|おどろ}かされるものがあります。{先日|せんじつ}、クラスで{一番|いちばん}{静|しず}かな{男|おとこ}の{子|こ}が、{国語|こくご}の{時間|じかん}に{自分|じぶん}で{作|つく}った{童話|どうわ}を{読|よ}みました。{不思議|ふしぎ}なことに、いつもはうるさい{子|こ}たちも、{最後|さいご}までじっと{聞|き}いていました。{読|よ}み{終|お}わったときの、あの{子|こ}のうれしそうな{顔|かお}といったらありませんでした。
>
> {正直|しょうじき}に{言|い}えば、{失敗|しっぱい}ばかりの{毎日|まいにち}で、{自分|じぶん}が{情|なさ}けなくなることもあります。それでも、{先生|せんせい}のように{子供|こども}を{尊重|そんちょう}できる{教師|きょうし}になりたいと{思|おも}っています。
>
> {寒|さむ}くなりますので、どうぞお{体|からだ}を{大切|たいせつ}になさってください。いつか{先生|せんせい}にお{会|あ}いして、{子供|こども}たちの{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いていただけたら、うれしい{限|かぎ}りです。
>
> {森|もり}あかり

{深|ふか}まってまいりました = has deepened (a seasonal opening for letters); {勤務|きんむ}{先|さき} = place of
work; {受|う}け{持|も}つ = to be in charge of a class; {情|なさ}けない = pathetic (N3). The
grammar of the lesson: うれしいことに, ものがあります, {不思議|ふしぎ}なことに, といったらありませんでした
(the polite past of といったらない), {限|かぎ}りです, and どれだけ〜か (どれだけ〜ことか without こと).

1. What happened to the writer this spring, and what is special about it?
2. What does the writer remember about Mr or Ms Yamashita?
3. What happened in the Japanese lesson, and what surprised the writer?
4. What would make the writer very happy?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The writer became a primary school teacher, and their first school is their old school
   ({母校|ぼこう}); they teach the same year their teacher taught them.
2. However busy the teacher was, they listened to every pupil until the end; the writer also
   remembers them writing replies in the notebooks until late.
3. The quietest boy in the class read a children's story he had written himself; strangely,
   even the noisy children listened quietly to the end.
4. To meet their old teacher one day and have the teacher listen to their stories about the children.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Dear Mr/Ms Yamashita,

Autumn is drawing on; I hope you are keeping well. This is Mori, who was in your class at
primary school.

The fact is that this spring I too became a primary school teacher. I'm happy to say that the
first school I've been sent to is my old school. I teach Year 3, the same year you taught us.

Every day when I stand in front of the children, I think of you. However busy you were, you
always listened to each and every pupil until they had finished. Only now do I really understand
how hard that must have been. I also remember well how you sat at the desk in the
classroom until late, writing replies in our home-school notebooks.

There is something astonishing about children's abilities. The other day, the quietest boy in
my class read out a story he'd written himself in our Japanese lesson. Strangely, even the
children who are usually noisy listened quietly to the end. I can't tell you how happy he looked
when he'd finished.

To be honest, my days are full of mistakes, and sometimes I feel hopeless. Even so, I want to
become a teacher who respects children the way you did.

It's getting colder, so please take good care of yourself. Nothing would make me happier than
to meet you one day and tell you about the children.

Akari Mori

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{驚|おどろ}いたことに、{全部|ぜんぶ}{一人|ひとり}でできました。
= To my surprise, they did it all by themselves.
この{子|こ}の{絵|え}には、{光|ひか}るものがありますね。
= There's real promise in this child's drawing.
{皆様|みなさま}にお{会|あ}いできて、うれしい{限|かぎ}りです。
= I'm delighted to meet you all.
{残念|ざんねん}なことに、{今日|きょう}は{休講|きゅうこう}です。
= Unfortunately, today's lecture is cancelled.
```

## Common mistakes

- ものがある about a concrete object: ×{教室|きょうしつ}に{面白|おもしろ}いものがある means "there's an
  interesting thing in the classroom". For an impression, the noun is the person or thing that
  has the quality: {彼|かれ}の{話|はなし}には{面白|おもしろ}いものがある.
- ×{残念|ざんねん}ことに: な-adjectives need な: {残念|ざんねん}なことに.
- ことに followed by a request: ×うれしいことに、{来|き}てください. What follows ことに is a fact.
- {限|かぎ}りだ about someone else: ×{母|はは}はうれしい{限|かぎ}りだ. It's your own feeling.
- Mixing up {限|かぎ}りだ (I couldn't be more…) with lesson 20's ない{限|かぎ}り (unless).
- {児童|じどう} and {幼児|ようじ}: {児童|じどう} is school age (in law, under 18; in everyday use,
  primary school pupils); {幼児|ようじ} is a small child before school.

## Key points

- 〜ものがある: there's something (impressive, hard, moving) about it; a judgement, formal.
- 〜ことに: at the start: to my surprise ({驚|おどろ}いたことに), unfortunately ({残念|ざんねん}なことに); a
  fact follows.
- 〜{限|かぎ}りだ: I couldn't be more…; your own feeling; formal (speeches and letters).
- どれだけ〜ことか, 〜ものだ: exclamations (review); 〜といったらない: indescribably (to recognize).
- New kanji: 童 児 幼 孫 訓 授 講 机 仲 尊 敬 賢 級. Write {授業|じゅぎょう}, {講義|こうぎ}, {教授|きょうじゅ},
  {訓練|くんれん}, {仲間|なかま}, {机|つくえ}, {孫|まご}, {幼|おさな}い, {敬語|けいご} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Hearsay and seeming: とか, という話だ, かのように, げ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Two questions run through this lesson: how did you hear it, and how does it look? Japanese
marks **[[hearsay]]** (information you got from someone else) carefully, and it has many ways of
describing **[[likeness]]** (looking like, seeming, as if). N3 gave you そうだ, らしい, ようだ,
みたい, っぽい, ということだ and とのことだ; this lesson adds the N2 ones.

{田中|たなか}さん、{来月|らいげつ}{結婚|けっこん}するとか。 — I hear Tanaka's getting married next month.
この{店|みせ}の{古着|ふるぎ}は、{全部|ぜんぶ}{店長|てんちょう}が{選|えら}んでいるという{話|はなし}だ。 — The story is that the manager picks all the second-hand clothes in this shop.
{彼|かれ}は{何|なに}も{知|し}らないかのように{笑|わら}っていた。 — He was smiling as if he knew nothing.
{子供|こども}は{新|あたら}しい{服|ふく}を{着|き}て、{得意|とくい}げな{顔|かお}をしている。 — The child is wearing new clothes and looks very pleased with themselves.
{気持|きも}ちのいい{食|た}べっぷりですね。 — It's a pleasure to watch you eat.

The theme is clothes, cloth and appearance: fabric and thread, garments and costumes, skin care,
dressing up, washing and looking after clothes. N3 lesson 16 had fashion basics, and many carried words
now take kanji: {帽子|ぼうし}, {眼鏡|めがね}, {服装|ふくそう}, {汗|あせ}, {洗濯|せんたく}, {磨|みが}く,
{塗|ぬ}る, {柔|やわ}らかい, {布団|ふとん}, {財布|さいふ}.

## I hear: 〜とか

At the end of a sentence, plain form + とか passes on something you've heard, a little vaguely:
"I hear that…, apparently…". It's softer and less certain than そうだ, and it's common in
conversation, in polite speech too, and in letters.

{駅前|えきまえ}の{古着屋|ふるぎや}、{来月|らいげつ}{閉店|へいてん}するとか。 — I hear the second-hand clothes shop by the station is closing next month.
{今年|ことし}の{冬|ふゆ}は{寒|さむ}くなるとかで、コートがよく{売|う}れているそうです。 — They say winter's going to be cold this year, so coats are selling well.
おじょうさん、{大学|だいがく}に{合格|ごうかく}なさったとか。おめでとうございます。 — I hear your daughter got into university. Congratulations.

(おじょうさん, someone else's daughter, is in kana: its kanji is off-list.)

Points:

- 〜とかで in the middle of a sentence gives a reason you've heard: {風邪|かぜ}をひいたとかで{休|やす}んで
  いる (he's off, with a cold or something).
- Nouns and な-adjectives take だ: {雨|あめ}だとか, {有名|ゆうめい}だとか.
- Don't confuse it with listing とか ({服|ふく}とか{靴|くつ}とか, N4). The hearsay とか ends the
  sentence or comes before で.

## The story is: 〜という{話|はなし}だ

〜という{話|はなし}だ is "the story is that…, I've heard that…". It's neutral and spoken, a little
more definite than とか. In casual speech: 〜って{話|はなし}だよ.

この{布|ぬの}は{手|て}で{織|お}ったものだという{話|はなし}です。 — I'm told this cloth was woven by hand.
あの{俳優|はいゆう}、{衣装|いしょう}を{全部|ぜんぶ}{自分|じぶん}で{選|えら}んでるって{話|はなし}だよ。 — Apparently that actor chooses all their costumes themselves.

> **Review: 〜ということだ, 〜とのことだ, 〜とみられる, 〜とされる (N3 lesson 22).** ということだ
> passes on information neutrally; とのことだ is the formal version for messages
> ({部長|ぶちょう}は{遅|おく}れるとのことです). In news and writing, 〜とみられる is "is thought to be"
> ({原因|げんいん}は{火|ひ}の{不始末|ふしまつ}とみられる) and 〜とされる is "is regarded as, is said to be"
> (めんは{肌|はだ}に{優|やさ}しいとされる: cotton is said to be kind to the skin; めん is in kana, as its kanji is off-list). The sheet "Hearsay and likeness" ranks them all by how sure
> the speaker is and how they heard.

## As if: 〜かのように, 〜かのようだ

〜かのように (N3 met it for recognition) is "as if", for something that isn't really so.
It often comes with まるで, or in writing あたかも.

| Before かのように | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {知|し}らないかのように, {見|み}たかのように |
| い-adjective | {暑|あつ}いかのように |
| noun / な-adjective + である, or だった | {本物|ほんもの}であるかのように, {夏|なつ}だったかのように |

{彼女|かのじょ}は{何|なに}もなかったかのように、{普段着|ふだんぎ}で{現|あらわ}れた。 — She turned up in her everyday clothes as if nothing had happened.
この{生地|きじ}は、まるできぬであるかのような{手触|てざわ}りだ。 — This fabric feels as if it were silk.
{彼|かれ}はあたかも{自分|じぶん}がデザインしたかのように{話|はな}した。 — He talked as though he had designed it himself.

(きぬ, silk, is in kana: its kanji is off-list.)

Before a noun, かのような: {夢|ゆめ}を{見|み}ているかのような{気分|きぶん} (a feeling as if I were
dreaming). At the end: 〜かのようだ.

### ようだ or かのようだ?

ようだ can be a guess ("it seems that"), and ような can be a plain comparison ("like"). The か of
かのようだ shows the speaker knows it isn't true: it's only an appearance.

| | 〜ようだ | 〜かのようだ |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | seems (a guess) / is like | as if (but it isn't) |
| Example | {外|そと}は{寒|さむ}いようだ (it seems cold outside: maybe it is) | {外|そと}は{冬|ふゆ}が{戻|もど}ってきたかのようだ (it's as if winter had come back: it hasn't) |
| Register | neutral | written, vivid |

{雪|ゆき}のように{白|しろ}い{肌|はだ} (skin as white as snow) is a plain simile; かのように needs a whole
clause, not just a noun: ×{雪|ゆき}かのように.

## Looking…: 〜げ

The stem of an adjective + げ (from {気|け}, "air, look") makes a な-adjective: "looking…, with an air
of…". It describes how someone seems to an observer. It's a little literary, and you'll meet it
most in stories and writing.

| Adjective | 〜げ | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {寂|さび}しい | {寂|さび}しげ | lonely-looking |
| {悲|かな}しい | {悲|かな}しげ | sad-looking |
| {楽|たの}しい | {楽|たの}しげ | cheerful |
| {不安|ふあん}な | {不安|ふあん}げ | anxious-looking |
| {得意|とくい}な | {得意|とくい}げ | proud, pleased with oneself |
| {自信|じしん}がある | {自信|じしん}ありげ | confident-looking |

{少年|しょうねん}は{寂|さび}しげな{後|うし}ろ{姿|すがた}を{見|み}せて、{帰|かえ}っていった。 — The boy went home, a lonely figure from behind.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{新|あたら}しいジャケットを{得意|とくい}げに{見|み}せてくれた。 — She proudly showed me her new jacket.
{何|なに}か{言|い}いたげな{顔|かお}だね。 — You look as if you want to say something.

〜たげ ({言|い}いたげ, from 〜たい) is "looking as if wanting to". いい + げ is irregular: よさげ
("looks good"), casual and recent.

げ and そう overlap: {楽|たの}しそうな{顔|かお} and {楽|たの}しげな{顔|かお} are both "a happy-looking face".
そう is everyday; げ is more literary. そう also predicts ({雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りそうだ: it looks like
rain), which げ can't do: ×{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りげ.

## The way someone does it: 〜ぶり, 〜っぷり

A noun or a verb's ます stem + ぶり is "the way someone does it", usually as you see it:
{仕事|しごと}ぶり (the way someone works), {話|はな}しぶり (the way someone talks), {生活|せいかつ}ぶり
(the way someone lives). With eating and drinking verbs it often becomes っぷり and sounds
admiring: {食|た}べっぷり, {飲|の}みっぷり.

{新人|しんじん}の{仕事|しごと}ぶりを{見|み}て、{店長|てんちょう}は{安心|あんしん}した。 — Seeing how the new employee worked, the manager was relieved.
{彼|かれ}の{話|はな}しぶりから、{服|ふく}が{本当|ほんとう}に{好|す}きなことが{分|わ}かる。 — You can tell from the way he talks that he really loves clothes.

After a length of time, ぶり is "for the first time in": {三年|さんねん}ぶりに{着物|きもの}を{着|き}た (I wore
a kimono for the first time in three years). N3's {久|ひさ}しぶり is this ぶり.

> **Review: 〜っぽい (N3 lesson 16).** Noun or stem + っぽい is "-ish, -looking": {子供|こども}っぽい
> (childish), {安|やす}っぽい (cheap-looking), {忘|わす}れっぽい (forgetful). It's casual. Compare
> {大人|おとな}っぽい{服装|ふくそう} (clothes that look grown-up) with {大人|おとな}らしい{服装|ふくそう} (clothes
> that suit a grown-up).

## Clothes, cloth and appearance: words

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| skin | {肌|はだ}, {素肌|すはだ}, {肌色|はだいろ}, {肌荒|はだあ}れ, {美肌|びはだ}, {保湿|ほしつ}, {日焼|ひや}け{止|ど}め, {美容|びよう}, メイク, {肌寒|はださむ}い, {肌触|はだざわ}り, {手触|てざわ}り |
| sweat and eyes | {汗|あせ}かき, {汗|あせ}ばむ, {汗|あせ}だく, {冷|ひ}や{汗|あせ}, {眼科|がんか}, {近眼|きんがん}, {肉眼|にくがん} |
| garments | {衣|ころも}, {衣服|いふく}, {衣類|いるい}, {衣装|いしょう}, {肌着|はだぎ}, {下着|したぎ}, {普段着|ふだんぎ}, {晴|は}れ{着|ぎ}, {古着|ふるぎ}, {毛皮|けがわ}, ジャケット, スカーフ, マフラー, ストッキング, スニーカー |
| dressing | {装|よそお}う, {正装|せいそう}, {変装|へんそう}, {着|き}こなし, コーディネート, {重|かさ}ね{着|ぎ}, {厚着|あつぎ}, {薄着|うすぎ}, {着付|きつ}け, {身|み}なり, {着心地|きごこち}, {色合|いろあ}い, ブランド, {衣替|ころもが}え, {衣食住|いしょくじゅう} |
| cloth and thread | {布|ぬの}, {布地|ぬのじ}, {生地|きじ}, {糸|いと}, {毛糸|けいと}, {織物|おりもの}, {織|お}る, {編|あ}む, {編|あ}み{物|もの}, {手編|てあ}み, {毛玉|けだま}, {毛布|もうふ}, {仕立|した}てる, {糸口|いとぐち}, {組織|そしき} |

| seeming | {本物|ほんもの}, あたかも, いかにも, {得意|とくい}げ, {若々|わかわか}しい |

Notes:

- {生地|きじ} is the cloth a garment is made of ({生地|きじ}が{厚|あつ}い); {布|ぬの} is cloth in general;
  {布地|ぬのじ} is cloth as material, a little formal. {生地|きじ} sounds like N4's きじ (an article).
- {衣服|いふく} is "clothing" in general, {衣類|いるい} "clothes" as a category (in shops, laundry),
  {衣装|いしょう} "costume" (for the stage, a wedding). {衣|ころも} is old-fashioned for clothes, and
  is also the coating on tempura.
- {衣替|ころもが}え is changing your wardrobe between seasons (traditionally in June and October).
- {糸口|いとぐち} is literally the end of a thread: a clue, a way in ({解決|かいけつ}の{糸口|いとぐち}).
  {組織|そしき} is an organization (and a tissue in biology): the kanji is the one for weaving.
- {汗|あせ}かき is a person who sweats a lot; {汗|あせ}だく is dripping with sweat (casual).
- {濯|すす}ぐ is to rinse; in print you'll also see すすぐ in kana, or other kanji.
- いかにも is "truly, just what you'd expect": いかにも{高|たか}そうな{服|ふく} (clothes that look
  every bit as expensive as they are). あたかも (as if) belongs with かのように and is written.
- {眼鏡|めがね} (N5's めがね) is a special reading: neither がん nor きょう.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: the body's surface, clothes, cloth and thread, and looking after things.

### The body's surface

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 肌 | skin | — | はだ | 6 | {肌|はだ}, {肌着|はだぎ}, {素肌|すはだ}, {肌寒|はださむ}い, {肌触|はだざわ}り |
| 汗 | sweat | カン | あせ | 6 | {汗|あせ}, {汗|あせ}かき, {冷|ひ}や{汗|あせ}, {汗|あせ}ばむ |
| 眼 | eye | ガン | まなこ | 11 | {眼科|がんか}, {近眼|きんがん}, {肉眼|にくがん}, {眼鏡|めがね} (special reading) |

- {汗|あせ} (N3) and {眼鏡|めがね} (N5) are now written with kanji.
- 眼 is the formal or medical "eye"; everyday 目 is still the word for eyes.

### Clothes

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 衣 | clothes, garment | イ | ころも | 6 | {衣服|いふく}, {衣類|いるい}, {衣装|いしょう}, {衣|ころも}, {衣替|ころもが}え, {浴衣|ゆかた} (lesson 25) |
| 帽 | cap, hat | ボウ | — | 12 | {帽子|ぼうし} |
| 装 | dress, wear; equip | ソウ, ショウ | よそお(う) | 12 | {服装|ふくそう}, {正装|せいそう}, {変装|へんそう}, {装|よそお}う, {衣装|いしょう} |

- {帽子|ぼうし} (N5) and {服装|ふくそう} (N3) are now written with kanji.
- 装 is ショウ in {衣装|いしょう}, ソウ elsewhere.

### Cloth and thread

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 糸 | thread | シ | いと | 6 | {糸|いと}, {毛糸|けいと}, {糸口|いとぐち} |
| 布 | cloth | フ | ぬの | 5 | {布|ぬの}, {布地|ぬのじ}, {毛布|もうふ}, {財布|さいふ}, {布団|ふとん} |
| 織 | weave | ショク, シキ | お(る) | 18 | {織|お}る, {織物|おりもの}, {組織|そしき} |
| 柔 | soft, gentle | ジュウ | やわ(らかい) | 9 | {柔|やわ}らかい, {柔道|じゅうどう}, {柔軟|じゅうなん} (lesson 30) |

- {財布|さいふ} (N5), {布団|ふとん} (N5), {柔|やわ}らかい (N4) and {柔道|じゅうどう} (N4) are now
  written with kanji.
- {織|お}る (weave) sounds like the humble おる (be) and {折|お}る (fold).
- 織 is シキ only in {組織|そしき}.

### Looking after things

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 磨 | polish, brush | マ | みが(く) | 16 | {磨|みが}く, {歯磨|はみが}き, {磨|みが}き, {靴磨|くつみが}き |
| 塗 | paint, coat | ト | ぬ(る) | 13 | {塗|ぬ}る, {塗料|とりょう} |
| 濯 | rinse, wash | タク | すす(ぐ) | 17 | {洗濯|せんたく}, {洗濯物|せんたくもの}, {洗濯機|せんたくき}, {濯|すす}ぐ |

- {磨|みが}く (N5), {歯磨|はみが}き (N4), {塗|ぬ}る (N3), {洗濯|せんたく} (N4), {洗濯物|せんたくもの} and
  {洗濯機|せんたくき} (N3) are now written with kanji.
- {磨|みが}く is also "polish (a skill)": {腕|うで}を{磨|みが}く (lesson 5's 腕).

Memory notes:

- 肌 is 月 (the flesh radical) and 几 (a small table): the flat surface of the body.
- 汗 is water (氵) and 干 (dry, lesson 19): the water that has to dry off you.
- 眼 is 目 (eye) and 艮: the eye looking steadily.
- 衣 shows a collar and the folds of a robe.
- 帽 is 巾 (cloth) and 冒: cloth on top of the head.
- 装 is 壮 (strong) over 衣 (clothes): dressing up to look strong.
- 糸 is a twisted thread, three loops and a tassel.
- 布 is a hand over 巾 (cloth): cloth in the hand.
- 織 is 糸 (thread) and 戠: threads put together, weaving.
- 柔 is 矛 (a spear) over 木 (wood): a pliant shaft that bends.
- 磨 is 麻 (hemp) over 石 (stone): rubbing with hemp on stone, polishing.
- 塗 is water (氵), 余 (left over, N3) and 土 (earth): wet earth smeared on.
- 濯 is water (氵) and 翟 (a pheasant's feathers): rinsing feathers clean.

```trace
肌汗眼衣帽装糸布磨塗柔織濯
```

## Dialogue: at a second-hand clothes shop

Two friends look round a second-hand clothes shop run by かおる. (Casual speech; the manager speaks politely.)

```dialogue
# In the shop
ひなた: ねえ、このお{店|みせ}、{前|まえ}は{劇団|げきだん}の{衣装|いしょう}を{作|つく}ってたって{話|はなし}だよ。
= Hey, the story is this shop used to make costumes for a theatre company.
そうた: へえ、だから{変|か}わった{服|ふく}が{多|おお}いのか。この{着物|きもの}の{生地|きじ}、すごくない？
= Huh, so that's why there are so many unusual clothes. Isn't the cloth of this kimono amazing?
ひなた: {手|て}で{織|お}った{布|ぬの}だね。{触|さわ}ってみて。{柔|やわ}らかくて、{何十年|なんじゅうねん}も{前|まえ}に{作|つく}られたものじゃないかのようだよ。
= That's hand-woven cloth. Feel it. It's so soft, it's as if it hadn't been made decades ago.
そうた: あ、ほんとだ。でも、いかにも{高|たか}そう。…あ、やっぱり{高|たか}い。
= Oh, it is. But it looks seriously expensive… Oh, it is.
ひなた: {店長|てんちょう}さん、{来月|らいげつ}セールするとか。それまで{待|ま}ったら？
= I hear the manager's having a sale next month. Why not wait till then?
そうた: うーん。でも、だれかに{買|か}われちゃいそうで{心配|しんぱい}。
= Hmm. But I'm worried someone else will buy it.
ひなた: あ、このジャケットもいいね。{肌触|はだざわ}りがいい。
= Oh, this jacket's nice too. It feels lovely.
そうた: {着|き}てみなよ。…うん、{似合|にあ}う。{大人|おとな}っぽいね。
= Try it on… Yeah, it suits you. Very grown-up.
ひなた: {本当|ほんとう}？じゃあ、これにしようかな。{店長|てんちょう}さーん、これ、{洗濯|せんたく}できますか。
= Really? Then maybe I'll get this one. Excuse me! Can this be washed?
かおる: それはクリーニングのほうが{安心|あんしん}ですね。{家|いえ}で{洗|あら}うなら、{手|て}で{優|やさ}しく{洗|あら}って、よく{濯|すす}いでください。
= It's safer to have it dry-cleaned. If you wash it at home, wash it gently by hand and rinse it well.
ひなた: {分|わ}かりました。
= All right.
そうた: …{見|み}て、{店長|てんちょう}さん、{得意|とくい}げな{顔|かお}してる。
= …Look, the manager looks very pleased with themselves.
ひなた: {古着|ふるぎ}の{話|はなし}になると、{話|はな}しぶりが{変|か}わるよね。{本当|ほんとう}に{好|す}きなんだろうな。
= The way they talk changes when it comes to second-hand clothes. They must really love them.
```

{似合|にあ}う = to suit (N4); {何十年|なんじゅうねん}も = for decades. Notice that ひなた passes on two things
heard from others in two different ways: って{話|はなし}だよ (the story is) and とか (I hear).
In the cloth line, かのよう shows the cloth really is old: it only feels new.

## Reading: an explanatory article

An article from a lifestyle magazine (である style) about looking after clothes.

> {日本|にほん}では、{昔|むかし}から{六月|ろくがつ}と{十月|じゅうがつ}に{衣替|ころもが}えをする{習慣|しゅうかん}がある。{学校|がっこう}の{制服|せいふく}も、{多|おお}くの{地域|ちいき}でこの{時期|じき}に{夏服|なつふく}と{冬服|ふゆふく}が{替|か}わる。{最近|さいきん}はれいだんぼうのある{生活|せいかつ}で、きせつを{感|かん}じにくくなったとも{言|い}われるが、{衣類|いるい}を{長|なが}く{大切|たいせつ}に{着|き}るためには、{今|いま}でも{意味|いみ}のある{習慣|しゅうかん}だという。
>
> {専門家|せんもんか}によると、{衣替|ころもが}えでいちばん{大切|たいせつ}なのは、しまう{前|まえ}に{必|かなら}ず{洗|あら}うことだ。{一度|いちど}しか{着|き}ていない{服|ふく}は、まるで{汚|よご}れていないかのように{見|み}える。しかし、{目|め}に{見|み}えない{汗|あせ}やひしが{生地|きじ}に{残|のこ}っていると、{半年|はんとし}{後|ご}に{黄色|きいろ}いしみになることがあるとされる。
>
> {洗|あら}った{衣類|いるい}は、よく{乾|かわ}かしてからしまう。ウールのセーターや{毛糸|けいと}の{物|もの}は、{洗濯機|せんたくき}ではなく{手|て}で{押|お}すように{洗|あら}い、{水|みず}で{軽|かる}く{濯|すす}ぐのがいいという{話|はなし}だ。{強|つよ}くこすると{毛玉|けだま}ができやすくなる。{干|ほ}すときは、ハンガーに{掛|か}けると{形|かたち}が{伸|の}びてしまうので、{平|たい}らに{置|お}いて{干|ほ}す。{強|つよ}い{日光|にっこう}も{色|いろ}が{薄|うす}くなる{原因|げんいん}になるので、{風|かぜ}の{通|とお}る{日|ひ}の{当|あ}たらない{場所|ばしょ}で{干|ほ}すのがいいとされている。
>
> {手間|てま}がかかるように{思|おも}えるが、このひと{手間|てま}で{服|ふく}のじゅみょうはずいぶん{変|か}わる。{祖母|そぼ}の{代|だい}から{着|き}られている{着物|きもの}が、{今|いま}もつややかな{色合|いろあ}いを{保|たも}っているのを{見|み}ると、{昔|むかし}の{人|ひと}のちえに{感心|かんしん}させられる。{安|やす}い{服|ふく}を{買|か}っては{捨|す}てる{時代|じだい}だからこそ、{一枚|いちまい}の{服|ふく}をていねいにあつかう{気持|きも}ちを{大切|たいせつ}にしたい。

ひし = sebum, the skin's oil (its second kanji is off-list); しみ = a stain; ひと{手間|てま} = a little
extra trouble; じゅみょう = lifespan (of a thing); つややか = glossy; {平|たい}ら = flat;
ちえ = wisdom; あつかう = to handle; ていねいに = with care. The hearsay and likeness words: とも{言|い}われる,
という (it is said), によると, かのように, とされる, という{話|はなし}だ.

1. When is {衣替|ころもが}え traditionally done, and why does the writer say it still matters?
2. Why should clothes you've worn only once be washed before you put them away?
3. How should a wool sweater be washed and dried, and why?
4. What does the writer want to value, and why "now especially"?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. In June and October. It still has a point because it helps you wear clothes for a long time
   and look after them.
2. They look as if they aren't dirty, but invisible sweat and skin oil left in the cloth can
   turn into yellow stains six months later.
3. By hand, pressing gently, and rinsed lightly; rubbing hard causes pilling. Dry it flat,
   because a hanger stretches it out of shape.
4. The attitude of looking after each garment carefully, precisely because it's an age when
   people buy cheap clothes and throw them away.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

In Japan there has long been a custom of changing your wardrobe in June and October. In many
areas school uniforms also switch between summer and winter versions at this time. It's said that
these days, with heating and air conditioning, we feel the seasons less, but the custom
reportedly still has a point if you want to wear your clothes for a long time and look after them.

According to experts, the most important thing when changing your wardrobe is to wash clothes
before you put them away. Clothes you've worn only once look as if they weren't dirty at all.
But if invisible sweat and skin oil are left in the cloth, they are said to turn into yellow
stains six months later.

Washed clothes should be put away only once they are fully dry. Wool sweaters and knitted things
are best washed not in the machine but by hand, pressing gently, and rinsed lightly in water, so
we're told. Rubbing hard makes them pill. When you dry them, a hanger will stretch them out of
shape, so lay them flat to dry. Strong sunlight is also said to fade the colours, so it's best to
dry them out of the sun, somewhere airy.

It may seem like a lot of trouble, but this little extra effort makes a big difference to how
long clothes last. When you see a kimono that has been worn since a grandmother's time still
keeping its glossy colours, you can't help admiring the wisdom of people in the past. Precisely
because this is an age when we buy cheap clothes and throw them away, I want to value the
attitude of handling each garment with care.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{来月|らいげつ}、{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}すとか。
= I hear you're moving next month.
まるで{本物|ほんもの}であるかのようですね。
= It's as if it were the real thing.
{得意|とくい}げな{顔|かお}をしていますね。
= You look very pleased with yourself.
いい{食|た}べっぷりですね。
= You've got a good appetite!
この{生地|きじ}は{肌触|はだざわ}りがいいです。
= This fabric feels nice against the skin.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{雨|あめ}とか for "I hear it'll rain": a noun needs だ, {雨|あめ}だとか, or a verb:
  {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}るとか.
- かのように after a bare noun: ×{本物|ほんもの}かのように in writing → {本物|ほんもの}であるかのように. (In
  casual speech {本物|ほんもの}かのよう is heard.)
- げ on any word: it goes on adjective stems (and a few set forms like {言|い}いたげ, {自信|じしん}ありげ).
  ×{食|た}べげ.
- げ for a prediction: ×{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りげだ. Use そう: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りそうだ.
- ぶり for a single action: {仕事|しごと}ぶり is the way someone works over time, not one task.
- {衣装|いしょう} read ×いそう: 装 is ショウ in this word.
- {生地|きじ} (cloth) read ×せいち: that's a different word (birthplace).

## Key points

- Hearsay: 〜とか (I hear; vague, polite too), 〜という{話|はなし}だ (the story is), ということだ / とのことだ
  (review), とみられる / とされる (news and writing).
- Likeness: 〜かのように / かのようだ (as if, but it isn't; まるで, あたかも), adjective stem + げ (looking…,
  literary), 〜ぶり / っぷり (the way someone does it), っぽい (review).
- New kanji: 肌 汗 眼 衣 帽 装 糸 布 磨 塗 柔 織 濯. Write {帽子|ぼうし}, {眼鏡|めがね}, {服装|ふくそう},
  {汗|あせ}, {洗濯|せんたく}, {磨|みが}く, {塗|ぬ}る, {柔|やわ}らかい, {財布|さいふ}, {布団|ふとん} with kanji from
  now on.

lessons.title: If only, if you dare: ものなら, ようものなら, ては
topics: ては and ていては
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last core lesson of the module puts feeling into conditions. "If" in Japanese can be plain
(たら, ば, と, なら, from N5 and N4), but N2 has conditionals that carry a speaker's attitude: a
wish you know is hopeless ("if only I could"), a warning in the form of a threat ("if you so
much as…"), a complaint about a habit ("if you keep doing that…") and a shrug ("if it happens,
well, then…").

できるものなら、{毎日|まいにち}{温泉|おんせん}に{入|はい}りたい。 — If only I could, I'd soak in a hot spring every day.
{一日|いちにち}でも{水|みず}やりを{忘|わす}れようものなら、すぐに{枯|か}れてしまう。 — If you forget to water it for even one day, it withers straight away.
そんなに{水|みず}をやっていては、{根|ね}がだめになってしまいますよ。 — If you keep watering it that much, the roots will be ruined.
{晴|は}れたら{晴|は}れたで、{日焼|ひや}けが{心配|しんぱい}だ。 — And if it's sunny, then I worry about sunburn.

The theme is outdoor leisure: gardening and plants, insects, beaches and swimming, hot springs
and staying over, cool and warm seasons. N3 had travel, onsen and many nature words in kana;
this lesson's kanji let you write {植物|しょくぶつ}, {枝|えだ}, {屋根|やね}, {枯|か}れる, {咲|さ}く, {緑|みどり},
{虫|むし}, {浴|あ}びる, {温泉|おんせん}, {涼|すず}しい and {暖|あたた}かい.

## If only I could: 〜ものなら

The dictionary form of a **[[potential]]** verb + ものなら is "if (by some chance) I could…", for
something you think is unlikely or impossible. The second half is usually a wish (〜たい, 〜てほしい)
or a challenge.

{行|い}けるものなら、{今|いま}すぐ{南|みなみ}の{島|しま}に{行|い}きたい。 — If only I could, I'd go to a southern island right now.
{戻|もど}れるものなら、{子供|こども}のころの{夏休|なつやす}みに{戻|もど}りたい。 — If only I could go back to the summer holidays of my childhood.
やれるものなら、やってみろ。 — Go on, do it, if you think you can. (a challenge; rough)

Points:

- Verbs that already mean "possible or not" also work: かなうものなら (if it could come true;
  its kanji is off-list).
- Casual: 〜もんなら.
- It's not a plain "if": for something likely, use たら or ば. ×{明日|あした}{晴|は}れるものなら{行|い}く.

## If you so much as…: 〜(よ)うものなら

The **[[volitional]]** + ものなら is quite different: "if you were to do (even a small thing), something
bad would follow". It exaggerates, often with でも or ちょっと, and the result is a disaster.

{少|すこ}しでも{遅|おく}れようものなら、{部長|ぶちょう}に{怒|おこ}られる。 — If you're even a little late, the department head tells you off.

| | 〜ものなら | 〜(よ)うものなら |

| Before it | potential (dictionary form) | volitional |
| Meaning | if only I could (unlikely) | if you were to… (disaster follows) |
| Second half | a wish or a challenge | a bad result |
| Example | {泳|およ}げるものなら{泳|およ}ぎたい | {泳|およ}ごうものなら{怒|おこ}られる |

## If you keep doing that: 〜ては, 〜ていては

The て form + は makes a conditional with a bad result: "if you do / if you keep doing that,
(something bad)". 〜ていては stresses that it goes on. The second half is often a negative or a
problem: 〜てしまう, 〜ない, だめだ, {困|こま}る.

そんなに{虫|むし}よけを{使|つか}っては、かえって{肌|はだ}に{悪|わる}い。 — If you use that much insect repellent, it's actually bad for your skin.

Compare N4's 〜ては{困|こま}る / 〜てはいけない: the same ては, fixed with a judgement. In casual
speech, 〜ちゃ / 〜じゃ: そんなに{食|た}べちゃ、{太|ふと}るよ.

ては has a second use you'll meet: two verbs in turn, repeated: {書|か}いては{消|け}し、{書|か}いては{消|け}す
(write and rub out, over and over). Here there's no "if"; it's a picture of a repeated action.

## If it happens, then…: 〜たら〜で, 〜ば〜で

The same word twice, once in a conditional and once with で, says "if it does happen, then that
brings its own (different) situation". Often it's a complaint that there's always a problem;
sometimes it's "and if it does, fine".

| verb: 〜たら〜たで | {降|ふ}ったら{降|ふ}ったで |
| verb: 〜ば〜たで | あればあったで |
| い-adjective: 〜ければ〜いで / 〜かったら〜かったで | {広|ひろ}ければ{広|ひろ}いで |
| noun, な-adjective: 〜なら〜で | {雨|あめ}なら{雨|あめ}で, {休|やす}みなら{休|やす}みで |

{庭|にわ}がなければ{寂|さび}しいし、あればあったで{手入|てい}れが{大変|たいへん}だ。 — Without a garden it's dreary, and if you have one, then keeping it up is hard work.
{雨|あめ}なら{雨|あめ}で、{旅館|りょかん}でゆっくり{温泉|おんせん}に{入|はい}ればいい。 — If it rains, then fine, we can just take it easy in the inn's hot spring.

> **Review: 〜さえ〜ば (N3 lesson 15) and 〜としたら (N3 lesson 19).** さえ〜ば is "as long as":

## To recognize: 〜(よ)うが〜まいが, 〜(よ)うと

The volitional + が / と, with lesson 18's まい, makes a written "whether or not", "no matter
whether":

{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ろうが{降|ふ}るまいが、{大会|たいかい}は{行|おこな}われる。 — Whether it rains or not, the tournament goes ahead.

You'll meet these in writing and in determined speech; at N2 you need to recognize them. They're
close to lesson 21's にかかわらず: {雨天|うてん}にかかわらず.

<summary>Answers</summary>

1. An hour by bus from the station, then a walk up a narrow slope; the reviewer advises
   travelling light (a lot of luggage makes it hard).
2. The outdoor bath fed straight from the spring, with a view over a valley; the water is
   soft and leaves the skin smooth.
3. If you leave the window open, insects come in (bring insect repellent); nights are cold even
   in summer (don't stay in light clothes; borrow a jacket to wear over the yukata).
4. At first it seemed inconvenient, but without them the time doing nothing, reading or cooling
   off while looking at the garden, felt wonderful.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

[The happiness of doing nothing at a little inn in the mountains] ★★★★☆

Worn out by work, I went to stay on my own, just for two nights. It's an hour by bus from the
station, and the last part is a walk up a narrow slope. It's only about fifteen minutes on foot, but with a lot
of luggage it's hard going,
so if you go, I recommend travelling light.

What I recommend most is the outdoor bath, fed straight from the spring. There's a
valley right in front of you, and since it was the season of fresh green leaves, it was like
bathing in the middle of the forest. The water is soft and leaves your skin smooth. If I could,
I'd come every week.

The food centres on local vegetables, and the daikon dish from their own garden was
especially good. There's a room-only plan, but there are no shops nearby, so I recommend meals.

There were things that bothered me too. Since it's in the mountains, if you so much as leave a
window open, insects pour in. If you don't like bugs, don't forget insect repellent. Also, nights
get quite cold, so even in summer, stay in light clothes and you'll catch a cold. You can borrow
a jacket to wear over your yukata, so don't be shy about asking.

There's no TV in the room and the Wi-Fi hardly works, so at first I thought it was inconvenient. But without them, time
spent reading or cooling off while looking at the garden, doing nothing, felt wonderful. Next time I'd
like to come in the autumn leaf season.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
できるものなら、もう{一度|いちど}{行|い}きたいです。
= If only I could, I'd like to go again.
{少|すこ}しでも{遅|おく}れようものなら、{大変|たいへん}です。
= If you're even a little late, there'll be trouble.
そんなに{水|みず}をやっていては、{枯|か}れてしまいますよ。
= If you keep watering it that much, it'll die.
{雨|あめ}なら{雨|あめ}で、{温泉|おんせん}を{楽|たの}しめばいいです。
= If it rains, then we'll just enjoy the hot spring.
```

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up the two ものなら. {行|い}けるものなら (potential) is a wish; {行|い}こうものなら (volitional)
  is a warning. ×{行|い}こうものなら{行|い}きたい.
- 〜ものなら for a likely event: ×{明日|あした}{休|やす}みなものなら{来|き}てね. Use たら: {休|やす}みだったら.
- 〜ては with a good result: ×{毎日|まいにち}{練習|れんしゅう}しては、{上手|じょうず}になる. ては leads to
  something bad; for a good result use ば or たら.
- 〜たら〜たで with two different verbs: the same word is repeated: {晴|は}れたら{晴|は}れたで, not
  ×{晴|は}れたら{降|ふ}ったで.
- {泊|と}まる and {止|と}まる, {泊|と}める and {止|と}める: same sound, different kanji. A car {止|と}まる;
  a guest {泊|と}まる.
- {一泊|いっぱく}, {二泊|にはく}, {三泊|さんぱく}: watch the sound changes.

## Key points

- potential + ものなら: if only I could (a wish against the odds); casual もんなら.
- volitional + ものなら: if you so much as… (a disaster follows).
- 〜ては / 〜ていては: if you (keep) doing that, something bad.
- 〜たら〜たで / 〜ば〜で / 〜なら〜で: if it happens, then (another situation).
- 〜(よ)うが〜まいが, 〜(よ)うと: whether or not, no matter (to recognize).
- New kanji: 植 枝 根 枯 咲 緑 虫 玉 浴 泊 泉 涼 暖. Write {植物|しょくぶつ}, {枝|えだ}, {屋根|やね},
  {枯|か}れる, {咲|さ}く, {緑|みどり}, {虫|むし}, {浴|あ}びる, {温泉|おんせん}, {涼|すず}しい, {暖|あたた}かい with
  kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Onomatopoeia
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese has a very large family of words that imitate sounds or paint a state: the rain
falls ざあざあ, a floor shines ぴかぴか, a child waits わくわく. Together they're called
**[[onomatopoeia]]** (オノマトペ). English has some (bang, splash, buzz), but Japanese uses far more of
them, in everyday speech, in children's books, in manga, in food adverts and even in doctors'
waiting rooms ("Is the pain ずきずき or ちくちく?"). Learners who skip them miss a great deal of the
colour of the language.

You know several already from earlier courses: ゆっくり, はっきり, ぐっすり, にこにこ, どきどき,
わくわく, いらいら, がっかり, のんびり, ぺこぺこ. This lesson sorts them into kinds, shows how they're
built, and adds ten new ones.

## Two kinds: giongo and gitaigo

Japanese grammar books divide onomatopoeia into two groups (and some writers add more):

| Kind | What it imitates | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **[[giongo]]** (ぎおんご) | real sounds: things, animals, people | ざあざあ (pouring rain), しとしと (soft, steady rain), ごしごし (scrubbing), ワンワン (a dog) |
| **[[gitaigo]]** (ぎたいご) | states, movements and feelings that make no sound | ぴかぴか (shining), つるつる (smooth, slippery), ふわふわ (soft and fluffy), わくわく (excited), そわそわ (restless) |

The first kanji of both names is off-list, so this course writes them in kana. Animal and human
voices (ワンワン, ニャー, げらげら) are sometimes called ぎせいご, and some writers call the feeling
words (いらいら, わくわく) ぎじょうご; you don't need the extra names, only the idea that gitaigo
"sound out" things that make no sound at all.

{雨|あめ}がざあざあ{降|ふ}っている。 — It's pouring. (giongo: you can hear it)
{雨|あめ}がしとしと{降|ふ}っている。 — A soft, steady rain is falling. (on the border: many dictionaries count it as gitaigo, the way the rain falls, since you barely hear it)
{床|ゆか}をぴかぴかに{磨|みが}いた。 — I polished the floor till it shone. (gitaigo: shine makes no sound)
{試験|しけん}の{結果|けっか}を{待|ま}って、そわそわしている。 — I'm restless, waiting for my exam results. (gitaigo: a feeling)

## How they're built

Most onomatopoeia are built from a root of one or two morae, in a few fixed shapes. The shape
itself carries meaning.

| Shape | What it suggests | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ABAB | repeated or continuing | ごろごろ, ざあざあ, ぽかぽか, そわそわ |
| ABっ / Aっ + と | once, quick, sudden | ぎゅっと (tightly, in one squeeze), ぱっと (in a flash), ほっと (with relief) |
| AっBり | a full, settled state | ぐっすり, はっきり, ぎっしり (packed tight), ひっそり (hushed) |
| AんBり | a soft, lingering state | ひんやり (pleasantly cool), のんびり, ぼんやり |
| ABん | one movement that resonates | ごろん (a roll over), ぽつん (alone) |

The sounds matter too. A voiced first consonant (with ゛) usually sounds bigger, heavier or
rougher than the plain one:

| Plain | Voiced |
|---|---|
| ころころ (a small thing rolling) | ごろごろ (a big thing rolling; thunder rumbling) |
| さらさら (dry and smooth, like sand or silky hair) | ざらざら (rough, gritty) |
| きらきら (twinkling, sparkling) | ぎらぎら (glaring, harsh) |
| とんとん (a light tap) | どんどん (pounding; also "rapidly") |

That's why ぎらぎら sounds unpleasant ({太陽|たいよう}がぎらぎら{照|て}る: the sun beats down) and
きらきら pretty ({星|ほし}がきらきら{光|ひか}る: the stars twinkle).

## How they work in a sentence

Onomatopoeia can play several roles, and the role often changes the accent:

- Adverb, often with と: {雨|あめ}がしとしと(と){降|ふ}る, ドアをとんとん(と)たたく. As adverbs most ABAB
  words fall after the first mora: [ふわふわ:1].
- する verb: いらいらする, わくわくする, ひんやりする ({朝|あさ}はひんやりしている: the mornings are
  cool).
- With の, に or だ, like a な-adjective or noun: ふわふわのパン (a fluffy loaf), ぴかぴかに{磨|みが}く,
  {床|ゆか}がつるつるだ. Used this way the ABAB words are usually flat: [ふわふわ:0].

ふわふわと{雲|くも}が{浮|う}かんでいる — clouds are floating gently.
ふわふわのタオル — a soft, fluffy towel.

The meaning can shift with the role: {床|ゆか}がつるつるすべる (the floor is slippery) and
つるつるの{肌|はだ} (smooth skin). Some words also have more than one meaning: ごろごろ is thunder
rumbling, a heavy thing rolling, and lazing about at home ({休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は{家|いえ}でごろごろしている).

## Feelings and the body

Gitaigo for feelings and bodily sensations are everyday words, and doctors use them too, because
they describe pain more exactly than adjectives do.

| Word | Feeling or sensation |
|---|---|
| わくわく | excited, looking forward to something |
| どきどき | heart pounding (nerves, fear or love) |
| いらいら | irritated, impatient |
| そわそわ | restless, fidgety, unable to settle |
| ずきずき | throbbing pain ({頭|あたま}がずきずきする) |
| ちくちく | prickling, stinging (a woollen jumper, a thorn) |
| ひりひり | smarting, burning (sunburn, spicy food) |

{日焼|ひや}けで{背中|せなか}がひりひりする。 — My back stings from sunburn.
この{毛糸|けいと}のセーターは{肌|はだ}がちくちくする。 — This wool jumper prickles against my skin.

## Onomatopoeia in manga

In manga, sound effects are drawn into the picture, usually in katakana, and they often say more
than the speech bubbles: ドーン (a boom, a dramatic moment), ガラッ (a door slid open hard), ゴゴゴ
(a menacing rumble), and even シーン for silence. Many are made up on the spot by the artist, so
you won't find them all in a dictionary. The katakana makes them stand out as sound, and
lengthening (ドーーン) or small っ (ガラッ) shows how long or how sudden the sound is.

## Onomatopoeia in food advertising

Shop windows, menus and packaging are full of texture words, because they make you imagine the
food in your mouth.

| Word | Texture |
|---|---|
| さくさく | crisp and light (pastry, tempura) |
| ふわふわ | soft and airy (pancakes, bread) |
| もちもち | soft, springy and chewy (mochi, some bread) |
| とろとろ | melting, thick and runny (cheese, a soft egg) |
| しゃきしゃき | crunchy and fresh (lettuce) |
| ぷりぷり | plump and springy (prawns) |

{外|そと}はさくさく、{中|なか}はふわふわ！ — Crisp outside, fluffy inside! (an advertising favourite)

## Ten new words

These join your vocabulary: オノマトペ, ぴかぴか, つるつる, ふわふわ, しとしと, ぽかぽか, ひんやり,
じめじめ, そわそわ, さくさく.

- ぽかぽか is pleasantly warm (spring sunshine, a body after a bath): {春|はる}の{日|ひ}がぽかぽかと
  {暖|あたた}かい.
- ひんやり is pleasantly cool to the touch or in the air: ひんやりした{朝|あさ}の{空気|くうき}.
- じめじめ is unpleasantly damp and humid: つゆはじめじめする (the rainy season is damp and muggy).
- ぴかぴか is shining, gleaming; ぴかぴかの{一年生|いちねんせい} is a brand-new first-year pupil.

## Dialogue: a café menu

Two friends choose a cake in a café. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# Choosing a cake
みゆ: {見|み}て、このメニュー。「ふわふわパンケーキ」「さくさくアップルパイ」…{全部|ぜんぶ}おいしそう。
= Look at this menu. "Fluffy pancakes", "crispy apple pie"… it all looks delicious.
けいた: 「もちもちワッフル」もあるよ。もちもちって、どんな{感|かん}じ？
= There are "chewy waffles" too. What's もちもち like?
みゆ: おもちみたいに、{柔|やわ}らかくて、かむと{少|すこ}し{押|お}し{返|かえ}してくる{感|かん}じ。
= Soft like mochi, and it pushes back a little when you bite it.
けいた: なるほど。{外|そと}は{雨|あめ}がしとしと{降|ふ}ってて{寒|さむ}いし、{温|あたた}かいものがいいな。
= I see. It's drizzling outside and cold, so I'd like something warm.
みゆ: じゃあ、とろとろチーズのグラタンは？
= Then how about the gratin with melting cheese?
けいた: いいね。…あ、でもぼく、ねこじたなんだ。{熱|あつ}いとしたがひりひりする。
= Sounds good… Oh, but I can't take hot food. If it's too hot my tongue stings.
みゆ: ふーふーして{食|た}べればいいじゃない。
= Just blow on it before you eat it.
けいた: そうする。みゆは？さっきからそわそわしてるけど。
= I will. And you? You've been fidgeting for a while.
みゆ: だって、きせつ{限定|げんてい}のケーキが{気|き}になって…。あ、{店員|てんいん}さんが{持|も}ってる、あのぴかぴかのやつ！
= Well, I can't stop thinking about the seasonal cake… Oh, the one the waiter's carrying, the shiny one!
```

{押|お}し{返|かえ}す = to push back; ねこじた = someone who can't take hot food (literally "cat's tongue"); した = tongue;
ふーふー = blowing on hot food; きせつ{限定|げんてい} = for this season only (きせつ's second kanji is off-list).

## Reading: a column

A short column from a newspaper's language corner (である style).

> {日本語|にほんご}を{学|まな}ぶ{人|ひと}がよく{驚|おどろ}くのは、オノマトペの{多|おお}さだという。{雨|あめ}ひとつとっても、ざあざあ、しとしと、ぱらぱら、ぽつぽつと、{降|ふ}り{方|かた}によって{言|い}い{方|かた}が{変|か}わる。{英語|えいご}なら「heavy rain」「light rain」と{形容詞|けいようし}で{言|い}い{分|わ}けるところを、{日本語|にほんご}では{音|おと}そのもので{表|あらわ}すのである。
>
> {面白|おもしろ}いのは、{音|おと}のしないものにもオノマトペがあることだ。{床|ゆか}がぴかぴかに{光|ひか}る、{肌|はだ}がつるつるになる、{春|はる}の{日|ひ}がぽかぽかと{暖|あたた}かい。どれも{音|おと}はしないが、{日本語|にほんご}の{話|はな}し{手|て}には、その{様子|ようす}が{目|め}に{浮|う}かぶかのように{感|かん}じられる。
>
> {料理|りょうり}の{世界|せかい}では、オノマトペは{特|とく}に{大切|たいせつ}だ。「さくさく」「ふわふわ」と{書|か}いてあるだけで、{食|た}べたことのない{人|ひと}にも{食感|しょっかん}が{伝|つた}わる。{外国|がいこく}から{来|き}た{料理人|りょうりにん}が「{日本|にほん}のお{客|きゃく}さんは、{味|あじ}と{同|おな}じくらい{食感|しょっかん}を{大切|たいせつ}にする」と{話|はな}していたのも、{当然|とうぜん}かもしれない。

{形容詞|けいようし} = adjective; {言|い}い{分|わ}ける = to use different words for; {食感|しょっかん} = texture
(of food); {料理人|りょうりにん} = a cook, chef.

## Key points

- Onomatopoeia (オノマトペ): giongo (ぎおんご) imitate real sounds; gitaigo (ぎたいご) paint states,
  movements and feelings that make no sound.
- Shapes: ABAB (repeated), Aっと (sudden, once), AっBり and AんBり (a settled state), ABん (one
  movement). Voiced sounds are bigger or rougher: ころころ / ごろごろ, さらさら / ざらざら.
- Roles: adverb (often + と, accent on the first mora), する verb, or with の / に / だ (usually flat).
- Manga writes sound effects in katakana; food adverts use texture words: さくさく, ふわふわ,
  もちもち, とろとろ.
- New words: オノマトペ, ぴかぴか, つるつる, ふわふわ, しとしと, ぽかぽか, ひんやり, じめじめ, そわそわ,
  さくさく.

lessons.title: Yōkai and folklore
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan's folk tales are crowded with strange creatures: a river imp with a dish of water on its
head, a red-faced mountain spirit with a long nose, a child-like spirit that brings luck to an old
house. They're called ようかい (its first kanji is off-list, so this course writes it in kana), and
they live on today in manga, anime, games, local festivals and souvenir shops. This lesson
introduces a few of the best known, the book that collected many of their stories, and how
yōkai are pictured today. It ends with an original legend that uses lesson 25's ものなら and
ようものなら.

## What is a yōkai?

ようかい are supernatural beings of folk belief: some frightening, some mischievous, some
helpful. They aren't quite ghosts. A ゆうれい (N4's ghost) is the spirit of a dead person, usually
someone with a grudge or an unfinished wish; a yōkai is a creature in its own right, tied to a
place (a river, a mountain, an old house) or to a thing. Many stories explain something people
feared or couldn't understand: children drowning in rivers, people lost in the mountains, a
house that suddenly grew rich or poor. Beliefs varied from region to region and changed over
the centuries, so the descriptions below are the common modern picture, not the only one.

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ようかい | a yōkai, a supernatural creature |
| {言|い}い{伝|つた}え | a legend handed down by word of mouth (lesson 8) |
| {民話|みんわ} | a folk tale |
| {怪談|かいだん} | a ghost story, a tale of the uncanny |
| {化|ば}ける | to take another form, to disguise oneself (by magic) |
| {正体|しょうたい} | someone's true form or identity |

{怪談|かいだん} sounds like N4's {階段|かいだん} (stairs), with the same flat accent: context tells them
apart. The kanji 怪 (lesson 2's {怪我|けが}) means "strange".

## Three famous yōkai

### The kappa

{河童|かっぱ} (a special reading: 河 is "river", 童 "child") is a water creature about the size of a
child, often green, with a beak, webbed hands and a shell on its back. On top of its head is a
{皿|さら}, a hollow like a dish, filled with water; if the water spills, it loses its strength.
Kappa are said to live in rivers and ponds, to pull people and horses into the water, and to love
cucumbers and sumo. The cucumber roll in sushi shops is called かっぱ{巻|ま}き, and many towns by
rivers use a cheerful kappa as their mascot. Some stories say that if you bow to a kappa, it bows
back, spills its water and becomes weak, so politeness can save your life.

### The tengu

てんぐ (its second kanji is off-list) live deep in the mountains. Today they're usually pictured
with a red face, a very long nose and the clothes of a mountain ascetic, and they can fly. Older
pictures often show them more like great birds, with beaks and wings. They were feared as spirits
that carried people off, and respected as guardians of the mountains; in some legends they teach
swordsmanship. {鼻|はな}が{高|たか}い ("a high nose") means "proud" in Japanese, and a boastful person is
sometimes said to have become a てんぐ: てんぐになる.

### The oni

おに (the kanji is off-list) are horned, fierce giants, often red or blue, wearing a tiger-skin
loincloth and carrying an iron club, a {金棒|かなぼう}. They appear in many folk tales, most famously as
the enemies Momotarō defeats. Every year on せつぶん, around the start of spring, families throw
roasted beans out of the house, shouting おには{外|そと}、{福|ふく}は{内|うち}! ("Out with the oni, in with good
luck!"). The saying おにに{金棒|かなぼう} ("an iron club for an oni") means something that makes the strong
even stronger.

## The Tōno stories and the zashiki-warashi

In 1910 the scholar {柳田国男|やなぎたくにお} (the first kanji of the family name is outside N2) published
『{遠野物語|とおのものがたり}』, a collection of stories from the Tōno area of Iwate, in the north-east
of Japan. A young man from Tōno who hoped to become a writer, ささききぜん, told him the
region's traditions, and やなぎた wrote them down. The book is often called the starting point of the study of Japanese
folklore. It includes kappa and, most famously, the ざしきわらし.

A ざしきわらし is a spirit like a small child that lives in the inner rooms of an old house. People
rarely see it, but they may hear footsteps or find small signs of its play. A house with a
ざしきわらし prospers; if it leaves, the family's luck runs out. Stories like this are especially
associated with the north-east, and some old inns there are known for "having" one.

## Yōkai in pictures, then and now

Yōkai became a favourite subject for artists in the Edo period. In 1776 the painter
とりやませきえん published a picture book of yōkai, the first of a series of four; later artists
often drew on his pictures, and many yōkai are still imagined much as he drew them. Later woodblock artists drew kappa, tengu and many others.

In the twentieth century the manga artist みずきしげる made yōkai popular again with his series
about a yōkai boy, which has been made into anime several times. More recently, games and anime
about befriending yōkai have been hits with children. Yōkai have also become a part of local
tourism: Tōno has a museum of its folk tales, and towns all over Japan have yōkai statues,
festivals and sweets. (Details change; check what's on if you plan to visit.)

## Dialogue: a museum of folk tales

A visitor asks a guide at a small museum of local legends. (Polite speech.)

```dialogue
# At the museum
ひろし: すみません、この{絵|え}は{何|なん}ですか。{頭|あたま}に{皿|さら}がのっていますね。
= Excuse me, what's this picture? It has a dish on its head.
みちこ: {河童|かっぱ}です。この{辺|あた}りの{川|かわ}には、{昔|むかし}から{河童|かっぱ}が{住|す}んでいるという{言|い}い{伝|つた}えがあるんです。
= That's a kappa. There's an old legend that kappa live in the rivers around here.
ひろし: {怖|こわ}いんですか。
= Are they frightening?
みちこ: {民話|みんわ}によって{違|ちが}います。{子供|こども}を{川|かわ}に{引|ひ}き{込|こ}む{怖|こわ}い{河童|かっぱ}もいれば、{助|たす}けてもらったお{礼|れい}に{魚|さかな}を{届|とど}ける{河童|かっぱ}もいます。
= It depends on the tale. There are frightening kappa that drag children into the river, and kappa that bring fish to thank someone who helped them.
ひろし: へえ、{優|やさ}しい{河童|かっぱ}もいるんですね。こちらの{鼻|はな}の{長|なが}いのは？
= Oh, so some kappa are kind. And this one with the long nose?
みちこ: てんぐです。{山|やま}の{神様|かみさま}のように{考|かんが}えられていました。{夜|よる}の{山|やま}で{道|みち}に{迷|まよ}った{人|ひと}は、てんぐに{連|つ}れていかれたと{言|い}われたそうです。
= That's a tengu. They were thought of as something like mountain gods. People who got lost in the mountains at night were said to have been carried off by a tengu.
ひろし: {正体|しょうたい}が{分|わ}からないものを、ようかいのせいにしたんでしょうか。
= Did people blame yōkai for things they couldn't explain?
みちこ: そういう{面|めん}もあるでしょうね。でも、{川|かわ}や{山|やま}は{危|あぶ}ないから{気|き}をつけなさい、という{昔|むかし}の{人|ひと}のちえでもあったんだと{思|おも}います。
= I expect that was part of it. But I think it was also the wisdom of people in the past, telling you to be careful because rivers and mountains are dangerous.
```

{引|ひ}き{込|こ}む = to drag in; {道|みち}に{迷|まよ}う = to lose your way; 〜のせいにする = to blame on;
ちえ = wisdom (its second kanji is off-list).

## Reading: an original legend

A short legend written for this lesson, in the style of a folk tale (である style, as such tales
are often retold in print). It isn't a traditional story.

> {昔|むかし}、ある{山|やま}あいの{村|むら}に、{深|ふか}いふちのある{川|かわ}が{流|なが}れていた。
>
> {村|むら}には{古|ふる}い{言|い}い{伝|つた}えがあった。{夕方|ゆうがた}、{日|ひ}が{沈|しず}んでから{子供|こども}が{一人|ひとり}で{川|かわ}に{近|ちか}づこうものなら、{河童|かっぱ}にふちの{底|そこ}へ{引|ひ}き{込|こ}まれてしまう、というのだ。だから{親|おや}たちは、{子供|こども}が{遊|あそ}びに{出|で}かけるたびに「{暗|くら}くなる{前|まえ}に{帰|かえ}ってきなさい」と{言|い}い{聞|き}かせた。
>
> ある{夏|なつ}の{夕方|ゆうがた}、たろうという{男|おとこ}の{子|こ}が、{川|かわ}べりで{泣|な}いている{小|ちい}さな{子|こ}を{見|み}つけた。{頭|あたま}に{皿|さら}のようなものがのっていて、その{皿|さら}はからからに{乾|かわ}いている。{河童|かっぱ}の{子|こ}だった。{日照|ひで}りで{川|かわ}の{水|みず}が{減|へ}り、ふちに{帰|かえ}れなくなっていたのだ。
>
> たろうは{怖|こわ}かった。しかし、{放|ほう}っておいては、この{子|こ}は{死|し}んでしまうかもしれない。たろうは{両手|りょうて}で{川|かわ}の{水|みず}をすくい、{河童|かっぱ}の{皿|さら}に{注|そそ}いでやった。{河童|かっぱ}の{子|こ}は{元気|げんき}を{取|と}り{戻|もど}し、{何度|なんど}も{頭|あたま}を{下|さ}げて、ふちへ{帰|かえ}っていった。
>
> その{夜|よる}、たろうの{家|いえ}の{戸|と}の{前|まえ}に、{大|おお}きな{魚|さかな}が{三匹|さんびき}{置|お}いてあった。それからというもの、その{村|むら}では、{川|かわ}で{子供|こども}がおぼれることは{一度|いちど}もなかったという。{村|むら}の{年寄|としよ}りは{今|いま}でも{言|い}う。「{会|あ}えるものなら、もう{一度|いちど}あの{河童|かっぱ}に{会|あ}って、お{礼|れい}を{言|い}いたいものだ」と。

ふち = a deep pool in a river (its kanji is off-list); {言|い}い{聞|き}かせる = to tell
(a child) firmly; {川|かわ}べり = the riverbank; {日照|ひで}り = a drought; すくう = to scoop up;
{注|そそ}ぐ = to pour; おぼれる = to drown; {三匹|さんびき} = three (fish, small animals; lesson 30's
匹). The grammar: {近|ちか}づこうものなら (if a child so much as went near), {放|ほう}っておいては (if he
left it), {会|あ}えるものなら (if only I could meet), and lesson 8's それからというもの (ever since).

## Key points

- ようかい: creatures of folk belief tied to places and things; ゆうれい are the spirits of the dead.
- {河童|かっぱ} (special reading): river creature with a dish of water on its head; loves cucumbers and
  sumo. てんぐ: red-faced, long-nosed mountain spirit. おに: horned giant with an iron club;
  せつぶん's beans.
- 『{遠野物語|とおのものがたり}』 (1910): やなぎたくにお's collection of Tōno folklore, told by ささききぜん;
  home of the ざしきわらし.
- Yōkai pictures: Edo-period picture books (1776 and after), then manga, anime and games.
- New words: ようかい, {河童|かっぱ}, てんぐ, おに, ざしきわらし, たぬき, {民話|みんわ}, {化|ば}ける,
  {怪談|かいだん}, {正体|しょうたい} ({言|い}い{伝|つた}え, used here, was taught in lesson 8).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.
