lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last module is about Japanese on the page and about the test itself. At N3 you learned the
**[[written style]]**: plain forms, である after nouns, clauses joined with the stem
({増|ふ}えており、, {高|たか}く、) and opinions such as と{考|かんが}えられる and べきである. Most N2
reading texts are written that way. They also use a layer of older **[[literary forms]]** that speech has almost
lost: a negative ending in ぬ, a "must" built on ねば, and phrases such as にいたる and
にほかならない. This lesson teaches them, so that the essays, columns and editorials of the rest of
the module (and of the exam) read smoothly.

{高齢化|こうれいか}が{進|すす}む{今|いま}、{地域|ちいき}で{支|ささ}え{合|あ}う{仕組|しく}みを{作|つく}らねばならない。 — Now that society is ageing, we must create ways for communities to support one another.

{知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に、{町|まち}から{子供|こども}の{声|こえ}が{消|き}えていた。 — Before anyone noticed, the voices of children had disappeared from the town.

{介護|かいご}は{家族|かぞく}だけの{問題|もんだい}ではなく、{社会|しゃかい}{全体|ぜんたい}の{問題|もんだい}にほかならない。 — Care isn't a problem for families alone: it is nothing less than a problem for society as a whole.

The theme is society and welfare: older people and care, taxes and benefits, disability,
inequality, groups and communities, and life in the suburbs. Population and trends
({少子化|しょうしか}, {高齢化|こうれいか}) are carried from N3; this lesson adds the words of the welfare
system and of the communities that live with it.

> **Review (N3 lesson 26).** The written style: {原因|げんいん}である, ではない, であった, であろう,
> であり、; stem joins {降|ふ}り、, {高|たか}く、, 〜ており、; the ず form {降|ふ}らず、 (する → せず,
> {来|く}る → {来|こ}ず); のである to explain; と{考|かんが}えられる, と{思|おも}われる, と{言|い}える,
> べきである. All of it is used below without comment. The reference sheet "Written style" has the
> full table.

## 〜ねばならない: written "must"

〜ねばならない is the written and formal form of 〜なければならない. It's made from the ない form:
drop ない and add ねば. する becomes せねば, and {来|く}る becomes {来|こ}ねば.

| Dictionary form | ない form | 〜ねばならない |
|---|---|---|
| {作|つく}る | {作|つく}らない | {作|つく}らねばならない |
| {考|かんが}える | {考|かんが}えない | {考|かんが}えねばならない |
| {急|いそ}ぐ | {急|いそ}がない | {急|いそ}がねばならない |
| する | しない | せねばならない |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}ない | {来|こ}ねばならない |

{社会保障|しゃかいほしょう}の{財源|ざいげん}をどう{確保|かくほ}するか、しんけんに{考|かんが}えねばならない。 — We must think seriously about how to secure the funding for social security.

{障害|しょうがい}のある{人|ひと}も{利用|りよう}できるよう、{駅|えき}の{設計|せっけい}を{見直|みなお}さねばならない。 — Station design must be rethought so that people with disabilities can use them too.

Notes:

- It lives in writing, speeches and formal statements. In conversation it sounds stiff or
  mock-serious, unless the speaker is quoting or making a vow:
  「{今日|きょう}こそ{部屋|へや}を{片付|かたづ}けねばならない」 said with a smile is a joke about one's own
  laziness.
- 〜ねばならぬ (with the ぬ below) is older still: speeches, slogans, novels set in the past.
- ねば alone is the written "if not": {急|いそ}がねば{間|ま}に{合|あ}わない (if we don't hurry, we won't
  make it). It's 〜なければ in dress clothes.
- The negative, "don't have to", is not ねば-based: write 〜なくてもよい or 〜{必要|ひつよう}はない.
- Lesson 17's ざるを{得|え}ない ("have no choice but") and べきである ("ought to", N3) are close
  relatives. ねばならない states a duty; べきである recommends; ざるを{得|え}ない admits there's no
  way out. The table at the end of this lesson puts them side by side.
- ねば is not a drill form: the conjugation drills stay with the N5 and N4 forms.

## 〜ぬ: the classical negative

ぬ is the **[[classical negative]]**, the negative of classical Japanese: the same job as ない. It attaches to the ない stem, like
ない: {知|し}らぬ, {行|い}かぬ, {見|み}ぬ, {言|い}わぬ; する → せぬ; {来|く}る → {来|こ}ぬ. Modern Japanese
keeps it in three places.

1. **Before a noun**, in set phrases and in writing. This is where you'll meet it most:

| Phrase | Meaning | Modern equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| {知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に | before one knew it | {知|し}らないうちに |
| {見知|みし}らぬ{人|ひと} | a stranger | {知|し}らない{人|ひと} |
| {思|おも}わぬ + noun | unexpected | {思|おも}いがけない |
| {予期|よき}せぬ + noun | unforeseen | {予想|よそう}しなかった |
| {変|か}わらぬ + noun | unchanging | {変|か}わらない |
| {絶|た}えぬ + noun | never-ending | {絶|た}えない |

{思|おも}わぬところで{昔|むかし}の{友人|ゆうじん}に{会|あ}った。 — I ran into an old friend somewhere I never expected.

{予期|よき}せぬ{事故|じこ}で、{電車|でんしゃ}が{大幅|おおはば}に{遅|おく}れた。 — An unforeseen accident made the trains very late.

2. **Before まま and うちに**, a little literary: {何|なに}も{言|い}わぬまま (without saying
   anything), {暗|くら}くならぬうちに (before it gets dark).
3. **At the end of a sentence**, only in old texts, proverbs and the speech of characters in
   historical dramas: {知|し}らぬが{仏|ほとけ} (ignorance is bliss: "not knowing, one is a Buddha").

Two things you already use come from ぬ. The polite negative ません is ます + ぬ (ませぬ, worn down to
ません), and the ん of casual 〜ん in western Japan and in older men's speech ({知|し}らん, {分|わ}からん)
is the same ぬ. Treat these as background: you don't need to produce ぬ, but you must recognize
it instantly, and never read it as a past or a command.

Don't confuse the negative ぬ with the ending of {死|し}ぬ (to die). And remember the order: ぬ follows the ない stem ({行|い}か + ぬ), never the
dictionary form (×{行|い}くぬ).

> **Review (lesson 18).** 〜まい is the written "won't" or "surely not": {二度|にど}と{行|い}くまい,
> {雨|あめ}は{降|ふ}るまい; する → するまい / すまい. With ぬ and ず it makes the set of written
> negatives: ず joins clauses, ぬ modifies nouns, まい ends the sentence with will or guess. None
> of them is a drill form.

## 〜べく: in order to (to recognize)

〜べく means "in order to, with the aim of" and is about as written as Japanese gets: reports,
company statements, news. It follows the dictionary form (する → すべく, also するべく) and is
followed by a verb of effort or action.

{人手不足|ひとでぶそく}を{補|おぎな}うべく、{介護|かいご}の{現場|げんば}に{新|あたら}しい{機械|きかい}が{導入|どうにゅう}された。 — To make up for the labour shortage, new machines were brought into care work.

In your own writing, 〜ために is always correct. Recognize べく; you'll rarely need to write it.

## 〜とする and 〜とされる: defining and regarding

〜とする has several jobs. Two are central to formal writing.

**In rules and definitions**, 〜とする means "shall be, is defined as". It's the voice of
regulations, membership rules and official guidance:

この{会|かい}の{会員|かいいん}は、{市内|しない}に{住|す}む{六十五歳|ろくじゅうごさい}{以上|いじょう}の{人|ひと}とする。 — Members of this association shall be residents of the city aged 65 or over.

{申|もう}し{込|こ}みの{期日|きじつ}は、{三月|さんがつ}{末|まつ}とする。 — The deadline for applications shall be the end of March.

**In arguments**, 〜とする sets up a supposition: "let's say, suppose". It's often with
かりに (supposing; its kanji is outside N2):

かりに{税|ぜい}を{上|あ}げるとする。その{場合|ばあい}、{最|もっと}も{負担|ふたん}が{重|おも}くなるのはだれだろうか。 — Suppose taxes were raised. In that case, who would bear the heaviest burden?

〜とされる is the passive: "is regarded as, is said to be". It reports a general or official
view without naming who holds it, and it's everywhere in news and textbooks:

{日本|にほん}は、{世界|せかい}でも{高齢化|こうれいか}が{最|もっと}も{進|すす}んだ{国|くに}の{一|ひと}つとされる。 — Japan is regarded as one of the most aged societies in the world.

この{制度|せいど}は、{多|おお}くの{家庭|かてい}を{助|たす}けたとされている。 — This scheme is said to have helped many households.

〜とされる sits between と{言|い}われる (people say) and と{考|かんが}えられる (it is thought, on
evidence): it sounds official and settled. Lesson 24 met it with とみられる; here it's a tool for
your own writing.

## 〜にいたる, 〜にいたって, 〜にいたるまで

いたる (to reach, to arrive at) is written in kana in this course; its kanji is outside N2. In
writing it turns up in three patterns.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| N / V にいたる | to reach, to end in (a stage or result) | {大|おお}きな{事故|じこ}にいたる |
| V にいたって(ようやく / はじめて) | only when it came to … (did …) | {問題|もんだい}が{深刻|しんこく}になるにいたって、ようやく… |
| A から B にいたるまで | from A right down to B; even | {子供|こども}から{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}にいたるまで |

{小|ちい}さな{誤解|ごかい}が{重|かさ}なり、{団体|だんたい}は{解散|かいさん}するにいたった。 — Small misunderstandings piled up, and in the end the organization was dissolved.

{住民|じゅうみん}が{声|こえ}を{上|あ}げるにいたって、{市|し}はやっと{調査|ちょうさ}を{始|はじ}めた。 — Only when the residents spoke out did the city finally start an investigation.

この{団地|だんち}では、{買|か}い{物|もの}から{病院|びょういん}の{送|おく}り{迎|むか}えにいたるまで、{住民|じゅうみん}が{助|たす}け{合|あ}っている。 — On this estate, residents help one another with everything from shopping right down to lifts to the hospital.

にいたる usually describes the end point of a process, often a serious one. にいたって stresses
that action came late. にいたるまで lists a range and stresses its far end, like まで with an
exclamation mark. 〜にいたっては ("as for …, the worst case") also exists; recognize it if you see it.

## 〜にほかならない: nothing other than

〜にほかならない says "is nothing other than, is precisely": it identifies one cause or one meaning
and rules out the rest. It follows a noun, or a clause + から / ため:

{福祉|ふくし}とは、{人|ひと}が{人|ひと}らしく{生|い}きるための{仕組|しく}みにほかならない。 — Welfare is nothing other than a system that lets people live as human beings should.

{町|まち}が{元気|げんき}を{取|と}り{戻|もど}したのは、{住民|じゅうみん}が{団結|だんけつ}したからにほかならない。 — The town got its energy back precisely because the residents pulled together.

ほか (other) is written in kana here, as in lesson 19's 〜ほかない; you'll also see
〜に{他|ほか}ならない. It's emphatic and written; in speech people say まさに〜だ or 〜そのものだ.

## Written opinions: であろう, と{言|い}えよう, のではなかろうか

The written style has softer and harder ways to end an opinion. N3 gave you と{考|かんが}えられる and
のではないだろうか. These are their more formal cousins.

| Speech or plain writing | Formal writing | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 〜だろう | 〜であろう | probably …, surely … |
| 〜と{言|い}えるだろう | 〜と{言|い}えよう | one could say that … |
| 〜のではないだろうか | 〜のではなかろうか | isn't it the case that…? |
| 〜なければならない | 〜ねばならない | must |
| 〜ないだろう | 〜まい | surely won't |

{今後|こんご}、{介護|かいご}を{必要|ひつよう}とする{人|ひと}はさらに{増|ふ}えるであろう。 — From now on, the number of people needing care will surely rise further.

{地域|ちいき}の{支|ささ}え{合|あ}いこそが、{最|もっと}も{確|たし}かなセーフティーネットだと{言|い}えよう。 — One could say that mutual support in the community is the surest safety net.

{制度|せいど}を{変|か}えるより{先|さき}に、{人|ひと}と{人|ひと}とのつながりを{作|つく}るべきではなかろうか。 — Shouldn't we build ties between people before changing the system?

- {言|い}えよう is the volitional of {言|い}える used as a guess (the old use of 〜よう, "it will
  probably be"). Likewise {考|かんが}えられよう, {分|わ}かろう.
- なかろう is the old form of ないだろう: い-adjectives had their own guess ending 〜かろう
  ({高|たか}かろう, よかろう). Today you'll meet it mostly in のではなかろうか and in a few phrases.
- These endings belong together with である. Don't use them in a です / ます text.

> **Review (lesson 9).** 〜つつある is the written "in the process of": {高齢化|こうれいか}が{進|すす}みつつある.
> It pairs well with this lesson's endings: {格差|かくさ}は{広|ひろ}がりつつあると{言|い}えよう.

## Duty and necessity, side by side

| Form | Strength and voice | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜なければならない | must (neutral; speech and writing) | {払|はら}わなければならない |
| 〜ねばならない | must (written, formal; a duty) | {払|はら}わねばならない |
| 〜べきである | ought to (a recommendation, a moral view) | {払|はら}うべきである |
| 〜ざるを{得|え}ない | have no choice but (lesson 17) | {払|はら}わざるを{得|え}ない |
| 〜{必要|ひつよう}がある | it is necessary (factual) | {払|はら}う{必要|ひつよう}がある |

All five can appear in an essay. Choose by what you mean: a duty (ねばならない), a recommendation
(べきである), reluctant acceptance (ざるを{得|え}ない) or a plain fact about what's needed
({必要|ひつよう}がある).

## Written words

These adverbs and conjunctions mark a text as written. Most are new; their spoken equivalents are
in brackets.

| Word | Meaning | Spoken |
|---|---|---|
| {極|きわ}めて | extremely (lesson 14) | とても, すごく |
| {著|いちじる}しい / {著|いちじる}しく | marked(ly), striking(ly) (lesson 20) | すごく{目立|めだ}つ |
| {一層|いっそう} | all the more | もっと, さらに |
| {依然|いぜん}として | still, as before | まだ{変|か}わらず |
| {未|いま}だ(に) | still (usually with a negative: still not) | まだ |
| いかに | how (much), to what extent | どんなに |
| {並|なら}びに | as well as (lists) | と |
| もしくは | or | または, か |
| かつ | and also | そして |
| {今日|こんにち} | nowadays (not "today") | {最近|さいきん}, {今|いま} |
| {我々|われわれ} | we (speaking for a group) | {私|わたし}たち |

{今日|こんにち}、{一人暮|ひとりぐ}らしの{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}は{珍|めずら}しくない。 — Nowadays, elderly people living alone are not unusual.

{手続|てつづ}きは{簡単|かんたん}かつ{無料|むりょう}である。 — The procedure is simple and free of charge.

{今日|こんにち} (こんにち) is the written "these days" and looks exactly like {今日|きょう} (today): read
the context. {我々|われわれ} was in kana at N3; its first kanji is lesson 2's, and 々 repeats it.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

In the suburbs of Tokyo there is a large housing estate built fifty years ago. It was once full of
young families raising children, and in the evenings, it is said, the square rang with children's
voices. But when the children grew up they left for central Tokyo, and only their parents'
generation remained. Now nearly half the residents are 65 or over, and many of them live alone. It
is a sight that can be seen all over Japan, nothing more and nothing less.

An ageing society is not in itself a bad thing. One could even say that being able to live long
is proof of an affluent society. The problem is that the ties between people weaken, and those who
need help can no longer be seen. The loneliness of living alone is hard for those around to notice,
unless the person concerned speaks up. On this estate, too, a few years ago, a man who collapsed in his
flat went undiscovered for several days. Fortunately his life was saved, but the residents were
deeply shocked. They realized that they had lived for decades without even knowing the faces of
the people next door.

The residents talked it over in the residents' association and came to the conclusion that,
rather than relying only on the authorities, they must act themselves. Using part of a subsidy
from the city, they rented an empty flat and opened a small café where anyone can drop in. It is run by the
residents' group, and the charge was set at a hundred yen a visit. Over tea and conversation it has
also become a place where people consult each other about care and tax paperwork. If
someone fails to come to the café for several days in a row, a resident who knows them goes to
see how they are. It is not a special scheme. But keeping an eye on one another in this way is
said to fill in the parts that public welfare services alone cannot cover.

What is interesting is that the people who support and the people who are supported are not fixed.
A woman who has trouble walking minds the shop, and a man who used to work for a company has taken
on the accounts. Recently students from a nearby university, and a foreign family who have just
moved onto the estate, have started coming too. Exchanges across the generations, from children right down to the elderly,
are beginning to grow. Nobody there is only on the receiving end.

Of course, relying only on the goodwill of residents is dangerous. When someone needs care,
professional help is required, and keeping the activity going needs the younger generation to
take part too. The authorities must not only provide money but think about ways to support such
efforts over the long term. Society will no doubt go on ageing. When it does, isn't what we need,
more than fine buildings, relationships in which people can call out to one another?

</details>

```speak
{何|なん}とかせねばならない。
= We must do something about it.
{知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に、{子供|こども}たちは{大人|おとな}になっていた。
= Before we knew it, the children had grown up.
{福祉|ふくし}とは、{人|ひと}が{人|ひと}らしく{生|い}きるための{仕組|しく}みにほかならない。
= Welfare is nothing other than a system that lets people live as human beings should.
{子供|こども}から{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}にいたるまで、だれもが{参加|さんか}できる。
= Everyone can take part, from children right down to the elderly.
{支|ささ}え{合|あ}いこそが{大切|たいせつ}だと{言|い}えよう。
= One could say that supporting one another is what matters most.
```

Read ねば, ぬ and であろう as written: they are never shortened in reading aloud. {今日|こんにち}
is こんにち, with the pitch on こ ({今日|こんにち} is [こんにち:1]), not {今日|きょう}.

## Common mistakes

- ×{行|い}くねばならない, ×しねばならない. ねば follows the ない stem: {行|い}かねば, and する
  becomes せねば.
- ×{知|し}らぬだった. ぬ has no past form; in modern writing the past negative is 〜なかった.
- Reading ぬ as a command or a past. {知|し}らぬ{人|ひと} is "a person one doesn't know", not
  "a person who knew".
- 〜べく after a past or a negative (×{行|い}ったべく, ×{行|い}かないべく). べく follows the
  dictionary form and states a purpose.
- にいたる for an ordinary arrival (×{駅|えき}にいたった). Use {着|つ}いた; にいたる is for reaching
  a stage or a result.
- にほかならない for a guess. It's an emphatic identification ("precisely this"), not "probably".
- Mixing であろう or ねばならない into a です / ます text. These belong to the である style.
- Reading {今日|こんにち} as きょう in an essay about society ("nowadays").

## Key points

- 〜ねばならない (ない stem + ねば; する → せねば) is the written "must"; 〜ねば alone is "if not".
- 〜ぬ is the classical negative: mostly before nouns ({知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に, {見知|みし}らぬ{人|ひと},
  {思|おも}わぬ, {予期|よき}せぬ) and in set phrases. Recognize it; ません and dialect 〜ん come from it.
- 〜べく: in order to (very written; recognize).
- 〜とする: "shall be" in rules, "suppose" in arguments; 〜とされる: "is regarded as".
- 〜にいたる (reach a stage), 〜にいたって (only when it came to …), 〜にいたるまで (right down to).
- 〜にほかならない: nothing other than, precisely.
- Formal endings: であろう, と{言|い}えよう, のではなかろうか, まい.
- Written words: {極|きわ}めて, {著|いちじる}しい, {一層|いっそう}, {依然|いぜん}として, {未|いま}だに,
  いかに, {並|なら}びに, もしくは, かつ, {今日|こんにち}.
- New kanji: 齢 祉 障 補 希 税 貯 豊 独 舎 郊 団 派.

The reference sheet "Written style" puts the spoken and written forms side by side. The words from
this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Word formation: prefixes and suffixes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese builds a great many words from a small set of pieces. You already know dozens of them
without having thought about it: {高齢化|こうれいか} is {高齢|こうれい} + 〜{化|か}, {不便|ふべん} is 〜{便|べん}
with {不|ふ}〜 in front, {会社員|かいしゃいん} is {会社|かいしゃ} + 〜{員|いん}. At N2 this stops being a
curiosity and becomes a skill. Newspaper and textbook Japanese is dense with these compounds, and
the JLPT N2 has its own question type for them, **[[word formation]]**: a word with a gap before or
after it, and four prefixes or suffixes to choose from.

{国際|こくさい}＿＿ — {化|か}, {性|せい}, {的|てき}, {感|かん}? → {国際化|こくさいか} (internationalization)

＿＿{関心|かんしん} — {不|ふ}, {非|ひ}, {無|む}, {未|み}? → {無関心|むかんしん} (indifference)

This lesson sorts the commonest **[[prefixes]]** and **[[suffixes]]** by meaning, shows how their sounds
change, and separates the combinations you must learn as words from the patterns you can use
freely. The theme words are the abstract words that these pieces build: states and situations,
extent and position, order, spans of time and completion.

## Three kinds of words

Japanese vocabulary comes from three sources, and they behave differently when words are built.

| Kind | What it is | Examples | Builds words with |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[Wago]]** ({和語|わご}) | native Japanese words | {山|やま}, {話|はな}す, {高|たか}い, {並|なら}ぶ | other wago, often with a sound change ({山|やま} + {川|かわ} → {山川|やまがわ}) |
| **[[Kango]]** ({漢語|かんご}) | words built from on'yomi, originally from Chinese | {状態|じょうたい}, {完了|かんりょう}, {福祉|ふくし} | kanji prefixes and suffixes: {無|む}〜, 〜{化|か}, 〜{性|せい} |
| **[[Gairaigo]]** ({外来語|がいらいご}) | loanwords, mostly from English, in katakana | データ, システム, ケア | some kango suffixes: データ{化|か}, システム{的|てき} |

Most prefixes and suffixes in this lesson are kango and attach to kango: {不|ふ} + {安定|あんてい},
{安全|あんぜん} + {性|せい}. Many also take gairaigo (デジタル{化|か}, スピード{感|かん}). They rarely
attach to wago, which have their own ways: {高|たか}さ (height), {話|はな}し{方|かた} (way of speaking).

A kanji compound read entirely with on'yomi is almost always kango; a word with okurigana
({並|なら}べる) or a kun'yomi ({幅|はば}) is wago. Knowing which you have tells you which pieces fit.

## The four negative prefixes: {不|ふ}〜, {無|む}〜, {非|ひ}〜, {未|み}〜

These are the commonest word-formation question at N2, because they all translate as "un‑, in‑,
non‑". Each has a core meaning, but in the end the combinations are fixed: learn each word with its
prefix.

| Prefix | Core meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| {不|ふ}〜 (ふ, sometimes ぶ) | not (negates a quality or state) | {不安|ふあん}, {不便|ふべん}, {不可能|ふかのう}, {不規則|ふきそく}, {不安定|ふあんてい}, {不平等|ふびょうどう}, {不足|ふそく}, {不注意|ふちゅうい}, {不十分|ふじゅうぶん}, {不器用|ぶきよう} |
| {無|む}〜 (む, sometimes ぶ) | there is no …, without | {無料|むりょう}, {無理|むり}, {無関心|むかんしん}, {無責任|むせきにん}, {無意識|むいしき}, {無断|むだん}, {無名|むめい}, {無事|ぶじ} |
| {非|ひ}〜 | not of, outside the bounds of | {非常識|ひじょうしき}, {非公開|ひこうかい}, {非公式|ひこうしき}, {非常|ひじょう}, {非現実的|ひげんじつてき}, {非正規|ひせいき} |
| {未|み}〜 | not yet | {未成年|みせいねん}, {未経験|みけいけん}, {未完成|みかんせい}, {未定|みてい}, {未知|みち}, {未解決|みかいけつ} |

Rules of thumb (tendencies, not laws):

- {無|む}〜 goes with a noun for something you can have or lack: {関心|かんしん} (interest),
  {責任|せきにん} (responsibility), {料金|りょうきん} (charge), {意識|いしき} (awareness). The result is
  "having no …".
- {不|ふ}〜 goes with a word that already describes a state or a quality, often a な-adjective:
  {安定|あんてい}, {規則|きそく}, {可能|かのう}, {平等|びょうどう}, {十分|じゅうぶん}. The result is "not …".
- {非|ひ}〜 says that something falls outside a category or a norm: {常識|じょうしき} (common
  sense), {公開|こうかい} (being public), {公式|こうしき} (official). It also forms adjectives with
  〜{的|てき}: {非現実的|ひげんじつてき} (unrealistic), {非科学的|ひかがくてき} (unscientific).
- {未|み}〜 always means "not yet": something that will or should happen later. {未完成|みかんせい}
  (not yet finished) is different from {不完全|ふかんぜん} (imperfect, flawed).

Pairs to compare:

{絵|え}はまだ{未完成|みかんせい}だ。 — The painting isn't finished yet.

{説明|せつめい}が{不完全|ふかんぜん}で、{誤解|ごかい}を{生|う}んだ。 — The explanation was incomplete (flawed) and caused a misunderstanding.

{会議|かいぎ}は{非公開|ひこうかい}で{行|おこな}われた。 — The meeting was held behind closed doors.

その{書類|しょるい}はまだ{公開|こうかい}されていない（{未公開|みこうかい}だ）。 — That document hasn't been made public yet.

Readings: {不|ふ} is ぶ in a handful of words ({不器用|ぶきよう} clumsy, {不気味|ぶきみ} eerie), and
{無|む} is ぶ in {無事|ぶじ} (safe) and {無礼|ぶれい} (rude). There are few; learn them as words.

## Other prefixes

| Prefix | Meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| {再|さい}〜 | again, re‑ | {再開|さいかい}, {再利用|さいりよう}, {再確認|さいかくにん}, {再放送|さいほうそう} |
| {超|ちょう}〜 | super‑, ultra‑ | {超高層|ちょうこうそう}ビル (skyscraper), {超大型|ちょうおおがた}; casual {超|ちょう}うれしい |
| {反|はん}〜 | anti‑, counter‑ | {反比例|はんぴれい} (inverse proportion), {反社会的|はんしゃかいてき} (antisocial), {反作用|はんさよう} |
| {副|ふく}〜 | vice‑, secondary | {副社長|ふくしゃちょう}, {副作用|ふくさよう}, {副業|ふくぎょう} |
| {諸|しょ}〜 | various, the many | {諸問題|しょもんだい}, {諸国|しょこく}, {諸外国|しょがいこく} |
| {各|かく}〜 | each | {各国|かっこく}, {各地|かくち}, {各自|かくじ} (each person), {各駅|かくえき} |
| {旧|きゅう}〜 | former, old | {旧型|きゅうがた}, {旧友|きゅうゆう} (an old friend) |
| {総|そう}〜 | total, general | {総額|そうがく}, {総数|そうすう}, {総合|そうごう} |
| {高|こう}〜 / {低|てい}〜 | high‑ / low‑ | {高性能|こうせいのう}, {高収入|こうしゅうにゅう}, {高品質|こうひんしつ}; {低温|ていおん}, {低価格|ていかかく}, {低所得|ていしょとく} |
| {半|はん}〜 | half | {半年|はんとし}, {半日|はんにち}, {半額|はんがく}, {半分|はんぶん} |
| {新|しん}〜 / {前|ぜん}〜 / {元|もと}〜 | new / former, previous / ex‑ | {新型|しんがた}, {新製品|しんせいひん}; {前社長|ぜんしゃちょう}; {元|もと}{会社員|かいしゃいん} |

- {各|かく} becomes かっ before k: {各国|かっこく} (also かくこく). {諸|しょ} and {各|かく} are written
  and formal: {各国|かっこく}の{代表|だいひょう} (the representatives of each country).
- {超|ちょう}〜 in writing builds serious words ({超高層|ちょうこうそう}); in casual speech it's an
  intensifier on almost anything ({超|ちょう}おいしい). Don't use the casual one in an essay.
- {元|もと}〜 is a wago prefix ("formerly"): {元|もと}{会社員|かいしゃいん}, {元|もと}{選手|せんしゅ}.
  {前|ぜん}〜 is the one just before the present one: {前社長|ぜんしゃちょう} is the previous president.

## Suffixes that make nouns and adjectives

| Suffix | Meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| 〜{化|か} | ‑ization, becoming | {高齢化|こうれいか}, {国際化|こくさいか}, {自由化|じゆうか}, {多様化|たようか}, デジタル{化|か} |
| 〜{性|せい} | ‑ness, ‑ity, the nature of | {安全性|あんぜんせい}, {可能性|かのうせい}, {重要性|じゅうようせい}, {多様性|たようせい} |
| 〜{的|てき} | ‑ic, ‑al (makes a な-adjective) | {社会的|しゃかいてき}, {一時的|いちじてき}, {基本的|きほんてき}, {積極的|せっきょくてき} |
| 〜{感|かん} | a sense of, a feeling of | {責任感|せきにんかん}, {安心感|あんしんかん}, {達成感|たっせいかん}, {一体感|いったいかん} |
| 〜{力|りょく} | the power or ability to | {想像力|そうぞうりょく}, {集中力|しゅうちゅうりょく}, {説得力|せっとくりょく}, {理解力|りかいりょく} |
| 〜{率|りつ} | rate, ratio | {合格率|ごうかくりつ}, {確率|かくりつ}, {比率|ひりつ}, {成長率|せいちょうりつ} |
| 〜{界|かい} | world, circles | {政界|せいかい}, {芸能界|げいのうかい}, {自然界|しぜんかい} |
| 〜{型|がた} | type, model | {大型|おおがた}, {小型|こがた}, {新型|しんがた}, {旧型|きゅうがた}, {血液型|けつえきがた} |
| 〜{式|しき} | style, method; ceremony | {和式|わしき}, {洋式|ようしき}, {日本式|にほんしき}; {卒業式|そつぎょうしき} |
| 〜{層|そう} | layer, age or social group | {年齢層|ねんれいそう}, {高齢層|こうれいそう}, {若年層|じゃくねんそう} |
| 〜{観|かん} | view of | {価値観|かちかん}, {人生観|じんせいかん}, {世界観|せかいかん} |
| 〜{制|せい} | system | {会員制|かいいんせい}, {予約制|よやくせい}, {税制|ぜいせい} |
| 〜{面|めん} | aspect, side | {精神面|せいしんめん}, {経済面|けいざいめん}, {安全面|あんぜんめん} |
| 〜{上|じょう} | in terms of, from the point of view of | {法律上|ほうりつじょう}, {教育上|きょういくじょう}, {歴史上|れきしじょう} |
| 〜{状|じょう} | letter; in the form of | {招待状|しょうたいじょう}, {案内状|あんないじょう}; {液状|えきじょう}, {粉状|こなじょう} |
| 〜{風|ふう} | in the style of, looking like | {和風|わふう}, {洋風|ようふう}, {学生風|がくせいふう}の{男性|だんせい} |

Notes:

- 〜{化|か} and 〜{性|せい} make nouns; 〜{的|てき} makes な-adjectives ({社会的|しゃかいてき}な{問題|もんだい},
  {一時的|いちじてき}に). 〜{化|か} nouns often take する: {多様化|たようか}する (to diversify).
- 〜{感|かん} has become very productive: スピード{感|かん}, {高級感|こうきゅうかん} (a sense of luxury).
  Use the established ones in writing.
- 〜{上|じょう} is lesson 7's ({契約上|けいやくじょう}): "from the standpoint of". Don't confuse it with
  〜{上|うえ} (on top of) or {上|うえ}で.
- 〜{面|めん} turns up in essays and reports: {経済面|けいざいめん}では{問題|もんだい}ないが、{安全面|あんぜんめん}に{不安|ふあん}が{残|のこ}る
  (economically it's fine, but doubts remain about safety).

## Money: 〜{費|ひ}, 〜{料|りょう}, 〜{代|だい}, 〜{賃|ちん}

Four suffixes all mean "cost, fee", and the word decides which one it takes. Tendencies:

| Suffix | Tendency | Words |
|---|---|---|
| 〜{費|ひ} | expenses of a type (budgets, records) | {生活費|せいかつひ}, {交通費|こうつうひ}, {食費|しょくひ}, {医療費|いりょうひ} |
| 〜{料|りょう} | a fee charged for a service or for use | {手数料|てすうりょう}, {入場料|にゅうじょうりょう}, {授業料|じゅぎょうりょう}, {保険料|ほけんりょう} |
| 〜{代|だい} | the price of a thing or service (everyday) | {電気代|でんきだい}, {食事代|しょくじだい}, {本代|ほんだい} |
| 〜{賃|ちん} | payment for transport, renting or work | {運賃|うんちん}, {家賃|やちん}, {賃金|ちんぎん} (lesson 1) |

{電気代|でんきだい} and {電気料金|でんきりょうきん} mean the same bill: 〜{代|だい} is the everyday word and
{料金|りょうきん} the one on the bill itself. When you meet a new money word, note its suffix.

## People: 〜{家|か}, 〜{者|しゃ}, 〜{員|いん}, 〜{派|は}

| Suffix | Tendency | Words |
|---|---|---|
| 〜{家|か} | someone with an art, a skill or a calling | {専門家|せんもんか}, {作家|さっか}, {政治家|せいじか}, {芸術家|げいじゅつか} |
| 〜{者|しゃ} | someone who does or is something | {研究者|けんきゅうしゃ}, {高齢者|こうれいしゃ}, {消費者|しょうひしゃ}, {未経験者|みけいけんしゃ} |
| 〜{員|いん} | a member of an organization | {会社員|かいしゃいん}, {公務員|こうむいん}, {店員|てんいん}, {会員|かいいん} |
| 〜{派|は} | a side in a debate, a school of thought | {賛成派|さんせいは}, {反対派|はんたいは}, {少数派|しょうすうは} |

〜{家|か} is read か here, け in a family name ({田中家|たなかけ}, the Tanaka family) and や in
{大家|おおや} (landlord). In listening questions, a lone 〜{家|か} is often in kana for that reason.

## Sound changes when words join

Three changes are common. You can't always predict them, but knowing them helps you hear and read.

1. **[[Rendaku]]** (voicing): the first consonant of the second part becomes voiced, mostly in wago
   compounds. {型|かた} → {大型|おおがた}, {方|かた} → {話|はな}し{方|かた} (no change here) but
   {夕方|ゆうがた}, {不足|ふそく} → {人手不足|ひとでぶそく}, {力|ちから} → {底力|そこぢから}. Kango suffixes
   mostly don't change: {想像力|そうぞうりょく}, {会社員|かいしゃいん}.
2. **Small っ** (gemination): a kanji ending in つ, ち, く or き often shortens before k, s, t or p
   sounds: {一|いち} + {周|しゅう} → {一周|いっしゅう}, {各|かく} + {国|こく} → {各国|かっこく},
   {学|がく} + {校|こう} → {学校|がっこう}.
3. **Half-voicing after ん or っ**: h becomes p: {反|はん} + {比例|ひれい} → {反比例|はんぴれい},
   {一|いっ} + {匹|ひき} → {一匹|いっぴき} (lesson 30).

## Words or patterns?

Some combinations are **[[lexicalized]]**: they are words in their own right, with their own meaning,
and you can't make similar ones at will. {無理|むり} isn't simply "no reason"; {非常|ひじょう} isn't
"not usual" but "emergency" (and {非常|ひじょう}に, "very"). These are vocabulary items, and the list
at the end of this lesson has many of them ({無関心|むかんしん}, {不可能|ふかのう}, {未成年|みせいねん},
{未経験|みけいけん}, {一時的|いちじてき}…; {再開|さいかい}, {大型|おおがた} and {総額|そうがく} were met in lessons 9–15).

Other combinations are **[[productive]]**: the pattern is alive, and writers create new words with it
every day. 〜{化|か}, 〜{性|せい}, 〜{的|てき}, 〜{感|かん}, {再|さい}〜 and {高|こう}〜 / {低|てい}〜 are the most
productive. You'll meet デジタル{化|か} or {再|さい}チャレンジ in an article, understand them at once,
and won't find them in a dictionary. In the JLPT, word-formation questions test established words,
so learn the common ones; in your own writing, use a new combination only when you've seen it used.

## Words for state, extent, position, order and time

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| State and situation | {状態|じょうたい}, {状況|じょうきょう}, {事態|じたい}, {実態|じったい}, {順調|じゅんちょう}, {固定|こてい}, {一定|いってい}, {固|かた}まる, {固|かた}める |
| Extent | {幅|はば}, {幅広|はばひろ}い, {大幅|おおはば}, {最低限|さいていげん}, {最大限|さいだいげん}, {並|な}み, {段階|だんかい} |
| Position | {中央|ちゅうおう}, {中間|ちゅうかん}, {周囲|しゅうい}, {周辺|しゅうへん}, {付近|ふきん}, {辺|あた}り, {囲|かこ}む |
| Order and process | {順|じゅん}, {順位|じゅんい}, {手順|てじゅん}, {過程|かてい}, {並|なら}べる, {並行|へいこう} |
| Time | {翌日|よくじつ}, {翌朝|よくあさ}, {翌月|よくげつ}, {翌年|よくねん}, {前半|ぜんはん}, {後半|こうはん}, {長期|ちょうき}, {短期|たんき}, {一時的|いちじてき}, {半|なか}ば, {前後|ぜんご}, {周期|しゅうき}, 〜{周年|しゅうねん}, {永久|えいきゅう}, {久|ひさ}しい |
| Completion | {完了|かんりょう}, {了解|りょうかい}, {未定|みてい}, {一周|いっしゅう} |

{状態|じょうたい} or {状況|じょうきょう}? {状態|じょうたい} is the condition a thing or person is in
({体|からだ}の{状態|じょうたい}, {車|くるま}の{状態|じょうたい}); {状況|じょうきょう} is the situation around
them, which changes ({経済|けいざい}の{状況|じょうきょう}, {今|いま}の{状況|じょうきょう}では). {事態|じたい} is a
situation that has developed, usually a bad one; {実態|じったい} is the true state behind appearances.

{翌|よく}〜 counts from a reference point: {試験|しけん}の{翌日|よくじつ} (the day after the exam). From
today, say {明日|あした}; from this year, {来年|らいねん}.

{前後|ぜんご} after a number means "about": {三十人|さんじゅうにん}{前後|ぜんご}, {五時|ごじ}{前後|ぜんご}. It works
on either side of the number, like ぐらい.

2. Why are kanji compounds so convenient for newspapers?
3. What danger does the writer see?
4. What advice does the writer give to learners of Japanese?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Western learning and institutions arrived all at once, and Japanese had no words for them, so
   scholars combined kanji into new words or gave old words new meanings ({社会|しゃかい} and
   {自由|じゆう} are said to have taken their present meanings then).
2. Kanji parts have clear meanings and are short ({安全性|あんぜんせい} in three characters instead of a

   that's also why headlines are strings of kanji.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Open a newspaper and you find a surprising number of words ending in 〜{化|か}, 〜{性|せい} and 〜{的|てき}:
{高齢化|こうれいか} (ageing), デジタル{化|か} (digitization), {安全性|あんぜんせい} (safety), {国際的|こくさいてき} (international). All
of them are words made by combining two or more parts. Japanese has created new words one after
another in this way, by linking short kanji parts together.

Many of these words are said to have multiplied in the Meiji era. When Western learning and
institutions arrived all at once, Japanese had no words to express them. So the scholars of the
time combined kanji to make new words, or gave old words new meanings. {社会|しゃかい} (society) and {自由|じゆう}
(freedom) are said to be words that came to be used in their present meanings at that time. Some,
it is said, were later taken into Chinese.

Kanji parts are convenient because their meanings are clear and they are short. Written out as
"the point of whether it is safe or not" it is long, but {安全性|あんぜんせい} takes just three characters. For a
newspaper, which must fit a lot of information into limited space, nothing could be handier. That
is also why headlines are so often strings of kanji, such as "service resumed" or "system to be
reviewed".

The parts aren't only kanji. Words made by adding a kanji part to a loanword, such as デジタル{化|か}
(digitization) and スピード{感|かん} (a sense of speed), are no longer unusual today. The other way
round, a kanji part is sometimes put in front, as in {再|さい}チャレンジ (a second try). One could say
that the freedom with which kango and loanwords combine is one of the great features of Japanese.

However, a handy tool has its dangers. Expressions such as "we will consider it positively" or "we
will respond flexibly" can seem to say something while in fact promising nothing. Add 〜{的|てき} and
you can make almost any word a little vague. A text full of kanji looks impressive, but that
doesn't mean it gets through to its readers.

For people learning Japanese as a foreign language, too, this system is a great ally. If you know
that {化|か} expresses "becoming so" and {性|せい} "that kind of nature", you can roughly imagine the meaning
of a word you're seeing for the first time. If you know {再|さい}, for example, you'll understand
{再開|さいかい}, {再利用|さいりよう} and {再確認|さいかくにん} at once. Every time you learn a part, the number of words you
can read grows by dozens. The shortcut to a wider vocabulary is to look at how words are put together, not just to memorize
them whole.

## Common mistakes

- ×{不関心|ふかんしん}, ×{無安定|むあんてい}, ×{不公開|ふこうかい}. The prefix belongs to the word:
  {無関心|むかんしん}, {不安定|ふあんてい}, {非公開|ひこうかい}.
- {未完成|みかんせい} for something flawed. {未|み}〜 is "not yet"; a flawed thing is
  {不完全|ふかんぜん}.
- ×{社会的|しゃかいてき}の{問題|もんだい}. 〜{的|てき} makes a な-adjective: {社会的|しゃかいてき}な{問題|もんだい}
  (or the noun {社会|しゃかい}{問題|もんだい}).
- Reading 〜{型|がた} as かた after a word ({大型|おおがた}, not ×おおかた, which is a different word:
  "most, probably").
- {翌日|よくじつ} for "tomorrow". {翌|よく}〜 counts from a day already mentioned; from today, use
  {明日|あした}.
- Using casual {超|ちょう}〜 ({超|ちょう}{大変|たいへん}) in writing.

## Key points

- Japanese words are wago (native), kango (on'yomi compounds) or gairaigo (loanwords). Kanji
  prefixes and suffixes attach mostly to kango, and some to gairaigo.
- {不|ふ}〜 "not" (a state), {無|む}〜 "no …", {非|ひ}〜 "outside, non‑", {未|み}〜 "not yet". Learn each
  word with its prefix.
- Prefixes: {再|さい}, {超|ちょう}, {反|はん}, {副|ふく}, {諸|しょ}, {各|かく}, {旧|きゅう}, {総|そう}, {高|こう} / {低|てい},
  {半|はん}, {新|しん}, {前|ぜん}, {元|もと}.
- Suffixes: 〜{化|か}, 〜{性|せい}, 〜{的|てき}, 〜{感|かん}, 〜{力|りょく}, 〜{率|りつ}, 〜{界|かい}, 〜{型|がた},
  〜{式|しき}, 〜{層|そう}, 〜{観|かん}, 〜{制|せい}, 〜{面|めん}, 〜{上|じょう}, 〜{状|じょう}, 〜{風|ふう}; money:
  〜{費|ひ}, 〜{料|りょう}, 〜{代|だい}, 〜{賃|ちん}; people: 〜{家|か}, 〜{者|しゃ}, 〜{員|いん}, 〜{派|は}.
- Sound changes: rendaku ({大型|おおがた}, {人手不足|ひとでぶそく}), small っ ({一周|いっしゅう},
  {各国|かっこく}), h → p ({反比例|はんぴれい}).
- Lexicalized words are vocabulary; productive patterns (〜{化|か}, 〜{性|せい}, 〜{的|てき}, 〜{感|かん})
  make new words.
- New kanji: 了 久 翌 順 央 周 囲 辺 幅 並 固 況 態.

The reference sheet "Word formation" collects the prefixes and suffixes in one place. The words
from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Building an argument: したがって, もっとも, ただし, というものだ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Most long N2 reading texts are arguments: a column, an essay or an editorial that makes a claim,
admits the other side, gives reasons and draws a conclusion. To follow one you need to see its
skeleton, and the skeleton is made of **[[conjunctions]]** (connectors): したがって (therefore), もっとも (that said),
ただし (provided that), {要|よう}するに (in short). The JLPT N2 tests this directly in the **text
grammar** task, where a passage has gaps and you choose the connector or the reference word that
fits.

{確|たし}かに{規則|きそく}は{必要|ひつよう}だ。もっとも、{理由|りゆう}の{分|わ}からない{規則|きそく}に{従|したが}うのは{難|むずか}しい。 — Rules are certainly necessary. That said, it's hard to obey a rule whose reason you can't see.

{規則|きそく}は{守|まも}るためにある。しかし、{守|まも}れない{規則|きそく}を{作|つく}っても{意味|いみ}がないというものだ。 — Rules exist to be kept. But making rules that can't be kept is surely pointless.

This lesson completes the connectors you met at N3, adds the patterns that end an argument
(〜というものだ, 〜というものではない), shows how an N2 argumentative text is built, and practises
the text grammar task. The theme is opinions and values: points of view, criticism, effects,
standards, rules followed or broken, and belief.

> **Review (N3 lesson 28).** しかし / でも / ところが; なぜなら〜からだ; そのため / したがって; その{上|うえ},
> しかも, {更|さら}に; {一方|いっぽう}, それに{対|たい}して, {逆|ぎゃく}に; {結局|けっきょく}; むしろ;
> {確|たし}かに〜が; つまり, すなわち, {要|よう}するに. These are carried and used below as known.

## Therefore: したがって, それゆえ

したがって (N3) is the written "therefore": a conclusion that follows logically from what was
just said. It's usually written in kana as a connector, though its verb {従|したが}う (to follow) is
this lesson's.

この{薬|くすり}は{効果|こうか}が{高|たか}い{一方|いっぽう}、{副作用|ふくさよう}も{強|つよ}い。したがって、{医師|いし}の{指導|しどう}のもとで{使|つか}わねばならない。 — This medicine is very effective but also has strong side effects. It must therefore be used under a doctor's guidance.

それゆえ says the same thing in a more literary way; ゆえに (or 〜ゆえ after a noun: {若|わか}さゆえの{失敗|しっぱい}, a mistake born of youth) is the old word inside it. Recognize both; in your
own writing, したがって or そのため is enough.

## That said: もっとも

もっとも at the start of a sentence adds a limit or an exception to what was just said: "that
said, mind you, though admittedly". The main statement stands; the もっとも sentence qualifies it.

{来月|らいげつ}から{料金|りょうきん}が{上|あ}がる。もっとも、{会員|かいいん}は{今|いま}までと{同|おな}じだ。 — Prices go up next month. Members, though, will pay the same as before.

{彼|かれ}の{意見|いけん}には{賛成|さんせい}だ。もっとも、{全部|ぜんぶ}ではないが。 — I agree with his opinion. Not all of it, mind you.

- It is a different word from {最|もっと}も (most, N3), though the two sound alike; this course
  writes the connector in kana.
- As a な-adjective, もっともな means "reasonable, natural": もっともな{意見|いけん} (a fair point),
  {怒|おこ}るのももっともだ (it's only natural to be angry).
- もっとも often ends with 〜が or 〜けれど, as a half-reluctant admission.

## Provisos: ただし and なお

ただし and なお (N4, N3) are the two connectors of notices and rules, and they're easy to mix up.

| | Meaning | What follows |
|---|---|---|
| ただし | however, provided that | an exception or a condition that limits what came before |
| なお | in addition, please note | extra information that doesn't change what came before |

{入館|にゅうかん}は{無料|むりょう}です。ただし、{特別展|とくべつてん}は{別料金|べつりょうきん}となります。 — Admission is free. Special exhibitions, however, are charged separately.

{受付|うけつけ}は{午前|ごぜん}{九時|くじ}からです。なお、{駐車場|ちゅうしゃじょう}はございませんので、{公共|こうきょう}{交通機関|こうつうきかん}をご{利用|りよう}ください。 — Reception opens at 9 a.m. Please also note that there is no car park, so please use public transport.

The test: if the second sentence takes something back from the first ("free — but not this"),
it's ただし. If it simply adds a separate point, it's なお. もっとも is close to ただし, but it's
the voice of a writer or speaker qualifying an opinion, not the voice of a rulebook.

## Summing up: {要|よう}するに, いわば, すなわち

| Connector | Job | Feel |
|---|---|---|
| {要|よう}するに (N3) | sums up: "in short, the point is" | spoken and written |
| {要|よう}は | the same, more casual | spoken |
| すなわち (N3) | restates exactly: "that is, namely" | written |
| つまり | restates or concludes | everywhere |
| いわば | offers an image or comparison: "so to speak, as it were" | written and spoken |
| {言|い}い{換|か}えれば | "to put it another way" | written |

{図書館|としょかん}は、いわば{町|まち}の{居間|いま}である。 — The library is, so to speak, the town's living room.

{要|よう}するに、{問題|もんだい}はお{金|かね}ではなく{時間|じかん}なのだ。 — In short, the problem isn't money but time.

いわば admits that what follows is a comparison, not literally true: いわば〜のようなものだ is a
common frame. すなわち defines; いわば paints a picture.

## Opening a sentence: それにしても, とはいえ

Two openers from earlier courses do a lot of work in arguments:

- それにしても (N3): "even so, all the same", after accepting a point: {理由|りゆう}は{分|わ}かった。それにしても{遅|おそ}すぎる (I understand the reason. Even so, it's far too late).
- とはいえ (lesson 1) as a sentence opener: "that said, granted". It's more written than
  それにしても and often turns a concession into the writer's real point:
  {規則|きそく}は{必要|ひつよう}だ。とはいえ、{多|おお}すぎる{規則|きそく}は{人|ひと}を{考|かんが}えなくさせる。

## 〜というものだ, 〜というものではない

〜というものだ presents a judgement as a general truth, often with feeling: "that's just how it
is, that's what … is (surely)". It follows a noun or a plain-form clause.

{困|こま}っている{人|ひと}を{助|たす}けるのが、{友|とも}だちというものだ。 — Helping someone in trouble is what friends are for.

{一度|いちど}の{失敗|しっぱい}で{全部|ぜんぶ}を{否定|ひてい}するのは、{乱暴|らんぼう}というものだ。 — Rejecting everything because of one failure is surely going too far.

〜というものではない (also 〜というものでもない) denies a simple formula: "it's not the case that
… just because …". It typically follows 〜ば / 〜たら / 〜ても / 〜さえ〜ば.

{規則|きそく}を{増|ふ}やせば{問題|もんだい}がなくなるというものではない。 — It's not as if adding more rules makes problems go away.

お{金|かね}さえあれば{幸|しあわ}せになれるというものでもない。 — Money alone doesn't make you happy.

〜というものではない is softer than 〜わけではない (N3) and different in use: わけではない denies
a conclusion someone might draw; というものではない rejects a too-simple rule. Lesson 5's
〜とは{限|かぎ}らない is close; というものではない sounds more like a moral.

> **Review.** 〜と{言|い}える / 〜とは{言|い}えない (lesson 5), 〜ざるを{得|え}ない (lesson 17) and
> 〜のではないだろうか (N3; lesson 26's 〜のではなかろうか) are the other endings of arguments. A
> careful essay uses several, so it doesn't sound either timid or bossy.

## How an N2 argumentative text is built

Most columns and essays on the N2 follow a pattern like this. Recognize the signposts and you can
find the writer's claim even when you don't know every word.

| Part | What it does | Typical signposts |
|---|---|---|
| Introduction | raises the question, often with an example or a common view | 〜と{言|い}われる, 〜という{人|ひと}が{多|おお}い, 〜だろうか |
| Counter-view | admits what the other side gets right | {確|たし}かに〜。, もちろん〜。, 〜という{意見|いけん}もある |
| Turn | swings back to the writer's side | しかし, だが, とはいえ, それにしても |
| Reasons | gives grounds and examples | なぜなら〜からだ, {例|たと}えば, まず / {次|つぎ}に, その{上|うえ} |
| Limits | admits exceptions without giving way | もっとも, ただし |
| Conclusion | states the claim | したがって, {要|よう}するに, 〜べきではないだろうか, 〜というものだ |

Two warnings. First, the writer's own view is almost never in the counter-view: a sentence after
{確|たし}かに or もちろん is there to be answered. Second, the claim is usually in the last paragraph
and often softened (〜のではないだろうか, 〜と{言|い}えよう). On the exam, the question "What is the
writer's opinion?" is answered there, not by the first strong sentence you read.

## Text grammar: connectors and reference words

In the text grammar task, you read a passage with numbered gaps and choose the word for each gap.
The gaps are of three kinds.

1. **[[Connectors]]** between sentences: しかし, したがって, もっとも, ただし, なお, {例|たと}えば, つまり.
   Ask what the relationship is: contrast, result, limit, addition, example, restatement.
2. **[[Reference words]]** (**[[demonstratives]]** in a text): この / その / あの, こうした / そうした (such),
   これ / それ. In writing, その and それ point back to something just mentioned; この and これ to
   something the writer is presenting as close or important; こうした sums up several things.
3. **Sentence endings and forms** that fit the writer's stance: 〜のではないだろうか, 〜わけではない,
   〜というものだ, 〜ざるを{得|え}ない.

A worked example (original text):

> {最近|さいきん}、「{規則|きそく}だから」という{理由|りゆう}だけで{子供|こども}を{注意|ちゅうい}する{大人|おとな}が{多|おお}い。（①）、{規則|きそく}の{意味|いみ}を{説明|せつめい}しなければ、{子供|こども}は{自分|じぶん}で{考|かんが}えなくなる。（②）{考|かんが}えない{習慣|しゅうかん}は、{大人|おとな}になってからも{残|のこ}る。（③）、{危険|きけん}なことについては、{説明|せつめい}より{先|さき}に{止|と}めるべきだが。

① しかし (contrast with the common practice just described; したがって would make the second
sentence a result of the first, which it isn't). ② こうした (sums up "not thinking for oneself";
あの would point to something both reader and writer already share). ③ もっとも (a limit on the
writer's own claim, ending in 〜が; なお would add unrelated information, and ただし is the voice of
a rule, not of a writer qualifying an opinion).

## Words for opinions and values

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| Points of view | {視点|してん}, {観点|かんてん}, {視野|しや}, {見解|けんかい}, {立場|たちば} (N3), {側面|そくめん}, {論点|ろんてん}, {前提|ぜんてい} |
| Arguing | {論|ろん}じる, {主張|しゅちょう} (N3), {説得|せっとく}する, {一理|いちり}, {賛否|さんぴ}, {正論|せいろん}, {一般論|いっぱんろん}, してき, むじゅん, りくつ, かいしゃく, ぶんせき, {定義|ていぎ}, {裏付|うらづ}け |
| Judging | {批評|ひひょう}, {批判的|ひはんてき}, {重視|じゅうし}する, {無視|むし}する, {合理的|ごうりてき}, {積極的|せっきょくてき}, {消極的|しょうきょくてき}, {基本的|きほんてき}, {本質|ほんしつ}, {根本|こんぽん} |
| Values and belief | {価値観|かちかん}, {意義|いぎ}, {理想|りそう}, {信念|しんねん}, {信頼|しんらい}, {祈|いの}り, へんけん, {重|おも}み, {自主性|じしゅせい} |
| Effects | {効果|こうか}, {逆効果|ぎゃくこうか}, {効率|こうりつ}, {効率的|こうりつてき}, {効|き}く, {可能|かのう}, {不可欠|ふかけつ}, {無効|むこう}, {水準|すいじゅん} |
| Rules followed or broken | {従|したが}う, {逆|さか}らう, {従来|じゅうらい}, {導入|どうにゅう}する, {指導|しどう}, {導|みちび}く, {押|お}し{付|つ}ける, {逆|ぎゃく}, {逆転|ぎゃくてん} |

{視点|してん} or {観点|かんてん}? {視点|してん} is where you look from ({子供|こども}の{視点|してん}: a child's
eye view); {観点|かんてん} is the criterion you judge by ({安全|あんぜん}の{観点|かんてん}から: from the
standpoint of safety). {視野|しや} is how much you can see: {視野|しや}が{広|ひろ}い (broad-minded).

Some words in the table were taught earlier and are reviewed here: {前提|ぜんてい} and {無効|むこう}
(lesson 7), {効率|こうりつ} (9), {賛否|さんぴ}, {意義|いぎ} and {定義|ていぎ} (11), {積極的|せっきょくてき} and
{消極的|しょうきょくてき} (14), {少|すく}なくとも (20). New in this lesson besides the table: {不当|ふとう},
{立証|りっしょう}, {祈願|きがん}, {逆説|ぎゃくせつ}, {主体的|しゅたいてき}, {受|う}け{身|み}.

{批判|ひはん} (N3) or {批評|ひひょう}? {批判|ひはん} points out what's wrong; {批評|ひひょう} weighs good
and bad, as a critic does.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for looking, judging, following and believing.

### Looking and judging

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 批 | criticize | ヒ | — | 7 | {批判|ひはん}, {批評|ひひょう}, {批判的|ひはんてき} |
| 視 | look at | シ | — | 11 | {視点|してん}, {重視|じゅうし}, {無視|むし}, {視野|しや}, {視線|しせん}, {視力|しりょく} |
| 準 | standard, level | ジュン | — | 13 | {水準|すいじゅん}, {基準|きじゅん}, {標準|ひょうじゅん}, {準備|じゅんび} |
| 可 | possible, allowed | カ | — | 5 | {可能|かのう}, {可能性|かのうせい}, {不可能|ふかのう}, {許可|きょか}, {不可欠|ふかけつ} |
| 効 | effect | コウ | き(く) | 8 | {効果|こうか}, {効率|こうりつ}, {有効|ゆうこう}, {無効|むこう}, {効|き}く |

- Carried words now in kanji: {批判|ひはん}, {準備|じゅんび}, {可能性|かのうせい}, {許可|きょか}, {有効|ゆうこう}.
  {基準|きじゅん} and {標準|ひょうじゅん} are lesson 13's words.
- 可 alone appears in notices: {持|も}ち{込|こ}み{可|か} (you may bring your own), and {不可|ふか}
  (not allowed). Lesson 15 met them.
- {効|き}く (to be effective) sounds like {聞|き}く; the kanji tells you which.

### Following and going against

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 従 | follow, obey | ジュウ | したが(う) | 10 | {従|したが}う, {従来|じゅうらい}, {従業員|じゅうぎょういん} |
| 逆 | reverse, against | ギャク | さか(らう) | 9 | {逆|ぎゃく}, {逆|ぎゃく}に, {逆効果|ぎゃくこうか}, {逆転|ぎゃくてん}, {逆|さか}らう |
| 導 | guide, lead | ドウ | みちび(く) | 15 | {導入|どうにゅう}, {指導|しどう}, {導|みちび}く |
| 換 | exchange, replace | カン | か(える) | 12 | {交換|こうかん}, {変換|へんかん}, {換気|かんき}, {転換|てんかん}, {言|い}い{換|か}える, {置|お}き{換|か}える, {乗|の}り{換|か}える |

- Carried words now in kanji: {逆|ぎゃく}に, {交換|こうかん}, {変換|へんかん}, {乗|の}り{換|か}える.
- {換|か}える, {替|か}える (lesson 10) and {変|か}える are all かえる. {変|か}える changes something;
  {換|か}える and {替|か}える replace one thing with another. {乗|の}り{換|か}える usually takes the kanji
  {換|か} ({乗|の}り{替|か}える in some texts); {言|い}い{換|か}える and {置|お}き{換|か}える nearly always do ({言|い}い{替|か}える is also seen).
- したがって is written in kana as a connector, as in N3, even though {従|したが}う is now in kanji.

### Touching, praying, the back side

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 触 | touch | ショク | ふ(れる), さわ(る) | 13 | {触|ふ}れる, {触|さわ}る, {感触|かんしょく}, {接触|せっしょく} |
| 祈 | pray | キ | いの(る) | 8 | {祈|いの}る, {祈|いの}り |
| 裏 | back, reverse | — | うら | 13 | {裏|うら}, {裏側|うらがわ}, {裏付|うらづ}け, {裏切|うらぎ}る |
| 振 | shake, wave | シン | ふ(る) | 10 | {振|ふ}る, {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}る, {振|ふ}り{向|む}く, {振|ふ}り{込|こ}む, {振動|しんどう} |

- Carried words now in kanji: {触|さわ}る, {祈|いの}る, {裏切|うらぎ}る, {振|ふ}り{込|こ}む (to pay by bank
  transfer).
- {触|さわ}る (N5) and {触|ふ}れる share the kanji. {触|さわ}る is a deliberate touch with the hand;
  {触|ふ}れる is lighter, can be accidental, and is also abstract: {問題|もんだい}に{触|ふ}れる (to touch
  on a problem), {法|ほう}に{触|ふ}れる (to break the law).
- {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}る and {振|ふ}り{向|む}く: both "to turn round", but only {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}る is used
  for looking back on the past.

Memory notes:

- 批 and 振 both have the hand radical (扌): a hand that strikes, a hand that shakes.
- 視 has 見 on the right: looking.
- 従 has the "going" radical (彳): walking behind someone, following.
- 逆 has 辶 (moving): moving the wrong way.
- 導 is 道 (way) over 寸 (a hand): a hand showing the way.
- 換 has 扌 too: a hand swapping one thing for another.
- 触 has 角 (a horn) on the left: an insect's feelers touching.
- 祈 has the altar radical (礻): praying at an altar.
- 裏 is 衣 (clothing) split open with something tucked inside: the lining, the back.
- 効 has 力 (strength) on the right: something that has an effect.

```trace
批視準可効従逆導換触祈裏振
```

## Dialogue: the rule about phones

At a secondary school, the student council is discussing a rule that bans phones at school. Rina
chairs; Daiki and Mei speak. (Polite, as in a meeting.)

```dialogue
# Student council meeting
りな: では、けいたいの{規則|きそく}について{意見|いけん}をお{願|ねが}いします。
= Now, opinions on the rule about phones, please.
だいき: ぼくは{規則|きそく}を{見直|みなお}すべきだと{思|おも}います。{緊急|きんきゅう}のとき、{家族|かぞく}に{連絡|れんらく}できないのは{危険|きけん}です。
= I think the rule should be reviewed. Not being able to contact your family in an emergency is dangerous.
めい: {確|たし}かにそういう{面|めん}もあります。でも、{持|も}ち{込|こ}みを{認|みと}めたら、{授業|じゅぎょう}{中|ちゅう}に{使|つか}う{人|ひと}が{出|で}てきませんか。
= There's certainly that side to it. But if we allow phones in, won't some people use them in class?
だいき: それは{使|つか}い{方|かた}のルールで{防|ふせ}げると{思|おも}います。{禁止|きんし}すれば{問題|もんだい}がなくなるというものではないでしょう。
= I think that can be prevented with rules on how they're used. Banning them doesn't automatically make the problem go away.
めい: なるほど、{一理|いちり}ありますね。もっとも、ルールを{守|まも}らない{人|ひと}は、どんなルールでも{守|まも}らないと{思|おも}いますけど。
= I see, there's something in that. Mind you, I think people who don't follow rules won't follow any rules.
りな: {要|よう}するに、{持|も}ち{込|こ}みは{認|みと}めて、{使|つか}う{時間|じかん}を{決|き}めるという{案|あん}ですね。
= So in short, the proposal is to allow phones but set times when they can be used.
だいき: はい。ただし、{試験|しけん}のときは{先生|せんせい}に{預|あず}けることにします。
= Yes. With the condition that during exams they're handed in to the teacher.
めい: それなら{賛成|さんせい}です。なお、{先生方|せんせいがた}の{意見|いけん}も{聞|き}いておいたほうがいいと{思|おも}います。
= Then I'm in favour. And I also think we should ask the teachers what they think.
りな: そうですね。では、この{案|あん}を{先生方|せんせいがた}に{提案|ていあん}するということで、いろんはありませんか。
= Right. Then, are there any objections to proposing this plan to the teachers?
だいき: ありません。
= None.
めい: ありません。{言|い}い{出|だ}したからには、だいきくんが{説明|せつめい}してね。
= None. Since you brought it up, Daiki, you can do the explaining.
だいき: えっ、ぼくですか。
= What? Me?
```

けいたい = a mobile phone; いろん = an objection (both have a kanji outside N2); {緊急|きんきゅう} =
an emergency; {預|あず}ける = to
hand over for safekeeping (lesson 7's kanji); {提案|ていあん} = a proposal; からには = since, now
that (lesson 11). Find the connectors: {確|たし}かに, でも, もっとも, {要|よう}するに, ただし, なお.

## Reading: should every rule be obeyed?

An opinion column from a newspaper's education page, in the である style.

> 「{規則|きそく}は{規則|きそく}だから{守|まも}りなさい」。{子供|こども}のころ、そう{言|い}われた{経験|けいけん}のある{人|ひと}は{多|おお}いだろう。{学校|がっこう}には、{髪|かみ}の{色|いろ}や{服装|ふくそう}から{放課後|ほうかご}の{過|す}ごし{方|かた}にいたるまで、{細|こま}かい{規則|きそく}がある。{中|なか}には、{理由|りゆう}を{聞|き}かれても{先生|せんせい}が{答|こた}えられないものさえあるという。{髪|かみ}が{生|う}まれつき{茶色|ちゃいろ}い{生徒|せいと}に、{黒|くろ}く{染|そ}めるよう{求|もと}めた{学校|がっこう}があったことも{報道|ほうどう}された。{近年|きんねん}、こうした{校則|こうそく}を{見直|みなお}す{学校|がっこう}が{増|ふ}えているが、それに{対|たい}しては{反対|はんたい}の{声|こえ}も{少|すく}なくない。
>
> {確|たし}かに、{規則|きそく}には{意味|いみ}がある。{多|おお}くの{人|ひと}が{一緒|いっしょ}に{過|す}ごす{場所|ばしょ}では、{全員|ぜんいん}が{同|おな}じルールに{従|したが}わなければ{混乱|こんらん}が{起|お}きる。{社会|しゃかい}に{出|で}れば、なっとくできない{決|き}まりにも{従|したが}わざるを{得|え}ない{場面|ばめん}がある。{学校|がっこう}はその{練習|れんしゅう}の{場|ば}だ、という{意見|いけん}にも{一理|いちり}ある。
>
> しかし、{理由|りゆう}を{説明|せつめい}できない{規則|きそく}を{押|お}し{付|つ}けることは、{教育|きょういく}として{逆効果|ぎゃくこうか}ではないだろうか。なぜなら、{子供|こども}が{学|まな}ぶのは「{規則|きそく}を{守|まも}ること」ではなく、「{考|かんが}えずに{従|したが}うこと」になってしまうからだ。{考|かんが}えずに{従|したが}う{習慣|しゅうかん}は、{大人|おとな}になっても{残|のこ}る。{会社|かいしゃ}で{不正|ふせい}が{見|み}つかったとき、「{上|うえ}の{指示|しじ}に{従|したが}っただけだ」と{話|はな}す{社員|しゃいん}の{姿|すがた}を、{私|わたし}たちは{何度|なんど}も{見|み}てきたのではないだろうか。{間違|まちが}った{指示|しじ}にも{逆|さか}らえない{大人|おとな}を{育|そだ}てることは、いわば{社会|しゃかい}の{安全|あんぜん}を{弱|よわ}めることにほかならない。
>
> {規則|きそく}を{増|ふ}やせばちつじょが{守|まも}られるというものではない。{大切|たいせつ}なのは、{規則|きそく}の{数|かず}ではなく、それを{守|まも}る{理由|りゆう}が{共有|きょうゆう}されているかどうかである。ある{中学校|ちゅうがっこう}では、{生徒|せいと}{自身|じしん}が{話|はな}し{合|あ}って{校則|こうそく}を{作|つく}り{直|なお}したところ、{違反|いはん}がかえって{減|へ}ったそうだ。{生徒|せいと}たちは{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つの{規則|きそく}について{必要|ひつよう}な{理由|りゆう}を{話|はな}し{合|あ}い、{説明|せつめい}できないものはなくした。{残|のこ}った{規則|きそく}は{以前|いぜん}より{少|すく}ないが、{生徒|せいと}にとっては「{自分|じぶん}たちのルール」になったのである。{自分|じぶん}たちで{決|き}めたことは{守|まも}る、というのは{人間|にんげん}にとってごく{自然|しぜん}なことである。{規則|きそく}は{上|うえ}から{与|あた}えられるものではなく、{共|とも}に{作|つく}るものでもあるのだ。
>
> もっとも、{何|なん}でも{生徒|せいと}に{任|まか}せればよいわけではない。{安全|あんぜん}や{健康|けんこう}にかかわる{規則|きそく}は、{議論|ぎろん}の{前|まえ}に{守|まも}らねばならない。ただし、その{場合|ばあい}でも、なぜ{必要|ひつよう}なのかを{説明|せつめい}する{責任|せきにん}は{大人|おとな}の{側|がわ}にある。したがって、{見直|みなお}すべきなのは{規則|きそく}そのものより、{規則|きそく}との{付|つ}き{合|あ}い{方|かた}なのだ。{子供|こども}に{求|もと}めるべきなのは{従順|じゅうじゅん}さではなく、{考|かんが}える{力|ちから}だと{言|い}えよう。

{放課後|ほうかご} = after school; {近年|きんねん} = in recent years (written); ちつじょ = order
(public order; its kanji are outside N2);
{共有|きょうゆう}する = to share; {作|つく}り{直|なお}す = to remake; {任|まか}せる = to leave to; {従順|じゅうじゅん}さ =
obedience; {指示|しじ} = instructions (N3). Find the argument's skeleton: introduction
(paragraph 1), counter-view ({確|たし}かに…{一理|いちり}ある), turn and reasons (しかし…なぜなら…),
the writer's claim (〜というものではない), limits (もっとも…ただし…) and conclusion
(したがって…{言|い}えよう).

1. What view does the writer admit in paragraph 2?
2. Why does the writer think unexplained rules are counterproductive?
3. What happened at the junior high school, and what does it show?
4. Which rules does the writer say must be followed before any discussion, and what is the
   writer's conclusion?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That rules have meaning: where many people spend time together, there's confusion unless
   everyone follows the same rules; in society you sometimes have to follow rules you don't agree
   with; and school can be the place to practise that (〜にも{一理|いちり}ある).
2. Because what children learn is not "keeping rules" but "obeying without thinking", a habit that
   stays into adulthood; raising adults who can't resist wrong instructions weakens society's
   safety.
3. The pupils discussed and remade the school rules themselves, and violations actually went down
   (かえって{減|へ}った). It shows that people keep rules they've decided on themselves.
4. Rules about safety and health; but even then adults must explain why. The conclusion: what
   needs rethinking is the way we relate to rules, and what we should ask of children is the power
   to think, not obedience.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"Rules are rules, so obey them." Many people were probably told that as children. At school
there are detailed rules covering everything from the colour of your hair and what you wear right
down to how you spend your time after school. Some, it is said, are rules whose reason even the
teachers can't give when asked. It has also been reported that a school asked a pupil whose hair
was naturally brown to dye it black. In recent years more and more schools have been reviewing such
rules, but there is no shortage of voices against it.

Certainly, rules have meaning. In a place where many people spend time together, there will be
confusion unless everyone follows the same rules. Once you go out into society, there are times
when you have no choice but to follow rules you can't agree with. There is also something in the
view that school is the place to practise this.

But isn't forcing rules whose reason can't be explained counterproductive as education? Because
what children then learn is not "keeping rules" but "obeying without thinking". The habit of
obeying without thinking stays with you into adulthood. How many times have we seen employees,
when wrongdoing is found at a company, say "I was only following instructions from above"? Raising adults who can't stand up even to
wrong instructions is, so to speak, nothing other than weakening the safety of society.

Adding more rules does not mean order will be kept. What matters is not the number of rules but
whether the reasons for keeping them are shared. At one junior high school, when the pupils
themselves talked it over and remade the school rules, violations actually decreased, it is said. The pupils discussed the reason each rule was needed
and got rid of the ones they couldn't explain. Fewer rules remained than before, but for the pupils
they had become "our own rules".
Keeping what you have decided for yourselves is a perfectly natural thing for human beings. Rules
are not only handed down from above; they are also something made together.

That said, it isn't the case that everything should be left to the pupils. Rules concerning
safety and health must be kept before any discussion. Even then, however, the responsibility to
explain why they are needed lies with the adults. Therefore, what should be rethought is not so
much the rules themselves as the way we relate to them. One could say that what we should ask of
children is not obedience but the power to think.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
もっとも、{例外|れいがい}もある。
= That said, there are exceptions.
{規則|きそく}を{増|ふ}やせばいいというものではない。
= It's not as if more rules are the answer.
{困|こま}ったときに{助|たす}け{合|あ}うのが{家族|かぞく}というものだ。
= Helping each other when things are hard is what family is for.
{図書館|としょかん}は、いわば{町|まち}の{居間|いま}だ。
= The library is, so to speak, the town's living room.
ただし、{試験|しけん}の{日|ひ}は{使用|しよう}できません。
= However, it can't be used on exam days.
```

もっとも at the start of a sentence has its own short pause after it, like "mind you,". Say
[もっとも:3] with the fall on と; the adverb {最|もっと}も (most) sounds the same.

## Common mistakes

- ただし for extra information. ただし limits or makes an exception; for an extra, separate point,
  use なお.
- Taking the counter-view for the writer's opinion. The sentence after {確|たし}かに or もちろん is
  there to be answered by しかし.
- 〜というものではない after a single fact (×{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ったというものではない). It denies a
  too-simple rule ("A doesn't automatically mean B"), so it usually follows 〜ば / 〜ても / 〜さえ.
- Writing {最|もっと}も for the connector もっとも ("that said"). Use kana.
- したがって in casual speech to a friend. It's written; in speech, だから.
- {視点|してん} and {観点|かんてん} used as if identical in every context: {子供|こども}の{視点|してん} (a
  child's eye view) but {安全|あんぜん}の{観点|かんてん}から (from the standpoint of safety).

## Key points

- したがって / それゆえ (therefore; それゆえ is literary), もっとも (that said; a limit on one's own
  point), ただし (an exception or condition), なお (additional information).
- {要|よう}するに / {要|よう}は (in short), すなわち (that is), いわば (so to speak), {言|い}い{換|か}えれば.
- それにしても and とはいえ open a sentence that turns back to the writer's view.
- 〜というものだ (that's what … is, surely); 〜というものではない (it's not as if …).
- The N2 argument: introduction, counter-view ({確|たし}かに), turn (しかし), reasons (なぜなら),
  limits (もっとも, ただし), conclusion (したがって, 〜のではないだろうか, 〜と{言|い}えよう).
- Text grammar: ask what each gap connects (contrast, result, limit, addition, example,
  restatement) and what each reference word points back to.
- New kanji: 批 視 準 可 効 従 逆 導 換 触 祈 裏 振.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading and listening practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is a workout. It has the kinds of texts the JLPT N2 reading section uses, from a
short notice to a long essay, and the five kinds of listening task, all original and at N2
length. Work through them as you would in the test: read the questions first, read the text once
for the gist, then go back for the details. The answers and translations are hidden, so try each
task before you look.

The kanji are thirteen that spell everyday words you've known for a long time in kana:
{改札|かいさつ}, {混|こ}む, {連絡|れんらく}, {回復|かいふく}, {事故|じこ}, {故障|こしょう}, {捨|す}てる, {拾|ひろ}う,
{冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}, {捜|さが}す. From now on they're written with kanji. The new words are those of
notices and exam papers: {期日|きじつ}, {保管|ほかん}, {復旧|ふっきゅう}, {見合|みあ}わせ, {設問|せつもん},
{下線|かせん}, {指示語|しじご}.

## Reading strategies

The N2 reading section has five kinds of text. Each needs a slightly different approach.

| Task | Text | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Short passages | 200 characters or so: a notice, an email, a short essay | Find the purpose: what is the reader asked to do, or what is the point? The last sentence often says it. |
| Mid-size passages | about 500 characters: an explanation, a column | Follow the logic paragraph by paragraph; questions often ask why, or what a phrase refers to. |
| **[[Integrated comprehension]]** | two short texts (A and B) on the same question | Find each writer's position first, then compare: where do they agree, where do they differ? |
| **[[Thematic comprehension]]** | a long essay of over 1,000 characters | Read for the writer's main claim; it's usually in the last paragraph. Mark the counter-views. |
| **[[Information retrieval]]** | a brochure, a timetable, rules with fees | Don't read it all. Read the question, note the conditions (who, when, how many), then find the rows that match. |

General habits:

- **Questions first.** Read the {設問|せつもん} before the {本文|ほんぶん}, so you know what to look for.
- **Reference words.** A question about {下線部|かせんぶ}の「それ」 or 「こうした{問題|もんだい}」 is answered
  in the sentences just before. Replace the {指示語|しじご} with what it points to and check that the
  sentence still makes sense.
- **The counter-view trap.** A sentence after {確|たし}かに or もちろん is the other side, not the
  writer's opinion (lesson 28).
- **Paraphrase.** The right choice rarely copies the text word for word; the wrong ones often do.
  Expect {直接|ちょくせつ}{会|あ}う in the text and {顔|かお}を{合|あ}わせる in the choice.
- **Time.** In the 105 minutes of the first part you also do vocabulary and grammar, so don't let
  one long passage eat the clock (lesson 30 has a timing plan).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for things you do every day: getting in touch, mixing, throwing away and picking up,
storing, searching, and a few that turn up in notices.

### Contact and getting better

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 絡 | entwine; connect | ラク | — | 12 | {連絡|れんらく}, {連絡先|れんらくさき} |
| 接 | touch, meet, join | セツ | — | 11 | {直接|ちょくせつ}, {面接|めんせつ}, {接続|せつぞく}, {接客|せっきゃく}, {接|せっ}する, {接近|せっきん} |
| 復 | return, again | フク | — | 12 | {復習|ふくしゅう}, {回復|かいふく}, {復旧|ふっきゅう}, おうふく |
| 札 | tag; paper money | サツ | ふだ | 5 | {札|ふだ}, {名札|なふだ}, {改札|かいさつ}, {千円札|せんえんさつ} |

- Carried words now in kanji: {連絡|れんらく}, {連絡先|れんらくさき}, {面接|めんせつ}, {接続|せつぞく},
  {接客|せっきゃく}, {復習|ふくしゅう}, {回復|かいふく}, {改札|かいさつ}. おうふく (a round trip) keeps
  its kana: its first kanji is outside N2.
- 札 is ふだ on its own and さつ in compounds: {千円札|せんえんさつ}, {改札|かいさつ}.
- {復旧|ふっきゅう} (restoration of a service) shows the small っ: フク + キュウ → ふっきゅう.

### Mixing, accidents and vessels

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 混 | mix; crowded | コン | ま(ぜる), ま(じる), こ(む) | 11 | {混|こ}む, {混雑|こんざつ}, {混乱|こんらん}, {混|ま}ぜる, {混|ま}じる |
| 故 | reason; the late | コ | ゆえ | 9 | {事故|じこ}, {故障|こしょう}, {故人|こじん}, 〜ゆえ(に) |
| 器 | vessel, device | キ | うつわ | 15 | {器|うつわ}, {食器|しょっき}, {楽器|がっき}, {容器|ようき}, {器用|きよう} |
| 暴 | violent, wild | ボウ | あば(れる) | 15 | {乱暴|らんぼう}, {暴力|ぼうりょく}, {暴風|ぼうふう}, {暴走|ぼうそう}, {暴|あば}れる |

- Carried words now in kanji: {混|こ}む, {混雑|こんざつ}, {混|ま}ぜる, {事故|じこ}, {故障|こしょう}, {楽器|がっき}.
- {混|ま}ぜる (transitive) and {混|ま}じる (intransitive, group 1) are a pair. {混|こ}む (to be crowded)
  is the same kanji with a different meaning.
- 故 as ゆえ is lesson 28's それゆえ; in kanji it appears in old-style writing: {若|わか}さ{故|ゆえ}.
  In this course ゆえ stays in kana.

### Throwing away, picking up, storing, searching

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 捨 | throw away | シャ | す(てる) | 11 | {捨|す}てる, {四捨五入|ししゃごにゅう} |
| 拾 | pick up | シュウ | ひろ(う) | 9 | {拾|ひろ}う, {拾得物|しゅうとくぶつ} |
| 蔵 | storehouse | ゾウ | くら | 15 | {蔵|くら}, {冷蔵|れいぞう}, {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ} |
| 捜 | search | ソウ | さが(す) | 10 | {捜|さが}す, {捜査|そうさ} |
| 底 | bottom | テイ | そこ | 8 | {底|そこ}, {到底|とうてい}, {底辺|ていへん}, {海底|かいてい} |

- Carried words now in kanji: {捨|す}てる, {拾|ひろ}う, {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}, {捜|さが}す, {捜査|そうさ}.
- {捜|さが}す and {探|さが}す: {捜|さが}す is for looking for something or someone lost ({落|お}とし{物|もの}を
  {捜|さが}す, {犯人|はんにん}を{捜|さが}す); {探|さが}す (N4) is for looking for something you want
  ({仕事|しごと}を{探|さが}す). In everyday writing {探|さが}す is commoner.
- {四捨五入|ししゃごにゅう} is rounding off: four and under are "thrown away", five and over "taken in".
- {到底|とうてい} (not … at all) always comes with a negative: {到底|とうてい}{間|ま}に{合|あ}わない.

Memory notes:

- 絡 has 糸 (thread) on the left: threads tangled together, a connection.
- 接, 捨, 拾 and 捜 all have the hand radical (扌): things you do with your hands.
- 拾 is 扌 + 合: a hand bringing things together, picking them up.
- 復 has 彳 (going): going back the same way.
- 混 has water (氵): things mixed in water.
- 器 is four mouths (口) round a dog (犬): a set of dishes.
- 暴 is 日 (the sun) over 共 and 水: the sun beating down, wild and violent.
- 蔵 has a plant top (艹): goods covered up and stored.
- 底 has a roof on top: the lowest part of a building.

```trace
絡接復札混故器暴捨拾蔵捜底
```

## Text 1: a library notice (short)

> **{市立|しりつ}{図書館|としょかん}からのお{知|し}らせ**
>
> {館内|かんない}の{拾得物|しゅうとくぶつ}は、{一階|いっかい}カウンターで{一週間|いっしゅうかん}{保管|ほかん}いたします。その{後|あと}は{警察|けいさつ}に{届|とど}けますので、お{心当|こころあ}たりの{方|かた}はお{早|はや}めにお{問|と}い{合|あ}わせください。なお、かさは{保管|ほかん}の{対象|たいしょう}{外|がい}とさせていただきます。
>
> また、{三月|さんがつ}{十日|とおか}（{月|げつ}）から{十四日|じゅうよっか}（{金|きん}）までは、{蔵書|ぞうしょ}{点検|てんけん}のため{休館|きゅうかん}いたします。この{期間|きかん}{中|ちゅう}に{返|かえ}す{期日|きじつ}が{来|く}る{本|ほん}は、{入口|いりぐち}の{返本|へんぽん}ポストにお{返|かえ}しください。ただし、CDやDVDは{故障|こしょう}の{原因|げんいん}になりますので、ポストには{入|い}れないでください。

{心当|こころあ}たり = an idea (of where something might be); {対象|たいしょう}{外|がい} = not covered;
{蔵書|ぞうしょ} = the library's books; {点検|てんけん} = inspection, checking; {返本|へんぽん}ポスト = a book-return box.

1. What happens to an item found in the library after a week?
2. Someone has to return a book and a DVD on 12 March. What should they do?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. It's handed over to the police ({警察|けいさつ}に{届|とど}けます). (Umbrellas aren't kept at all.)
2. Put the book in the return box at the entrance; the DVD must not go in the box (it can break),
   so it has to wait until the library reopens on 15 March.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

**Notice from the city library.** Items found in the library are kept at the ground-floor counter
for one week. After that they are handed in to the police, so if you think something may be
yours, please enquire as soon as possible. Please note that umbrellas are not kept.

The library will also be closed from Monday 10 to Friday 14 March for an inventory of the
collection. Books due back during this period should be returned to the return box at the
entrance. CDs and DVDs, however, can be damaged, so please don't put them in the box.

</details>

## Text 2: a business email (short)

> **{件名|けんめい}：ご{注文|ちゅうもん}{商品|しょうひん}の{発送|はっそう}について**
